pages.raw_text:
The Foundations of Celestial 
Reckoning
The Foundations of Celestial Reckoning gives the reader direct access to the foun-
dational documents of the tradition of calculation created by astronomers of the 
early Chinese empire between the late third century bce and the third century ce. 
The paradigm they established was to shape East Asian thought and practice in 
the field of mathematical astronomy for centuries to come. It was in many ways 
radically different from better known traditions of astronomy in other parts of the 
ancient world.
This book includes full English translations of the first three systems of math -
ematical astronomy adopted for use by imperial astronomical officials, together 
with introductory material explaining the origin and nature of each system, 
and a general introduction to the work as a whole. The translations, which 
are accompanied by the original Chinese text, give a consistent rendering of 
all technical terms, and include detailed explanatory notes. The text in which 
the second of the three systems is found also includes a unique collection of 
documents compiled around 178 
ce by two experts in the field, one of whom 
was the author of the third system translated in this book. Using material tran -
scribed from government archives of the two preceding centuries, these scholars 
carefully document and review controversies and large-scale official debates 
on astronomical matters up to their own time. Nothing equivalent in detail 
and clarity has survived from any other ancient culture. The availability of the 
totality of this material in English opens new perspectives to all historians of 
pre-modern astronomy.
Christopher Cullen is Emeritus Director of the Needham Research Institute, 
Emeritus Fellow of Darwin College, and Emeritus Honorary Professor of the 
University of Cambridge. He is editor of the Needham Research Institute Series 
(Routledge).

pages.raw_text:
Scientific texts provide our main source for understanding the history of science 
in the ancient and medieval world. The aim of this series is to provide clear and 
accurate English translations of key scientific texts accompanied by up-to-date 
commentaries dealing with both textual and scientific aspects of the works and 
accessible contextual introductions setting the works within the broader history of 
ancient science. In doing so, the series makes these works accessible to scholars 
and students in a variety of disciplines including history of science, the sciences, 
and history (including Classics, Assyriology, East Asian Studies, Near Eastern 
Studies and Indology).
Texts will be included from all branches of early science including astronomy, 
mathematics, medicine, biology, and physics, and which are written in a range of 
languages including Akkadian, Arabic, Chinese, Greek, Latin, and Sanskrit.
Forthcoming
The Medicina Plinii
Kai Broderson
Al-Battānī’s Kitāb al-Zīj al-Sābi’ and its Latin Translation
Emilia Calvo and Rosa Comes Maymo
Scientific Writings from the Ancient and Medieval World
Series editor: John Steele, Brown University, USA

pages.raw_text:
This book contains translations of a number of Chinese documents relating to 
astronomy, dating from around the beginning of the Common Era. They include 
three complete astronomical systems of the type known as li 曆, and two other 
documents in which contemporary developments in techniques of astronomical 
calculation are described and debated.
Ancient material of this kind has until now remained largely unavailable to 
Western historians of astronomy – except for the very small number who happen 
to be able to read classical Chinese. Yet if it had not been for the accident of the 
language barrier, I believe that this material might long have played a major role in 
any account of the development of astronomy in the ancient world. There are two 
main reasons why I believe that to be the case.
In the first place, the documents presented here in translation come from a 
culture that gave astronomy and astronomers a level of importance in government 
structures unsurpassed elsewhere, both in antiquity and in later times up to the last 
few centuries. All the documents studied here were either compiled under official 
patronage of some kind, or were drawn from material in government archives. 
They therefore exemplify and indeed owe their preservation over the last two 
millennia to the unique importance of astronomical activity and historical record-
keeping for the Chinese imperial state from the third century 
bce to its fall in 1911.
Second, a striking feature of these documents is that they come from a time 
when a number of basic innovations in astronomy were taking place. In compari-
son, in the ancient Mediterranean world we have very detailed documentation of 
the highly developed techniques of calculation used in the Greek-speaking world 
in the second century of the Common Era, thanks to the survival of the work of 
Ptolemy of Alexandria.
1 But if we look for some indication of how (for instance) 
the ecliptic was first adopted by Ptolemy’s predecessors as the primary reference 
frame for the motions of the sun, moon and planets, little direct evidence survives.
2 
By contrast, the Chinese material translated here gives us a first-hand record of

This book contains translations of a number of Chinese documents relating to 
astronomy, dating from around the beginning of the Common Era. They include 
three complete astronomical systems of the type known as li 曆, and two other 
documents in which contemporary developments in techniques of astronomical 
calculation are described and debated.
Ancient material of this kind has until now remained largely unavailable to 
Western historians of astronomy – except for the very small number who happen 
to be able to read classical Chinese. Yet if it had not been for the accident of the 
language barrier, I believe that this material might long have played a major role in 
any account of the development of astronomy in the ancient world. There are two 
main reasons why I believe that to be the case.
In the first place, the documents presented here in translation come from a 
culture that gave astronomy and astronomers a level of importance in government 
structures unsurpassed elsewhere, both in antiquity and in later times up to the last 
few centuries. All the documents studied here were either compiled under official 
patronage of some kind, or were drawn from material in government archives. 
They therefore exemplify and indeed owe their preservation over the last two 
millennia to the unique importance of astronomical activity and historical recordkeeping for the Chinese imperial state from the third century 
bce to its fall in 1911.
Second, a striking feature of these documents is that they come from a time 
when a number of basic innovations in astronomy were taking place. In comparison, in the ancient Mediterranean world we have very detailed documentation of 
the highly developed techniques of calculation used in the Greek-speaking world 
in the second century of the Common Era, thanks to the survival of the work of 
Ptolemy of Alexandria.
1 But if we look for some indication of how (for instance) 
the ecliptic was first adopted by Ptolemy’s predecessors as the primary reference 
frame for the motions of the sun, moon and planets, little direct evidence survives.

the efforts made by one expert to convince his colleagues that the ecliptic must be 
adopted not only as the preferred frame for calculations of solar, lunar and plan-
etary motions, but also for constructing observational instruments. This innova -
tion is also clearly reflected in changes in the ways that the three systems I have 
translated deal with celestial motions. To take another example from several, the 
documents in this book show clearly how the moon’s varying speed was first 
observed, analysed and made predictable. Taken together, they show us how the 
East Asian tradition of doing astronomical calculations – what has been called 
the ‘Han paradigm’
3 – was created and consolidated.
I hope that historians of astronomy more familiar with what happened at the 
other end of the Eurasian continent will find that a reading of this material helps 
them to see more familiar texts in a fresh light, and introduces them to a new field.
The explanatory material that accompanies the ancient material presented in 
this book is mainly intended to help the reader understand the technical features 
of the texts translated, and for that purpose I go into all the detail necessary. Each 
document is prefaced by a special introduction in which its origins and particular 
features are described, and the translations are accompanied by explanatory com-
ments, with a number of worked examples. Apart from that, I sketch the historical 
and cultural context needed to convey a basic idea of what purposes these docu-
ments served, who produced them, and how they were evaluated. This book is 
not, therefore, an attempt to write a social, intellectual and political history of the 
numerical and quantitative aspects of Chinese astronomy in the period with which 
it deals, although it does provide access to some of the most important source 
material for writing a book of that kind. I expect that any reader of this work will 
see the need for such a history; in another book completed more or less in parallel 
with this one I have attempted to fill that need.
4 That book and the present one will, 
I hope, be regarded as complementary.

The Qin, followed by the Han, established an entirely new form of government, 
under which the country was administered by a non-hereditary corps of salaried 
officials, each of whom was ultimately responsible to the emperor. These officials 
were selected on the basis of their competence in the skills needed for their work, 
which demanded as a minimum a good standard of literacy and a level of numeracy 
sufficient to enable them to report on the expenditure under their control.
6 This 
pattern of rule was followed for most of the next two millennia, up to the final 
dissolution of the imperial system with the fall of the Qing 清 dynasty in 1911.

into a number of effectively independent states, closely related in culture and 
language, always in competition for dominance or protection, and sometimes in 
a state of open warfare with each other. This period of disunion is conventionally 
divided into the Spring and Autumn Chun qiu 春秋 period (c.771

4 General introduction
the Spring and Autumn to the time when Qin conquered all other states to establish 
its empire.
Historians of the imperial age preserved traditions of earlier periods of unified 
rule before the disunion of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States. The earli-
est of these was said to have been the Xia 夏 dynasty, conventionally dated from 
the end of the third millennium bce to the first half of the second. The subsequent 
Shang 商 (or Yin 殷) dynasty was said to have been overthrown by the Zhou 周 
near the end of the second millennium bce, and the Zhou kings maintained their 
power until they were forced to flee their capital in 771 bce.8 There has never been 
doubt about the historicity of the Zhou, but many Western historians discount the 
idea that anything like a ‘Xia dynasty’ ever existed and maintained central control 
of a large territory. As for the Shang, the latter part of the dynasty is well attested 
by finds from the 1920s onwards of inscribed animal bones used for divination, 
deposited in caches at the site of the last Shang capital at Anyang 安陽, and giving 
names of Shang kings close to those recorded by historians of the imperial age. 
But none of these ancient kingdoms had a form of government resembling that of 
the Qin and Han.
The kings of Zhou, of whom we know the most, were supported by groups of 
closely interrelated aristocratic clans, to whom the governance of the royal terri -
tories was entrusted in a way that bears some resemblance to the feudal system as 
pictured by historians of medieval Europe. These were the clans that, after the fall 
of Western Zhou power, set themselves up as the de facto rulers of the competing 
states of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods. In many cases these 
rulers eventually abandoned their Zhou feudal rank titles such as gong 公 ‘duke’ 
or bo 伯 ‘count’ in favour of the title wang 王 ‘king’, which was by strict propriety 
reserved for the king of Zhou himself, their theoretical sovereign. It was the king 
of Qin who eventually managed to overthrow his rivals in other states and establish 
imperial rule over the whole of what was often called Tian xia 天下 ‘[All that is] 
under Heaven’. To symbolise the radical political change brought about by his 
victory, he adopted the ancient title di 帝, commonly translated as ‘emperor’ when 
applied to human rulers, but which also carries strong suggestions of divine status. 
As we shall see, the rulers of Han continued this practice.
The keeping of detailed and carefully dated records of important activities has 
been an essential part of the work of officials in many cultures. In the huge East 
indexes. Hong Kong; London, was accorded immense respect by Chinese scholars because it was 
supposedly edited by Confucius (Kong Qiu 孔丘, 551–479 bce). For our purposes, the Spring and 
Autumn Annals are particularly relevant because as well as containing a long series of dates in the 
luni-solar calendar, they also contain 37 dated references to solar eclipses, which were often used by 
later Chinese scholars as test cases to evaluate the accuracy of systems of astronomical calculation.
8 The original Zhou capital was near the site of what was later to become Han dynasty Chang’an; the 
fleeing Zhou rulers were reestablished under the protection of powerful vassals at Luoyang, where 
they maintained a certain level of prestige, but without effective power, until 256 
bce when their line 
was extinguished by Qin. Like the Han, the Zhou dynasty is therefore conventionally subdivided 
into Western and Eastern periods.

Asian empires that concern us, this record-keeping took on a correspondingly 
large importance. The creation and preservation of official records relates to the 
material translated in this book in two separate ways. In the first place, no such 
records could be produced without a universally accepted system of calendrical 
dating, centrally promulgated and used throughout the empire, and without such 
a system no coordinated advance planning would have been possible. Second, the 
official record formed the basis for periodical reflection on the past in the form of 
historical writing, both by officials delegated by the imperial government as well 
as by some private individuals. A major part of this writing consists of a series 
of what westerners call ‘dynastic histories’ but Chinese scholars term ‘standard 
histories’ zheng shi 正史, each of which typically gives a relatively full account 
of the history and institutions of a given dynasty, as well as biographical details of 
the people (mostly men) who played a major role in that history.
Three of the standard histories will be of particular importance in our 
discussions:
Shi ji 史記 literally ‘Records of the [Grand] Clerk’, or ‘Records of the Histo-
rian’. This work was written by Sima Qian 司馬遷 (c. 145–86 
bce), who took 
up a task begun by his father and completed it around 90 bce. It is a compre-
hensive account of the world as known to him from earliest times up to his own 
day. As the state archivist, Sima Qian had access to the records of the imperial 
government, and to whatever remained of the records of the pre-imperial age.
Han shu 漢書 literally ‘Book of Han’, usually rendered as ‘History of the 
[Western] Han dynasty’. This work was written by Ban Gu 班固 (32–92 
ce), and 
completed after his death by his sister Ban Zhao 班昭 and others. It covers 
the history of the Western Han dynasty from 206 bce up to the end of the time 
when Wang Mang was in power.
Hou Han shu  後漢書 literally ‘Book of Later Han’, usually rendered as 
‘History of the Later [or Eastern] Han dynasty’. Most of the text is due to 
Fan Ye 范曄 (398–445 
ce); the monographs are by Sima Biao 司馬彪 
(c. 240–c. 306 ce) and were added to Fan Ye’s text later. It covers the history 
of the Eastern Han dynasty from the restoration after Wang Mang up to the 
end of the dynasty in 220 
ce.

6 General introduction
who compiled it could not avoid making calculations based on the movements of 
the sun and moon, and discussing and evaluating the basis of such calculations, 
both in observational and mathematical terms. The official monographs relating to 
calendrical matters during the early imperial age therefore include a great deal of 
what would in modern English be called ‘astronomy’, and it is from such mono-
graphs as well as from related material that the material of this book is drawn. 
Typically, the methods for astronomical calculations summarised in official mono-
graphs were set out in the form of documents known as li 曆, and it is to these 
that we now turn.
1.2 WHAT WAS A LI 曆, AND WHAT DID IT DO?
Chapters 2, 3 and 4 of this book contain translations, to which I have added explan-
atory commentary, of three ancient Chinese li, all of which date from the first three 
centuries of the Common Era:
The Triple Concordance li (San tong li 三統曆), completed about 10 ce
The Han Quarter Remainder li (Han si fen li 漢四分曆), promulgated in 85 ce
The Uranic Manifestation li (Qian xiang li 乾象曆), created around 200 ce.
Such documents were central to pre-modern Chinese attempts to use calculation 
to predict the motions of the heavenly bodies – principally the sun and moon, but 
also the five visible planets. These calculations formed the basis of the calendar, 
the provision of which was held to be an important state responsibility, as well as 
setting a standard of expected regularity in celestial phenomena, departure from 
which might require specialist interpretation as a portent of good or ill. These 
three translations are followed by two documents in Chapter 5, the first of which

both in observational and mathematical terms. The official monographs relating to

1.2 WHAT WAS A LI 曆, AND WHAT DID IT DO?
Chapters 2, 3 and 4 of this book contain translations, to which I have added explanatory commentary, of three ancient Chinese li, all of which date from the first three 
centuries of the Common Era:
The Triple Concordance li (San tong li 三統曆), completed about 10 ce
The Han Quarter Remainder li (Han si fen li 漢四分曆), promulgated in 85 ce

setting a standard of expected regularity in celestial phenomena, departure from 
which might require specialist interpretation as a portent of good or ill. These

General introduction 7
signifying ‘foot’ (and hence ‘motion step by step through a sequence’) has replaced 
the element ri 日 representing ‘sun’ or ‘day’.10 The word *rêk/li was used with a 
number of related senses, such as ‘count’, ‘calculate’ and ‘sequence’. In the con-
texts that interest us, li can refer to a calendar, in the sense of a piece of writing 
setting out an ordered sequence of days, of the kind that one might keep on one’s 
desk to consult when planning activities. More abstractly the word might refer 
to the entire system of constants and algorithms that generates a calendar – or, 
returning towards the concrete, a document in which such a system is expounded 
and its operation explained, i.e. the kinds of document translated in this book. Li 
might thus be rendered as ‘calendrical system’, or (following Nathan Sivin) as 
‘astronomical system’.
11 Of those two renderings, the latter seems preferable in 
that it takes account of the fact that a typical li does not simply enable us to calcu-
late when months and years will begin and end, but also enables us to calculate the 
times when lunar eclipses might be expected, and even to predict the motions of 
the planets. In this translation, I shall however often simply render li as ‘system’.
1.2.1 Calculating a calendar
A basic requirement for a li was that it should enable those who used it to predict 
when the months and years that structured human life should begin. The funda -
mental unit of time was the day, which in the early imperial period was counted 
as running from midnight to midnight, all days being presumed to be the same 
length.
12 A month was always a whole number of days, and, as we shall see shortly, 
could be either 29 or 30 days long. Ideally, the first day of a lunar month was 
supposed to contain the instant of conjunction of sun and moon (often called in 
English ‘new moon’). But since at this period in China the lunation was held to 
be of constant length, so that the system in effect predicted the mean rather than 
the true conjunction, that might not always be the case, even if the calendar was 
10 Thus, in explaining the statement of the Hou Han shu that a scholar had studied the San tong li 
三統歷 ‘Triple Concordance system’, the commentator refers to San tong li 三統曆 without any 
sign that he expects the reader to be concerned by the change of character used: see Hou Han shu, 
35, 1207.
11 On the range of meanings of li, see for instance Nathan Sivin (2011) “Mathematical astronomy and 
the Chinese calendar,” in Calendars and years II: astronomy and time in the ancient and medieval 
world. J. M. Steele. Oxford, Oxbow Books, 39–51, 41–42.
12 No explicit definition of the day ri 日 is found in the sources translated in this book. It is however 
clear that one day is effectively taken to be the interval between the sun’s return to the same position 
relative to the observer’s meridian. We might therefore say that the mean solar day was used; the 
actual solar day can be from about 20 seconds shorter to about 30 seconds longer than the mean 
value. To avoid giving a misleading impression of precision, I use the term ‘day’ without qualifica-
tion. The slow secular deceleration of the earth’s rotation due to tidal friction makes the modern 
mean solar day a few hundredths of a second longer than it was in Han times, but this effect need 
only concern us when making retrospective calculations of solar eclipses: see for instance the 
discussion in F. R. Stephenson and L. V . Morrison (1995) “Long-term fluctuations in the earth’s 
rotation: 700 bc to ad 1990.” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series A: 
Physical and Engineering Sciences 351 (1695): 165–202.

8 General introduction
well managed. In fact the interval between conjunctions may vary by up to about a 
quarter of a day from the mean interval, of which a modern value is 29.53059 days 
(to seven significant figures). The current English term for this interval is ‘mean 
synodic month’. I prefer to use the term ‘lunation’ rather ‘synodic month’ in this 
book, so as to avoid the risk of confusion with the civil month, which must always 
be a whole number of days. The Chinese word yue 月 (of which the most basic 
meaning is ‘moon’) can refer to either the lunation or the civil month; I translate 
according to the context. The simplest procedure would have been to translate as 
‘moon’ throughout, but unfortunately this is ruled out by the way this word as a 
time measure has been used by some Western authors to give a quaintly exotic 
impression (‘many moons ago . . .’).
The year contained a whole number of months, normally though not always 12 
as we shall see, and hence contained a whole number of days. Whereas the month 
was an attempt to follow lunations with whole numbers of days, in China the year 
was an attempt to follow the cycle of the seasons (represented astronomically by 
the return of the sun to winter solstice) using a whole number of lunar months. The 
underlying solar cycle was treated as being of constant length,
13 but the approxima-
tion to this period in terms of whole lunar months was necessarily a rougher one 
than the approximation of the lunation in terms of whole days. The common word 
for ‘year’ used in the texts of li was sui 歲. Like yue, sui may sometimes refer to 
the calendrical unit, the civil year consisting of a whole number of months and 
thus a whole number of days, and sometimes to the actual underlying astronomi-
cal period, i.e. the cycle from one winter solstice to the next. The term nian 年, 
however, also normally translated as ‘year’, always refers in a calendrical context 
to the civil year, the administrative unit consisting of either 12 or 13 whole lunar 
months, and hence containing a whole number of days.
We have spoken of the need to determine the days on which (for instance) lunar 
months should begin and end, and solstices should fall – but in order to do so we 
clearly need a reference system independent of the luni-solar calendar. This was 
provided by the cycle of sexagenary day names. This system is much more ancient 
than the documents discussed in this book, and is found in many texts, ranging 
from Shang oracle inscriptions written on bone in the second millennium 
bce up 
to traditional calendars produced today.
13 In modern terms, the interval between winter solstices is close to the so-called tropical year, for 
which a modern mean value is 365.24219 days, although this equivalence is less simple than might 
be thought. See Jean Meeus and Denis Savoie (1992) “The history of the tropical year.” Journal 
of the British Astronomical Association  102 (1): 40–42. In the period we are discussing, it was 
assumed that at winter solstice the sun always returned to the same position relative to the stars – as 
we might put it nowadays, the sidereal and tropical years were taken to be equivalent, whereas in 
fact the sidereal year (modern mean value 365.25636 days) is about 20 minutes longer because of 
the steady westwards shift of the sun’s winter solstice position due to the phenomenon of preces-
sion. I therefore avoid both modern terms in this book, and refer to the interval between solstices 
as ‘the solar cycle’ or sometimes ‘the cycle of the seasons’. This also avoids any confusion with 
the civil year, which unlike the solar cycle contained a whole number of days.

General introduction 9
The sexagenary name of a day is composed of a pair of characters, one chosen 
from a cycle of 10 characters taken in sequence (the ‘heavenly stems’ tian gan 天干; 
Table 1.1), and the other taken from a sequence of 12 characters (the ‘earthly 
branches’ di zhi 地支; Table 1.2).14
The result was a pair of characters, often referred to as gan zhi  干支, that 
repeated after 60 days. See Table 1.3, which shows the repetition of the first char-
acter of the pair after 10 pairs, whereas the second character repeats after 12 pairs.
When a sexagenary day name occurs in a translated text, I render it by a com -
bination of a transliteration of the name plus a number indicating its place in the 
60-day cycle (its ‘sexagenary day number’). Thus for instance 甲寅 is rendered 
as jiayin.51.
The gan zhi sexagenary cycle of day-names seems to have followed a single 
unbroken sequence from as early as it can be checked against independently 
dated events, such as solar eclipses, of which reliable records in the Spring and 
Autumn annals begin in the late eighth century 
bce. It is thus possible to correlate it 
reliably with the day-sequence most used by historians of astronomy, the Julian 
date (JD), which is counted in days from zero starting at Greenwich noon on

antiquity of the sets of characters used in the sequences of stems and branches: see the discussion 
in Endymion Wilkinson (2000) Chinese history: a manual. Revised and enlarged. Cambridge, MA, 
Harvard University Press, 175–178. In the period discussed here, the stems and branches may be 
said to have functioned as mere conventional signs.

10 General introduction
January 1, 4713 bce.15 Since that day was a guichou.50 day, the sexagenary day 
number of all subsequent Julian dates may easily be calculated.16
This, then, is the core task of a li: to predict in advance the days of the sexa -
genary cycle when the significant dates of a given year of the luni-solar calendar 
will fall. The necessary calculations were made by the responsible officials well 
before the start of the year in question, and embodied in documents promulgated 
throughout the empire. Ultimately the data produced were copied into what must 
have been many thousands of annual written calendars for the use of both officials 
and private individuals.
15 All dates in this book are given in the Julian calendar, normally used by modern historians as a 
common reference system for the time before the Gregorian reform of 1582 ce. This calendar is 
based on the system introduced at Rome by the reforms of Julius Caesar in 45 bce, and modified 
by Augustus 40 years later. For convenience of dating, scholars project back the use of the Julian 
system into periods long before the time of Julius Caesar: this is the so-called proleptic Julian 
calendar.
16
 Two minor complications need to be taken into account here. First, because the Julian date is 
counted from noon, the Greenwich guichou.50 day in question ran from JD −0.5 to JD +0.5. 
Second, because of the difference in longitude, days in East Asia begin and end earlier than days 
at Greenwich. Thus, for instance, the longitude of the Western Han capital at Chang’an was 108° 
51.48′ E, which corresponds to a time difference of about 7.2 hours, 0.30 day. As a result, the rel-
evant guichou.50 day at Chang’an ran from JD −0.8 to JD +0.2. Such considerations are of course 
important when an astronomical event such as a lunar eclipse might be recorded near the beginning 
of a day in China, leading to it falling on a different sexagenary day from that on which it would 
have been predicted using Greenwich time.

which was necessary from time to time since in fact the mean interval between

Another necessary periodical adjustment is shown by the fact that this calen -
dar has 13 month-rows, not the regular 12: an extra ‘intercalary’ month, run yue 
閏月has clearly been added to this year to allow the pause needed for the cycle 
of the seasons (about 365¼ days) to catch up with the shorter period defined by 
12 lunar months (about 354 days).
18
Some days have other notations in addition to the sexagenary name: thus the 9th 
day of the 12th month-row is marked with the day-name guiyou.10, but below that 
is the marking dong zhi 冬至 ‘winter solstice’. In the transcription, this and other 
events in the solar cycle marked on the original are represented as follows: Spring 
Equinox, SprE; Summer Solstice, SS; Autumn Equinox, AE; Winter Solstice, WS. 
These represent the mid-points of the four seasons. The beginnings of each season 
are also marked, as BSpr, BS, BA and BW. These eight instances are the so-called 
ba jie 八節 ‘eight nodes’. For simplicity, a number of markings of purely hemero-
logical significance have been omitted from this transcription.
19
All the data on this calendar are precisely as calculated in accordance with 
the li in official use in 69 bce, whose basic structures were embodied in the later 
rewriting and expansion translated in this book as the San tong li 三統曆 ‘Triple 
Concordance’ system.
1.2.2  Beyond the calendar: calibrating the seasons  
and graduating the heavens
While the ‘eight nodes’ represent the smallest subdivisions of the solar cycle 
marked on calendars in early imperial times, a li such as the ones studied in this 
book will in fact enable us to calculate a further set of subdivisions of which the 
‘eight nodes’ are a subset, the so-called er shi si qi 二十四氣 ‘24 qi’, a term some-
times paraphrased as ‘the 24 solar seasons’.
20 During the period under discussion, 
the 24 qi can refer either to the 24 instants dividing the time interval between two 
successive winter solstices into equal periods, or to the periods beginning with 
18 It is thought that the insertion of intercalary months may originally have been carried out on an ad hoc 
basis – one simply waited until it became obvious that the calendar was getting a month ahead of the 
seasons, as evidenced by a whole range of natural phenomena ranging from the behavior of plants and 
animals to the appearance of the heavens – and then inserted an extra month to restore order to the 
system. But by the beginning of the imperial period such things were done systematically. See also note 
48 on this change. The principles used in the systems we shall study are outlined later in this chapter.
19
 Discussions of these will be found in Christopher Cullen, ‟Calendars and calendar making in Qin 
and Han times: books of fate and popular culture in early China.ˮ The daybook manuscripts of the 
Warring States, Qin, and Han. D. Harper and M. Kalinowski. Leiden: Brill, 2017 (forthcoming).
20 The term qi plays a vital role in Chinese cosmology, including medicine. No single translation cap-
tures the complete range of meaning contained in this word: scholars have used ‘vapor’, ‘breath’, 
‘pneuma’, ‘energy’ and several others. I prefer to follow A. C. Graham in leaving qi untranslated: 
see A. C. Graham (1989) Disputers of the Tao: philosophical argument in ancient China. La Salle, 
IL, Open Court, 101 and elsewhere.

General introduction 13
those instants. If the qi are numbered so that number 1 is winter solstice, then the 
odd-numbered qi are designated as ‘medial qi’ zhong qi 中氣, and the even-numbered 
qi as ‘nodal qi’ jie qi 節氣.21 Each of the qi has a name based on the phenomena cor-
responding to that season, such as da han 大寒 ‘Great Cold’ (the 3rd  qi) or bai lu 
白露 ‘White Dew’ (the 18th). Taking the example of the Han Quarter Remainder 
system, the second one translated in this book, the interval between winter solstices 
is 365¼ days, and so each of the 24 qi follows at intervals of:
365 ¼ days ÷ 24 = 15 7⁄32 days.
The eight nodes marked on calendars thus follow one another at three times this 
interval, i.e. 45  21⁄32 days, which explains why most of them are marked on the 
calendar at intervals of 46 whole days rather than 45.
The medial qi play an important role in deciding where intercalary months 
should fall. The interval between two medial qi in our example system will be  
30 14⁄32 days, which is clearly longer than the interval between mean lunations, a 
little over 29½ days. As a result, it will happen from time to time that a lunation 
occurs that just fits between two medial qi without including either of them. In 
the period we are discussing, the month corresponding to the lunation would be 
designated as intercalary – which is just what has happened to the month following 
the first month of the 69 
bce calendar.22 The medial qi known as yu shui 雨水 ‘Rain 
Water’, not marked on the calendar, in fact fell on the last day of the first month 
(the first row of the calendar), while the next medial qi, Spring Equinox, fell on 
the first day of the month but one after that, corresponding to the third row of the 
calendar. This was designated as the second month, with the intervening month 
on the second row, which contains no medial qi, being labeled as an intercalary 
first month.
So much, then, for divisions of time as marked on a calendar for everyday use. 
A li would normally also enable us to divide up the motions of the sun, moon and 
planets relative to the heavens into intervals known as du 度.
23 One du in the early 
imperial period was taken to be the amount of displacement of the sun from one 
day to the next as it makes its annual circuit of the heavens – an amount which 
at that time was assumed to be constant. The number of du corresponding to a 
complete circuit of the heavens was thus equal to the number of days in one solar 
cycle in the system in use. As already mentioned, in the period we are consider -
ing it was assumed that the winter solstice position of the sun was fixed relative to 
the stars. In the Triple Concordance system there is no explicit mention of exactly  
21 Note that some sources may refer to all 24 qi collectively as jie qi, while still subdividing odd and 
even as described here.
22 As we shall see in Chapter 2, the value used for the length of the solar cycle in 69 bce was very 
slightly larger than the value given in Huai nan zi , with a corresponding slight increase in the 
interval between medial qi.
23 This word, anciently * dâkh, appears to be the exopassive form of another word written with the 
same character, modern duo, anciently *dâk (‘to measure, calculate’), hence giving du the sense 
‘what is measured, a measure’: Schuessler (2007), 218.

14 General introduction
what path the sun was following, but it is referred to a system of reference, the 28 xiu 
宿 ‘lodges’, each one named after an asterism in the Chinese system, and whose 
widths were effectively defined in terms of the time interval between transits of 
the meridian by the leading stars of the asterisms associated with each lodge.
24 
That meant, in modern terms, that the lodges were defined in terms of intervals of 
right ascension (R.A.); they might also be said to be defined by intervals marked 
on the celestial equator. If therefore the sun moves by 1 du per day with reference 
to this system, that would mean it moved at a steady speed in right ascension. It 
does not however do this; in fact it moves at an approximation to constant speed 
with respect to the ecliptic, a great circle inclined at an angle of about 23½°, 24 
du, to the equator, and its daily change of right ascension therefore varies with its 
position on the ecliptic.
25 Predictions of solar position thus had a built-in error.
We must stress, however, that it would be anachronistic to say that the Triple Con-
cordance held that the sun moved uniformly with respect to the equator, since the 
equator/ecliptic distinction does not seem to have been an issue for astronomers at 
the time Liu Xin wrote down the specification of his system. By the end of the first 
century 
ce, however, the issue had been raised.26 In the Han Quarter Remainder we 
are however told explicitly that while we initially reckon the motion of the heavenly 
bodies with respect to the equator (chi dao 赤道 ‘The Red Road’), we are to add cor-
rections in order to convert the resulting positions to positions on the ecliptic (Chinese 
huang dao 黃道 ‘The Yellow Road’); what is more, we are given two listings of lodge 
widths, one with reference to the equator and one with reference to the ecliptic.
27 In the 
Uranic Manifestation system, the equatorial/ecliptic distinction is taken for granted, 
24 See Chapter 2, Proc. 2.8, and the list of lodge widths given in Proc. 2.29, also Cullen (forthcoming), 
Chapter 5. It is nowadays clear that the habit of some authors of calling these ‘lunar lodges’ has no 
basis. The xiu have no special link with the moon: see Christopher Cullen (2011c) “Translating 宿 
*sukh/xiu and 舍 *lhah/she: ‘lunar lodges’, or just plain ‘lodges’?” East Asian Science, Technology 
and Medicine (33): 80–92.
25 The inequality of solar motion with respect to the ecliptic (the ‘solar anomaly’) was first noted in 
East Asia by Zhang Zixin 張自信 c. 560 ce. He spent 30 years on an ‘island in the sea’, devoting 
his time to accumulating and analyzing observations of the sun, moon and planets made using an 
armillary sphere. See the account in Sui shu, 20, 561, and Nathan Sivin (2009) Granting the sea-
sons: the Chinese astronomical reform of 1280, with a study of its many dimensions and a transla-
tion of its records. New York, Springer, 297, where the name is written in Wade-Giles as Chang 
Tzu-hsin. For the history of this topic in the ancient Mediterranean world, where Callippus is said 
to have detected the inequality of the seasons (a result of the variation in solar motion) in 330 
bce, 
see James Evans (1998) The history and practice of ancient astronomy. New York; Oxford, Oxford 
University Press, 210–216.
26 See the discussion of this point by Jia Kui given in Chapter 5 of this book, and Cullen (2000), 
352–382.
27 See Chapter 3, Proc. 3.48 and Proc. 3.50. The method for converting from one coordinate system 
to another is however flawed, as discussed in Cullen (2000), 352–382.

General introduction 15
and on that basis we proceed to a discussion of lunar latitude – the distance of the 
moon from the ecliptic, on which it is assumed that the sun is located.28
It is not enough to establish a unit for the measurement of celestial motion – a 
reference point is needed if our measurements are to tell us where things are. In the 
ancient and mediaeval west, the reference point for the moving heavenly bodies 
was the ‘First Point of Aries’, i.e. the beginning of the sign of the zodiac named 
after the asterism Aries, which position is taken to be that of the sun at the spring 
equinox.
29 From the equinox, the signs of the zodiac are laid out at equal intervals 
of 30° round the ecliptic, so that the sun might be said to be at (say) seven degrees 
of Aries about a week after the equinox. In early imperial China, the situation was 
rather more complicated.
In the first place, the basic system of division of the heavens inherited from antiq-
uity was not graduated in longitude based on the ecliptic, but was (as explained 
above) equivalent to the modern division of the heavens in right ascension, based 
on the equator. Moreover, instead of 12 equal divisions there were the 28 lodges, 
whose widths varied from 33 du to as little as 2 du. A position might be given as 
being so many du in a given lodge, but the task of working out how far that position 
was from (say) the winter solstice required one to add up the various widths of all the 
intervening lodges. The essentially equatorial lodge system continued to be used as 
a reference frame for celestial positions even after it was recognized that the ecliptic 
was the more appropriate reference for calculating solar, lunar and planetary motion.
Finally, we may mention the less frequently used system of the 12 ci 次 ‘sta-
tions’. This was an equal division of the heavens into 12, associated with the 
(approximately) 12-year cycle of Jupiter round the heavens. Each station had a 
name, and was defined by the position amongst the lodges at which it began and 
ended. The stations were positioned so that each one began with the position of 
the sun at a ‘nodal qi’, and centred on its position at a ‘medial qi’.
1.3 HOW DID A LI WORK?
The essential structures of a li were extremely simple. To calculate a calendar 
of the type shown in Figure 1.1, it was only necessary to have the following 
information:
1
 A defined moment of ‘system origin’ li yuan 曆元.
28 See for instance Chapter 4, Proc. 4.53, which discusses how the lunar latitude previously calculated 
may be used to find the moon’s north polar distance from the north polar distance of the sun.
29 Around 130 bce this position was actually located at the westwards end of the asterism in question, 
so that the sun in its annual eastwards motion round the heavens entered Aries just at the spring 
equinox. Because of the phenomenon of precession, the equinox has shifted westwards and is now 
found in Pisces, the Fishes. See Evans (1998), 101–104.

General introduction 15
and on that basis we proceed to a discussion of lunar latitude – the distance of the 
moon from the ecliptic, on which it is assumed that the sun is located.28
It is not enough to establish a unit for the measurement of celestial motion – a 
reference point is needed if our measurements are to tell us where things are. In the 
ancient and mediaeval west, the reference point for the moving heavenly bodies 
was the ‘First Point of Aries’, i.e. the beginning of the sign of the zodiac named 
after the asterism Aries, which position is taken to be that of the sun at the spring 
equinox.
29 From the equinox, the signs of the zodiac are laid out at equal intervals 
of 30° round the ecliptic, so that the sun might be said to be at (say) seven degrees 
of Aries about a week after the equinox. In early imperial China, the situation was 
rather more complicated.
In the first place, the basic system of division of the heavens inherited from antiquity was not graduated in longitude based on the ecliptic, but was (as explained 
above) equivalent to the modern division of the heavens in right ascension, based 
on the equator. Moreover, instead of 12 equal divisions there were the 28 lodges, 
whose widths varied from 33 du to as little as 2 du. A position might be given as 
being so many du in a given lodge, but the task of working out how far that position 
was from (say) the winter solstice required one to add up the various widths of all the 
intervening lodges. The essentially equatorial lodge system continued to be used as 
a reference frame for celestial positions even after it was recognized that the ecliptic 
was the more appropriate reference for calculating solar, lunar and planetary motion.
Finally, we may mention the less frequently used system of the 12 ci 次 ‘stations’. This was an equal division of the heavens into 12, associated with the 
(approximately) 12-year cycle of Jupiter round the heavens. Each station had a 
name, and was defined by the position amongst the lodges at which it began and 
ended. The stations were positioned so that each one began with the position of 
the sun at a ‘nodal qi’, and centred on its position at a ‘medial qi’.
1.3 HOW DID A LI WORK?
The essential structures of a li were extremely simple. To calculate a calendar 
of the type shown in Figure 1.1, it was only necessary to have the following 
information:
1
 A defined moment of ‘system origin’ li yuan 曆元.
28 See for instance Chapter 4, Proc. 4.53, which discusses how the lunar latitude previously calculated 
may be used to find the moon’s north polar distance from the north polar distance of the sun.
29 Around 130 bce this position was actually located at the westwards end of the asterism in question, 
so that the sun in its annual eastwards motion round the heavens entered Aries just at the spring 
equinox. Because of the phenomenon of precession, the equinox has shifted westwards and is now 
found in Pisces, the Fishes. See Evans (1998), 101–104.

16 General introduction
This was normally chosen as an instant when all the essential data of the cal -
endar were thought to have been simultaneously in their initial states. The time of 
day would thus be midnight, so that a new day was beginning. That day would be 
the first day of the first month according to the month count used for such calcula-
tions (which was normally two months before the first civil month – see below). 
The (mean) conjunction of sun and moon would coincide with that midnight, as 
would the instant of winter solstice. It was also usual for the day in question to be 
one whose sexagenary day-name was the first of the 60-day cycle, jiazi.1.
2 Defined lengths for all important calendrical cycles
Since winter solstices and mean luni-solar conjunctions recur at constant inter-
vals, all we need to know is the length of each cycle, and we can then count off 
completed cycles to find the sexagenary days on which all subsequent solstices 
and mean conjunctions will fall.
However, this will not in itself enable us to tell when the first month of a new 
year will fall. To do that, we need to have a rule telling us exactly when intercalary 
months are to be inserted in the calendar, as is essential to deal with the problem 
that 12 lunar months are about 11 days shorter than the cycle of the seasons defined 
by the recurrence of winter solstice. In all three of the systems translated in this 
book, intercalation was based in part on the rule that 19 complete solar cycles 
from winter solstice gave a period precisely equal to 235 mean lunations – i.e the 
interval between one mean conjunction and the next. Early in the Western Han, the 
Huai nan zi 淮南子 compendium (presented to the emperor in 139 
bce), evidently 
basing itself on this assumption and the 365¼ day value for the solar cycle, tells us 
that a mean lunation is 29 499⁄940  days in length.30 The precise equivalence of these 
two periods – which were in general not reckoned to be whole numbers of days – 
implied the equivalence of two calendrical intervals, i.e. 19 years and 235 months, 
both of which were of course whole numbers of days. Since 235 = 19 × 12 + 7, it 
is clear that in 7 of those 19 years there must have been an intercalary month. In 
the West the 19-year intercalation rule is called the ‘Metonic period’, after Meton, 
the fifth century 
bce Athenian, although it was probably in use in Babylonia before 
his time.31 No name is associated with this innovation in China. All we know is that 
by some time in the pre-imperial period the tradition had been established that 19 
years should contain seven intercalary months. Who first proposed this rule, and 
why and when, we simply do not know. Presumably long experience of running 
a calendar by more ad hoc methods eventually suggested that these assumptions 
30 See Huai nan hong lie ji jie 3, 105. See also John S. Major, with an appendix by Christopher Cul-
len (1993) Heaven and earth in early Han thought: chapters three, four and five of the Huainanzi. 
Albany, State University of New York Press, 95.
31 See Evans (1998), 185–186, and for the Babylonian background J. P. Britton (2007) “Cal -
endars, intercalations and year-lengths in Mesopotamian astronomy,” in Calendars and 
years: astronomy and time in the ancient Near East. J. M. Steele. Oxford, Oxbow Books, 
115–132, 127.

General introduction 17
led to regularity. There are signs from the dates recorded in historical sources that 
such calendrical practices were systematised some time in the Spring and Autumn 
period, i.e. during the period from the eighth to fifth centuries 
bce.32
The problem is not completely solved at this point, since we still have to decide 
exactly where in the calendar each intercalary month must be inserted; all we can 
tell on the basis of the rule just given is that if the extra months are regularly dis-
tributed there will be one about every three years. Before 104 
bce, it was customary 
for intercalary months to be inserted at the end of the selected civil year. Since the 
civil year then began with the 10th month according to the usual month-count, the 
intercalary month was labelled as a ‘latter 9th month’ hou jiu yue 後九月. Thereafter, 
when the basic form of the first of our three systems came into use, intercalations 
could be inserted at any point in the calendar. As we have seen, in the 69  bce 
calendar illustrated above the choice of the month in the second row as an interca-
lary month was determined by the fact that no ‘medial qi’ fell within it. It would 
thus have been designated as the ‘intercalary standard [i.e. 1st] month’ run 
zheng yue 閏正月, since an intercalary month continues the numbering of the 
preceding month. It is clear that the first month of a year can never itself be 
an intercalary month – although it can follow an intercalary 12th month in 
the preceding year.
1.3.1 A note on the planets
In early imperial China, the motions of the five visible planets were not marked 
in calendars for normal official business and daily life. This is perhaps a reflection 
of their lack of ominous significance for the mass of the population at this period: 
the planets do not play a role in the ri shu 日書 ‘Day-book’ prognosticatory texts 
that appear to have circulated widely in early imperial times. All three li translated 
here do however include methods for predicting planetary motions and periods of 
visibility (the latter being essential since no planet is visible when the line of sight 
to it passes close to the sun). The reason seems clear: while ordinary people did 
not need to concern themselves with the planets, planetary movements were in 
principle capable of being interpreted as predicting the good or ill fortune of the 
state itself, or of prominent persons in the state. Most important in this regard were 
instances where a planet was seen to depart from its normal pattern of motion – a 
notion that is meaningless unless a system is in place to tell us what that normal 
pattern should be.

33 An example of the role of simple predictive rules in (we may say) generating  portents for experts

China: Prediction and Divination in the Wu xing zhan.” Early Science and Medicine 16: 218–251.

18 General introduction
As with the sun and moon, the basic principle behind planetary calculations 
was that of reckoning repeated cycles of fixed length beginning from a time in 
the past when all five planets were at some initial position. Within each cycle 
of planetary motion, the planet was specified as performing a fixed sequence of 
movement – moving far enough from the sun to be visible, performing a pattern 
of direct (eastwards) and retrograde (westwards) motion, and once more getting 
too close to the sun to be seen. A system origin sufficient to enable calculations 
relating only to the sun and moon might be placed some way back in the past – but 
given the lengths of planetary cycles, a system origin that also saw the planets 
together at their initial positions might have to be placed very far back in the 
past indeed in order to be consistent with contemporary observation. Thus for 
example, in the Triple Concordance system, predictions of solar and lunar phe -
nomena might be made using as origin the winter solstice preceding the civil year 
that began in 104 
bce, while planetary calculations necessitate the use of a ‘High 
Origin’ 143,127 years earlier.
Documents from the early imperial period show clear evidence of specialists in 
li discussing how they might predict solar and lunar phenomena more accurately 
than their predecessors. Given the very public nature of the calendrical documents 
that were based on such predictions, this is not surprising. I am not aware, how-
ever, of any explicit discussions in the period covered by this book centring on the 
improvement of planetary predictions.
34 Ptolemy, on the other hand, complains at 
some length about his lack of systematic observational data, and notes the difficul-
ties of observing planetary phenomena.35 The only innovation in the way planetary 
motions are calculated amongst the three systems translated in this book is more 
a matter of presentation than of substance: while the Triple Concordance begins 
by calculating the time of first dawn visibility (or apparent morning rising, or 
heliacal rising) for a given planet, the other two systems first find the moment of 
conjunction with the sun. But since the Triple Concordance (like the other systems) 
assumes that visibility begins and ends when the planet is a fixed distance from the 
sun, the difference is not highly significant in terms of the underlying calculations.
A complete cycle of a planet’s movement relative to the sun is a synodic cycle, 
and the time taken for that is its synodic period. Synodic periods are not fore -
grounded in the systems translated in this book. Instead we are given two integer 
numbers, one in effect giving us a number of synodic periods, and the other giving 
us a whole number of years (or more precisely solar cycles) during which precisely 
that number of synodic periods elapses. If we calculate the synodic periods implied 
in terms of solar cycles, and take these as equivalent to tropical years, then those 
implied by all three systems agree to three decimal places with modern mean 
The approach to the relation between prediction and portents that I take there was suggested by 
David Brown (2000) Mesopotamian planetary astronomy-astrology. Groningen, Styx, 146–156.
34 The earliest substantive comparison of the planetary predictions of different systems known to me 
is found in Jin shu, 17, 500–502; it occurs in an account of discussions which took place around 
220 to 226 ce.
35 Almagest IX.2, in Toomer (1998), 420–423.

General introduction 19
values in the case of Jupiter (1.092 tropical years), Saturn (1.035 tropical years), 
Venus (1.599 tropical years) and Mercury (0.317 tropical years). Only in the case 
of Mars do we find a discrepancy: the Triple Concordance implies a synodic period 
of 2.137 tropical years, while the other two systems imply 2.134 tropical years, 
compared with the modern value of 2.135 tropical years. It is worth stressing that 
these are mean values, and that any given synodic cycle of a planet may depart 
significantly from the mean duration: in the case of Jupiter the duration may vary 
by a day or two, but in the case of Mars the variation may be of the order of a 
week. If one adds to that the fact that actual planetary visibility as reported by a 
given observer will not in general be well predicted by the planet’s elongation from 
the sun alone, but will depend on a complex interaction with horizon phenomena 
and the observer’s personal characteristics,
36 it will be clear that predictions of 
planetary phenomena by the means available in early imperial China were likely 
to be somewhat approximate. Indeed, it cannot be said that the prediction of the 
movements of the planets ever claimed the same degree of attention from Chinese 
specialists in li as they did in some other parts of the pre-modern world.
37
In ancient western Eurasia the planets were given names that associated them 
with deities. In China, each planet might be referred to by one of two possible 
names, one of which linked the planet with one of the ‘Five Phases’ wu xing 五行 
which were seen as fundamental to the basic processes of the cosmos,
38 and the 
second more descriptive:39
五星之合於五行， 水合於辰星， 火合於熒惑，金合於太白， 木合於歲星, 
土合於填星．
The correspondence between the Five Stars and the Five Phases: Water cor -
responds to the Chronogram Star [Mercury], Fire corresponds to Dazzling 
36 See the discussion in Cullen (2011a), 193–249.

‘Season Granting system’ of 1280 ce studied by Sivin was the most sophisticated example of a li 
ever produced. But it simply borrowed the planetary data of another system from the preceding 
century, and like all its predecessors made no attempt to represent planetary latitudes.
38 These are five phases of cosmic activity named as Water, Fire, Wood, Metal and Earth. They are not 
physical substances or elements in the ancient Greek sense, and they are certainly not simply the 
materials from which their names are taken. These five phases are a key part of a scheme of what 
has been called ‘correlational cosmology’ in which the main aim is not to answer the question ‘what 
substance is this thing made of?’ but rather ‘how does this relationship or activity resemble other 
relationships or activities?’ For a discussion, see for instance Graham (1989), 319–356. Note that 
‘Earth’ in this scheme renders tu 土, meaning ‘earth’ in the sense of ‘soil’, not ‘Earth’ meaning the 
part of the cosmos on which we live, di 地, the cosmic correlate of Heaven tian 天. When both words 
occur in the same passage, I indicate the distinction by writing ‘Earth [di 地]’ and ‘Earth [tu 土]’.

20 General introduction
Deluder [Mars], Metal corresponds to Great White [Venus], Wood corre -
sponds to the Year Star, and Earth corresponds to the Garrison Star [Saturn].
(Han shu 21a, 985)
1.4 DATES
Since the purpose of a li was to facilitate dating, it is necessary to say something 
about how dates were specified. First, the year: for all normal civil dating purposes, 
the year was designated by a regnal year of an emperor – for instance 180  bce was 
Wen di yuan nian 文帝元年 ‘The first year of Wendi’. Wendi is the conventional 
English designation for the emperor whose personal name (never used in his life-
time) was Liu Heng 劉恆, and who reigned from 180 to 157 bce. Di 帝 corre-
sponds to our ‘emperor’, and like the Latin ‘Augustus’ has semi-divine connotations. 
Wen 文 ‘civilised, cultivated’ was a posthumous title, shi 謚, supposedly summing 
up his particular virtues. During his lifetime the emperor might have been referred 
to in the third person by some phrase such as jin shang 今上 ‘The present One on 
High’. To complicate matters, during the Western Han, it became the custom for

Wen 文 ‘civilised, cultivated’ was a posthumous title, shi 謚, supposedly summing

standard (or New Year)’ and the tian zheng 天正 ‘Celestial standard’, the latter 
being of course the one used in astronomy. More rarely, the 12th Xia month is called 
the di zheng 地正 ‘Terrestrial standard’. The moment of li yuan ‘system origin’ 
normally fell at the start of the first day of the first Celestial month.
Within any given month, one might find a day designated simply by its sexage-
nary day name, or by its number within the month. The first day had a name of its 
own, shuo 朔 ‘beginning’, and the last day was also often labeled as hui 晦 ‘dark’ 
(i.e. of the moon).
1.5 HOW WAS A LI CALCULATED?
The principles of using a li to generate astro-calendrical predictions is best illus -
trated with specific examples, which will be given with the translations that follow. 
But some broad principles may be sketched out here.
The indispensable starting point is always to find the number of years that have 
elapsed since the ‘system origin’ li yuan 曆元 up to the start of the year of interest. 
Then, supposing for instance that we wish to find the sexagenary day name of the 
first day of the first astronomical month corresponding to that year, we might first 
find how many months correspond to that number of years, a process which will 
require us to have a means of determining how many intercalary months have been 
inserted since the instant of system origin. Then, assuming that we have a value in 
days for the length of the mean lunation (which is a basic element in any li), we 
may easily find the total number of days elapsed since the time of system origin 
up to the mean conjunction which falls on the first day of the desired month. We 
already know the sexagenary day name of system origin (usually jiazi.1), so we 
may find the sexagenary day name we need by adding the number of days elapsed 
to the sexagenary number of system origin, and casting out completed cycles of 60.
In practice, the calculation is simplified in two main ways, discussed in the 
following sections.
1.5.1 Elimination of completed cycles
In any given li, the conditions of system origin will repeat in whole or in part at 
certain fixed intervals, the length of which will depend on the way that the basic 
constants of the system relate to one another. Thus, for instance, in the Triple Con-
cordance system, the mean conjunction of sun and moon will once more coincide 
with midnight beginning the first astronomical month after 1539 years from the 
instant of system origin – although the day then beginning will not in general be 
a jiazi.1 day as it was at system origin. In fact the sexagenary day number will 
increase by 40 at the start of each 1539-year period. Therefore, after three such 
periods, 4617 years, the sexagenary day number will at last repeat (since it has 
increased by 3 × 40 = 120 = 2 × 60). If we are doing calculations relating to a 
year far from system origin, and our only interest is in the sun and moon, we may 
thus simply subtract whole multiples of 4617 from the years elapsed, thereby

22 General introduction
decreasing the size of the numbers in all subsequent calculations. We may then also 
cast out any remaining multiples of 1539, making allowance for the shift in initial 
day number. All this helps to keep the numbers as small as possible.
1.5.2 Means of calculation, and scaling to avoid fractions
There are no signs in any of our texts of the physical means by which calculations 
were carried out. But it is reasonable to conclude that they were not done any 
differently from the way that other calculations were carried out at this period, 
which was by the use of rod numerals.
42 Numbers were laid out on a flat surface 
in a grid-like arrangement, using arrays of short rods to represent the digits from 1 
to 9,
43 with units at the right and higher order digits to the left using decimal place 
value. When a zero would be written in modern notation, a space would be left. As 
a calculation proceeded, rods representing parts of the result would be laid down, 
and some digits of the given numbers would be removed, until the final result was 
obtained. The abacus was not used in China until a thousand years later than the 
period we are discussing, and written calculations using common Chinese numer-
als did not come into use until the seventeenth century.
Suppose we are working with the Triple Concordance system, which defines 
the length of the mean lunation as 29 43⁄81 days. In words, this number would have 
been written as er shi jiu ri ba shi yi fen ri zhi si shi san 二十九日八十分日之四十三, 
literally ‘twenty-nine days, [and] of eighty-first parts of a day, forty-three’. That 
will imply that if we are trying to calculate the instant of some given mean con -
junction in the future, we shall have to handle a mixed number, represented by a 
three-layered array of rods with the upper layer representing the 29 whole days, 
the next representing the number of 81st parts ( fen 分) of a day, and the lowest 
of the three layers representing the denominator 81, as in Table 1.4:

General introduction 23
This method of representing a mixed number is the result of the layout used to 
perform a division operation, in which the dividend would originally have been in 
the middle row with the divisor below it, and the integer quotient and remainder 
would have been formed as shown here as the division proceeded.
If we want to multiply this number by (for instance) 32 to find the number of 
days in 32 lunations, we would first multiply the 29 by 81 and add the 43 to it to 
turn everything into 81st parts, then multiply by 32. After that we would have to 
perform long division to produce another quotient and remainder laid out over the 
divisor 81 as above. To avoid this complication, the Triple Concordance system 
does not work with raw days when dealing with lunations, but ‘scales up’ days by 
81, the ‘day factor’ ri fa 日法, so that the number of days in a lunation is trans -
formed into 29 × 81 + 43 = 2392, the so-called lunation factor yue fa 月法 – which 
is of course the number we would have begun any multiplication by obtaining. We 
perform any necessary calculations at this scale, and only when we need to come 
back down to earth with an actual number of days do we count how many times 
the number calculated contains 81 to find the whole days, while the remainder 
becomes the numerator of any fractional part of a day, with 81 as the denominator. 
The great mathematical thinker of the third century 
ce, Liu Hui 劉徽, referred to 
this method of avoiding fractions:
若有分以乘其實而長之則亦滿法乃為全耳.
If there are fractions [lit. ‘parts’], then one can multiply the dividend so as 
to scale it up [lit. ‘enlarge it’], so that it does fill the divisor. Then one has a 
whole [number].
(Jiu zhang suan shu 九章算術 1, commentary,  
in Guo Shuchun 郭書春 2004: 1, 15
45)
Both of these features will be found in all three of the systems translated in this 
book. In addition, each system provides extra assistance to the calculator by giv-
ing values for a number of auxiliary constants that are derived from the basic 
constants, but are provided already calculated as a time saver. An example from 
the Triple Concordance system is ‘Reckoning Surplus’ ce yu 策餘 [8,080], which 
represents the number of days above whole multiples of 360 in 1539 years. Each 
system will of course have its own distinctive set of such numbers.

24 General introduction
have been determined by observing two successive instants when the sun’s north 
polar distance was at a maximum (and hence it was at winter solstice), and noting 
the time interval between them as accurately as possible. Or it may have been the 
case that rough estimates of the date of winter solstice made many years apart 
enabled the underlying value to be determined with fair accuracy. In reality, we 
have no direct evidence of what took place when an explicit value for the length 
of the solar cycle was first stated.
46 From the early imperial age, we begin to hear 
statements that the observation of the noon shadow of a gnomon reaching its 
maximum length for the year might serve as evidence that a given day was that of 
winter solstice – but this was only one of the phenomena connected with the season 
in early sources. Others included the behaviour of animals, birds and insects, and a 
rise in the water level in wells.
47 If we look at the two most ancient winter solstice 
dates on record, both of which come from the Spring and Autumn period (one for 
656 
bce and one from 523 bce), we find that both are dated two days before the 
date on which the actual winter solstice fell.48 The winter solstice assumed by the 
Grand Inception system for midnight on 25 December 105 bce was 28 hours later 
than the actual instant of solstice – see the Introduction to the Triple Concordance 
system in chapter 2, note 3. The noon shadow of a gnomon changes very slowly 
near a solstice, and Nakayama Shigeru has estimated that a 1-cm uncertainty in 
the winter solstice shadow could lead to a 4- to 5-day uncertainty in determining 
the solstice date, so if a gnomon was used to check these determinations the error 
was within a reasonable range.
49
The moon posed a somewhat easier problem than the sun, since its cycle of 
phases is easy to follow by simply looking at its changing appearance from day 
to day.
If one attempted to match this cycle with a month consisting of whole days, then 
it would soon be obvious that these months should normally alternate between 29 
and 30 days in length, with an occasional pair of 30-day months in succession. 
In fact, in the quarter-remainder type system first described in Huai nan zi , the 
length of the underlying lunar cycle was defined by the adoption of 365¼ days as 
the length of the solar cycle, taken with the 19-year cycle of seven intercalations. 
The reform of 104 
bce conversely defined the solar cycle length on the basis of the 
intercalation cycle and a pre-defined value for the lunar cycle.
In 104 bce new constants were introduced. The pattern of intercalations was 
preserved, but the mean lunation was defined as a new value, 29 43⁄81  days – which 
is in fact only very slightly different from 29  499⁄940 days, the value of mean luna -
tion implied by previous practice, and found in the Huai nan zi book cited above.

General introduction 25
were made at this time, it is clear from the historical record that the basic motive 
for this change was to make the divisor of day parts into the cosmologically sig -
nificant number 81. This is the fourth power of 3, the number representing the 
principle of yang 陽, which pertains to the heavens as opposed to earth, to male 
as opposed to female, and to light as opposed to darkness.
50 This change naturally 
dictated a slight adjustment in the length of the solar cycle in order to maintain 
the pattern of intercalation. A century later, when Liu Xin created his Triple Con-
cordance system on the basis of the Grand Inception, he further elaborated these 
theoretical underpinnings, drawing heavily on the influential cosmological texts 
which by his day had become attached to the ancient divination handbook known 
as the Yi jing 易經 Book of Change.
51 In 85 ce the Grand Inception constants were 
replaced by those in use before 104 bce, but with a newly defined system origin; 
this time the reason given in the texts was not cosmological, but was supposedly 
based on a long programme of observation. In the early third century 
ce the last of 
our three translated systems – the Uranic Manifestation system – was created, and 
this time it seems that what happened was a simultaneous adjustment of the solar 
cycle length and the time of system origin to achieve maximum consistency with 
past records of observation as well as contemporary phenomena. Such interlocking 
adjustments became the pattern followed in succeeding centuries.
1.7  A NOTE ON TRANSLATING COMPUTATIONAL 
PROCEDURES
The main aim of my translation is to enable a reader who cannot read classical 
Chinese to understand and appreciate the nature of these ancient texts. An essential 
part of that understanding and appreciation must be to see how the texts specifies 
computation procedures, using named quantities and simple arithmetical instruc-
tions. For each quantity I have provided a translated name that matches as closely 
as possible the meaning of the name in Chinese, an approach that follows the 
pattern set by Nathan Sivin.
52 I have tried to avoid writing obviously ‘Chinese’ 
English, while following the original wording as closely as possible. Thus, for 
instance, to take an example from the Triple Concordance system, the initial list 
of constants contains the following, giving the value of one constant:

General introduction 25
were made at this time, it is clear from the historical record that the basic motive 
for this change was to make the divisor of day parts into the cosmologically sig -
nificant number 81. This is the fourth power of 3, the number representing the 
principle of yang 陽, which pertains to the heavens as opposed to earth, to male 
as opposed to female, and to light as opposed to darkness.
50 This change naturally 
dictated a slight adjustment in the length of the solar cycle in order to maintain 
the pattern of intercalation. A century later, when Liu Xin created his Triple Concordance system on the basis of the Grand Inception, he further elaborated these 
theoretical underpinnings, drawing heavily on the influential cosmological texts 
which by his day had become attached to the ancient divination handbook known 
as the Yi jing 易經 Book of Change.
51 In 85 ce the Grand Inception constants were 
replaced by those in use before 104 bce, but with a newly defined system origin; 
this time the reason given in the texts was not cosmological, but was supposedly 
based on a long programme of observation. In the early third century 
ce the last of 
our three translated systems – the Uranic Manifestation system – was created, and 
this time it seems that what happened was a simultaneous adjustment of the solar 
cycle length and the time of system origin to achieve maximum consistency with 
past records of observation as well as contemporary phenomena. Such interlocking 
adjustments became the pattern followed in succeeding centuries.
1.7 A NOTE ON TRANSLATING COMPUTATIONAL 
PROCEDURES
The main aim of my translation is to enable a reader who cannot read classical 
Chinese to understand and appreciate the nature of these ancient texts. An essential 
part of that understanding and appreciation must be to see how the texts specifies 
computation procedures, using named quantities and simple arithmetical instructions. For each quantity I have provided a translated name that matches as closely 
as possible the meaning of the name in Chinese, an approach that follows the 
pattern set by Nathan Sivin.
52 I have tried to avoid writing obviously ‘Chinese’ 
English, while following the original wording as closely as possible. Thus, for 
instance, to take an example from the Triple Concordance system, the initial list 
of constants contains the following, giving the value of one constant:

§ 10. Circuits of Heaven 562,120. Multiplying the Lunation Factor [2392] by 
Rule Months [235], one obtains Circuits of Heaven.
The expression zhou tian 周天 is literally a verbal phrase ‘Circuiting heaven’, but 
I have allowed myself the flexibility of making it into a noun phrase since I am, 
after all, translating into a language that uses verbal phrases in such contexts much 
less frequently than classical Chinese does. Again, I have reversed the order of 
the reference to multiplication, which actually reads ‘By Rule Months multiplying 
the Lunation Factor’, which is rather unnatural. The numbers in square brackets 
after Lunation Factor and Rule Months are added in my translation by way of con-
venient reminders of the values of the quantities referred to, which are normally 
only stated explicitly in the text when they are defined, as seen here in the case of 
Circuits of Heaven.
At no stage in my translation or explanatory comments have I replaced a name 
by an algebraic symbol, nor have I introduced modern algebraic notation, proce-
dures which have no analogue in the Chinese astronomical literature.
53 I have how-
ever allowed myself some simple arithmetic in my commentary to (for instance) 
explain the significance of the calculation above, which is that Circuits of Heaven 
[562,120] is in fact equal to the number of days in Concordance Factor [1539] 
solar cycles, or the number of days in one solar cycle at a scale of Concordance 
Factor [1539]. Since the sun moves 1 du in a day, it is also the number of du in a 
complete circuit of the heavens, at a scale of Concordance Factor [1539] – hence, 
perhaps, its name. There is nothing in such calculations that goes beyond what a 
Han scholar with a basic understanding of numbers could not have managed. But I 
have deliberately not gone further than that. Readers interested in other approaches 
may consult, for instance, the study of Michel Teboul.
54

sented this material. The page below comes from the Wu ying dian 武英殿 ‘Hall of 
Martial Brilliance’ woodblock printed edition of the standard histories, produced 
under the patronage of the Qianlong emperor in 1739.
The text runs in columns reading from top to bottom, ordered from right to left. 
The text cited above is in the sixth column. The next column refers to the calcula-
tion of a different constant – so it may be seen that the basic divisions of the text 
are easy to distinguish in the original. Although the form of the wood-block printed 
characters is a little different from modern printing, the reader will be able to see 
that there is no essential difference of content or form, apart from the fact that 
the Zhonghua edition adds punctuation. The pre-modern reader would have been 
expected to supply this by himself or herself, either mentally while reading, or by
