28 General introduction
marking in small circles with a brush to mark major divisions. We may say that for 
the pre-modern reader punctuation was an expression of their understanding of the 
text, whereas the modern reader expects understanding to be in part mediated by 
the punctuation that is supplied.
55 I hope it is clear, however, that presenting the 
text in the modern manner does not significantly distort the way the pre-modern 
Chinese reader would have interacted with the mathematical and astronomical 
content of material of this kind. In my translations I have noted a few instances 
where my translation of more complex listings does involve significant editorial 
intervention in formatting, designed to help the reader better understand the struc-
ture of what is being presented.
It may be helpful to give a few notes on the ways in which calculations are 
specified in the text.
Addition: for instance, in the Triple Concordance system, we read
以章月加閏法， 得月周．
Which I translate as:
Adding Rule Months [235] to Intercalation Factor [19], one obtains Lunar 
Circuits.
We might render the first part of this text more literally as ‘By Rule Months [235] 
increase Intercalation Factor [19]’, but the resemblance is so close that the more 
natural English expression above seems permissible. Both subtraction and multi-
plication are also expressed in ways similar to the structures of modern English.
This is not the case when we look for processes analogous to what we call 
‘division’. What we find is in effect two halves of the process called ‘Euclidean 
division’ in the Western tradition. Euclidean division is the process that sees one 
integer, the ‘dividend’ (say 17) divided by another integer, the ‘divisor’ (say 5) to 
yield a ‘quotient’ (3) and a ‘remainder’ (2). In another part of the Triple Concor -
dance text we are concerned with the quotient only
盈統法得一度
[Take the number previously calculated and] obtain 1 du for each filling of the 
Concordance Factor [1539].
Thus, we find how many times 1539 can be ‘filled’ by being taken from the number 
already calculated, and that gives us the number of du sought. Elsewhere attention 
is centred on the remainder:
以章月除月元餘，則入章月數也．
55 As a result, disagreements between scholars about the meaning of a text passage may take the form 
of disagreement about how the text should be punctuated. A few issues of that kind will occur in 
the translations given below.

General introduction 29
Cast out Rule Months [235] from Months Origin Remainder, then [what 
remains] is the number of months entered into the Rule.
Here we are to subtract 235 from Months Origin Remainder until the amount 
remaining is less than 235, and that remainder will be the number of months we 
have advanced into the current uncompleted group of 235 months.
But quite frequently both quotient and remainder are of interest to us:
盈元法得一，名曰積日，不盈者名曰小餘．
[Take the number previously calculated and] obtain 1 for each filling of the 
Origin Factor [4,617]. [The number obtained] is called Accumulated Days; 
what does not fill is called the Lesser Remainder.
We first find how many times 4617 can be ‘filled’ by being taken from the number 
already calculated, and that number of times is Accumulated Days. The number 
left over, less than 4617, is the Lesser Remainder.
Many readers will no doubt recognise the similarity between the systematic way 
that the calculation procedures given above are set out and modern programming 
languages.
56 While working on these texts for much of the last two decades, I 
have exploited this aspect of them by constructing Excel spreadsheets for each of 
the three systems translated in this book. In these spreadsheets I have set out the 
successive stages of all calculations in Chinese and in translation, accompanied 
by cells in which the calculations specified are performed automatically and the 
results obtained at each stage are displayed. The spreadsheets are arranged so 
that all that is required is to enter the year for which results are required, and all 
parameters for that year (such as the dates of the first days of months, solstices and 
equinoxes, and planetary phases) are then calculated and displayed on a series of 
worksheets, with each stage of calculation clearly visible. Many of these calcula-
tions can be performed using standard Excel functions, but I have found it con -
venient to supplement these by constructing a number of special functions using 
Visual Basic, a simple language that interfaces easily with Excel. Spreadsheets 
of this kind not only enable one to find and compare the predictions of different 
systems reliably and quickly, but are also useful means for checking whether one’s 
understanding of the way the systems work is correct.
57

The three astronomical systems translated here were written over the course of 
two centuries, and they present their material somewhat differently. Nevertheless, 
certain basic features are common to all three, and this makes it possible to present

30 General introduction
them in a fairly consistent way without too much editorial interference. At the 
most basic level, I have numbered all paragraphs of translation in a given system 
in one continuous sequence. The paragraphs themselves usually reflect the way 
the original text is arranged (see Figure 1.2), but in some cases I have subdivided 
further for the sake of presentational clarity. The great majority of the text is pre-
sented as a series of units consisting of either two or three items. The first item of 
a given unit is the Chinese text itself. There then follows the English translation by 
myself, preceded by a paragraph number. After that there may be an explanatory 
comment, distinguished from the translation by the use of a different typeface and 
text alignment, and terminated by a horizontal line, followed by the Chinese text 
of the next unit to be translated.
An exception are the paragraphs or parts of paragraphs that state the purpose 
of the calculations set out in text that follows. These I have labelled in a separate 
sequence within each system as ‘Procedures’, numbering them as ‘Proc. 2.1’ and 
so on. I hope the structural clarity that results may justify the modification of 
the original format. I have also used the ‘Procedure’ style of heading to label 
important calculation tools such as tables of data. Other subheadings reflect the 
presence of subheadings in the text, such as mu 木 ‘Wood [Jupiter]’ to introduce 
a list of constants relating to that planet. In some cases I have supplied a sub -
heading not found in the text in order to make clear the nature of the material 
that follows; when I do that, the heading is in square brackets, as [Solar and 
Lunar Constants].
In the Chinese text, the use of round and square brackets thus (算)[策] indicates 
that the first character is to be deleted and the second substituted for it. Such revi-
sions to the received text are mostly due to the Zhonghua editors. Where I have 
not agreed with the editors, or have proposed a revision of my own, I have added 
a note to that effect.
1.9 ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS
I have made particular use of the writings of a number of previous scholars in 
trying to elucidate difficult parts of the texts translated in this book. For all three 
li, I have frequently turned to the writings of Li Rui 李銳 (1768–1817), who left 
detailed explanations of the processes of calculation that they describe.
58 For the 
Triple Concordance system, I have used the work of Wang Xianqian 王先謙,59 and  
58 Li Rui 李銳 (1768–1817) (1993b) Li shi yi shu  李氏遺書 (Transmitted works of Mr Li). Zhong 
guo ke xue ji shu dian jitong hui, tian wen juan 中國科學技術典籍通彙天文卷 (Compendium of 
classic texts of Chinese science and technology, astronomical section). Bo Shuren 薄樹人. Beijing, 
Henan Educational Press, vol. 2, 701–818.
59 Wang Xianqian 王先謙 (1900, reprinted 1959) Han shu bu zhu  漢書補注 (The Han shu, with

also of Nōda Churyō 能田忠亮 and Yabuuti Kiyosi 藪內清.60 The fact that specific

I hope, be taken as indicating any wish to minimise the value of their work, and 
the extent to which I have benefitted from it. There are a number of well-known 
studies in East Asian languages (and to a lesser extent in Western languages) which

writings of an individual scholar, but it is often hard to separate general influence 
from specific borrowing. I am grateful to all those who have worked on this field 
in the past, and am conscious of how much easier my task has been made by what 
they accomplished. 
I would like to express my gratitude to John Steele (Brown University), who as 
Series Editor read the first draft of this book with close attention and made many 
valuable suggestions. I assume entire responsibility for any errors that remain. 
Both Stacey Carter as Production Editor and Sheri Sipka as Project Manager were 
patient, helpful and vigilant during the transformation of a very complex manu -
script into a published book. I am deeply grateful to Catherine Jami (CNRS, Paris), 
for her support, understanding, and acutely perceptive scholarly advice over the 
years during which I have worked on this project.
Les Martinières, August 2016

2.1 INTRODUCTION
2.1.1 An astronomical system and its cr eator
The San tong li 三統曆 ‘Triple Concordance system’ is a collection of data and 
procedures for calculation, preserved in the text of the Han shu 漢書 (Writings/
documents on the Han), a history of the Western Han dynasty (206 bce–9 ce) edited 
by Ban Gu 班固 (32–92 ce) with the help of his sister Ban Zhao 班昭 (45–116 ce), 
which reached final form in the early second century ce. It is our earliest extant 
example of a complete li.
The Triple Concordance system as we have it today was the work of Liu Xin 
劉歆 (c. 50 bce–23 ce). As a youth, he was a friend of Wang Mang 王莽 (45 bce–23 ce), 
who rose to power in the Han court through his family connections with the 
empress. In 9 ce, after having been the effective ruler for some years, Wang caused 
the boy who held the throne as nominal Han sovereign to go through a ceremony 
of abdication in his favour, and took the throne as emperor, with the title Xin 新 
‘New’ for his dynasty (Han shu 99a, 4099–4100). Liu Xin became one of Wang’s 
chief ministers, and provided intellectual support for his claim to be patterning 
his government on the model of antiquity, and to be drawing power from the 
fundamental cycles of the cosmos. Liu Xin’s construction of a new astronomi -
cal system was part of that support. Despite his membership of the old imperial 
clan, Liu Xin survived a number of political purges during the next three decades, 
including some involving his own children, until in 23 
ce he was executed after 
the discovery of a plot to assassinate Wang and restore the Han to power. Wang 
Mang himself died not long after, as his palace was stormed by Han restorationist 
forces. The Triple Concordance system remained in use until it was replaced by 
a new Han system in 85 
ce. That system, the Han Quarter Remainder system, is

but there is no doubt that it already contained the foundation elements used in the

The Triple Concordance system 33
calendar, and the dates of the major events in the solar cycle, such as the solstices 
and equinoxes. This is made clear by the fact that excavated calendars of the first 
century 
bce (such as the 69 bce specimen discussed in Chapter 1) contain dates 
exactly as they would have been calculated in accordance with the Triple Concor-
dance system. The process that led to the adoption of the Grand Inception system 
for official use was a complex one. I have told this story elsewhere,
1 but for our 
purposes we may mention two significant points.
Motivation, and inauguration of the system
The decision to carry out a reform of the official li in 104 bce had already been 
taken as long ago as 113 bce, when a certain Gongsun Qing 公孫卿 persuaded the 
emperor, Wudi 武帝, that this would enable him to emulate the mythical Yellow 
Emperor (Huang di 黃帝) of remote antiquity and become an immortal.2 Gongsun 
Qing claimed that in order to achieve this it was essential that a new system origin 
should be adopted which would reproduce the conditions of the time when the Yel-
low Emperor had supposedly achieved immortality. This could be done by taking 
the winter solstice of late 105 
bce as falling on the first day of the first astronomical 
month, which would be a jiazi.1 day. No special astronomical observations seem 
to have been carried out at the time this decision was made. It was however noted 
that the calendar then in use predicted that the solstice of late 113 
bce would fall 
on the first day of the first astronomical month, a xinsi.18 day, which would have 
suggested that conditions in 105 bce might be close to those specified. As we learn 
from the content of the emperor’s edict at the time of the reform, it was taken that 
the winter solstice and conjunction of sun and moon coincided at the start of a day 
corresponding to December 25, 105 
bce, which was a jiazi.1 day, the normal con-
ditions at a system origin. On that date, the emperor in person took part in solemn 
ceremonies to mark this new beginning. In fact, at local midnight commencing that 
day at the Western Han capital of Chang’an (modern Xi’an), the sun was already 
more than 28 hours past winter solstice, and the moon was about 17 hours past 
conjunction with the sun.
3 But neither fact would have been easy to observe with 
the means available at the time. It is not until the early Eastern Han that we begin 
to hear complaints that the Triple Concordance system predicts conjunctions of

eternity of blissful existence free of need and suffering. Immortals might allow mortals to perceive 
them if they so wished, but usually chose to enjoy life far from the centres of human labour and 
conflict. See Michael Loewe (1979) Ways to paradise: the Chinese quest for immortality. London,

3 In modern terms, the longitudes of sun and moon would have been observed as 271.2° and 279.3°,

34 The Triple Concordance system
sun and moon too late, as would have been expected – see the account in the docu-
ments translated in Chapter 5.
The introduction of the factor 81
As mentioned in Chapter 1, the Grand Inception modified what appear to have 
been the previously generally accepted foundational parameters of the luni-solar 
calendar, which were a solar cycle of 365¼ days in length, and the precise equiva-
lence of 19 solar cycles to 235 mean lunations (the intercalation cycle known as the 
‘Metonic period’ in the West). This dictated a mean lunation 29 499⁄940 days in length. 
The Grand Inception retained the intercalation cycle, but modified the mean lunation 
length to 29 43⁄81 days. In quantitative terms this is a tiny change, since  499⁄940 = 42.999⁄81 (to 5 
significant figures in the numerator). The motive was not empirical, but was rather 
the wish to introduce into the system the cosmologically significant number 81, 
which as mentioned in Chapter 1 was not only the fourth power of the quintessen-
tially yang number 3, but also represented the volume of the pitchpipe sounding the 
fundamental note of the scale, ‘Yellow Bell’ huang zhong 黃鐘. Since music was 
held to embody the same cosmic order as was exemplified in the heavens, it would 
have been highly satisfying to see the motions of sun and moon governed by this 
number. We read in the imperial edict giving sanction to this change:
黃鐘為宮
 [. . .] 自是以後， 氣復正
The pitchpipe Yellow Bell sets the fundamental note of the scale [. . .] So from 
now on, the [seasonal] qi return to order.
(Shi ji 26, 1260)4
2.1.2 Structure of the system
I limit myself here to sketching the theoretical structure of the system, without any 
detailed attempt to discuss how the constants used were derived in practice. In the 
comments following the translations of the definitions of constants, I have included 
some references to the cosmological basis of those constants in the numerical 
structures thought to be inherent in the Book of Change Yi jing 易經. This text, 
originally an ancient handbook of divination, had by the early imperial period been 
supplemented by material expounding a scheme of numerological relations held 
to be of fundamental cosmic significance.
5
Like all astronomical systems in this period, the Triple Concordance system was 
built on two main foundations. The first was a ‘system origin’ – a moment in the

past when everything in the system was at its initial position, and from which all 
calculations were to start. For calculations relating to the sun and moon, the winter 
solstice of late 105 
bce was such a moment. But as we shall see, for calculations 
involving the planets a point much more remote in time was required. The second 
foundation was a set of constants on which all calculations were based. These 
included the lengths of certain cyclical periods after which the heavenly bodies 
returned to given states. For the Triple Concordance, the most important such period 
was the Origin period of 4617 years, after which the sun and moon came back to 
their initial positions at the same time of the same day of the same month of the 
year, and on the same sexagenary day. This and other periods are discussed below.
Let us look at these two foundations of the system in more detail.
System origin
As already indicated, if we only want to make calculations about the sun and moon, 
including such phenomena as solstices, equinoxes, conjunctions of sun and moon 
(and thus the first days of lunar months) and lunar eclipses, we may use the day the 
system was inaugurated, when it was assumed that winter solstice and conjunction 
of sun and moon
6 coincided at midnight beginning the first day of the first Celestial 
month, which was also a jiazi.1 day, on December 25, 105 bce in the proleptic 
Julian calendar. However, the Triple Concordance system specification frequently 
talks about counting off years from a much more distant point, the shang yuan 
上元 ‘High Origin’, without unfortunately saying exactly where that point is. For 
that information, we have to look at another piece of Liu Xin’s writing preserved 
in the Han shu, his Shi jing ‘Canon of the Ages’.
7 At one point, this tells us:
漢曆太初元年，距上元十四萬三千一百二十七歲．
In the Han system, the first year of the Han Grand Inception reign period was 
distant from High Origin by 143,127 years.
(Han shu, 1023)
Counting back 143,127 years from the winter solstice of 105 
bce, we find ourselves 
at the winter solstice calculated according to the Triple Concordance as falling on 
December 2, 143,232 
bce. Now since 143,127 = 32 × 4617, i.e. a whole number 
of Origin periods, the luni-solar conditions at this High Origin would have been 
taken to be exactly identical to those at the winter solstice of 105 
bce. So what was 
the purpose of using such a distant starting point for calculations?
The aim, as we shall see when we come to look at the parts of the Triple Con-
cordance dealing with the planets, was to find a moment in the past that not only

36 The Triple Concordance system
saw the sun and moon at their initial positions, but did the same for the five visible 
planets. For these, the recognised initial conditions were that they were all taken to 
be in conjunction with one another at a standard distance to the west of the sun, so 
that (in theory) they had just become visible at dawn – which they certainly were 
not in late 105 
bce.8 Given the lengths and incommensurabilities of the planetary 
cycles, it was necessary to look far back in the past to find such a moment that 
led to acceptably accurate predictions of planetary positions during the time the 
Triple Concordance was in use, while also being suitable for predictions of luni-
solar conditions.
Cycles and constants
For the Triple Concordance, the most important elements in the list of cycles are:
The Rule: zhang 章. In all the systems we shall be discussing, the Rule cycle 
can be interpreted as saying that 19 sui 歲 are equivalent to 235 yue 月. 
Now, as mentioned in Chapter 1, there is ambiguity in both these terms. Sui 
can mean the precise length of the solar cycle, i.e. the interval between 
winter solstices, consisting of 365 days and a fraction of a day, or it may 
refer to the calendrical unit of the civil year, consisting of a whole number 
of lunar months (and hence of a whole number of days). Yue can mean the 
precise length of a (mean) lunation, consisting of 29 days and a fraction of 
a day, or it can refer to the calendrical unit of the lunar month, which consists 
of a whole number of days. Thus the equivalence embodied in a Rule means 
either and both of the following:
19 solar cycles are precisely equivalent to 235 lunations. So if a Rule 
begins with coincidence of winter solstice and conjunction (as at 
system origin), so will all subsequent Rules. However, since the period 
elapsed is not a whole number of days, the coincidence will not neces-
sarily occur at midnight as it did at the moment of system origin.
19 civil years contain 235 lunar months. Thus, since 235 = 19 × 12 + 7, 
there must be 7 intercalary months in 19 years. So if the Rule began 
on the first day of the first astronomical month, so will all subsequent 
Rules.
The Concordance tong 統: 1539 sui, 81 Rules. Winter solstice and mean con-
junction once more coincide at midnight. A Concordance is a whole number 
of days, months and years, and so that we may see that 1539 sui signifies 
both 1539 solar cycles and 1539 civil years, both of them precisely.
The Origin yuan 元: 4617 sui (solar cycles or civil years), three Concor -
dances. Winter solstice and mean conjunction coincide at midnight, and 
8 In later systems, such as the Han Quarter Remainder and Uranic Manifestation, the planets were 
taken to be in conjunction with the sun at system origin.

elapsed is not a whole number of days, the coincidence will not necessarily occur at midnight as it did at the moment of system origin.
19 civil years contain 235 lunar months. Thus, since 235 = 19 × 12 + 7, 
there must be 7 intercalary months in 19 years. So if the Rule began 
on the first day of the first astronomical month, so will all subsequent 
Rules.
The Concordance tong 統: 1539 sui, 81 Rules. Winter solstice and mean conjunction once more coincide at midnight. A Concordance is a whole number 
of days, months and years, and so that we may see that 1539 sui signifies 
both 1539 solar cycles and 1539 civil years, both of them precisely.
The Origin yuan 元: 4617 sui (solar cycles or civil years), three Concor -
dances. Winter solstice and mean conjunction coincide at midnight, and 
8 In later systems, such as the Han Quarter Remainder and Uranic Manifestation, the planets were 
taken to be in conjunction with the sun at system origin.

The Triple Concordance system 37
the day then beginning is once more at the same place in the sexagenary 
cycle (normally jiazi.1) as was system origin.
As noted in Chapter 1, a major practical function of these cycles is to reduce 
the size of the numbers that appear in calculations, since whole numbers of the 
relevant cycles can be cast out at the start of the process.
In order to make it possible to run all the basic luni-solar calculations underlying 
the Triple Concordance system, the values of two constants are needed:
Lunation Factor yue fa 月法 [2,392]
Day Factor ri fa 日法 [81]
Combined in the division (Lunation Factor) / (Day Factor) these last two constants 
give the number of days in one mean lunation, 29  43⁄81. As noted in Chapter 1, to 
avoid fractions most calculations are carried out using days at a scale of Lunation 
Factor, with a final division to find whole days and parts.
We may compare this to a modern value for the ‘mean synodic month’, 29.5306 
days (to six significant figures). Since 29 43⁄81 = 29.5309 to the same precision, the 
two values agree to within 0.0003 day, just under half a minute. Now a civil month 
has to be a whole number of days. The lunation length given here is a little longer 
than the average length of 29.5 days that would result from a strict alternation of 
short months of 29 days and long months of 30 days, and so it is clear that there 
should be two successive long months from time to time in order to keep months 
in step with the lunation – just as we saw in the case of the 69 
bce calendar dis-
cussed in Chapter 1.
From Rule Months, Lunation Factor and Day Factor, we may calculate the num-
ber of days from one winter solstice to the next as being 365 385⁄1539  days, which is 
365.2502 days to four decimal places – about 11 minutes longer than the modern 
value for this period.
9
In addition, the system contains sets of constants and calculation procedures 
for predicting the motions of the five naked-eye planets. These assume that, to 
use modern terms, the synodic period of each planet (i.e. the interval between its 
conjunctions with the sun) is constant, which is something of an approximation, 
and that exactly the same pattern of motion is repeated by a given planet in each 
of its synodic cycles.

‘Sequence Constants’ which gives similar data for each of the planets, and ‘The Five 
Pacers’ which details the movements of each of the five planets during one complete

38 The Triple Concordance system
synodic cycle. ‘Concordance Workings’ specifies how luni-solar phenomena are to 
be calculated, and ‘Sequence Workings’ does the same for the planets. The text ends 
with a number of shorter sections, giving details of certain calendrical cycles and the 
widths in du of the 28 lodges, the unequal divisions used to define motion round the 
heavens. As noted in Chapter 1, the lodge system may be characterised in modern 
terms as an equatorial division of the heavens into slices of right ascension, and a 
modern reading of the text might conclude that it was assumed that the motions of 
the sun and moon could be treated as uniform with respect to the celestial equator – 
whereas in fact the ecliptic is a much more appropriate reference frame for the sun 
and moon, and likewise the planets. This would be an anachronistic view, however, 
since the equatorial/ecliptic distinction depends on a view of the heavens as a celes-
tial sphere, and was not yet a live issue at the time Liu Xin and his predecessors 
wrote.
10 For a recognition of this distinction we must wait until the introduction of 
the Han Quarter Remainder system 70 years or so after Liu Xin’s time.
The text translated here is a complete specification of the Triple Concordance 
system, apart from the statement of the High Origin mentioned earlier, in the gen-
eral form and style that was to become standard for all later systems. It was, how-
ever, not the only writing by Liu Xin preserved in the Han shu. It is preceded in 
chapter 21a by a treatise on what may be called cosmological metrology, in which 
the significance of the standard weights and measures is explained, including the 
pitches and lengths of the pipes defining the musical scale (Han shu 21a, 956–972). 
Before giving us this treatise, Ban Gu warns us that he has ‘removed heretical 
expressions’, an understandable precaution given Liu Xin’s support for the deposed 
Wang Mang. After this the editor or editors then give us (Han shu 21a, 973–979), a 
brief sketch of the history of li from the mythical times of ‘High Antiquity’ down 
to the time of Liu Xin; this material is translated in Chapter 5 of this book, where it 
appears in the role of a curtain-raiser to the major collection of historical documents 
by Cai Yong and Liu Hong on developments in li in the first and second centuries 
ce. 
It is followed (Han shu 21a, 979–986) by more material apparently originating with 
Liu Xin, in which the values of key constants in the Triple Concordance system are 
derived from cosmological considerations: much of this material is either repeated 
in the Triple Concordance specification, or is cited in my explanatory comments. 
The Triple Concordance specification translated here forms the first part of the next 
chapter (Han shu 21b, 991–1011). There then follows a document under the title 
Shi jing 世經 ‘Canon of the Ages), in which we are given a series of chronological 
and calendrical notes on historical records from High Antiquity down to the first 
century 
ce.11 If, as seems highly likely, this document was originally composed by 
Liu Xin,12 it has obviously been supplemented by the Han shu editors, since it ends

in progress on Liu Xin’s Canon of the Ages.” Asia Major xiv(2): 27–70.
12 Thus, the editors state that Liu Xin zuo san tong li ji pu yi shuo chun qiu 作三統曆及譜以說春
秋 ‘Wrote the Triple Concordance system and a listing which explained the Spring and Autumn

The Triple Concordance system 39
with material referring to events in the decades following his death. I have made 
references to some of these data in notes on the schematic chronological tables 
given near the end of the Triple Concordance specification.
2.1.4 Text used
The text used here follows the version published in chapter 21b of Han shu  
漢書 (History of the Western Han dynasty), Ban Gu 班固 (32–92 ce), Zhonghua, 
Beijing, punctuated edition of 1962. There is no reason to doubt that the text we 
have today is substantially identical with what was composed by Ban Gu and his 
co-editors. Moreover, from the comments of those Western Han editors it seems 
likely that what we read in this text is essentially what Liu Xin wrote. Page num-
bers given thus ‘– 991 –’ follow that edition. I have also made extensive use of the 
online searchable version that forms part of the Scripta Sinica site maintained by 
Academia Sinica, Taibei, which uses the same pagination, as I have for the other 
documents I translate.
2.2 TEXT, TRANSLATION AND COMMENTS
– 991 –
漢書卷二十一下
律曆志第一下
Han shu chapter 21b
Monograph on harmonics and astronomical systems, 1b
統母
2.2.1 Concordance constants
日法八十一．元始黃鐘初九自乘，一龠之數，得日法．
§1 Day Factor 81. At the Origin Initiation, the First 9 of the Yellow Bell multiplies 
itself, which is the number of the first pitchpipe; one obtains the Day 
Factor.
This number is the divisor of the fractional part of days in a (mean) lunation. As 
the text states, it is supposed to be derived from considerations of mathematical 
harmonics, for which the fundamental note is the one named ‘Yellow Bell’. The 
fourth power of the yang number 3 is 81, and when multiplied by 10, which (as 
noted in section § 2) is the conclusion of the series of five yang numbers (odd) 
[Annals]’ Han shu, 21a, 979. Much of the ‘Canon of the Ages’ is devoted to showing how the 
dates given in the Spring and Autumn [Annals]  can be explained consistently with the Triple 
Concordance.

Together with Lunation Factor [2392] (see below), Day Factor defines the number

閏法十九， 因為章歲． 合天地終數，得閏法．
§2 Intercalation Factor 19, taken as the basis for Rule Years. Joining the ultimate 
numbers of Heaven and Earth, one obtains the Intercalation Factor.
This is the number of civil years, 1 Rule, containing seven intercalary months, 
making a total of 19 × 12 + 7 = 235 months. Alternatively, we may say that 19 solar 
cycles are precisely equal to 235 lunations.
13 The pattern of intercalations within 
years repeats at this interval. The first day of the first month of each 19-year period 
contains the instant of coincidence of winter solstice and conjunction, but not 
necessarily at midnight or on a jiazi.1 day.
From data and procedures given later in the text, it may be calculated that the time 
of day of the coincidence advances by 20/81 day each Rule.
The meaning of the ‘ultimate numbers of Heaven and Earth’ is clarified in a passage 
from the Book of Change quoted by Liu Xin in his earlier discussion of cosmologi-
cal theory:
故易曰 ： 「天一地二， 天三地四， 天五地六， 天七地八， 天九地十． 天數五， 地數五
‘Thus the Changes say ‘1 for Heaven, 2 for Earth, 3 for Heaven, 4 for Earth, 5 
for Heaven, 6 for Earth, 7 for Heaven, 8 for Earth, 9 for Heaven, 10 for Earth: 
five Heavenly numbers and five Earthly numbers.’
(Han shu 21a, 983)
9 and 10 are simply the last pair of numbers in the list, and when added they 
make 19.
13 Or in modern terms, 19 tropical years are precisely equal to 235 synodic months. My reasons for 
preferring to speak of ‘solar cycles’ and ‘lunations’ in discussions of li are set out in Chapter 1.

In Intercalation Factor [19] solar cycles, the moon makes 235 circuits of heaven rela-

might say that 19 tropical years is taken as precisely equal to 235 synodic months

a quantity that will be a whole multiple of solar cycles, or, in calendrical terms, a

Now to get 19 solar cycles is precisely equal to 235 lunations, and
235 = 47 × 5, while 135 = 27 × 5.
Hence we multiply New and Full Moons Coincidence [135] by 47, and obtain 6345 
lunations = 6345 × 19/235 solar cycles = 513 solar cycles.
We might expect the latter quantity to be given some name, such as ‘Coincidence 
Years’, but somewhat strangely it is not separately defined in the text: see however 
its use by Li Rui in Proc. 2.12. By contrast, in the Han Quarter Remainder system, a 
fuller list is given, based on the same prediction scheme:

月數 Month Number: 135
食法 Eclipse Factor: 23
Liu Hong’s Uranic Manifestation system uses a slightly different basis, with 1882 
eclipses in 11,045 lunations. Since 1882/11,045 = 23.0032/135, the difference is 
not large.

2.2.2 Sequence constants
In this part, which gives basic constants for the movement of each of the planets 
in turn, it is helpful to bring forward some general matters relevant to much of 
what follows.
First, as mentioned in Chapter 1, each planet has two names: one descriptive and 
the other indicating its correlation with one of the Five Phases. This correlation also 
implies an association with a number from one to five that will be relevant to the 
way the constants for that planet are calculated. The preceding chapter of Han shu 
has the following discussion by Liu Xin:
五星之合於五行，水合於辰星，火合於熒惑，金合於太白， 木合於歲星，土合於填星． 
三辰五星而相經緯也． 
天以一生水，地以二生火，天以三生木，地以四生金，天以五生土．
The correspondence between the Five Stars and the Five Phases: Water cor -
responds to the Chronogram Star [Mercury], Fire corresponds to Dazzling 
Deluder [Mars], Metal corresponds to Great White [Venus], Wood corresponds 
to the Year Star, and Earth [tu 土] corresponds to the Garrison Star [Saturn]
The three Chronograms [sun, moon and stars] and Five Planets: they are warp 
and weft.
Heaven produces Water with 1. Earth [di 地] produces Fire with 2. Heaven pro-
duces Wood with 3. Earth [di 地] produces Metal with 4. Heaven produces Earth 
[tu 土] with 5.

2.2.2 Sequence constants
In this part, which gives basic constants for the movement of each of the planets 
in turn, it is helpful to bring forward some general matters relevant to much of 
what follows.
First, as mentioned in Chapter 1, each planet has two names: one descriptive and 
the other indicating its correlation with one of the Five Phases. This correlation also 
implies an association with a number from one to five that will be relevant to the 
way the constants for that planet are calculated. The preceding chapter of Han shu 
has the following discussion by Liu Xin:
五星之合於五行，水合於辰星，火合於熒惑，金合於太白， 木合於歲星，土合於填星． 
三辰五星而相經緯也． 
天以一生水，地以二生火，天以三生木，地以四生金，天以五生土．
The correspondence between the Five Stars and the Five Phases: Water cor -
responds to the Chronogram Star [Mercury], Fire corresponds to Dazzling 
Deluder [Mars], Metal corresponds to Great White [Venus], Wood corresponds 
to the Year Star, and Earth [tu 土] corresponds to the Garrison Star [Saturn]
The three Chronograms [sun, moon and stars] and Five Planets: they are warp 
and weft.
Heaven produces Water with 1. Earth [di 地] produces Fire with 2. Heaven produces Wood with 3. Earth [di 地] produces Metal with 4. Heaven produces Earth 
[tu 土] with 5.

central to the whole discussion of planetary predictions in the Triple Concordance 
system. The character 見 can represent two different but closely related words. One 
is the common transitive verb ‘to see, to visit’, pronounced jian in modern stan -
dard Chinese, and probably pronounced something like *ken in the period when 
the Triple Concordance was written. The other is an intransitive verb, xian (ancient

*gen), meaning ‘to appear, become visible’.16 It is the latter word that the character 
represents in the present context. Thus, for instance, at the beginning of the text 
describing the motions of Jupiter (see section § 92), we have: chen shi xian 晨始見. . . 
‘It first appears at dawn’. The precise significance of this phrase is that after a period 
when the planet was too close to the sun to be seen, the eastwards motion of the sun 
allows the planet to rise long enough before the sun for it to be briefly visible in the 
east before the dawn sunlight blots it out. This event is variously known in English 
as the ‘apparent morning rising’
17 of the planet, or alternatively its ‘heliacal rising’ or 
‘first morning rising’. When on the contrary the distance between the sun and the 
planet decreases to the point where the planet can no longer be seen, the planet is 
said to fu 伏 ‘disappear’ or ‘become invisible’ (literally ‘hide’), as in for instance section 
§ 110 . . . bai ba shi si ri er fu 百八十四日而伏, ‘it disappears after 184 days’.
When we say of a planet that it ‘first appears’ the English translation is simply 
reproducing the verbal function of the Chinese term xian. In many instances, how-
ever, attempting to translate xian as a verb would produce an unnatural effect in 
English. Thus when one of the constants listed below is identified by the words xian 
shu ye 見數也 , I have chosen to translate as ‘[This] is the Appearance Number’: see 
section § 25. In the case of the outer planets, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, the word 
‘Appearance’ in this sense can either refer to the event of the planet first ‘appear-
ing’, or to the period of time that begins with an Appearance and ends with the 
next Appearance, a property it has in common with some other astro-calendrical 
expressions. Thus for instance in section § 104, we have for Jupiter yi xian, san bai 
jiu shi ba ri 一見，三百九十八日
 . . . ‘One Appearance is 398 days’. In modern terms, 
an Appearance is a synodic cycle.

the sun begins to approach them from the west, so that eventually they are only 
visible for a short time before they set in the west not long after dusk. Then, when 
the sun gets close enough for its light to blot them from view, they disappear until 
once more becoming visible just before dawn. For the ‘inner planets’ Mercury and 
Venus, the situation is a little more complex. The planets can first appear either in

The Triple Concordance system 53
One stalk from the right hand heap is placed between the ring and little fingers 
of the left hand.
The left hand heap is then counted through by fours, and the remainder (four or 
less) is inserted between ring finger and middle finger.
The same is done with the right hand heap, and the remainder is inserted between 
the middle and index finger.
The total stalks in the fingers will then be either 5 or 9.
The two remaining heaps are then put together, and the process repeated twice. 
On each trial, one will have either 4 or 8 stalks between the fingers.
If the sequence of stalks is 5, 4, 4, the result is a yang line. A total of 49 − 5 − 4 − 4 = 
36 stalks will remain in the two heaps.
If it is 9, 8, 8, the result is a yin line. A total of 49 − 9 − 8 − 8 = 24 stalks will remain 
in the two heaps.
The process is then repeated to find the next of the six lines.
Thus if six  yang lines are produced, yielding the hexagram 乾 Qian ‘Uranic’, 
the total of the remainders will be 6 × 36 = 216; if six  yin lines are produced, 
yielding the hexagram 坤 Kun ‘Chthonic’ the total of the remainders will be 
6 × 24 = 144.
– 993 –

The Triple Concordance system 67
‘The Year Number of the Great yin is the Year Number of Mercury 9216. The 
Year Number of the Great Yang is the Year Number of Mars 13,824.’
(Li Rui 李銳 (1768–1817) 1993: 718A)
Thus: (Mercury Year Number [9216] + Mars Year Number [13,824]) / 2 = 11,520.
But what is the significance of the number 11,520? To understand that, we have to 
consider how divination with the Book of Change was carried out. It has already been 
noted in section § 22 that when a  yang line is produced using manipulation of 
yarrow stalks, a remainder of 36 is produced, and when a yin line is produced, the 
number is 24: see section § 22. Since each of the 64 hexagrams in the book has six 
lines, which show all possible combinations of yin and yang, then there will be 6 × 
64 = 374 lines, of which 192 will be  yang and 192 yin. The total remainders will 
then be
Yang: 192 × 36 = 6912
Yin: 192 × 24 = 4608
The total of the remainders is thus 6912 + 4608 = 11,520.
As the Book of Change notes:
二篇之策萬有 一千五百二十 當萬 物之數也
commentary: 二篇三百八十四爻陰陽各半合萬 一千五百二十 策
‘The Reckoning of the two sections [of the Book of Change] is 11,520, which 
matches the number of the myriad creatures.
Commentary: In the two sections [of the Book of Change] there are 384 lines, 
with half yin and half yang. Together that makes a Reckoning of 11,520.’
(Zhou yi 周易 7, Xi Ci 繫辭 (a), 153B in Shi san jing zhu shu edn.  
(Ruan Yuan 阮元 1973 reprint of original of 1815))
以星行率減歲數，餘則見數也．

later sections, in each of which we are given the mean rate of motion of the planet 
averaged over its entire synodic cycle.

通其率，故曰日行千七百二十八分度之百四十五．

§ 151. Making the r ates compatible, thus we may say that in one day it travels 
7355/13,824 du.
In each case, the denominator of the fraction is the Year Number for the planet, 
the number of years during which it makes Appearance Number of Appearances. 
The numerator is the quantity referred to in this section as ‘Star [sc. planet] Motion 
Rate’.
Now if, for example, Jupiter moves on average 145/1728 du/day, then since the sun 
moves 1 du/day, and (in this period of Chinese history) a solar cycle is the time 
during which the sun makes a complete circuit relative to the stars, as well as the 
interval between winter solstices, in 1728 solar cycles Jupiter will make 145 circuits 
relative to the stars, and hence the number of circuits it will make relative to the sun 
will be
1728 − 145 = 1583, the Appearance Number for Jupiter.
Similar calculations apply to Saturn and Mars. We may tabulate:

晨始見，去日半次．
§92 It first appears at dawn, distant half a station from the Sun.
A station, ci 次, is in principle one of the 12 ‘Jupiter stations’ defined in section 2.2.7; 
these vary in width between 30 and 31 du. However, in the general method for cal-
culating Appearances of planets, we are simply told that planets will appear ‘15 du 
behind the Sun’: see Proc. 2.18. A detailed examination of the figures given for the 
motions of each planet implies slightly different values for their distances from the 
sun at an Appearance. Thus for instance in the case of Jupiter, section § 97 implies 
that one of its ‘stations’ would be 30 + 1,661,286/7,308,711 du wide (30.227 du 
to 5 significant figure), while for Saturn it would be 30 + 8,433,600/19,275,975 du 
(30.438 du to the same precision). Mars has the largest station width, at 32.250 du, 
which would make ‘half a station’ more than 16 du rather than 15 du. Such differ-
ences are however simply the result of dividing the planet’s visible motion into a 
few sections where the daily motion is defined using simple fractions, leaving the 
invisible motion, where it moves from visibility on one side of the sun to visibility 
on the other side, to make the total motion compatible with the defined duration 
of the synodic period. They have no practical observational significance.

§97 It moves direct once more, moving 2/11 du per day, for 111 days and

2.2.4 Concordance workings
推日月元統， 置太極上元以來， 外所求年，盈元法除之， 餘不盈統者， 則天統
甲子以來-1001-年數也． 盈統， 除之， 餘則地統甲辰以來年數也． 又盈統， 除之, 
餘則人統甲申以來年數也． 各以其統首日為紀
Proc. 2.1. To predict the Origin and Concordance of sun and moon:
§173 Set out [the years] from the High Origin of the Supreme Ultimate, with 
[the year] sought outside [the count]. Cast out what fills the Origin Factor 
[4617]. In the case of a remainder that does not fill the Concordance 
Factor [1539], then that is the number of years since the Celestial Con -
cordance jiazi.1. If it fills a Concordance Factor [1539], cast that out, 
then that is the number of years since the Terrestrial Concordance 
jiachen.41. If it fills a further Concordance Factor [1539], cast that out, 
then that is the number of years since the Anthropic Concordance 
jiashen.21. In each case, take the day of the Concordance Head as the 
start of the count.
EXAMPLE: Suppose our target year is the Chinese civil year that began in the 
spring of 102 bce. As usual, we shall in fact calculate data for the Celestial year 
that begins two months earlier, near the winter solstice of 103 bce. We are told 
elsewhere (in Liu Xin’s Shi Jing 世經 ‘Canon of the Ages’ Han shu p. 1023) that
漢曆太初元年，距上元十四萬三千一百二十七歲．
‘The first year of the Han Taichu reign period was distant from High Origin by 
143,127 years.’
The first civil year of the Taichu (‘Grand Inception’) period began in spring 
104 
bce. So 102 bce must be 143,127 + 2 = 143,129 years from High Origin. In 
modern terms, that means that the time interval between the winter solstice at 
High Origin and the winter solstice (in late 103 
bce) preceding the start of this 
civil year is 143,129 years.
The text however conceives that we number the year beginning at High Origin 
as number one, and then stop at the year before our target year, which will be 
number 143,130. The numerical results are of course identical, but the conceptual 
difference is clear.

Proc. 2.2. To predict the Celestial Standard Month:24
§174 Multiply Rule Months [235] by the number of years of entry into the 
Concordance, and obtain 1 for each filling of Rule Years [19]. This is 
called Accumulated Months. What does not fill is called Intercalation 
Surplus. If Intercalation Surplus is 12 or above, the year has an intercala -

with the sequence of Medial Qi, which begins each year with the Winter Solstice. 
At the start of a Rule, winter solstice coincides with the conjunction beginning 
the Celestial First Month. This condition recurs at the beginning of the next Rule, 
but the conjunction with which the first winter solstice of that Rule coincides is 
seven later than the one that would have been indicated if winter solstices were 
separated by exactly 12 lunations each. So each successive winter solstice is 7/19 
of a lunation later than its predecessor with respect to its Celestial First Month 
conjunction, and it is the total of this lag that is represented by Intercalation 
Surplus. As stated, 24 months is the number of months between the start of the 
current Concordance and the start of the first month of this Celestial year. As the 
text points out, the Terrestrial and Anthropic (or Civil) years begin one and two 
months later.

Turning first to the Accumulated Days, 708, this is the number of days from the 
start of the current concordance to the start of the first day of the first month of 
the present Celestial year.
708/60 = 11 remainder 48
So 11 complete 60-day cycles and 48 odd days have elapsed since the start of the 
current concordance, and thus 48 is the Greater Remainder. Following the instruc-
tions, then if the first day is number 1 and we are to count 48, the day ‘outside the 
count’, the day of conjunction, is number 49.
Now the head of the current concordance was day jiazi.1. So the conjunction for 
the first month of this Celestial year falls on cyclical day renzi.49.
The Lesser Remainder, 60, is the fraction of a day by which the (mean) conjunc -
tion starting this month falls after midnight, at a scale of Day Factor [81] – i.e. the 
conjunction falls 60/81 day after midnight.
Since the mean interval between conjunctions will be
2392/81 days = 29 + 43/81 days
it is clear that 29 and 43 are the amounts we must add to the Greater and Lesser 
Remainders to get to the next conjunction. Since
38 + 43 = 81
it is clear that if the Lesser Remainder at the start of this month is 43 or more, then 
a whole extra day will have to be counted before we get to the next conjunction, 
which will be 30 days away rather than 29, giving a ‘long month’ as stated. At the 
start of this month the Lesser Remainder is 60, so the month is long. The figures 
for the first quarter, and the full moon follow from the fact that:
2392/4 = 598
and 598/81 = 7 remainder 31.
It is assumed that the lunar phases are equally spaced.

The Triple Concordance system 93
of a mean lunation by which the winter solstice near the beginning of this year 
lags behind the conjunction of the first Celestial month, and this increases by 7/19 
of a lunation from one winter solstice to the next.
Now there are 12 medial qi in a year. So the lag between a medial qi and its preced-
ing conjunction must increase steadily from medial qi to medial qi by 7 / (12 × 19) 
= 7/228 of a mean lunation. When the total lag for a given medial qi builds up to 
greater than 228/228 of a mean lunation, then that medial qi falls after the next 
mean conjunction, and the lunation preceding that medial qi contains no medial 
qi at all, since the previous medial qi fell just before the previous mean conjunction.
The convention is that each medial qi corresponds to a month in the Celestial Year, 
and hence a month without a medial qi is anomalous. That month is therefore 
counted as intercalary; it bears the same number as the preceding month, with 
the prefix run 閏 ‘intercalary’.
Since we are counting up the increasing lag in units of (1/228) of a mean lunation, 
and the Intercalation Surplus is in (1/19) of a lunation, it is clear that the initial mul-
tiplication by 12 is needed to convert the Intercalation Surplus to the correct scale, 
since 12 × 19 = 228. We then find how many times we need to add 7 to this until we 
reach a total exceeding 228. Having found this number, then if we start counting with 
winter solstice taken as #1, and if (say) 3 additions of 7 are required, the 4th qi will be 
the one ‘outside the count’ that has shifted onto or past the next mean conjunction.
The reference to the medial qi (immediately after an intercalary month) possibly fall-
ing on the second day of the month rather than on the first day deals with the fact that 
the maximum lag that can occur at a medial qi that does not create an intercalation 
is 227/228 lunation. At that point, the medial qi will fall just before the conjunction 
following the conjunction to which that medial qi ‘belongs’, the gap in days being:
(2392/81) × (1/228), which is just under 0.13 day.
The lag of the next qi after the next conjunction will be
(227 + 7) / 228 lunations = 234/228 lunations.
That means it will go 6/228 of a lunation past the following conjunction, leaving 
a whole lunation without a medial qi in it – an intercalary month.
Now 6/228 lunation = (6/228) × 2392/81 days
= 0.78 day to 2 significant figures.
Clearly therefore this qi could fall on the day after the day of the conjunction, if the 
conjunction falls more than 0.22 day after midnight on the first day of the month.
EXAMPLE: Applying these principles to our target year of 102 
bc, we proceed as 
follows. Since the Intercalation Surplus is 14, we calculate:
14 × 12 = 168
and
(228 − 168) / 7 = 8, remainder 4

94 The Triple Concordance system
Thus if winter solstice is medial qi number 1, we shall need to move 9 steps further 
on from that before the total lag exceeds 228. That will take us to medial qi number 
10 (which is the 21st of the 24 qi). Some thought will show that if this is to be in 
its proper month, which is of course the 10th Celestial month, then the preceding 
month must be ‘intercalary 9th’, since it will contain no medial qi, and will follow 
the 9th month. An intercalary 9th Celestial month corresponds to an intercalary 7th 
Civil month. This, then is a mathematically consistent way of deciding when an inter-
calary month is to be counted, on the basis that the appropriate medial qi should fall 
within any normal lunation, counted from one instant of conjunction to the next.
However, it appears that this is not how the system was operated in practice. In 
deciding when to count an intercalary month in the almanac, the only factor that 
seems to have been considered in practice was whether the medial qi in question 
fell within the whole days allocated to that month. That means a month would miss 
being intercalary if a medial qi that really belonged to the preceding lunation fell 
on its first day (counted from midnight), but before the actual instant of conjunc-
tion. In such a case, that month would in effect ‘steal’ the preceding conjunction, 
saving itself from intercalary status, but making the preceding month intercalary.
Concrete archaeological evidence of this practice may be found on an excavated 
calendar for 12 
bce.25 The first days of the first three (civil, Xia count) months are 
given as follows:
正月大己亥朔
閏月小己巳朔
二月大戊戌朔春分
Standard [i.e. first] month. Long [i.e. 30 days]. Jihai.36, first day
Intercalary month. Short [i.e. 29 days]. Jisi.6, first day
Second month. Long [i.e. 30 days]. Wuxu.35, first day. Spring equinox
Here we see that an intercalary month is stated to begin on day jisi.6; it is inter -
calary month 1. But if we set out the precise times of inceptions of lunations and 
medial qi as in Table 2.2, we can see that the Triple Concordance appears to make 
a different prediction.
The times for lunation and medial qi inception are shown with full calculated preci-
sion, at a common denominator of Origin Factor [4617]. It is clear that the month 
after month 2 must be intercalary, since Spring Equinox falls slightly before the 
instant of lunation inception for that month, and Grain Rains falls slightly after the 
instant of lunation inception for the next month. If however we work with whole 
days only, we obtain a different sequence as in Table 2.3.

seek the 24 qi, treble the Lesser Remainder, and add to the Greater 
Remainder 15, to the Lesser Remainder 1010. In predicting the 24 qi, 
[which are] the sub-divisions of the medial [qi], use the Origin [Factor 
[4617]] as the factor in each case.
The Eight Nodes begin with the first qi, followed at intervals of three qi by numbers 
4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, and 22. Each of the Eight Nodes shifts the day number by (1/8) × 
562,120/1539 = 70,265/1539 days, which is 45 days remainder 1010, as stated 
here. The interval between two qi is: (1/24) × 562,120/1539 = 70,265 / (1539 × 3).

推五行，其四行各七十三日，統(歲)[法]分之七十七． 中央各十八日, 統法分
之四百四． 冬至後，中央二十七日六百六分．
Proc. 2.7. To predict the Five Phases:
§179 Four of these phases are 73 days, and 77 Concordance Factor [1539] parts. 
The Central [Phase] is in each case 18 days and 404 Concordance Factor 
[1539] parts.
§180 After the winter solstice, the Central [Phase] is 27 days and 606 parts.
At a scale of Concordance Factor [1539], the year has 562,120 parts.
562,120/5 = 112,424 and 112,424/1539 = 73 remainder 77
Now 112,424/4 = 28,106, and 28,106/1539 = 18 remainder 404
So it is clear that the first figure is the result of dividing the year into five equal 
parts. We then allocate one quarter of each of these five parts to Earth, the cen -
tral phase.
The last sentence is somewhat obscure; following the notes of Li Rui (Li Rui 
李銳 (1768–1817) 1993: 724B), it may be interpreted as a means of applying 
the Five Phases to the four seasons. From winter solstice to Establishment of 
Spring is 45 days, and 1010/1539 days. One removes 18 days and 404 parts 
during which Earth reigns, to leave 27 days and 606 parts within which water 
reigns before the central phase begins – and so on for spring (wood), summer 
(fire), autumn (metal) and once more winter (water). The text is not explicit 
about whether the period before each solstice and equinox is to be allocated 
in the same way.

du of the star where the conjunction marker is entered.

98 The Triple Concordance system
Assuming that at the start of the system Accumulated Days are zero, then ‘outside 
the count’ will be the first du of the lodge Ox.
推其日夜半所在星，以章歲乘月小餘，以減合晨度．小餘不足者，破全度．
Proc. 2.9. To predict the star where the sun is located at midnight:
§182 Multiply the Lesser Remainder of the month by Rule Years [19], and by 
that diminish the du of the mark-point for the conjunction. If the Lesser 
Remainder is insufficient, break a whole du [into parts].
The Lesser Remainder for a month is a fraction of a day at a scale of 81. Multiply -
ing this by 19 converts to a scale of 19 × 81 = 1539, the Concordance Factor, used 
for fractions of a du. Since (by definition) the sun moves 1 du in a day, subtract -
ing this amount from the du for the conjunction gives the du for the preceding 
midnight.
推其月夜半所在星， 以月周乘月小餘，盈統法得一度，以減合晨度．
Proc. 2.10. To predict the star where the moon is located at midnight:
§183 Multiply the Lesser Remainder of the month by Lunar Circuits [254], and 
obtain 1 du for each filling of the Concordance Factor [1539], and by that 
diminish the du of the mark-point for the conjunction.
Since Lunar Circuits [254] is the number of circuits of the sky performed by the 
moon while the sun performs Rule Years [19] circuits, the motion of the moon 
since midnight may obviously be found by substituting 254 for 19 in the previous 
calculation.
推諸加時， 以十二乘小餘為實，各盈分母為法，數起於子，算外，則所加辰也．
Proc. 2.11. To predict the time of occurrence:
§184 Multiply the Lesser Remainder by 12 to make the dividend, and in 
each case take the factor to be the divisor for filling the parts, and 
number off from zi.1 [the cyclical character designating the first of the 
twelve double-hours]. Outside the count, then that is the double-hour 
of occurrence.
To find the time in (1/12) days, we must multiply by 12 the fraction of the day, 
which will be the Lesser Remainder divided by the appropriate divisor.

Proc. 2.12. To predict lunar eclipses:
§185 Set out the Accumulated Months in Coincidence Remainder Years. Multiply 
by 23, and cast out what fills 135. As for what does not fill, count one 
month for each addition of 23, until it fills 135. With the number you 
obtain, count off from the [Celestial] first [month]. Outside the count, then 
that is the lunar eclipse. At its time of occurrence, it is at the double-hour 
[mark] directly opposite to the sun.
On this passage Li Rui comments:
置入統歲.盈會 歲五百一十三.除去之.不盈者會餘 歲也.以章月乘之.盈章 歲得一
為積月.今案三統不見會 歲之數.當置入統以來積月盈會月除去之.餘即會餘 歲積
月也.
‘Set out years into the Concordance. As for what fills Coincidence Years 513, cast 
it out. What does not fill is Coincidence Remainder Years. Multiply that by Rule 
Months [235]. Obtain 1 for each filling of Rule Years [19] to make Accumulated 
Months. NOTE: in the Triple Concordance [system] ‘Coincidence Years’ does not 
appear. One has to set out the months into a Concordance, and then cast out 
what fills Coincidence Months [6345]. The remainder is the ‘Accumulated Months 
in Coincidence Remainder Years’’.
(Li Rui 李銳 (1768–1817) 1993: 725)
Li Rui is correct in saying that the quantity he calls Coincidence Years [513] is not 
defined in the Triple Concordance text. Instead we are given Coincidence Months 
會月 [6345]: see section § 14. Obviously:
Coincidence Months [6345] × Rule Years [19]/Rule Months [235]
= Coincidence Years [513]. There are three such periods in a Concordance, 1539 years.
His interpretation of the slightly puzzling phrase 會餘歲積月 does produce the cor-
rect result. Eclipse prediction is based on the idea that here will be 23 lunar eclipses 
in 135 lunations (or 23/135 of an eclipse per month), and hence the calculation in 
the text follows, yielding the number of eclipses in the Coincidence so far, i.e. by the 
beginning of the first Celestial month of this year. As for the remainder, that represents 
the parts of an incomplete eclipse, at a scale of 135. We then calculate how many 
more months must elapse, adding 23 eclipse parts per month, and thus find in what 
month the eclipse parts will add up to 135 or more, so a further eclipse takes place.

and at an altitude of about 70°. The eclipse was penumbral, with about ¾ of the

2.2.5 Sequence workings
推五星見復，置太極上元以來，盡所求年，乘(大統)27見復數，盈歲數得一，則
定見復數也． 不盈者名曰見復餘．見復餘盈其見復數，一以上見在往年，倍一
以上， 又在前往年，不盈者在今年也．
Proc. 2.13. To predict the Appearances or Returns of the Five Stars [sc. ‘Planets’]:
§186 Set out the years from the High Origin of the Great Ultimate that exhaust 
the year sought, and multiply the Appearance or Return Numbers. Count 
1 for each filling of the Year Number, then this is the Determined Appear -
ance or Return Number. The remainder is called the Appearance or Return 
Remainder. When the Appearance or Return Remainder fills its [appropri -
ate] Appearance or Return Number, if [it does so] 1 [time] or more then 
it is in the past year; if it is 2 [times] or more, then again it is in the year 
before the past year, but if it does not fill it, it is in the present year.
We are instructed to calculate:
Years × (Appearance Number) / (Year Number).
Suppose for example that we have 10,000 years since High Origin.
Then 10,000 × 1583/1728 = 9160, remainder 1520.
The figure of 9160 is the number of whole Appearance cycles that has taken place 
to date. There remains 1520/1728 of a cycle partly completed, and 1520 is the 
Appearance or Return Remainder. In this case, 1520 < Appearance Number [1583].
Now one Appearance takes 1728/1583 years. So since we have 1520/1728 of an 
Appearance, this has taken the following time since the start of the Appearance;
(1520/1728) × [1728]/1583) year = 1520/1538 year, just under a year.
Clearly, if the Remainder had been greater than 1538, the Appearance would have 
started over a year ago. In the case of Jupiter we can never actually have a case where 
the time elapsed since the last Appearance is as much as 2 years, since there is about 
one Appearance a year. However, in the case of Mars this could certainly happen.
27 These two characters ‘the great concordance’ do not seem to belong here, and I omit them from 
the translation.

solstice, and the station from  Xingji .1. Outside the count, that is the Medial

At the midpoint of each station is one of the ‘Medial Qi’, i.e. the odd-numbered

which is the ﬁ rst du of Ox. In the Triple Concordance, the starting position of the 
planets was half a station to the west of the sun at High Origin, which fell at winter 
solstice – hence at the beginning of the station Xingji.

Remainder) / (Origin Factor) is simply the number of whole days from the start 
of the current Origin Cycle up to the start of the Medial Qi in which the current 
Appearance occurs.
The remainder from this division is the Lesser Remainder, i.e. the fraction of a day 
after midnight at which the actual Medial Qi begins, at a scale of Origin Factor 
[4617]. Given that the first day of an Origin is jiazi.1, we can use this result to predict 
the cyclical day of the start of the Medial Qi in which the Appearance takes place.
The reference to the winter solstice is a puzzle. Li Rui (Li Rui 李銳 (1768–1817) 1993: 
726A) says that it is just given as an example of a possible Medial Qi. Maybe he is 
right. But if we emend 則(冬)至[日] then we have ‘then that is the day of Arrival’, 
which fits the calculation and refers back to the stated aim of the procedure.
From one Medial Qi to the next is: 562,120 × 4/4617 days = 30 + 2020/4617 days. 
Clearly if there is already a Lesser Remainder of 2597 elapsed after midnight at the 
start of the Medial Qi, then by the end of the Medial Qi 4617 will have accumu-
lated and an extra day is to be counted. The Medial Qi will therefore be 31 days 
rather than 30 days long, if we reckon it as running from the midnight before its 
actual instant of inception to the midnight preceding the instant of inception of 
the next Medial Qi. This note is not strictly relevant to the topic, but the point was 
not made earlier when qi inceptions in general were discussed without reference 
to planetary motions.
推朔日， 以月法乘月元餘，盈日法得一， 名曰積日，餘名曰小餘． 小餘三十八
以上， 月大．數除積日如法， 算外， 則星見月朔日也．
Proc. 2.17. To predict the day of conjunction:
§193 By the Lunation Factor [2392] multiply the Months Origin Remainder, 
counting one for each filling of the Day Factor [81]. This is called Accu-
mulated Days, and the remainder is called Lesser Remainder. If the Lesser 
Remainder is 38 or more, then the month is long. Count off and cast out 
according to the method, and outside the count is the conjunction day for 
[this] Appearance of the planet.
Months Origin Remainder (calculated above) is the number of whole months 
from the start of the last Origin to the start of the month in which the Appear -
ance of the planet takes place. The calculation specified converts this to days and 
(1/81) days, since (Lunation Factor) / (Day Factor) = 2392/81 = 29 + 43/81, the 
length of a mean lunation. Since one month is 29 + 43/81 days long, an initial 
Lesser Remainder of 38 will produce a whole day in the course of the month, 
so that the month is long. Given that the first day of an Origin is jiazi.1, we can 
use this result to predict the cyclical day of the start of the month in which the 
Appearance takes place, and hence we may predict on which day of the month 
it occurs, as is done shortly.

推入中次日度數，以中法乘中餘，以見中法乘其小餘并之，盈見中日法得
一，則入中日入次度數也．中(次)[以]至日數，次以次初數，算外，則星所
見[及日](日及)29 所在度數也．(求夕)30 在日後十五度．
Proc. 2.18. To predict the number of days and number of degrees of entry into 
a Medial [Qi] or station:
§194 By the Medial [Qi] Factor [140,530] multiply the Medial [Qi] Remainder, 
multiply Appearance Medial [Qi] Factor [1583] by the Lesser Remainder 
and combine them. Obtain one for each filling of the Appearance Medial 
[Qi] Day Factor, then this is the number of days into the Medial [Qi] and 
the number of du into the Station. In the case of a Medial [Qi] count from 
the day of the Arrival [of the Medial Qi], and in the case of a Station 
count from the start of the Station. Outside the count, then that is the day 
on which the planet appears and of the du in which it is located, that is 
15 du behind the Sun.
Medial [Qi] Remainder is the fraction of a Medial Qi uncompleted at the start of 
the Appearance last commenced before the end of the present year, at a scale of 
Appearance Medial Qi Factor [1583].
Medial [Qi] factor (140,530) is the number of days in one Medial Qi, at a scale of 
the Origin Factor [4617].
Thus the product of these is the number of days forming part of an uncompleted 
Medial Qi contributed by one Appearance, at a scale of 1583 × 4617 = Appearance 
Medial [Qi] Day Factor (7,308,711).
The Lesser Remainder is the fraction of a day (at a scale of Origin Factor 4617) after 
midnight when the instant of inception of the Qi falls.
So multiplying this by Appearance Number [1583] gives us that fraction of a 
day, once more at a scale of 4617 × 1583 = Appearance Medial Qi Day Factor 
(780,711).
When we obey the instruction to combine these two results, the total is the num-
ber of days from the midnight commencing the day in which the current Medial 
Qi falls to the instant of the Appearance, at a scale of Appearance Medial Qi Factor 
(780,711).

1817) (1993), 726B.
30 I omit these two characters, which mean ‘in the evening’. The object here is to find the Appearance 
of the planet, that is its first dawn appearance, when it is ‘behind the sun’ in the normal sense of 
the word, i.e. to its west. In the evening, the sun is (in the same sense) in advance of the sun, i.e. 
to its west, when it is last seen.

106 The Triple Concordance system
By following the instruction ‘Obtain one for each filling of the Appearance Medial 
[Qi] Day Factor’ the scale will be changed from Appearance Medial [Qi] Day Factor 
(780,711) to days (or du of solar motion).
We were told in Proc. 2.14 that we should count off from Xingji ‘Star Marker’, 
the first of the 12 stations. At High Origin, the sun began from the mid-point 
of this station, which is winter solstice. In the Triple Concordance system, 
however, the planets were all half a station, ci 次, about 15 du, to the west of 
the sun (‘behind the sun’), as this section reminds us and were thus at the 
start of Xingji. The date we have calculated is indeed the date of the planet’s 
Appearance – but to find the position of the planet, the du must be counted 
off from the start of each station.
推入月日數，以月法乘月餘，以見月法乘其小餘并之，盈見月日法得一, 則入
月日數也．并之大餘，數除如法，則見日也．
Proc. 2.19. To predict the number of days of entry into a month:
§195 By the Lunation Factor [2392] multiply the Lunation Remainder [15,079], 
and combine it with the Appearance Lunation Factor [30,077 = 19 × 1583] 
multiplied by the Lesser Remainder. Count one for each time this fills the 
Appearance Lunation Day Factor [2,436,237 = 1583 × 1539 = 1583 × 19 
× 81], then this is the number of days of entry into the month. Combine 
it with the Greater Remainder, and count and cast out according to the 
method, then that is the day of Appearance.
Now Lunation Remainder is the fraction of a month, at a scale of Appearance 
Lunation factor (30,077 for Jupiter), remaining between the end of the most recent 
lunation and the Appearance itself.
Lunation Factor is the number of days in a month scaled up by 81.
Multiplying these together gives days at a scale of (1583 × 19 × 81). The Lesser 
Remainder for the month is the fraction of a day (at a scale of 81) after midnight at 
which the inception of the lunation actually falls. Multiplying this by Appearance 
Lunation Factor (30,077 = 19 × 1583) again gives days at a scale of 1583 × 19 × 81.
Thus adding the above two quantities and dividing by the Appearance Lunation 
Day Factor (2,436,237 = 1583 × 1539 = 1583 × 19 × 81) gives (as the integral part) 
the number of days from the midnight of the start of the civil month at which the 
Appearance occurs.
The Greater Remainder is the amount by which one counts forward from the 
Concordance Head to find the cyclical day of the start of the month. By count-
ing forward again from this it is easy to find the cyclical day of the Appearance, 
as stated.

[Qi] of the next Appearance.
Accumulated Medial [Qi] [13] is the number of whole Medial [Qi] in one Appear-
ance. The Medial Qi Origin Remainder is the number of whole Medial Qi up to 
the current Appearance over and above whole numbers of Origin Medial [Qi]. So 
adding the first to the second increases the whole number of Medial [ Qi] to take 
account of a further Appearance. As for the fractions, we add the fractional Medial 
[Qi] contributed by one Appearance [157] to the fraction we had at the beginning 
of the current Qi, and if a whole Qi results we add it on to the previous result. Hence 
the Qi for the next Appearance results.
推後見月，加積月於月元餘，加後月餘於月餘，盈其法得一，從月元餘,  
除數如法，則後見月也．
Proc. 2.21. To predict the month of the next Appearance:
§197 Add Accumulated Months [13] to Lunation Origin Remainder. Add the 
later Lunation Remainder [15,079] to the Lunation Remainder [for the 
start of the present Appearance]. Obtain 1 if the factor is filled, and let 
that go with the Lunation Origin Remainder. Then cast out and count off 
according to the method, and that is the month of the next Appearance.
Since Appearances follow one another at fixed intervals, we can find the time 
of the Appearance following the one we have just calculated by adding on the 
appropriate number of months and fractions of a month to represent the time 
interval elapsed.

推朔日及入月數，如上法

Proc. 2.24. To predict the evening Appearance from the morning Appearance, 
or from the evening Appearance to predict the morning Appearance:
§200 In each case, follow the method above.
推五步，置始見以來日數，至所求日，各以其行度數乘之． 其星 (當作度?)若
日有分者，分子乘全為實，分母為法．其兩有分者， 分母分度數乘全, 分子從
之， 令相乘為實，分母相乘為法， 實如法得一， 名曰積度． 數起星初見(星宿)所
在宿度，算外，則星所在宿度也．
Proc. 2.25. To predict the Five Pacers:
§201 Set out the number of days since the first Appearance, up to the day sought. 
Multiply each by its number of du of motion. If the du or the days have 
parts, let the numerator of the parts multiply the whole number to make the 
product, and let the denominator of the parts be the divisor. If they both have 
parts, let the denominators of the parts [each] multiply the [corresponding] 
whole number, and let the numerator of the parts be added thereunto, then 
let the [results] be multiplied together to make the product. Let the denomina-
tors be multiplied together to make the divisor, and obtain one as the product 
corresponds to the divisor. This is called Accumulated Degrees. Count starting 
from the lodge degree where the first Appearance of the star is situated, and 
outside the count, that is the lodge degree where the star is situated.
Here we are told how to use the data given in section 2.2.3 to find the position of 
the planet on any given day after its appearance, by sampling adding up the total 
motion during the different phases to date.

The Triple Concordance system 109
Proc. 2.26. To predict the location of the Year:
§202 Set out [years] from the High Origin, with the year sought outside. Cast 
out what fills Year Number [for Jupiter] [1728 = 12 × 144]. What does 
not fill, multiply it by 145. Take 144 as the factor. Obtain 1 for each accord 
with the factor. That is called Accumulated Stations. What does not fill is 
called Stations Remainder. If Accumulated Stations fills 12, cast it out. 
What does not fill is called True Stations. Count off this number from [the 
station] Xingji.1, and outside the exhausted count, then that is the station 
where it is. If you wish to know the ‘Grand Year’ Tai sui, cast out 60 from 
the stations, and with the remainder that does not fill, count off starting 
from bingzi.13.
As we have seen in the Introduction to this system, the High Origin for the Triple 
Concordance is 143,127 years (31 periods of Origin Years [4617]) before the winter 
solstice of 105 
bce, which preceded the civil year of 104 bce when the Grand Incep-
tion was inaugurated.
The stations, ci 次, referred to here are 12 equal divisions of the circuit of the heav-
ens, which are defined with reference to the 28 lodges in part G below. In pre-
imperial times, the expectation was that Jupiter would move through one station 
each year – hence its name sui xing 歲星 ‘The Year Star’ – and thus traverse 144 
stations in 144 years.
The name of the station in which Jupiter was located also served to locate a 
given year in a 12-year cycle. An equivalent chronological function was served 
by the so-called Grand Year, a marker which moves through the 12 celestial 
branches (often called the 12 chen 辰 ‘markpoints’ in this context) in the normal 
sequence zi 子, chou 丑 and so on. Since the annual west to east displacement 
of Jupiter in the heavens is opposite to the normal east to west labelling of 
the stations in terms of the branches, the ‘Grand Year’ is often referred to by 
Western scholars as ‘counter-Jupiter’: see for instance (Needham, Joseph and 
Wang Ling 1959: 402–403). We may also find ‘Grand Year’ interpreted as in 
the present instance, where it refers to the number of a year in the full ganzhi 
sexagenary form.
In this section, Liu Xin revises the traditional scheme, using data based on those 
given in section § 105, which imply that Jupiter moves through 145 stations in 
144 years. This motion through one extra station in that period was referred to 
by some later writers as chao ci 超次 ‘skipping a station’ (see below). In modern 
terms, we may say that the older scheme implied that the sidereal period of Jupi -
ter (the time taken for it to make a complete circuit of the heavens) was 12 years, 
whereas Liu Xin’s change was equivalent to making the sidereal period 11.92 years 
(to 4 significant figures), somewhat closer to the modern value of 11.87 years. Liu 
Xin’s revision of the annual rate at which Jupiter moved against the background 
of the stars was not in itself problematic. Later astronomical systems made further

110 The Triple Concordance system
changes – the Han Quarter Remainder system used data for Jupiter implying a 
sidereal period very close to the modern value.
The situation is made more complex for Liu Xin by the fact that he preserves the 
strict correspondence between the planet Jupiter’s movement through the 12 sta-
tions and the movement of the chronological marker which was the ‘Grand Year’. 
Thus in the same way that Jupiter will ‘skip a station’, every 144 years, the Grand 
Year will ‘skip a markpoint’ chao chen 超辰, and the sexagenary year number will 
jump forward by one. This is a major complicating factor in chronological reckon-
ing, affecting the sexagenary cycle of years as well as the Grand Year. It thus leads 
to a discrepancy between Liu Xin’s year-names and those in the system used from 
the Eastern Han onwards, which form a continuous sequence during all subse -
quent years unbroken by ‘skipping’, and were also projected back into the past 
for purposes of historical reference.
Suppose, for example, that High Origin is a bingzi.13 year as Liu Xin tells us. If we 
want to know the sexagenary year number of the year civil year corresponding 
to 104 
bce, which followed the winter solstice of 105 bce, then we know that the 
‘[years] from the High Origin, with the year sought outside’ are 143,127.
Following the procedure set out in the text, we cast out whole multiples of Jupiter 
Year Number [1728], which is number of years in which 12 station skips take place, 
amounting to a complete circuit, since 1728 = 12 × 144
So 143,127 = 1728 × 82 + 1431
Proceeding as specified:
1431 × 145 = 207,495
and 207,495 = 1440 × 144 + 135
So Accumulated Stations is 1440. Casting out 12, we get zero, since
1440 = 120 × 12.
So the station is simply Xingji.1, as at High Origin.
Casting out 60, we find
1440 = 60 × 24, so the sexagenary year number is bingzi.13, as at High Origin.
However, according to the continuous sequence of numbering used in the East -
ern Han and thereafter, the sexagenary year number of the civil year beginning 
in 104 
bce is not bingzi.13, but dingchou.14. This discrepancy is a result of Liu Xin’s 
‘station-skipping’ procedure.
There are however only a few years after the adoption of the Grand Inception 
reform in 104 bce for which this a problem. The discrepancy of one step in the cycle 
continues up to and including 96 bce, which Liu Xin would calculate as jiashen.21, 
and the later system would make yiyou.22. In the next year, 95 bce, Liu Xin’s system 
skips another station, and so both systems make the year bingxu.23. Thereafter
