both systems remain in step for the rest of the Western Han, and were still in step 
in 10 ce, around the time when Liu Xin composed his system; both Liu Xin and 
the later system would have made the sexagenary name of that year gengwu.7. 
Theoretically another station skip should have occurred in 50 ce, 144 years after 
the previous one, so that the systems would therafter have been out of step again. 
But by then it appears that station-skipping was no longer practiced for sexagenary 
year-names. The Grand Inception origin year is stated to have been dingchou.14 in 
debates of the second century 
ce (Chapter 5, § 52, § 59, § 60) making it clear that 
Lu Xin’s practice has been abandoned. Full discussion of relevant chronological 
questions will be found in (Liu Tan 劉坦 1955).
贏縮．傳曰 ： 「歲棄其次而旅於明年之次， 以害鳥帑， 周楚惡之． 」 五星之(盈)
[贏]縮不是過也． 過次者殃大， 過舍者災小， 不過者亡咎． 次度． 六物者,歲時(
數)日月星辰也． 辰者， 日月之會而建所指也．
Proc. 2.27. Excess and shortfall:
§203 The [Zuo] zhuan [Duke Xiang 襄 28th year] says: ‘The Year [star] has 
rejected its station and moved on to the station for the next year, harming 
both the Bird and its Tail [i.e. the kingdoms corresponding to the asterisms 
Phoenix Fire 鶉火and Phoenix Tail 鶉尾], so Zhou and Chu [which cor -
respond to those asterisms] will find it baleful’. The excess or shortfall of 
the Five Stars [sc. Planets] is not a transgression of this kind. If there is 
transgression of a [Jupiter] station, the harm is great; if there is a trans-
gression of a lodge, the disaster is small. If there is no transgression, there 
is no damage: it is just shifting to a different degree. The six things: the 
Year [star], the seasons, the sun, the moon, the stars and the markpoints. 
‘Markpoint’ means where the sun and moon meet, and which is pointed 
to by the Establishment [of the Dipper].
The record that Liu Xin cites from the Zuo zhuan refers to the year 545 bce, and 
is clearly intended to show that ‘station-skipping’ was recognised well before his 
own day. He goes on to explain that the appearance of Jupiter in the wrong station 
(‘transgression’ guo 過) is much more serious omen than the lesser discrepancy 
of positions involved in a shift from one lodge to a neighbouring lodge, which he 
terms ‘excess or shortfall’. As the commentators on the Zuo zhuan passage note, 
according to the Triple Concordance system, in 545 
bce Jupiter should have been in 
station number 1, xingji 星紀 ‘Star Marker’ so the implication is that it had moved 
on to station number 2, xuan xiao 玄枵 ‘Dark Hollow’. The ‘Bird’ and the ‘Tail’ are 
explained as referring to two stations (number 8 and 9) which are more or less 
opposite to the two Jupiter stations mentioned, and hence are open to baleful 
influence from their direction. In fact according to modern calculations Jupiter was 
close to the lodge Heart that year, which is in station 11, da huo 大火 ‘Great Fire’. See 
(Ruan Yuan 阮元 1973 reprint of original of 1815: Zuo zhuan, 38, 23b, page 653A).

112 The Triple Concordance system
The mention of the ‘Establishment’ jian 建 refers to the concept of the dou jian  
斗建 ‘Dipper Establishment’. This is a schematic view based on the fact that if we 
look at the Northern Dipper (Ursa Major) at the same time of night throughout a 
year, the end of its ‘handle’ (δ  to η Uma) will rotate by about 30° each month, 
so that it points in directions which are taken as indicating the positions of the 12 
branches round the horizon. Thus, in the last few centuries 
bce the handle would 
be pointing straight down at the horizon in the late evening around the winter 
solstice – and thus indicating the point on the horizon corresponding to the 
branch (or ‘markpoint’, chen 辰), which is number 1, zi 子 lying due north. This is 
therefore the ‘markpoint’ corresponding to the first Celestial month, which does 
of course begin with a conjunction (‘meeting’) of the sun and moon. The next 
month at the same time of night the handle will have rotated about 30° anticlock-
wise, so that the direction on the horizon indicated by the handle approximates 
to the position of markpoint number 2, chou 丑, 30° to the east of north, and so 
on month by month. This highly schematic view clearly has only a rough cor -
respondence to reality, and is probably derived from the diviners’ devices known 
as shi 栻 ‘[cosmic] models’, which show the heavens as a flat disk bearing the 
Dipper, rotating above a flat square earth: see (Cullen, Christopher 1981). The 
scheme is fully elaborated in the Huai nan zi 淮南子 book, completed by 139 
bce: 
see (Huai nan hong lie ji jie 3, 110–112) and (Major, John S., with an appendix by 
Christopher Cullen 1993: 106–108).

112 The Triple Concordance system
The mention of the ‘Establishment’ jian 建 refers to the concept of the dou jian 
斗建 ‘Dipper Establishment’. This is a schematic view based on the fact that if we 
look at the Northern Dipper (Ursa Major) at the same time of night throughout a 
year, the end of its ‘handle’ (δ to η Uma) will rotate by about 30° each month, 
so that it points in directions which are taken as indicating the positions of the 12 
branches round the horizon. Thus, in the last few centuries 
bce the handle would 
be pointing straight down at the horizon in the late evening around the winter 
solstice – and thus indicating the point on the horizon corresponding to the 
branch (or ‘markpoint’, chen 辰), which is number 1, zi 子 lying due north. This is 
therefore the ‘markpoint’ corresponding to the first Celestial month, which does 
of course begin with a conjunction (‘meeting’) of the sun and moon. The next 
month at the same time of night the handle will have rotated about 30° anticlockwise, so that the direction on the horizon indicated by the handle approximates 
to the position of markpoint number 2, chou 丑, 30° to the east of north, and so 
on month by month. This highly schematic view clearly has only a rough cor -
respondence to reality, and is probably derived from the diviners’ devices known 
as shi 栻 ‘[cosmic] models’, which show the heavens as a flat disk bearing the 
Dipper, rotating above a flat square earth: see (Cullen, Christopher 1981). The 
scheme is fully elaborated in the Huai nan zi 淮南子 book, completed by 139 
bce: 
see (Huai nan hong lie ji jie 3, 110–112) and (Major, John S., with an appendix by 
Christopher Cullen 1993: 106–108).

120 The Triple Concordance system
2.2.9 [The Nine Roads]
九章歲為百七十一歲， 而九道小終． 九終千五百三十九歲而大終． 三終而與
元終九會．31
§263 The Nine Roads [reach their] Lesser Conclusion in 9 Rule Years [19], 
making 171 years. [They reach their] Greater Conclusion in Nine [Lesser] 
Conclusions, [making] 1539 years. 3 [Greater] Conclusions conclude with 
Origin [Years [4617]], making 9 Coincidences.
Exactly what any given Han dynasty author means by the ‘Nine Roads’ is not 
always clear. In the next section Liu Xin tells us that the Nine Roads relate to the 
sun. From the references to ‘Coincidences’, which are the periods over which lunar 
eclipses repeat, it seems that there might be some link with eclipses.
171 years = 9 × 19 years as stated, and three of these Lesser Conclusions do indeed 
make 1539 years, a Concordance, which is presumably the Greater Conclusion. Three 
of these make Origin Years [4617]. Coincidence Years is not explicitly defined in the 
initial listing, but Coincidence Months [6345] is defined in section § 14, and this is 513 
years, the period during which a pattern of 1081 lunar eclipses is repeated.
9 × 513 = 4617, so the statement above is correct.
The ‘Nine Roads’ may refer to the nine tables that follow shortly below, each of 
which contains 27 Rule Heads; since a Rule has 19 years, each table therefore cov-
ers 27 × 19 = 513 years, which is Coincidence Years, and 9 of these do, as before, 
make an Origin, covering all nine tables.
For Jia Kui on the other hand, a century after Liu Xin, the ‘Nine Roads’ referred to 
the paths followed by the moon during each of the nine years taken for the moon’s 
point of maximum speed (in modern terms the perigee) to make a complete circuit 
of the heavens.
32
陽以九終， 故日有九道． 陰兼而成之， 故月有十九道．陽名成功， 故九會
而終． 四營而成易， 故四歲中餘一，四章而朔餘一， 為篇首， 八十一章而
終一統．
§264 The Yang concludes with 9: thus the Sun has Nine Roads; the  yin joins 
with and completes it; thus the Moon has 19 Roads. The Yang is said to 
be completing and achieving: so it concludes in 9 Coincidences. Four 
processes [of manipulation of the yarrow stalks] form the Changes: so in 
4 years the Medial [Qi] remainder is 1; in four Rule [Years [19]] the

before Led Ox’, which appear to be intruded commentary.
32 See Cullen (forthcoming), chapter 6.

Conjunction Remainder is 1 making a Section Head. In 81 Rule [Years 
[19]] then that concludes 1 Concordance [1539].
In 4 years the change the change in Lesser Remainder of the Winter Solstice is 1, 
since 1 year is
365 + 385/1539 days,
and 4 × 385 = 1540,
so the Lesser Remainder is indeed 1.
In 4 Rule Years [19] = 76 years, then we have 4 × 235 months, and one month 
is 29 + 43/81 days.
4 × 235 × 43 = 499 × 81 + 1, so Lesser Remainder is as specified.
The interest here is clearly a comparison with Quarter-Remainder methods, in 
which 4 Rules is a bu 蔀. Note that Sima Qian calls his bu a jia zi pian 甲子篇.
2.2.10 [Concordances and Rule Heads]
In order to find the sexagenary day of the first month of a given year (and hence 
of all subsequent months), we need to know the sexagenary day on which the 
current Concordance began: see Proc. 2.3. The material that follows is intended 
to make it possible to find that information.
First, let us recall the relationship between the three main periods underlying calen-
drical calculations – the Origin, the Concordance, and the Rule. At the beginning of 
each Origin period (4617 years), winter solstice and conjunction coincide at midnight 
beginning a jiazi.1 day. Each Origin contains three Concordance periods (1539 years). 
At the beginning of each Concordance, winter solstice and conjunction coincide at 
midnight, but not necessarily on a jiazi.1 day. Each Concordance contains 81 Rule 
periods of 19 years. Since 19 solar cycles is precisely equal to 235 lunations, at the 
beginning of each Rule, winter solstice and [mean] luni-solar conjunction coincide as 
at system origin, but not necessarily at midnight, and not necessarily on a jiazi.1 day.
I have arranged the information in the text into nine lists, each consisting of three 
groups of nine cyclical days on each list, making a total of 243 sexagenary days. 
Each sexagenary day is the first day of a Rule, a ‘Rule Head’ zhang shou 章首. The 
first list begins with a Rule Head which is also an Origin Head, yuan shou 元首, as 
well as the Concordance Head, tong shou 統首 of the first of the three Concords in 
this Origin. This is the winter solstice preceding 104 
bce, the first year of the Taichu 
太初 ‘Grand Inception’ reign period.
The second list begins with the second Rule Head in the Origin, and so on until we 
reach the ninth list, which begins with the Ninth Rule Head.
Returning to the first list, the next Rule Head below the first is the 10th, which 
begins 9 × 19 = 171 years later, followed by the 19th, and so on, until we have the 
first group of 9 rule heads at the same interval, ending with Rule Head number 73.

122 The Triple Concordance system
The next Concordance begins with Rule Head 82 in the first list, at the head of the 
next group of nine Rule Heads in that list, next to which is marked er tong 二統 
‘2nd Concordance’. It concludes with Rule Head 162 in the ninth list.
The third Concordance begins with Rule Head 163 at the head of the last group 
of 9 Rule Head in the first list, and is marked san tong 三統 ‘3rd Concordance’. It 
concludes with Rule Head 243 in the ninth list.
The total of 243 Rule Heads in the nine lists contain 243 × 19 = 4617 years, an Origin.
In each list, the three groups of nine Rule Heads belonging to each concordance are 
labeled at their end with the characters zhong 中, ji 季 and meng 孟 respectively. These 
characters are also associated with the three months of a season, taken in the order 
meng, zhong, ji. The rationale for the usage in this case is not clear. In this connec-
tion, it is noteworthy that several commentators feel that the current way the data 
are listed in the text may not be the original layout.
33 However, the usage of meng 孟 
by Liu Xin himself suggests that the terms in the present text are correctly positioned: 
see footnote 99. In Proc. 2.1, the three Concordances were labelled Celestial tian 天, 
Terrestrial di 地, and Anthropic ren 人, which parallels the three different first months 
of the year, corresponding to the 11th, 12th and 1st Xia count months respectively.
A number of the Rule Heads are annotated with various important historical dates 
that happened to fall at that Rule Head in whatever Origin they were situated.
I have arranged the information in the text into tabular form to help the modern 
reader grasp how it is structured. However, the arrangement in pre-modern ver -

from the Wu ying dian edition of 1739.

The Triple Concordance system 133
 §265 Set out the Greater Remainder 39, and a Lesser Remainder 61; count off 
and cast out according to the method, in each case starting out from the 
Concordance Head. To seek the next Rule, it is appropriate to add to the 
Greater Remainder 39, and to the Lesser Remainder 61, in each case 
exhausting the 81 Rules [that make up a Concordance]. 
  Days/lunation = Lunation Factor [2392]/Day factor [81]. So the days in one Rule 
of 235 lunations are: 235 × 2392/81 = 6939 remainder 61. And since 6939 mod 
60 = 39, it is clear that to go from conditions at one Rule Head to the next we 
simply add 39 to the Greater Remainder and 61 to the Lesser Remainder as stated.  
 推篇， 大餘亦如之， 小餘加一． 求周至，加大餘五十九， 小餘二十一． 
 Proc. 2.31. To predict the Section: 
 §266 The Greater Remainder is similar to it, and to the Lesser Remainder add 
1. To seek Circuits Culmination, add to the Greater Remainder 59, the 
Lesser Remainder 21. 
  If (as seems to be the case) a Section is four Rules, then since the days in four Rules 
are:  
  4 × 235 × 2392/81 = 27,759 + 1/81, and  
  27,759 = 462 × 60 + 39,  
  one adds 39 to the Greater Remainder as in the previous section, and 1 to the 
Lesser Remainder.  
  Circuits Culmination 57 is three Rules (see section § 21), and thus contains  
  3 × 235 × 2392/81 days = 346 × 60 + 59 + 21/81 days  
  so one adds 59 to the Greater Remainder and 21 to the Lesser Remainder, as speci-
ﬁ ed here.  
 2.2.11 Appendix 1: intercalations in theory and practice 
 The method described in the main text (see Proc. 2.4) for locating an intercalary 
month essentially deﬁ nes a month as intercalary if the lunation to which it corre-
sponds (a period which could not run from midnight to midnight, since it is not a 
whole number of days) does not contain the instant of a medial  qi . The calculation 
makes use of the concept of ‘intercalation surplus’. 
 However it seems that the actual method used in practice for locating interca-
lations was slightly different. Instead, a month was taken to be intercalary if the 
instant of a medial  qi  was not located in the whole days making up the month – a 
period slightly different from the lunation. If the medial  qi  fell close to the end 
of a month, then different results might be produced, since the lunation might be 
over while the month continued for several hours. The  qi  might therefore still fall 
within the month, while falling outside the lunation.

3.1 INTRODUCTION
3.1.1 The system and its backgr ound
The system described here is often simply referred to as the ‘Quarter Remainder’ (or 
more literally ‘Fourth Part’) system, Si fen li 四分曆. However, the usage preferred 
in this book is ‘Han Quarter Remainder’ system, Han si fen li 漢四分曆, which is 
the term used by Li Rui in his account of this particular system, and which serves to 
identify it uniquely. ‘Quarter Remainder’ without qualification refers to a general type 
of system, of which a number of different examples are known, each of which pro-
duces different results when used to calculate basic calendrical data such as the dates 
of solstices, equinoxes and mean conjunctions of sun and moon. The only essential 
point that such systems have in common is that all of them assume that the interval 
between winter solstices is precisely 365¼ days; additionally, all known systems of 
this type use the equivalence of 235 lunations to 19 solar cycles as a basis for finding 
when intercalary months should be inserted. As already mentioned in C
 hapter 1, it 
seems very likely that all the methods for making calculations relating to calendrical 
astronomy known before 104 
bce were based on the ‘Quarter Remainder’ datum.
The Han Quarter Remainder system was officially adopted in 85 ce, but the 
impulse that led to its creation was given decades earlier. I summarise here the 
account set out in Hou Han shu, zhi 2, translated in Chapter 5 of this book.
In 32 
ce, less than a decade after the beginning of Eastern Han, two high offi -
cials memorialised that the Triple Concordance system, created by Liu Xin on the 
basis of the fundamental data fixed by the Grand Inception system in 104 
bce, was 
predicting conjunctions of sun and moon markedly later than what was actually 
observed, so that the moon’s first crescent might actually be visible on the first 
day of the lunar month marked in the civil calendar – something which ought 
never to occur. But with the dynasty still engaged in re-establishing its power 
base, the emperor felt there was no time to attend to such matters ( Hou Han shu, 
zhi 2, 3025). In 62 
ce, the lunar eclipse predicted by the Triple Concordance for 
September 8 in fact fell on the preceding day, and the attention this drew led to a 
year-long programme of observation, as a result of which it was eventually decided 
in late 69 
ce that calculations of crescents and full moon dates should be made 
using methods based on Quarter Remainder methods. But as yet no new system 
The Han Quarter  
Remainder system
Han si fen li 漢四分曆

The Han Quarter Remainder system  139
was introduced, in part we are told because it was not yet possible to decide on 
a system origin li yuan 曆元 to replace that used by the Triple Concordance. So 
the dates when lunar months began and ended were calculated as before (ibid.).
Finally, in 85 ce, the obvious mismatch between the heavens and the system in 
use – by then seen to be about ¾ day – was finally confronted. It was also noted that 
the predicted seasonal positions of the sun amongst the stars were five du ahead 
of its actual positions. Order were given to Bian Xin 編訢 and Li Fan 李梵, two 
experts in li, to look into the matter and make proposals for reform. On March 18 
of that year, the emperor issued an edict commanding that their proposals should 
be put into effect, and the Triple Concordance was abandoned in favour of the Han 
Quarter Remainder system (Hou Han shu, zhi 2, 3026).
3.1.2 Authorship of the text
As noted below, the text translated here comes from the third of the monographs 
originally written by Sima Biao 司馬彪 (c. 240–c. 306 
ce), and later incorporated 
in the Hou Han shu . From Sima Biao’s note at the end of this monograph, it is 
clear that the description of the Han Quarter Remainder system we have now was 
authored, or at least edited, near the end of the Eastern Han:
光和元年中， 議郎蔡邕、 郎中劉洪補續律曆志， 邕能著文， 清濁鍾律， 洪
能為筭， 述敘三光． 今考論其業， 義指博通， 術數略舉， 是以集錄為上下
篇， 放續前志， 以備一家．
In the first year of the Guanghe period [178 
ce], the Gentleman for Consulta-
tion Cai Yong, and the Palace Gentleman Liu Hong expanded and extended 
the Monograph on the Pitchpipes and [Astronomical] System. Yong was able 
in setting out writings, and in the tuning of bells and pitchpipes, while Hong 
was able in calculations, and in giving an ordered account of the Three Lumi-
naries. Now I have examined and evaluated their work: its ideas are broad and 
general, and [the details of ] numerical procedures are succinct and complete. 
Therefore I have collected their records into a first and second chapter, and 
have let them serve as a continuation of the Former Treatise, in order to make 
up a complete body of doctrine.
(Hou Han shu, zhi 3, 3082)
The ‘second chapter’ referred to is the second monograph of the Hou Han shu  
(translated in Chapter 5), and the ‘Former Treatise’ is the monograph on harmon-
ics and the astronomical system made up of chapters 21a and 21b in the Han shu. 
What we have here is therefore not merely the guide to calculation methods that 
was presumably compiled by Bian Xin and Li Fan c. 85 
ce, but also contains reflec-
tions on the system by two great experts writing a century later. One of them, Liu 
Hong, was the creator of the Uranic Manifestation system that is the third of the 
systems to be translated in this book. All this goes a long way to explain some of 
the more discursive features of the text before us, and naturally increases its value 
as a historical source considerably.

140 The Han Quarter Remainder system 
3.1.3 Structur e of the system
This is essentially as already outlined in the account given of quarter-remainder 
type systems in Chapter 1. As mentioned there, a significant departure from pre-
vious practice is that the Han Quarter Remainder shows clear recognition of the 
distinction between the celestial equator and the ecliptic.
3.1.4 Organisation of the text
Unlike the specification of the Triple Concordance system in the Han shu, the divi-
sions of the text, though evident by their content, are not generally marked by any 
kind of heading. The opening section of the text is preceded by the heading 
li fa 曆
法 ‘Methods for [astronomical] systems’, but it is possible that this heading is really 
intended to label the whole text. This long section contains material of a type not 
found in close association with other early system descriptions. It reflects explicitly 
on the basis and significance of astronomical systems, and explains to some extent 
at least how some of the basic parameters of the system are derived from observa-
tion. We can see clearly the influence of Cai Yong and Liu Hong in all this.
Next comes a section in which we are given a list of 17 constants relating to the 
cycles of the sun and the moon; these will form the basis of future calculations. 
There follows a paragraph on the subject of the cycles by which lunar eclipses may 
be predicted, with a list of relevant constants.
The next section gives the core procedures of the system, which specify how in 
any given year one may calculate all basic calendrical data, such as the cyclical 
days on which months begin, and the location of any intercalary months, together 
with the dates of the 24 qi which divide the interval between winter solstices into 
equal parts. We learn how to find the location of the sun and moon with reference 
to the system of 28 lodges on any date and at different times of day, and how to 
predict lunar eclipses.
Three sections then follow on the topic of planetary motions. First, we are given 
the basic constants underlying the motion of each planet, then told how to use them 
to calculate when each planet will be in conjunction with the sun. Finally we are 
given for each planet a kind of ‘motion template’ dividing up the movement of 
the planet from one conjunction to the next into subdivisions, and specifying the 
daily motion of the planet for each subdivision, ending with a short note on how 
the data from this ‘template’ may be used to calculate from day to day where the 
planet is in relation to the system of 28 lodges.
Next follow three tables. The first lists the months of the year, giving for each 
the name of the odd-numbered qi (medial qi, zhong qi  中氣) which should be 
found in that month if intercalations are properly carried out. The second table lists 
the 28 lodges, with their widths in du with reference to the celestial equator, and 
the third lists lodge widths with reference to the ecliptic. The first table includes 
‘advance and retardation numbers’ intended to be used for conversion from one 
reference system to the other.

The Han Quarter Remainder system  141
The final substantive section of the text specifies how to calculate which stars 
will be seen on the meridian at dawn and dusk at any time of the year. This is 
accompanied by a tabulation of data for each of the 24 qi into which the solar 
cycle is divided, including the position of the sun in the lodge system, the noon 
shadow of a standard gnomon, the north polar distance of the sun, the duration of 
light and darkness, and the stars ‘centred’ on the observer’s meridian at dusk and 
dawn.
[^1] Then the System Origin is specified, and the text closes with a historical 
discussion, recounting innovations in astronomical systems from High Antiquity 
up to the adoption of the current system, and reviewing the source materials on 
which the account given in this text is based.
3.1.5 Methods of calculation
These follow the basic principles outlined in Chapter 1. One feature that marks this 
system out from the other two translated in this book is the fact that it sometimes gives 
more than one method for achieving the same result, the second being introduced by 
the phrase yi shu 一術, literally ‘one method’. Once more, the impression is given that 
the text is not intended simply as a practical set of instructions to produce a calendar, 
but also has a more discursive purpose, reflecting the interests of its authors and editors.
3.1.6 T ext used
The following text follows the version in Hou Han shu 後漢書 (History of Eastern 
Han dynasty), Fan Ye 范曄 (398–445 ce), Zhonghua, Beijing: punctuated edition 
of 1963. Page numbers given thus ‘– 991 –’ follow that edition. Fan Ye’s main 
text was completed near the end of his life. However, the monographs found in 
the present edition were added later, using material from an earlier and now lost 
work by Sima Biao 司馬彪 (c. 240–c. 306 
ce).[^2]

142 The Han Quarter Remainder system 
3.2.1 Methods for  [astronomical] systems
昔者聖人之作曆也， 觀琁璣之運， 三光之行， 道之發斂， 景之長短， 斗綱 
(之)[所]建， 青龍所躔， 參伍以變， 錯綜其數， 而制術焉．
§1 When in former times the sages created [astronomical] systems, they watched 
the turning of the xuan ji, the motions of the Three Luminaries, the expansion 
and contraction of the Roads, the growing and shrinking of the shadow, the 
establishment of the Dipper mainstay, and the orbit of the Caerulean Dragon. 
The Three [Luminaries] and the Five [Planets] changed [their positions], and 
they wove together the numbers, so that they were able to make them into 
methods [for calculation].
This introduction underlines a radical difference of approach between its 
authors and Liu Xin, creator of the Triple Concordance system. Whereas he 
claimed to have derived the constants of his system from cosmological con-
siderations, this system claims that its basic data are drawn from observation. 
This approach, it is claimed, represents a return to the practice of the ancient 
sages who created human culture in the mythical past. Some of the terms 
used here require a little explanation. ‘ Xuan ji’ refers to the pole star of the 
Han period, β Ursae minoris; the changing meanings of this term are discussed 
in (Cullen, Christopher and Farrer, Anne S. L. 1983); the ‘Three Luminaries’ 
are the sun, moon and stars; the ‘Roads’ are the paths of the sun and moon; 
the ‘Establishment of the Dipper’ refers to the changing directions indicated 
by the handle of the Dipper when first seen at dusk in successive months (see 
section § 3); the ‘Caerulean Dragon’, which more usually refers to one of the 
four creatures associated with groups of constellations correlated with the four 
directions here refers to the sexagenary name of the year (see sections § 5 
and § 18).
天之動也， 一晝一夜而運過周， 星從天而西， 日違天而東． 日之所行與運周， 在
天成度， 在曆成日． 居以列宿， 終于四七， 受以甲乙， 終于六旬．
§2 In the movement of Heaven, the turning in one day and night is more than 
a circuit. The stars follow Heaven in moving westwards, while the sun goes 
against Heaven in moving eastwards. The motion of the sun and its turning 
round its circuit forms the du in Heaven and the days in the system. It dwells 
in the ordered lodges, which terminate in four sevens; it is received in the 
cyclical signs, which terminate in six decades.
The expression ‘one day and night’ refers to a complete solar day, in which the sun 
returns to the same position relative to the observer. If we count from the moment 
of noon, this is the interval between two instants when the sun is on the meridian

The Three [Luminaries] and the Five [Planets] changed [their positions], and 
they wove together the numbers, so that they were able to make them into 
methods [for calculation].
This introduction underlines a radical difference of approach between its 
authors and Liu Xin, creator of the Triple Concordance system. Whereas he 
claimed to have derived the constants of his system from cosmological considerations, this system claims that its basic data are drawn from observation. 
This approach, it is claimed, represents a return to the practice of the ancient 
sages who created human culture in the mythical past. Some of the terms 
used here require a little explanation. ‘ Xuan ji’ refers to the pole star of the 
Han period, β Ursae minoris; the changing meanings of this term are discussed 
in (Cullen, Christopher and Farrer, Anne S. L. 1983); the ‘Three Luminaries’ 
are the sun, moon and stars; the ‘Roads’ are the paths of the sun and moon; 
the ‘Establishment of the Dipper’ refers to the changing directions indicated 
by the handle of the Dipper when first seen at dusk in successive months (see 
section § 3); the ‘Caerulean Dragon’, which more usually refers to one of the 
four creatures associated with groups of constellations correlated with the four 
directions here refers to the sexagenary name of the year (see sections § 5 
and § 18).

天成度， 在曆成日． 居以列宿， 終于四七， 受以甲乙， 終于六旬．
§2 In the movement of Heaven, the turning in one day and night is more than 
a circuit. The stars follow Heaven in moving westwards, while the sun goes 
against Heaven in moving eastwards. The motion of the sun and its turning 
round its circuit forms the du in Heaven and the days in the system. It dwells 
in the ordered lodges, which terminate in four sevens; it is received in the 
cyclical signs, which terminate in six decades.
The expression ‘one day and night’ refers to a complete solar day, in which the sun 
returns to the same position relative to the observer. If we count from the moment 
of noon, this is the interval between two instants when the sun is on the meridian

due south of the observer. If we count from the moment of midnight, the sun is 
still crossing the meridian line, but below the horizon in the north.
The statement that ‘the turning in one day and night is more than a circuit’ 
refers to the fact that since the sun is moving from west to east against the 
background of the celestial sphere with the fixed stars (which turns from east to 
west), it follows that from one noon to the next (or one midnight to the next), 
since the sun has returned to the same position relative to the observe, the 
celestial sphere has turned a full revolution, plus the sun’s daily motion, which 
is in fact 1 du.

§3 ‘The sun and moon push one another on’. The sun is slow and the moon 
is fast. When they share a position, that is called a conjunction. The slow 
[i.e. the sun] is ahead and the fast [i.e. the moon] is behind. When they 
are one part near and three parts distant, that is called a crescent. When 
they are opposite one another, so that they divide Heaven down the middle, 
that is called opposition. When the fast reaches the slow, so that its bril -
liance is exhausted and its form is hidden, that is called darkening [as on 
the last day of a lunar month]. When darkening and conjunction have 
joined and separated, and the Dipper Establishment shifts by a sign, that 
is called a month.
The first sentence refers to the Book of Change, which contains the following 
passage:
日往則月來， 月往則日來， 日月相推而明生焉.

§4 Through the motion of the sun and moon, there is winter and there is sum -
mer. Between winter and summer, there is spring and there is autumn. Thus 
when the sun moves through the northern regions, that is called winter; 
through the western regions it is called spring; through the southern regions 
it is called summer, and through the eastern regions it is called autumn. 
When the sun’s path extends out southwards, it goes ever further from the 
pole, and the shadow becomes ever longer, and when distance and length 
reach their extreme, then winter culminates there. When the sun’s path draws 
in towards the north, it goes ever closer to the pole, and the shadow is ever 
shorter, and when nearness and shortness reach their extreme, then summer 
culminates there. Between the two extremes [sc. ‘solstices’], the path is even 
and the shadow is true, and spring and autumn are divided there.
The ‘regions’ through which the sun moves are the four quarters of the heavenly 
sphere corresponding to its position during the four seasons. The labelling as 
‘north’ and so forth in the third sentence is conventional rather than directional. 
The meaning becomes literal in the rest of the section, where it is stated that 
when the sun is at its northernmost the season is summer, and when it is at its 
southernmost the seasons is winter.
– 3056 –
日周于天， 一寒一暑， 四時備成， 萬物畢改， 攝提遷次， 青龍移辰， 謂之歲．歲
首至也， 月首朔也． 至朔同日謂之章， 同在日首謂之蔀， 蔀終六旬謂之紀，歲
朔又復謂之元． 是故日以實之， 月以閏之， 時以分之，歲以周之， 章以明之，
蔀以部之， 紀以記之， 元以原之． 然後雖有變化萬殊， 贏朒無方， 莫不結系于
此而稟正焉．
§5 The sun circuits round Heaven: there is one cold and one heat, the four 
seasons are all complete, the myriad creatures are all changed, the sheti [i.e. 
the 12 cyclical characters referring to years] shift their station, and the Cae -
rulean Dragon [i.e. the sexagenary name of the year] moves its mark-point. 
This is called a sui. The head of the sui is the [winter] solstice, and the head 
of the yue is the conjunction. When the solstice and the conjunction fall on 
the same day, that is called a Rule [Head].When this takes place at the head 
of a day [i.e. midnight], this is called an Obscuration [Head]. When an 
Obscuration has terminated the six decades, that is called an Era [Head]. 
When the sui and the conjunction both return, that is called an Origin [Head]. 
So for the day one fills it, for the yue one intercalates it, for the season one 
divides it, for the sui one circuits it, for the Rule one illuminates it, for the 
Obscuration one sections it, for the Era one records it, and for the Origin 
one traces it to the source. Only when this is done, then even if there are 
transformations and a myriad variations, and expansions and contraction

without limitation, then there is nothing that is not bound up with these and 
are endowed and rectified by them.
I have deliberately refrained from providing a translation of the term ‘ sui’ 歲 and 
‘yue’ 月 in this section, which illustrates rather well the double reference involved 
in the use of these words, as was discussed in Chapt er 1. In its first occurrence ‘sui’ 
evidently refers to the calendrical unit that we may call the civil year, normally 
consisting of 12 whole months of either 29 or 30 whole days each. However, we 
are next told that the ‘sui’ starts at winter solstice – which is by no means always 
the case for the civil year, so that the reference is clearly to what I have chosen to 
call the ‘solar cycle’. As already explained, in the period covered by this book it was 
assumed that the winter solstice was at a fixed position relative to the stars, so that 
(in modern terms) the tropical and sidereal years were equal. Similar considerations 
apply to the choice between the translations ‘month’ and ‘lunation’ for yue 月.
The other periods mentioned are explained below: see section § 18. Their durations 
are:
Rule: 19 years
Obscuration: 76 years
Era: 1520 years
Origin: 4560 years
The sentence beginning ‘So for the day one fills it .  . .’ cont ains a number of 
plays on words, sometimes involving assonance.

the drips go down and counts the divisions, and by examining the centred 
stars, dusk and dawn are created.

sel’  is a simple outflow clepsydra, with the aid of which we are to time the

the particular], and on coming across some [category] 5 one expands it’; ‘one 
seeks out the profound and draws forth the obscure, hooks out the deep and 
brings near the distant’, so that there is nothing that is recondite or hidden, 
whatever its subtlety may be. So Yin and Yang have their division, cold and 
heat have their regularities, ‘Heaven and Earth are made authentically manifest, 
and the Sun and Moon are made authentically brilliant.’

§10 It was Chongli [= Zhuanxu 顓頊, grandson of the Yellow Emperor] who 
was the first to bestow his august patronage on these methods, inaugurate 
this heritage and make the Heavenly brilliance pure and radiant. It was Xi 
and He who played a glorious part in taking up the Sage Lord’s command 
to accord with august Heaven, to set up canons, sequences and counterparts 
for the Three Markers [the sun, moon and stars], in order to grant their 
tasks to the people, setting up intercalations to correct the seasons, and thus 
completing the year’s accomplishments. It was [King] Tang and [King] Wu

who achieved complete success in taking Metal and Fire as their counterparts,[^6] 
changing the Mandate and creating ordinances, regulating the calendar and 
making clear the seasons, being responsive to Heaven and making the people 
amenable. But then it came to the time of decay of kingly virtue, when 
above there was disorder by rulers who lacked the Way, and below stupid 
Clerks lost [the thread]. In the time of Xiahou [sc. the Xia dynasty], the Xi 
and He officials were debauched by wine, abandoning the seasons and 
disordering the days, whereupon [the marquis of] Yin proceeded against 
them. Tchou
7 [last Ruler of the Shang dynasty] was debauched and tyran -
nous, abandoning the sexagenary sequence of days, and King Wu punished 
him. For one who is able to clarify these matters authentically, their rise is 
swift; for those who turn back and do harm, their fall is sudden. How great 
it is, like telling of the sustaining cords of Heaven and Earth, and the solid 
work of Lords and Kings. Thus the Sage treasures these things, and the 
Gentlemen exerts his diligence therein.
The basis element of this story, which takes us from mythical rulers of High 
Antiquity down to the undoubtedly historical early kings of the Zhou dynasty 
c. 1 046  bce, are repeated in a number of accounts such as the present one. See 
also the material from the Han shu translated in Chap ter 5. The point being made 
is that good and effective rulers ensure that effective astronomical systems are 
adopted.
夫曆有聖人之德六焉：以本氣者尚其體， 以綜數者尚其文， 以考類者尚其
象， 以作事者尚其時， 以占往者尚其源， 以知來者尚其流．
§11 There are six ways in which the virtue of the Sage is contained in an 
[astronomical] system. By taking the qi as basic, it exalts the form [of 
Heaven]. By threading together the numbers, it exalts the patterns [of 
Heaven]. By examining the categories, it exalts the counterparts [of Heaven]. 
By carrying out its task, it exalts the seasons [of Heaven]. By divining from 
what is past, it exalts the source, [which is Heaven]. By knowing what is 
to come, it exalts the onwards movement [of Heaven].

§13 The twenty-first du of Dipper is [the position of the Sun when it is at] the 
maximum distance from the pole. When the sun is situated there it is the 
winter solstice: that is the time when all things begin to be produced. Thus

from winter solstice, the months give precedence to the establishment zi

and time of day is made even with midnight.

At the winter solstice of the ancient Yellow Emperor, Xia, Yin, Zhou and Lu 
systems,[^9] the sun is at the Establishment Star, and the Establishment Star is 
our modern Dipper Star.
(Hou Han shu, zhi 2, 3027)

§15 In the process of producing the numbers of the astronomical system, one 
sets up [armillary] instruments and gnomons,[^10] in order to compare the solar 
shadows. When the shadow is longest the sun is most distant; this is the 
starting point for the degrees of heaven. The sun sets out from that starting 
point, and makes a sui when it has circuited. However the shadow does not 
return: the shadow returns to its starting point after four circuits, 1461 days, 
and so this represents the termination of the sun’s motion. Casting out 
circuits from the days, one obtains 365 and ¼, which is the number of days 
in a sui. The sun moves one du in a day, so [this figure] is also the du in 
[a circuit of] the heavens.

152 The Han Quarter Remainder system 
it is the termination of lunar motion. Casting out solar circuits from lunar 
circuits, one obtains the number of [lunar] circuits in a solar cycle. Casting 
out one solar circuit from that leaves a remainder of 12  7/19 which is the 
number of times the moon moves through more than a circuit and meets 
the sun, which is the number of lunations in a solar cycle. If [by that quan-
tity] one casts out from the days in a solar cycle, that makes the number 
[of days in] a lunation. When the remainder parts of lunations [in a solar 
cycle] fill the factor, one gets a month, and when a month is formed the 
year is a large one [i.e. with an intercalary month].
This section describes the astronomical basis and implications of the Rule Cycle, 
which will be referred to in section § 18, and is also used in the other two systems 
translated in this book. Since the moon will actually move past the sun 254 − 19 = 
235 times, the implication is that 19 solar cycles are precisely equal in duration to 
235 lunations. Since 235 = 19 in 12 + 7, we must insert seven intercalary lunar 
months in the course of 19 civil years in order to maintain correspondence between 
the months and the seasons.
254/19 = 13 + 
7⁄19, the number of lunar circuits of heaven in a solar cycle.
Thus 12 + 7⁄19 is the number of lunations in a solar cycle.
The number of days in a lunation is:
(365 ¼) (1 2 + 7⁄19) = 29 499⁄940 days
The reference to ‘filling the factor’ works as follows:
One solar cycle = 12 + 
7⁄19 lunations
Two solar cycles = 24 + 14⁄19 lunations
Three solar cycles = 36 + 21⁄19 lunations = 36 + 1 + 2⁄19 lunations
Thus the 3rd civil year must contain an extra month in order to keep in step with 
the solar cycle, since the fractional parts of a month have built up to more that 
19, which is ‘the factor’, more specifically the ‘Rule Factor’; see section § 24.

one sets out the 12 Medial [Qi] in order to fix the places of the months. 
When a conjunction occurs without a Medial [Qi], that makes an intercalary 
month. The start of a Medial [Qi] is called a Nodal [Qi], and together with 
the Medials these make the 24 qi. If by this one casts out from the days of 
one year, that makes the number of days in one qi. If the fractions accumulate to complete one day, that makes an Extinction. If one adds up the 
fractions of the qi of a year, then if these accord with their factor, that

makes one Year Extinction. The Extinction fractions are divided amongst 
the terminating Medials; the Medials are terminated at the winter solstice. 
When the fractions at the winter solstice accumulate to accord with their 
factor, one gets one day, and this is concluded after four years.
We have already met the ‘no medial qi’ rule for intercalation in the Triple Concor-
dance system.
The number of days in one Qi is:
(365 ¼) /2 4 = 15  7⁄32
The meaning and application of the term ‘Extinction’ is made clear in detail in

月分成閏， 閏七而盡， 其歲十九， 名之曰章． 章首分盡， 四之俱終， 名之曰蔀. 
以一歲日乘之， 為蔀之日數也． 以甲子命之， 二十而復其初， 是以二十蔀為
紀 ．紀歲青龍未終， 三終歲後復青龍為元．
§18 The fractions of a lunation complete an intercalation, and these intercalations 
are exhausted after seven. The years are 19, which is called a Rule. When 
the fractions at the head of a Rule are exhausted, and the fours are all 
terminated, this is called an Obscuration. If one multiplies by the days of 
one year, this is the number of days of an Obscuration. If one counts off 
by the sexagenary day name [lit. ‘the jiazi’], it returns to the beginning 
[after] 20. So 20 Obscurations make an Era. In the years of an Era the 
Caerulean Dragon is not yet concluded, so after three completions of [this 
number of] years one returns to the Caerulean Dragon, making an Origin.
In the first two sentences, we are reminded that seven intercalations take place in 
a Rule cycle of 19 years. Since however 19 solar cycles are
365¼ days × 19 = 6939¾ days
we shall have to finish four Rules – an Obscuration, 76 years – before we have 
a whole number of days, and winter solstice and conjunction once more coincide 
at midnight. Since an Obscuration contains 27,759 days, we shall need 20 
Obscurations – an Era, 1520 years – before the days elapsed are a multiple of 60 
and the sexagenary day name repeats. But since 1520 is not a multiple of 60, 
we need three Eras – an Origin, 4560 years – before the sexagenary year number 
returns to system origin conditions. This section makes it plain that the term 
‘Caerulean Dragon’ is being used as a name for the sexagenary year-name. This 
usage can be traced back to the Huai nan zi book in the second century 
bce: see 
(Huai nan hong lie ji jie  3, 125–126) and (Major, John S., with an appendix by 
Christopher Cullen 1993: 133–135).

This is how the figures work out:
The notion of a cycle of 23 lunar eclipses in 135 months predates the Eastern 
Han. The cycle begins with a lunar eclipse at the full moon of the first month 
of the cycle, and the last eclipse falls at the full moon of the 131st month. 
The next lunar eclipse is at full moon of the first month of the next 135-
month cycle.
135/23 = 5 + 20/23, so this is the mean number of months between eclipses – 
although actual eclipses must of course be separated by whole numbers of 
months, since they must fall at full moon.
The mean number of months in a civil year taken over a complete Rule of 19 
years is 235/19.
So the mean number of eclipses per year is given by:
(235/19) / (135/23) = (235 × 23) / (19 × 135)
Dividing top and bottom by 5, we obtain:
(47 × 23) / (19 × 27)
= 1081/513
= 2 + 55/513 which is the mean number of eclipses in one year.
Now an Obscuration is 4 × 19 = 76 years
So in an Obscuration, the number of eclipses is:
(4 × 19) × (47 × 23) / (19 × 27)
= (4 × 47 × 23) / 27
= 4324/27
So in 27 Obscurations there are 4324 eclipses. Note that since there are 940 
months in an Obscuration, 27 Obscurations contains:
27 × 940/135 = 188 cycles of 135 months, each with 23 eclipses in the same 
pattern.
27 Obscurations is 27 × 76 = 27 × 4 × 19 = 2052 years. This is an Obscura -
tion Coincidence.
However 2052 mod 60 = 12, so the sexagenary year number of successive 
Obscuration Coincidences will shift by this amount. Taking 5 Obscuration 
Coincidences would bring return of the sexagenary year number, but the 
result would not yet be a multiple of the Origin Factor (4560). This results 
when we take 4 × 5 = 20 Obscuration Coincidences since:
20 × 2052 = 41,040 = 9 × 4560

Cast out Era Factor [1520] from the remainder. Number from the Heaven

The text seems slightly garbled near the end though it is clear what is intended. 
The proposed emendation by the editors deals with the problem; its length sug -
gests that a scribe may have skipped a column of characters. The further emendation 
of ‘Era’ to ‘Obscuration’ is also helpful.
The aim of this section is to find the sexagenary number (year-name) of the year 
now beginning. We do this by finding the sexagenary number of the first year 
of the current Obscuration, and then counting forward. The requisite data are 
provided in Table 3.1.
First we cast out whole Origins, since all relevant conditions repeat in an 
Origin. Since an Origin is three Eras, we then establish which of the three 
Eras of the current Origin we are in. That tells us which of the three main 
columns (in the modern format – rows in the original) we should be using. 
The columns are named after Heaven, Earth and Man – Celestial, Terrestrial 
and Anthropic. Each column has in its first row the sexagenary number of its 
first year.
Each column has 20 rows, containing the sexagenary numbers of the first year

How does this table work?
We begin in the year designated gengchen.17, whose first day is jiazi.1. This is the 
head of an Origin [4560], an Era [1520], an Obscuration [76] and a Rule [19].
Since 1520 = 25 × 60 + 20, then one Era later the year-name will have increased 
by 20, to become gengzi.37; another Era later it will be gengshen.57. The next 
Era will start again in year gengchen.17.
However, 1520 × 365.25 = 7980 = 133 × 60.
So a whole number of sexagenary day cycles has elapsed from the start of one 
Era to the next, and the day name of the first day of the Rule that begins the 
first Obscuration of each new Era in the sequence is unchanged.
If however we begin from the original starting point, but go forward only one 
Obscuration, 76 years, to the start of the second of the 20 Obscurations that 
make up the initial Era, then since 76 = 60 + 16, the year-name must increase 
by 16 from gengchen.17 to bingshen.33.
Also, since 76 × 365.25 = 462 × 60 + 39, the day name changes from jiazi.1 to 
guimao.40.

Proc. 3.5. To predict the Celestial Standard [Month]:
§46 Set out the years into the Obscuration and subtract one. Multiply by Rule 
Months [235]. Count one for each Rule Factor [19] filled. Call this Accu-
mulated Months. The remainder is the Intercalation Remainder. If it is 12 
or more, this year has an intercalation.
This section and the next aim to predict the sexagenary day name of the first day 
of the first month of the current year according to the Celestial count. We start 
from the beginning of the current Obscuration, at which we are guaranteed that 
midnight, conjunction beginning the first Celestial month and winter solstice coin-
cide. We already know (from Proc. 3.3) the sexagenary day name with which the 
Obscuration begins. Here we aim to find how many whole months have elapsed 
since the start of the Obscuration, and to predict whether the current civil year has 
an intercalary month or not.
The first procedure deals with the fact that ‘years into the obscuration’ 入 蔀 年 
means the ordinal number of year in the Obscuration. Since we want the number 
of years from the start of the Obscuration to the start of the current year, we 
have to subtract one from this number. Then we use the fact that 235 months 
are exactly equivalent to 19 years to find how many whole months have elapsed 
since the start of the Obscuration.
The remainder will be a fraction of a month at a scale of Rule Factor [19]. This 
is the Intercalation Remainder, and may be taken as the pending fraction of a 
new intercalary month representing the amount by which the start of the new 
year is in advance of its ideal date, which should coincide with winter solstice. 
Now since 235/19 is 12 + 7/19, it is clear that by the end of the year we are now 
starting the Intercalation Remainder will have increased by 7. So if at the start 
of the current year this Remainder is 12 or more, the Remainder will at least have 
reached 19 by the end of the year, calling for a delay of a whole month before 
the next year starts – which requires an intercalary month to be inserted in the 
current year, as stated.
The Intercalation Remainder will also be useful in later calculations. In that con -
nection, it should be noted that it can also be explained in connection with the

sequence of Medial Qi, which begins each year with the Winter Solstice. At the 
start of a Rule, winter solstice coincides with the conjunction beginning the 
Celestial First Month. This condition recurs at the beginning of the next Rule 19 
years later, but the conjunction with which the first winter solstice of that Rule 
coincides is seven later than the one that would have been indicated if winter 
solstices were separated by exactly 12 lunations each. So each successive winter 
solstice is 7/19 of a lunation later than its predecessor with respect to its Celestial 
First Month conjunction, and it is the total of this lag that is represented by 
Intercalation Remainder.
推天正朔日，
置入蔀積月， 以蔀日乘之， 滿蔀月得一， 名為積日， 不滿為小餘， 積日以六十
除去之， 其餘為大餘， 以所入蔀名命之， 筭盡之外， 則前年天正十一月朔日
也． 小餘四百四十一以上， 其月大． 求後月朔， 加大餘二十九， 小餘四百九十
[九]， 小餘滿蔀月得一， 上加大餘， 命之如前．
Proc. 3.6. T o predict the day of Celestial Standard Conjunction:
§47 Set out the Accumulated Months into the Obscuration. Multiply by Obscura -
tion Days [27,759]. Count one for each Obscuration Months [940] filled. 
Call that Accumulated Days. The remainder is the Lesser Remainder. Cast 
out 60 from the Accumulated Days. The remainder is the Greater Remainder. 
Count off from the [sexagenary] name of the Obscuration, and outside the 
exhausted count will be the day of Celestial Standard Conjunction in the 
eleventh [civil] month preceding the [civil] year. If the Lesser Remainder is 
441 or greater, the month is long. To find the conjunction day of the next 
month, add 29 to the Greater Remainder, and 499 to the Lesser Remainder. 
Count one each time the Lesser Remainder fills Obscuration Months [940]. 
Take that unit up to the Greater Remainder. Count off as before.
We now use the previous result to find the actual day of the Celestial Standard 
Conjunction, which begins the first Celestial month. First we convert the Accu-
mulated Months into days by using the fact that 27,759 days are precisely equal 
to 940 months. The whole days resulting from this procedure tell us how many 
whole days have elapsed from the midnight commencing the current Obscuration 
up to midnight beginning the current year. Since we are interested in sexagenary 
day names, we can usefully cast out 60 from this amount to form the Greater 
Remainder as specified in order to find the sexagenary day name of the first day 
of the current year.
To take an example: if we are in the second year of the Obscuration, Accumulated 
Months will be 12. Since:
12 × 27,759/940 = 354 remainder 348
and 354 mod 60 = 54

Proc. 3.6. T o predict the day of Celestial Standard Conjunction:
§47 Set out the Accumulated Months into the Obscuration. Multiply by Obscura -
tion Days [27,759]. Count one for each Obscuration Months [940] filled. 
Call that Accumulated Days. The remainder is the Lesser Remainder. Cast 
out 60 from the Accumulated Days. The remainder is the Greater Remainder. 
Count off from the [sexagenary] name of the Obscuration, and outside the 
exhausted count will be the day of Celestial Standard Conjunction in the 
eleventh [civil] month preceding the [civil] year. If the Lesser Remainder is 
441 or greater, the month is long. To find the conjunction day of the next 
month, add 29 to the Greater Remainder, and 499 to the Lesser Remainder. 
Count one each time the Lesser Remainder fills Obscuration Months [940]. 
Take that unit up to the Greater Remainder. Count off as before.
We now use the previous result to find the actual day of the Celestial Standard 
Conjunction, which begins the first Celestial month. First we convert the Accumulated Months into days by using the fact that 27,759 days are precisely equal 
to 940 months. The whole days resulting from this procedure tell us how many 
whole days have elapsed from the midnight commencing the current Obscuration 
up to midnight beginning the current year. Since we are interested in sexagenary 
day names, we can usefully cast out 60 from this amount to form the Greater 
Remainder as specified in order to find the sexagenary day name of the first day 
of the current year.
To take an example: if we are in the second year of the Obscuration, Accumulated 
Months will be 12. Since:
12 × 27,759/940 = 354 remainder 348
and 354 mod 60 = 54

month. [Thus] there may be adjustments back and forth, and these are 
determined by [the position of] the Medial qi.
In Proc. 3.5, it was determined whether the current year contains an intercalary 
month. If there is an intercalary month, this procedure finds where it will come 
in the sequence of months. The key to making this decision is to look for a luna -
tion within which no medial qi is located. That lunation normally corresponds 
to an intercalary month – with, as we shall see, a slight adjustment to allow for 
certain borderline conditions.
We begin by finding Intercalation Remainder, the remainder from:
(Years into Obscuration) × 235/19.
The whole number result of this division is the total number of whole mean 
lunations elapsed from the start of the current Obscuration up to the conjunc -
tion which began the current (Celestial) year, which will include some lunations 
corresponding to intercalations in previous years.
The remainder represents the amount in (1/19) of a mean lunation by which the 
winter solstice near the beginning of this year lags behind the conjunction of the 
first Celestial month, and this increases by (7/19) of a lunation from one winter 
solstice to the next. Now there are 12 medial qi in a year. So the lag between a 
medial qi and its preceding conjunction must increase steadily from medial qi to 
medial qi by
(7/19) / (12) = 7/228 of a mean lunation.
Since we are counting up the increasing lag in units of (1/228) of a mean lunation, 
and the Intercalation Remainder is in (1/19) of a lunation, it is clear that the initial 
multiplication by 12 is needed to convert the Intercalation Remainder to the correct 
scale, since 12 × 19 = 228. When the total lag for a given medial qi builds up to 
greater than 228/228 of a mean lunation, then that medial qi falls after the next mean 
conjunction, and the lunation preceding that medial qi contains no medial qi at all, 
since the previous medial qi fell just before the previous mean conjunction. The month 
corresponding to that lunation is therefore counted as intercalary; it bears the same 
number as the preceding month, with the prefix run 閏 ‘intercalary’.
We then find how many times we need to add 7 to the scaled up Intercalation 
Remainder until we reach a total exceeding 228. Having found this number, then 
if we start counting with winter solstice taken as #1, and if (say) 3 additions of 
7 are required to reach 228, the 4th qi will be the one ‘outside the count’ that 
has shifted onto or past the next mean conjunction.
Suppose for example that the Intercalation Remainder is 14 for this year. That 
means the winter solstice lagged 14/19 of a lunation behind the Celestial First 
Month conjunction. In order for an intercalation to occur, we therefore need the 
remainder to increase by
19 − 14 = 5

We multiply by 12 to obtain 60, thus converting the scale from 19 to 228, and 
then count off sevens from this, each seven representing a medial qi past winter 
solstice that must pass before an intercalation is triggered.
Now 60/7 = 8, remainder 4
So it will take 9 more medial qi after winter solstice, the first medial qi, before 
we accumulate the required remainder of 228. Thus it will be the 10th medial qi 
that will lag its corresponding (10th) conjunction by enough to take it past the 
next (11th) conjunction. The 10th lunation therefore contains no medial qi. It will 
thus be counted as the lunation of the intercalary 9th month, and it is the next 
lunation that will contain the 10th medial qi and thus correspond to the 10th 
month of the Celestial count. Of course the intercalary 9th Celestial month is the 
intercalary 7th civil month; we reach that number if we start counting from the 
11th civil month of the preceding year, rather than the first Celestial month.
What is the point of the statement that we should count a month ‘for each 
completed four’? This relates to a practice that we have already noted in the 
period when the Triple Concordance was in use – although as we have seen 
there is no explicit description in the system itself. The practice was that if the 
medial qi falls so near the next conjunction that it actually falls within the same 
day as that conjunction, then it is counted as falling within the next lunation. 
As a result, an intercalary month will be counted one month earlier than would 
otherwise have been the case. The ‘completed four’ method gives us a rough 
and ready way of telling when this shift might be called for. We may note that:
4/228 of a lunation is (4/228) × (29 
499/940) days
= 478/940 days to 3 significant figures, just over half a day.
So the ‘completed four’ method places the qi in the next lunation if that qi falls 
within half a day before the conjunction, so that the current lunation corresponds 
to an intercalary month. If the interval is larger than 4/228 but less than 7/228 
day, the next month will be intercalary.

The length of the mean lunation is (29 + 499/940) days, defined by:
[Obscuration Days [27,759]]/[Obscuration Months [940]]
Taking a quarter of this, we obtain:
(7 + (359 + ¾) / 940) days for the interval between the events considered here. 
Hence the additions specified to the Greater and Lesser Remainders, with allow -
ance for a whole extr a day mounting up as the factor of 940 is filled.
The final section deals with the timing of the phase during the day. It seems, 
however, that specialists in li did not naturally think of their timings as starting 
from midnight, but preferred to think how much of the night was past, starting 
from dusk (when the night clepsydra was started) and running to dawn (when 
the day clepsydra was started). The night lengths given later for the principal 
seasons (see Table 3.11) are summarised in Table 3.3. The Lesser Remainders 
correspond to half the night length, 940 representing a whole day and night:

ke Lesser Remainder

From this it is clear that the figure of 260 is a rounded value for the time from mid-
night to dawn at the equinoxes in Lesser Remainder terms, designed to indicate 
roughly whether the phase is occurring during the hours of darkness at the start of 
the day. It is unclear why we are not told how to tell whether the phase falls after 
dusk on a given day, but that would be easy enough to deal with if required. From 
the final statement, it is evident that the whole of a given night was reckoned as 
belonging for astronomical (and hence divinatory) purposes to the day in which 
it began. Hence (in modern terms) an event at 2:00 am on Tuesday would be 
reckoned as having taken place during the night of Monday.

The length of the mean lunation is (29 + 499/940) days, defined by:
[Obscuration Days [27,759]]/[Obscuration Months [940]]
Taking a quarter of this, we obtain:
(7 + (359 + ¾) / 940) days for the interval between the events considered here. 
Hence the additions specified to the Greater and Lesser Remainders, with allow -
ance for a whole extr a day mounting up as the factor of 940 is filled.
The final section deals with the timing of the phase during the day. It seems, 
however, that specialists in li did not naturally think of their timings as starting 
from midnight, but preferred to think how much of the night was past, starting 
from dusk (when the night clepsydra was started) and running to dawn (when 
the day clepsydra was started). The night lengths given later for the principal 
seasons (see Table 3.11) are summarised in Table 3.3. The Lesser Remainders 
correspond to half the night length, 940 representing a whole day and night:
Table 3.3
 Night lengths for the four principal qi
ke Lesser Remainder
winter solstice: 65 305.5
summer solstice: 35 164.5
spring equinox: 55.8 262.26
autumn equinox: 55.2 259.44
From this it is clear that the figure of 260 is a rounded value for the time from midnight to dawn at the equinoxes in Lesser Remainder terms, designed to indicate 
roughly whether the phase is occurring during the hours of darkness at the start of 
the day. It is unclear why we are not told how to tell whether the phase falls after 
dusk on a given day, but that would be easy enough to deal with if required. From 
the final statement, it is evident that the whole of a given night was reckoned as 
belonging for astronomical (and hence divinatory) purposes to the day in which 
it began. Hence (in modern terms) an event at 2:00 am on Tuesday would be 
reckoned as having taken place during the night of Monday.

置入蔀年減一， 以沒數乘之， 滿日法得一， 名為積沒， 不盡為沒餘． 以通法乘 
積沒， 滿沒法得一， 名為大餘， 不盡為小餘． 大餘滿六十除去之， 其餘以蔀名
命之， 筭盡之外， 前年冬至前沒日也． 求後沒， 加大餘六十九， 小餘四， 小餘滿
沒法， 從大餘， 命之如前， 無分為滅．

The Han Quarter Remainder system  171
Proc. 3.11. Method to predict Extinction and Obliteration:
§52 Set out years of entry into the Obscuration and subtract one. Multiply  
by Extinction Number [21], and obtain one for each filling of the Day 
Factor [4]. Called this Accumulated Extinctions. What is not exhausted 
is Extinction Remainder. Multiply Accumulated Extinctions by Compat -
ibility Factor [487], and count one for each filling of Extinction Factor 
[7]. Call this the Greater Remainder. What is not exhausted is the Lesser 
Remainder. As the Greater Remainder fills 60, cast it out, and count off 
the remainder from the Obscuration [sexagenary day] name. Outside the 
exhausted count, that is the Extinction Day before the winter solstice of 
the preceding [civil] year. To predict the next Extinction, add 69 to the 
Greater Remainder, and 4 to the Lesser Remainder, and as the Lesser 
Remainder fills the Extinction Factor [7], let that go with the Greater 
Remainder, and count off as before. When there are no fractions, that is 
Obliteration.
Since the interval from one winter solstice to the next is 1461/4 days, and this is 
equal to
360 + 5¼ = 360 + 21/4 days
winter solstices do not all occur on the same sexagenary day. It would however 
be very convenient if they did. To deal with this problem, we do something akin 
to intercalation, by considering a ‘basic’ solar cycle of 360 days, in which all qi 
are assumed to fall on the same cyclical day as the preceding year. We then allow 
for the fact that extra days do in fact accumulate at the rate of 21/4 per solar 
cycle, so that the cyclical days on which qi fall shift further through the sexage -
nary sequence. The total number of whole extra days accumulated to date is 
the Accumulated Extinctions.
The question then arises as to when precisely the extra days amounted to the 
whole number which is Accumulated Extinctions: that day is the Extinction 
Day.
Now the number of days in the year is 1461/4, and each year accumulates an 
extra 21/4 days. So each day in the year contributes:
(21/4) / (1461/4) days = 7/487 days
(So NB that each of the 24 qi contributes (21/4) / 24 = 7/32 days. Thus each 
whole day of a qi may be taken as contributing 7 / (15 × 32) days)
487 is the Compatibility Factor and 7 is the Extinction Factor, as indicated. 
Alternatively, we may say that each day of Extinction takes
487/7 = 69 + 4/7 days
Hence multiplying Accumulated Extinctions by 487 and dividing by 7 gives us 
the number of days from the start of the current Obscuration to the moment of 
Extinction. Since 487/7 = 69, remainder 4, adding these numbers as specified

172 The Han Quarter Remainder system 
will take us to the next Extinction Day. If on any given Extinction Day there is 
no fractional remainder, that is an Obliteration.
一術，
以(為)[十]五乘冬至小餘， 以減通法， 餘滿沒法得一， 則天正後沒也．
Proc. 3.12. Another method:
§53 Multiply the Lesser Remainder of the winter solstice by 15, and subtract from  
Compatibility Factor [487]. Obtain 1 as the remainder fills Extinction Factor 
[7], then that is the Extinction after the Celestial Standard [conjunction].
The Lesser Remainder of the winter solstice is the remainder when years into the 
Obscuration are multiplied by Day Remainder [168] and divided by Medial [ Qi] 
factor [32]. It takes on the values 0,8,16 and 24 over a four-year cycle.
Since one year contributes 21/4 days towards an Extinction, each of the 24 qi 
contributes (21/4) / 24 = 7/32 days. So .  . . each of the 15 days of a qi may be 
taken as contributing 7 / (15 × 32) days).
So if we have a Lesser Remainder at the usual scale of 32, that has taken [Lesser 
Remainder] × 15/7 days to accumulate, and that is the time since the last Extinc -
tion. Thus, since Extinctions are 487/7 days apart, the time to the next Extinction 
is (487 − 15 × [Lesser Remainder]) / 7 days – as specified.
Checking in detail:
The gaps from the previous Extinction to the winter solstice commencing 
the second year of the Obscuration is:
365 − 5 × 487/7
since there were five Extinctions before the winter solstice
= 5 × (73 − 487/7)
= 5 × (511 − 487) / 7
= 5 × (24/7)
= 15 × (8/7)
So the next year the gap will be twice this, at
15 × (16/7)
And in the next year the gap will be:
15 × (24/7)
And these gaps are in each case (Lesser Remainder for winter solstice) × 15/7.
Clearly therefore we can find the gap from winter solstice to the subsequent 
extinction by subtracting these amounts from 487/7 as specified.

置入蔀積月以[蔀]日乘之， 滿大周除去之， 其餘滿蔀月得一，

The Han Quarter Remainder system  173
– 3064 –
名為積度， 不盡為餘分． 積度加斗二十一度， 加二百三十五分， 以宿次除之,
不滿宿， 則日月合朔所在 (星)[宿] 度也． 求後合朔， 加度二十九， 加分四百九
十九， 分滿蔀月得一度， 經斗除二百三十五分．
Proc. 3.13. T o predict the du where the conjunction is located:
§54 Set out the Accumulated Months of entry into the Obscuration, multiply by 
Obscuration days [27,759], and cast out and discard what fills Greater 
Circuits [343,335]. As for the remainder, obtain 1 for each filling of Obscu-
ration Months [940]. Call this Accumulated Du. What is not exhausted is 
Remainder Parts. To the Accumulated Du, add the 21 du of Dipper, with 
[its] 235 parts, and then for each Lodge cast out in succession. When it 
does not fill a Lodge, then that is the du of the Lodge
13 at which the sun 
and moon are located at their conjunction. To seek the next conjunction, 
add to the du 29, and add to the Parts 499, obtaining 1 du as the Parts fill 
Obscuration Months [940], and casting out 235 Parts as you pass through 
Dipper.
Accumulated Months have already been calculated for the conjunction of the first 
Celestial (and hence subsequent) months in Proc. 3.6. Obscuration Days [27,759] 
is the number of days in a month at a scale of Obscuration Months [940], so the 
multiplication specified produces the number of days elapsed at the instant of 
conjunction (and hence number of du moved by the sun), including fractional 
parts, at a scale of Obscuration Months [940]. Greater Circuits [343,335] = 365¼ 
× 940, so this represents the du in a complete circuit at the same scale. Casting this 
out gives the number of du moved by the sun past its starting point at winter 
solstice – which is also the du moved by the moon at the time of the conjunction, 
since its position coincides with that of the sun.
If we want to locate the present position of the sun and moon in the lodge 
system, then we have to take account of the fact that in the system used by the 
Han Quarter Remainder, winter solstice position of the sun is at 21¼ du of 
the lodge Dipper. Thus to count movement of the sun from the start of Dipper 
we have to add this amount, with the ¼ du in the form 235/940. We then move 
through the lodge system casting out the different extensions of each lodge in 
turn until we find which lodge the sun is located in at the time of the conjunc -
tion. As the text notes, when we pass through Dipper again (which is in all 
26
235/940 du across) we must remember to deduct the fraction as well as the 
whole du of this lodge.
Since the length of a mean lunation is 29 499/940 days, this is also the number of 
du that the sun moves between conjunctions. By adding this amount we can 
move from the position just calculated to the next conjunction position.

174 The Han Quarter Remainder system 
The received text runs 置入蔀積月以日乘之 ‘Set out the Accumulated Months 
of entry into the Obscuration, multiply by days’ which is clearly defective. I 
emend following the version of Li Rui, which involves only the insertion of 蔀 
‘Obscuration’ before ‘days’, and produces an exact result for the position of 
moon and sun at the moment of conjunction: see (Li Rui 李銳 (1768–1817) 
1993: 760B).
The editors of the Zhonghua edition adopt a more complex emendation, in 
accordance with the views of Qian Daxin 置入蔀積(月)[日]以(日)[蔀月]乘之 ‘Set 
out the Accumulated Days of entry into the Obscuration, and multiply by Obscu-
ration Months [940]’ : see Hou Han shu, zhi 3, 3063. However, this only produces 
the position of the moon and sun on the midnight of the day on which the 
conjunction falls, not at the moment of conjunction itself. Li Rui’s simpler read -
ing is clearly preferable.
一術，
以閏餘乘周天， 以減大周餘， 滿蔀月得一， 合以斗二十一度四分一， 則天正合
朔日月所在度．
Proc. 3.14. Another method:
§55 Multiply Circuits of Heaven [1461] by Intercalation Remainder, and by that 
subtract from Greater Circuits [343,335], obtaining 1 as the remainder fills 
Obscuration Months [940]. Join with it the 21 du ¼ of Dipper, and this is the 
du where the sun and moon are located at the Celestial Standard conjunction.
Intercalation Remainder is the fraction of a month at a scale of 19 by which the 
conjunction of Celestial New Year falls in advance of the winter solstice. Now the 
days in a lunation (and hence the du moved by the sun between conjunctions) are 
given by:
19 × Circuits of Heaven [1461]/Obscuration Months [940].
Since as before the number of du in a whole circuit is represented by
Greater Circuits [343,335]/Obscuration Months [940],
the procedure described here moves us backwards from the sun’s winter solstice 
position to its location at the preceding conjunction, as required.
推日所在度，
置入蔀積日之數， 以蔀法乘之， 滿蔀日除去之， 其餘滿蔀法得一， 為積 
度， 不盡為餘分． 積度加斗二十一度， 加十九分， 以宿次除去之， 則夜半日所
在宿度也． 求次日， 加一度． 求次月， 大加三十度， 小加二十九度， 經斗除十 
[九]分．

The Han Quarter Remainder system  175
Proc. 3.15. T o predict the du where the sun is located.
§56 Set out the number of Accumulated Days entered into the Obscuration, and 
multiply it by Obscuration Factor [76]. Cast out and discard Obscuration 
Days [27,759], and obtain 1 for each time the remainder fills Obscuration 
Factor [76], which is Accumulated Du, while what is not exhausted is 
Remainder Parts. To the Accumulated Du add the 21 du of Dipper and add 
19 parts, then cast out and discard the Lodges in sequence, and that is the 
degree of the Lodges where the sun is located at midnight. To seek the next 
day, add 1 du. To seek the next month, add 30 du for a long [month] and 
29 du for a short [month]. When passing through Dipper cast out the 19 
parts.
At the beginning of an Obscuration cycle, the sun is at winter solstice. Each day 
thereafter it moves 1 du. Since the days in a solar cycle, and hence the du moved 
in that cycle, are given by:
Obscuration Days [27,759]/Obscuration Factor [76] = 365¼,
The procedure given yields the du from winter solstice moved by the sun in the 
current cycle, and the rest follows. ‘19 parts’ here are 19/76 = ¼.
一術，
以朔小餘減合[朔]度分， 即日夜半所在． 其分(三)[二]百(二)[三]十五約之,
十九乘之．
Proc. 3.16. Another method:
§57 By the Lesser Remainder for the conjunction subtract from the du and parts 
for the conjunction, then that is where the sun is located at midnight. As 
for the parts simplify them by 235, multiplying by 19.
The Lesser Remainder is the fraction of a day, at the scale of Obscuration Months 
[940] by which the conjunction falls after midnight, and hence it gives the angular 
movement of the sun between these instants. It will be recalled that the factor 
giving the scale of Parts in the calculation of the sun’s midnight position was 
76. To convert to this from a scale of 940 requires a multiplication of the parts 
by 235/19, as specified.
推月所在度，
置入蔀積日之數， 以月周乘之， 滿蔀日除去之， 其餘滿蔀法得一， 為積
度， 不盡為餘分． 積度加斗二十一十[九]分， 除如上法， 則所求之日夜半月

Proc. 3.17. T o predict the du where the moon is located:
§58 Set out the number of Accumulated Days entered into the Obscuration, and 
multiply them by Lunar Circuits [1016]. Cast out and discard what fills 
Obscuration Days [27,759], and obtain 1 for each time the remainder fills 
Obscuration Factor [76], which is Accumulated Du, while what is not 
exhausted is Remainder Parts. To Accumulated Du add the 21 [ du] and 19 
parts of Dipper, and cast out according to the method above, then that is the 
degree of the Lodges where the moon is located at midnight on the day 
sought. To seek the next day, add 13 du and 28 parts. To seek the next month, 
for a long [month] add 35 du and 61 parts, but if the month is small add 22 
du 33 parts. If the parts fill the factor obtain 1 du, and in passing through 
Dipper cast out 19 parts. When in the last ten days of winter the Moon is 
in Spread and Heart, take note of it; this refers to the time between the [end] 
boundary of the day clepsydra up to the end of the [night] clepsydra.
Lunar Circuits [1016] is the number of circuits of Heaven made by the moon in an 
Obscuration, during which the sun only makes 76 circuits. So 1016/76 gives the 
factor by which the moon’s speed is greater than the sun’s. Since Accumulated 
Days is the number of du moved by the sun since the start of the Obscuration, 
multiplying by this factor gives the du moved by the moon. Subtraction of Obscura-
tion Days [27,759] before dividing by Obscuration Factor [76] removes the whole 
circuits from the result.

this we may find that the motion for 30 days is:
30 × 1016/76 du = 401 du and 4 parts.

and 61 parts given in the text for 30 days, from which the figure for a short 29 
day month follows immediately. An error is of course introduced by the assump -
tion that the month is a whole number of days long.

Proc. 3.20. T o seek the du entered by the sun at dusk:
§61 By the parts moved by the sun from midnight to dawn, subtract from 
Obscuration Factor [76], and the remainder is the parts moved from midnight 
to dusk. If you add this to the du and parts where the sun is located at 
midnight, this is the du where the sun is located at dusk.
This works because if as usual we assume that solar motion is constant, the move-
ment from midnight to dawn is equal to the movement from dusk to midnight.

術曰：置其節氣夜(半)[漏]之數， 以月周乘之， 以二百除之， 為積分． 積分滿
蔀法得一， 以增夜半度， 即(明)月[明]所在度也．
Proc. 3.21. T o predict the du and parts entered by the moon at dawn:
§62 Method: set out the number for the night clepsydra for the Nodal qi, and 
multiply by Lunar Circuits [1016], then cast out 200, making [the number 
obtained] Accumulated Parts. Obtain 1 for each time Accumulated Parts 
fills Obscuration Factor [76], and by that increase the midnight du, then 
that is the du where the moon is located at dawn.
Since Lunar Circuits [1016] gives the circuits of Heaven made by the moon while 
the sun is making Obscuration Factor [76] circuits, using this instead of the 76 
in the earlier calculation uses the moon’s speed instead of the sun’s, as appropri-
ate. The later division by 76 is performed because unlike the case of the sun the 
moon will have moved more than one du in the given time, so it is not sensible 
to leave the motion in parts.
