Proc. 3.27. T o predict lunar eclipses:
§68 Set out the year of entry into Obscuration Coincidence [2052]. Subtract 
one. Multiply by the Eclipse Number [1081]. Count one for each full Year 
Number [513]. This is called Accumulated Eclipses. The remainder is the 
Eclipse Remainder.
For convenience of exposition, I have divided this procedure into three sections, 
of which this is the first.
An Obscuration Coincidence begins with an eclipse at full moon of its first Celestial 
month, as was the case in the month beginning at System Origin ‘Year of entry’ is 
the number of the target year in the Obscuration Coincidence; subtracting one gives 
us the interval in years from the start of the Obscuration Coincidence to the start 
of the current Celestial year. Since there is a complete cycle of 1081 lunar eclipses 
in 513 years, beginning with an eclipse at full moon of the first month, with another 
at full moon of the first month of the next cycle, the calculation prescribed year tells 
us how many lunar eclipses (within that Obscuration Coincidence) have taken place 
by the beginning of the target year. Thus in the first year of the Obscuration Coin-
cidence, the result is zero. In the second year, the result is found from:
1 × 1081/513 = 2 remainder 55
Thus two eclipses have already occurred in the first year (in addition, i.e. to the 
one at the full moon following the start of the Obscuration Coincidence) and 55 
is the Eclipse Remainder representing in effect the fraction accumulated by the 
start of this year of an eclipse that will ‘mature’ as the current year progresses.

月數． 當先除入章閏， 乃以十二除去之， 不滿者命以十一月， 筭盡之外， 則 
前年十一月前食月也．
§70 Remove multiples of the Rule Months [235] from Accumulated Months. 
The remainder is the number of months into the Rule. First one takes out 
the intercalations that far into the Rule. Then one removes multiples of 12. 
As for the remainder, count from the eleventh month, and outside the 
exhausted count that is the month of the eclipse before the eleventh month 
of the preceding [civil] year.
This part of the procedure removes from Accumulated Months the months before 
this eclipse that are whole Rules or whole years (including intercalary months). 
The result is the months into the relevant year (which is the one before the target 
year) when this eclipse occurs. From what follows, it seems clear that the inter -
calary months removed include those in the current year up to the time of the 
eclipse, so the result will be the actual number of the month of eclipse in the 
Celestial count, allowing for any preceding intercalations.

月數． 當先除入章閏， 乃以十二除去之， 不滿者命以十一月， 筭盡之外， 則

§70 Remove multiples of the Rule Months [235] from Accumulated Months. 
The remainder is the number of months into the Rule. First one takes out 
the intercalations that far into the Rule. Then one removes multiples of 12. 
As for the remainder, count from the eleventh month, and outside the 
exhausted count that is the month of the eclipse before the eleventh month 
of the preceding [civil] year.
This part of the procedure removes from Accumulated Months the months before 
this eclipse that are whole Rules or whole years (including intercalary months). 
The result is the months into the relevant year (which is the one before the target 
year) when this eclipse occurs. From what follows, it seems clear that the inter -
calary months removed include those in the current year up to the time of the 
eclipse, so the result will be the actual number of the month of eclipse in the 
Celestial count, allowing for any preceding intercalations.

Proc. 3.29. T o seek the next eclipse:
§72 Add 5 months and 20 parts, with one for the count of months when the 
factor is filled. Count it off according to the factor, and when the parts are 
exhausted there is an eclipse above the count.
Since there are Eclipse Factor: [23] eclipses in Month Number [135] months, the 
mean interval between eclipses will be
135/23 months = 5 20/23 months.
Hence the process specified here to locate the next eclipse.
推月食朔日術曰：
置食積月之數， 以二十九乘之， 為積日． 又以四百九十[九]乘積月， 滿蔀月 
得一， 以并積日， 以六十除之， 其餘以所會蔀名命之， 筭盡之外， 則前年天正

Proc. 3.30. T o predict the day of conjunction [which begins the month] with 
a lunar eclipse:
§73 Set out the number of Accumulated Months of the eclipse, multiply it by 
29, to make Accumulated Days. Further, multiply Accumulated Months by 
499, and count one for each filling of Obscuration Months [940], adding 
this to the Accumulated Days. Cast out multiples of 60, and count off the 
remainder from the name of the Coincidence Obscuration. Outside the count 
that is exhausted, then that is the conjunction day [of the month] with a 
lunar eclipse before the Celestial First Month of the preceding year.
All this follows from the fact that there are 29 499/940 days in a lunation .

加大餘十四， 小餘七百一十九半， 小餘滿蔀月為大餘， 大餘命如前， 則食 
日也．

The Han Quarter Remainder system  183
Proc. 3.31. T o seek the day of the eclipse:
§74 Add to the Greater Remainder 14, and to the Lesser Remainder 719 and 
½. As the Lesser Remainder fills Obscuration Months [940] let that count 
as Greater Remainder, and counting off the Greater Remainder as before, 
then that is the day of the eclipse.
The additions specified simply add half the length of a lunation, the interval 
between conjunction and opposition.
求後食朔及日，
皆加大餘二十七， 小餘六百一十五． 其月餘分不滿二十者， 又加大餘二 
十九， 小餘四百九十九． 其食小餘者， 當以漏刻課之， 夜漏未盡， 以筭上為
日．
Proc. 3.32. T o seek the conjunction [of the month] with the next eclipse and 
the [actual] day:
§75 In each case add 27 to the Greater Remainder, and 615 to the Lesser Remain -
der. Where the parts for the month do not fill 20, further add 29 to the Greater 
Remainder and 499 to the Lesser Remainder. The Lesser Remainder for the 
eclipse should be compared with the clepsydra graduations. Where the night 
run is not exhausted, count one back to make the day.
The aim here is to predict the sexagenary day and time of day of the next eclipse. 
To get to these figures, we multiply the days in a lunation by the lunations from 
one eclipse to another, on the basis that eclipses can normally be expected at 
intervals of five lunations:
5 × (Obscuration Days [27,759]/Obscuration Months [940])
= 147315/940
Since 147 = 2 × 60 + 27, we can see that the sexagenary day number must increase 
by 27, and the extra parts of a day (at a scale of 940) will be 615, as specified.
Recalling that the mean interval between eclipses is 5 20/23 lunations it is clear 
that the reference to ‘where the parts for the month do not fill 20’ identifies 
the situation where the interval since the last eclipse is not yet long enough 
for another eclipse to be expected. In that case, we simply add a lunation’s 
worth of days and parts as specified to get to the conjunction of the next 
month.
The final sentence refers to the practice already seen in Proc. 3.10, where an 
event occurring during the hours of darkness after midnight is counted as occur -
ring on the previous day.

一術，
以歲數去上元， 餘以為積月， 以百一十二乘之， 滿月數去之， 餘滿食法得一,
則天正後食．
Proc. 3.33. Another method:
§76 Cast out Year Number [513] from [the years since] High Origin. [From 
the] remainder make Accumulated Months, and multiply by 112. Cast out 
what fills Month Number [135], and for the remainder obtain one for each 
filling of Eclipse Factor [23], then this is the eclipse after Celestial First 
Month.
As Li Rui notes, the start of this text is elliptical. It is however possible to make 
sense of the details that are given here if we consider how the first eclipse of a 
given Celestial year can in fact be predicted. 14 The steps would be as follows:
(1)  Cas t out Year Number [513] from years since High Origin. This removes 
complete cycles of eclipses, so that we are counting years from the near -
est year in which an eclipse occurs at opposition of the first Celestial 
month.
(2)  W e then take the resulting years, and convert them to months, by multiply -
ing by 235 and dividing by 19. We take the whole number result of this, 
which is Accumulated Months from the start of the nearest year in which an 
eclipse occurs at opposition of the first Celestial month up to the start of 
the present year.
(3)  No w we multiply by Eclipse Factor [23] and cast out whole multiples of 
Month Number [135]. The result will be (at the scale of Month Number) the 
fraction of an eclipse that has been completed between the last eclipse and 
the start of the first Celestial month. It will be a number greater than zero 
and less than 135. Let us call this Eclipse Remainder.
(4)  If w e subtract this number from 135, the result will tell us how far we 
have to go until the first eclipse after Celestial First Month is complete. 
Now each month, 23/135 of an eclipse is completed. Thus to find the 
number of months to be counted until the next eclipse is complete 
will be:
(135 − Eclipse Remainder) / 23
Now what is proposed here is to multiply Accumulated Months by
112 = (135 − 23)
This represents the amount by which one month falls short of a whole eclipse.

The Han Quarter Remainder system  185
Then we are to cast out multiples of 135; each of these multiples is a whole 
eclipse’s worth: thus, for example, if we consider an instant at the start of the 
10th month of the sequence, when Accumulated Months is 9, we get:
9 × 112 = 1008
1008 mod 135 = 63
7 multiples of 135 have been cast out, meaning we are 7 eclipses short of the 
number that would have occurred if there had been eclipses at the rate of one a 
month; there have been nine months, so there should have been two eclipses so 
far: this is indeed the case, since there were eclipses in the first and seventh month.
Each month we move forward increases the total by (135 − 23). The 135 repre -
sents a further eclipse missed in that month, and thus the number of misses 
normally goes up by 1 a month, as it should. But from time to time the accu -
mulation of 23s passes the total of 135 – and when that happens a month passes 
without the total of missed eclipses increasing – which is what happens when 
an eclipse actually takes place.
Further, for a month in which an eclipse actually falls,
(23 × Accumulated months) = a multiple of 135. So clearly
(135 − 23) × Accumulated months = a multiple of 135.
For the next month, when Accumulated Months increases by 1, the left-hand 
side of the equation will increase by 135 and decrease by 23. The increase of 
135 will not affect the result when 135 is cast out.
Thus to find the next eclipse, we can count up 23 each month until we reach 135.
Now returning to our example, where we had 9 Accumulated Months, from 63 
to the next full eclipse missed is
135 − 63 = 72
72 = 3 × 23 + 3
So the number of fillings of 23 is 3. The next eclipse after the start of the 10th month 
of the sequence is indeed three months onwards, in the 13th month of the sequence.

with the factor, and with the number of counts obtained begin from zi for 
midnight. Then outside the exhausted count is the double-hour of 
occurrence.
This procedure can be applied to find the time of day of all lunar phenomena, 
not just eclipses. The ‘factor’ here is Obscuration Months [940], which is the 
scale factor for the Lesser Remainder of months. Multiplication by 12 and division 
by 940 converts the Lesser Remainder into (1/12) days, i.e. converts the fraction 
of a day into double hours.
The day is divided into 12 ‘double-hours’, named after the 12 cyclical signs. The 
first double-hour is labelled zi 子, and centres on the moment of midnight. Thus 
only half of it is actually in the day counted from midnight, and it is for that 
reason that we begin by subtracting a half-factor, before counting off the whole 
factors for each subsequent whole double-hour.

以百乘其小餘， 滿其法得一刻；不滿法(法)什之， 滿法得一分． 積刻先

不滿夜漏半者， 乃減之， 餘為昨夜未(晝)[盡]， 其弦望其日．
Proc. 3.35. T o predict the ke of the clepsydra run from water filling:
§78 Multiply the Lesser Remainder by 100. Obtain one ke for each time it fills 
its factor. As for what does not fill, multiply it by ten, and obtain one fen 
for each time it fills the factor. From the accumulated ke, first subtract half 
the night clepsydra for the Nodal qi entered; the remainder is the amount 
of the daytime water filling. If it exceeds the day clepsydra, cast that out, 
and the remainder is the amount of the night water filling. If the ke do not 
fill half the night clepsydra, then subtract [the ke] from it, and the remainder 
is the unexpired part of the preceding night. The crescents and full moons 
[are counted on] that day.
The Lesser Remainder tells us the fraction of a day (at a scale of Obscuration Months 
[940] by which a given event falls after midnight. First we convert this into ke and 
tenths of ke, at the rate of 100 ke to the day. The time from midnight to dawn is

midnight is greater than this, we have moved into the hours of daylight, and 
subtraction will tell us how far we are into that daytime clepsydra run. If the event 
is late enough, it will move into the clepsydra run for the next night, and we 
subtract the day clepsydra run to find out how far that is. If however the time of 
the event past midnight is less that half the night length, then we may calculate

3.2.5 [Planetary constants]
Proc. 3.36. [Derivation of planetary constants]:
五星數之生也， 各記於日， 與周天度相約而為率．
§79 As for the production of the numbers for the five planets, each is reckoned 
with reference to the Sun, and a rate is made by making it congruent with 
the du of the circumference of heaven.
Cycle Rate: number of conjunctions between planet and sun
Solar Rate: number of complete circuits of the sun round the heaven while Cycle 
Rate conjunctions occur – i.e. the number of years required for that.
So for instance, for the Wood Star (Jupiter) has
Cycle Rate: 4327
Solar Rate: 4725
For every 4725 circuits of the heavens by the sun, Jupiter makes 4327 conjunctions.
That means that during these 4725 solar circuits, it moves through (4725 − 4327) 
= 398 circuits.
以章法乘周率為(用)[月]法， 章月乘日率， 如月法， 為積月月餘．
§80 By multiplying the Cycle Rate by the Rule Factor [19] one makes the 
Lunation Factor, then Rule Months [235] multiplies the Solar Rate, and 
[from the number of] accords with the Lunation Factor, one makes the 
Accumulated Months and the Lunation Remainder.
Cycle Rate × Rule Factor [19] gives the number of Conjunctions in Solar Rate years, 
at a scale of Rule Factor: this is Lunation Factor.
Rule Months [235] × Solar Rate gives the number of months in the years of Solar 
Rate, at a scale of Rule Factor [19].
Hence dividing the second result by the first gives the months in one conjunction 
(Accumulated Months) and the remainder is at a scale of Lunation Factor.

§79 As for the production of the numbers for the five planets, each is reckoned

the du of the circumference of heaven.
Cycle Rate: number of conjunctions between planet and sun
Solar Rate: number of complete circuits of the sun round the heaven while Cycle 
Rate conjunctions occur – i.e. the number of years required for that.
So for instance, for the Wood Star (Jupiter) has
Cycle Rate: 4327
Solar Rate: 4725
For every 4725 circuits of the heavens by the sun, Jupiter makes 4327 conjunctions.
That means that during these 4725 solar circuits, it moves through (4725 − 4327) 
= 398 circuits.

Rate, at a scale of Rule Factor [19].

§85 T aking it by harmonising the Solar Rates, obtain for the termination of the 
five planets 29,991,621,582,300. Take as many of these as the Obscuration 
[factor] to make this compatible with the Origin [factor].
The Solar Rates are:
Wood (Jupiter) 4725 = 5 × 945 = 5 × 5 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 7
Fire (Mars) 1876 = 2 × 2 × 7 × 67
Earth (Saturn) 9415 = 5 × 7 × 269
Metal (Venus) 4661 = 59 × 79
Water (Mercury) 1889 = prime
The number given above is the lowest common multiple of these, and its factors are:
4 × 5 × 5 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 7 × 59 × 67 × 79 × 269 × 1889
An Origin is 4560 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 × 19
To make the result a multiple of the Origin, we thus need to multiply by  
2 × 2 × 19 = 76, an Obscuration Factor.
This also produces a multiple of Origin Concidence [41,040] = 9 × Origin Factor 
[4560], and so repetition of a lunar eclipse at the full moon of the first Celestial 
month is also ensured: see Proc. 3.1.
The result of this calculation will thus be the period after which all the initial 
conditions of the system at High Origin (see section § 256) will repeat. This is 
not an important quantity in the calculations underlying the Han Quarter Remain-
der, nor is it used elsewhere in the system. Neither the Triple Concordance system 
nor not the Uranic Manifestation system contain anything similar.

§87 Solar Rate: 4725.
The Cycle Rate is the number of conjunctions of Jupiter with the sun (not 
counting the initial conjunction at High Origin) that take place while the sun 
performs Solar Rate circuits of the heavens, i.e. in Solar Rate solar cycles. 15 If 
Jupiter were a fixed star, these numbers would be equal. The number of con -
junctions (Cycle  Rate) is however less than the number of solar cycles elapsed 
(Solar Rate), since Jupiter is itself performing circuits of the heavens in the same 
direction as the sun, but more slowly. The difference 4725 − 4327 = 398 is the 
number of complete circuits of the heavens performed by Jupiter in Solar Rate 
solar cycles.

§92 Lesser Remainder 847.
These quantities enable us to find the date and time of the conjunction of sun 
and moon falling at the start of the lunation within which the conjunction of 
the sun and Jupiter occurs. The first is the amount to be added to the cyclical 
day number with which the system began, once for each conjunction. The second 
is the fraction of a day (at a scale of 940) to be added to the instant of midnight 
for each conjunction.
We convert the Conjunction Accumulated Lunations to days, on the basis that 
one Obscuration contains precisely 27,759 days or 940 months:
13 × 27,759/940 = 383 + 847/940
847/940 is the fraction of a day after midnight when falls the solar-lunar conjunc-
tion beginning the lunation in which the first conjunction after High Origin of 
Jupiter with the sun occurs. To find the cyclical day name of the first day of the 
corresponding month, we calculate:
383 mod 60 = 23,
which is to be added to the cyclical day number with which the system began.
虛分， 九十三．
§93 V oid Parts 93.
940 − 847 = 93
This is the fraction of a day remaining after the conjunction just considered 
occurs.

(b) The part of a month left over in one conjunction after discarding the 
whole months in Accumulated Months (Lunation Remainder)
Let us carry out the calculation for Jupiter, for which we have:
Conjunction Accumulated Lunations: 13
Lesser Remainder 847
Lunation Remainder: 41,606
So in a conjunction, we have 13 complete lunations, which consist of a whole 
number of days, plus a fraction of a day equal to 847/940 days. After that 
we have 41,606 / (4327 × 19) of a lunation.
First let us convert the second quantity to days. Since Obscuration Days is 
27,759 and Obscuration Months is 940, the result is:
(41,606 / (4327 × 19)) × (27,759/940)
= (41,606 × 27,759) / (82,213 × 940)
= 1,154,940,954
To make the fractions ‘communicate’ we may now transform the 847/940 day to:
847 × 82,213 / (82,213 × 940) = 69,634,411
Now 1,154,940,954 + 69,634,411 = 1,224,575,365
and 1,224,575,365 / (82,213 × 940) = 15 remainder 65,372,065
Now the remainder here is at a scale of 82,213 × 940. If we simplify by 19 × 235 
to give a remainder of 14,641, that makes the scale 4 × 4327, which is the Day and 
Du Factor.
日度法， 萬七千三百八．
§96 Day and Du Factor 17,308.
4 × 4327 = 17,308
This is the denominator for two quantities:
(a)  The fr actional part of days above whole days and whole months for one 
conjunction.
(b)  The fr actional parts of a du moved by Jupiter relative to the stars from one 
conjunction to another.
It is clear that these fractions must differ by exactly ¼, since the sun moves at  
1 du/day, and thus after 365 days it still has to move ¼ du in ¼ day to reach the 
position from which Jupiter has shifted by an angle whose fractional part is (b). 
Thus the same divisor will apply to both fractions.
積度， 三十三．
度餘， 萬三百一十四．

One full conjunction matures each time the Conjunction Remainder becomes 
equal to Solar Rate = 4725 for Jupiter. In one solar cycle, the fraction of a con -
junction that is added is (Cycle Rate) / (Solar Rate) = 4327/4725 for Jupiter. So 
Conjunction Remainder increases by Cycle Rate each solar cycle.
Now if Conjunction Remainder = Cycle Rate at year’s end, it was clearly zero at the 
start of the solar cycle, i.e. the cycle began with a conjunction at winter solstice.
If Conjunction Remainder < Cycle Rate at the solstice at year’s end, then clearly 
the conjunction was less than a year ago, i.e. within the present year.
If Conjunction Remainder > Cycle Rate at the solstice at year’s end, then the 
conjunction was more than one year ago, i.e. before the start of the present 
year.
If Conjunction Remainder >2 × Cycle Rate at year’s end, then the conjunction 
was more than two years ago.
The interpretation of the sentence 不得焉退歲 seems supported by the later usage 
of 退歲 to mean the years one has to step back from the present year to find a 
year with a conjunction: see section § 163.

from jiazi.1, and outside the count is the conjunction day of the month of 
the planet’s conjunction.
The ‘conjunction day’ here is the day of the solar-lunar conjunction that begins 
the month in which the conjunction falls. The procedure is a simple conversion 
of whole months into days and fractions of a day at a scale of Obscuration 
Months [940], using the equivalence:
Obscuration Days [27,759] = Obscuration Months [940]
We then cast out multiples of 60 from the whole days to find the shift of the 
cyclical day number from the initial value at High Origin.
推入月日，
以蔀日乘月餘， 以其月法乘朔小餘， 從之， 以四千四百六十五約之， 所得 
(得)滿日度法得一， 為入月日， 不盡為日餘． 以朔命入月日， 筭外， 星合日也．
Proc. 3.40. T o find the days entered into the month:
§161 By Obscuration Days [27,759] multiply Lunation Remainder, and by the 
Lunation Factor multiply the Lesser Remainder for the conjunction [i.e. 
the luni-solar conjunction beginning this lunation], and let it go with [the 
previous result]. Simplify by 4465, and for what you obtain, get one for 
each filling of the Day and Du Factor, to make the days entered into the 
month. What is not exhausted is the Day Remainder. Count off the days 
entered into the month from the conjunction [day], and outside the count 
is the day of [the planet’s] conjunction.
Lunation Remainder here is used in the second of its two meanings, i.e. the 
fractional part of a lunation from the solar-lunar conjunction at the start of the 
month to the instant of planetary conjunction, at a scale of Lunation Factor, 
which is Cycle Rate × 19. However, the end result of this procedure has to be in 
days at a scale of Cycle Rate × 4.
Now days convert to lunations as follows:
Lunations = Days × Obscuration Months [940]/Obscuration Days [27,759]
So in this procedure, we start with:
Lunations × (Cycle Rate × 19), then multiply by 27,759 and divide by 4465, 
to produce:
Lunations × (Cycle Rate × 19) × 27,759/4465
= (Days × 940/27,759) × (Cycle Rate × 19) × 27,759/4465
= (Days × Cycle Rate) × 940 × 19/4465

Proc. 3.41. T o predict the du of conjunction:
§162 By circuit s of heaven multiply Du Parts. As this fills Day and Du Factor, 
obtain 1 to make Accumulated Du. What is not exhausted makes Du 
Remainder. Count off the du from 21¼ du of Dipper. Outside the count, 
that is the du where the star has its conjunction.
Du Parts is the fraction of a solar cycle between the last winter solstice and the 
current conjunction of the sun with the planet; see section § 156. As shown 
there, (Circuits of Heaven) × Du Parts / (Day and Du Factor) gives the distance 
moved by the sun from winter solstice (at 21¼ du of Dipper) to conjunction 
with the planet, as specified here.
The integral result of the calculation, Accumulated Du, is the number of du moved 
by the sun between winter solstice and conjunction. It is therefore the number 
of days elapsed from winter solstice to conjunction.
The remainder is in du at a scale of
(Day and Du Factor) / (Circuits of Heaven)

204 The Han Quarter Remainder system 
Number [21]. Count one for each filling of the Day Factor [4], to make the 
Greater Remainder, and let what is not exhausted be the Lesser Remainder. 
Count off the Greater Remainder from the jiazi, and then that is the day of 
the winter solstice for the Celestial first month in the year of the planet’s 
conjunction.
What are the ‘years stepped back’? It is clear that the result of:
(Years to High Origin) − (Years Stepped Back + 1)
gives the interval in years from High Origin to the winter solstice preceding the 
conjunction. We recall that in calculating ‘High Origin’, we were told to include 
the current year. If ‘Years Stepped Back’ are the count from the present year back 
to when the conjunction actually occurred, this makes sense. Suppose that we 
find that we are in year 100, but the conjunction occurred the year before the 
present year, then clearly there was an interval of 98 years from High Origin to 
the winter solstice before the conjunction.
Why cast out 80?
80 × 365¼ = 29,220 = 487 × 60
So casting out 80 solar cycles removes whole multiples of 60-day shifts of jiazi. 
To find out the shift that has occurred, we have to look at the effect of the 
remaining multiple of 5.25 days.
Extinction Number [21] is the days and day fraction above 360, at a scale of Day 
Factor [4], since 21/4 = 5¼. Thus the calculation of the Greater Remainder as 
given here gives us the shift in cyclical day number. Lesser Remainder gives us 
the fraction of a day by which the solstice falls after midnight, at a scale of Day 
Factor [4].
以周率[乘]小餘， 并度餘， 餘滿日度法從度， 即(正)[至]後星合日數也， 命以
冬至．
§164 By Cycle Rate multiply the Lesser Remainder , and add it to Du Remainder, 
and let the number of times this [combined] Remainder fills Day and Du 
Factor go with the Du. Then this is the number of days after the solstice that 
the planet’s conjunction [takes place]. Count it off from the winter solstice.
Lesser Remainder is the fraction of a day by which the solstice falls after midnight, 
at a scale of Day Factor [4]. Multiplication by Cycle Rate raises the scale to
4 × Cycle Rate = Day and Du Factor, as required.
Du Remainder (like Month Remainder) has two meanings:
1. The fr actional part of the angular motion of the planet between conjunc -
tions, given once for each planet in the initial listing of constants.

2. The fr actional part of the angle moved by the sun from winter solstice to 
conjunction. This is at a scale of Day and Du Factor, as required.
Here we are using it in sense 2. So adding the two quantities together gives us the 
amount by which the conjunction falls after midnight, at a scale of Day and Du 
Factor.
Any whole du are then added to the du calculated above, which are the Accumulated 
Du for predicting the du of conjunction.
Thus (since the sun moves at one du/day) we have the days elapsed at the conjunc-
tion since midnight beginning the day of winter solstice, as required.

Proc. 3.43. T o find the month of the next conjunction:
§165 Add Conjunction Accumulated Lunations to the Months of Entry into the 
Year, and add the Month Remainder to the Month Remainder, counting one 
for each filling of Lunation factor and letting that go with the Months of Entry 
into the Year. If the Months of Entry into the Year fill 12, cast it out, reckoning 
into that any intercalary month. As for the remainder, count off as before, and 
outside the count, that is the month of the next conjunction. For Venus and 
Mercury, if one adds to a dawn appearance one gets a dusk appearance, and 
if one adds to a dusk appearance one gets a dawn appearance.
求朔日，
以大小餘加今所得， 其月餘得一月者， 又[加大]餘二十九， [小餘四百九十
九， ]小飾滿蔀月得一， (如)[加]大餘， 大餘命如前．
Proc. 3.44. T o find the conjunction day:
§166 By the Greater and Lesser Remainders add to those you now obtain, and 
when from the Month Remainder you get one month, further to the Greater 
Remainder add 29, and to the Lesser Remainder 499, and when the 
Lesser Remaind er fills Obscuration Months [940] obtain 1, and add to the 
Greater Remainder, then the Greater Remainder is counted off as before.
This section and the two following simply add on one conjunction’s worth of 
constants onto the values already obtained, to find the values for the next con -
junction of the planet with the sun.

求入月日，
以入月日[日]餘加今所得， 餘滿日度法得一， 從日． 其前合月朔小餘(不)滿
其虛分者， 空加一日． 日滿月先去二十九， 其後合月朔小餘不滿四百九十九,
又減一日， 其餘命如前．
Proc. 3.45. T o find the day of entry into the month:
§167 By the Days of Entry Into the Month, and the Day Remainder add to those 
you now obtain. As the remainder fills Day and Du Factor obtain 1, and 
let it go with the days.
求合度，
以積度度餘加今所得， 餘滿日度法得一從度， 命如前， 經斗除如周率矣．
Proc. 3.46. T o find the du of conjunction:
§168 Add the Accumulated Du and the Du Remainder to what you have obtained, 
and as the remainder fills the Day and Du Factor let it go with the du. 
Count it off as before, and as you pass through Dipper cast out what 
accords with Cycle Rate.
3.2.7 [Planetary motions]
In what follows, I have added brief notes to show the internal consistency of the 
figures given for the duration of the various phases of each planet, and the 
movement of the planet during the phases.
The data given here are in general different from those given in the Triple Concor-
dance system. Single phases in the Triple Concordance are here often divided into 
two phases, each with a different rate of motion. I have indicated the smaller number 
of cases where the data of the Triple Concordance have been adopted unchanged. 
Overall, however, the differences are such as to suggest a conscious effort to con-
struct a system that gave a better representation of the planets’ observed motions.
The Uranic Manifestation system, on the other hand, adopts the planetary data 
of the Han Quarter Remainder almost entirely, with minor adjustments to the 
motion in the invisible phases to adapt them to the different basic constants of 
the system.
木，
Wood [Jupiter]
晨伏， 十六日七千(二)[三]百二十分半， 行二度萬三千八百一十一分，

§169 in the case of Jupiter. Thus we may calculate where the planet will be 
when first seen in the east at dawn.
(術)[行]分母乘之， 分(日)如[日]度法而一， 分不盡如(法)半[法]以上， 亦得一,
§248 Let the denominator for motion parts multiply it, and obtain one for each 
time the parts accords with the Day and Du Factor, and if the parts not 
exhausted accord with half the factor or greater, then accordingly obtain 
one.
The result of this rule is that we only calculate planetary positions to within 1 du. 
Thus 1.2 du counts as 1 du, and 1.7 du counts as 2 du.
而日加所行分， 滿其母得一度． 逆順母不同， 以當行之母乘故分， 如故母， 
如一也．
§249 Then [each] day add the parts moved, obtaining one du as the denominator 
is filled. If the denominators for retrograde and direct motion are not the same, 
by the denominator appropriate to the [type of] motion multiply the given 
parts, and as they accord with the given denominator, that counts as one.
This refers to the fact that the daily rate of motion in the planet may involve 
fractional amounts with different denominators in different phases.
留者承前， 逆則減之， 伏不書度．
§250 For a station, uphold the previous [value], for retrogradation then subtract 
it, and for invisibility do not write down the du.
經斗除如行母， 四分具一． 其分有損益， 前後相放．
§251 When it goes through [the lodge] Dipper, corresponding to the motion 
denominator, take one in four. The parts have their increase and decrease, 
but what goes before and after are related.
When the planet moves through the lodge Dipper, of width 21¼ du, we subtract 
the fraction and calculate accordingly, to find how far the planet has moved into 
the next lodge.
其以赤道命度， 進加退減之． 其步以黃道．

in (Cullen, Christopher 2007a), about 30  y ears before this table was composed, 
Zhang Heng 張衡 did produce a tabulation at intervals of 3 or 4 du, probably 
based on careful measurements on a graduated sphere, which made such a true 
interconversion possible. See also (Cullen, Christopher 2000). Here, however, the 
combination of the figures given and the stated widths of the lodges on equator 
and ecliptic serve a different and somewhat unexpected purpose, which is in 
effect to transform uniform motion with respect to the equator into uniform 
motion with respect to the ecliptic – which is clearly an impossibility. It is pos -
sible that these figures represent a not very successful attempt to respond to 
criticisms by Jia Kui 賈逵 of the practice of calculating the motion of the sun on 
the basis of uniform motion with reference to the equator rather than the ecliptic: 
see the translation given in this book, Chapt
 er 5, and (Cullen, Christopher forth -
coming: chapter 6).

Proc. 3.51. [The basis of the solar table]:
§253 For producing the distance of the Yellow Road from the pole, and the 
solar shadow, one relies on the [armillary] instrument and the gnomon. 
For producing the clepsydra divisions, multiply the differences in distance 
from the pole by the differences for the Nodal qi, with a difference of 1 
ke being counted as this accords with the varying distance, then let them 
be added and subtracted. For the production of dusk and dawn [centred 
stars], multiply the du of Heaven by the day clepsydra, and subtract from 
it the night clepsydra, counting 1 for 200, to make the Determined Du. 
By that subtract from the du of Heaven, and the remainder is [the du of 
the] dawn [centred star]. Add one to the Determined Du to make [the du 
of the] dusk [centred star]. If there is a remainder, four-fold it; if it accords 
with the factor once, that is shao ‘Lesser’, if twice, that is ban ‘Half’ , and 
if three times, that is tai ‘Greater’. What is not exhausted, three-fold it; 
if it accords with the factor that is qiang ‘Strengthened’ –  let it make up 
qiang [even if] the remainder is [only] over half of the factor. When there 
are 3 qiang that is shao, and when there are four shao that is a du. Two

Proc. 3.51. [The basis of the solar table]:
§253 For producing the distance of the Yellow Road from the pole, and the 
solar shadow, one relies on the [armillary] instrument and the gnomon. 
For producing the clepsydra divisions, multiply the differences in distance 
from the pole by the differences for the Nodal qi, with a difference of 1 
ke being counted as this accords with the varying distance, then let them 
be added and subtracted. For the production of dusk and dawn [centred 
stars], multiply the du of Heaven by the day clepsydra, and subtract from 
it the night clepsydra, counting 1 for 200, to make the Determined Du. 
By that subtract from the du of Heaven, and the remainder is [the du of 
the] dawn [centred star]. Add one to the Determined Du to make [the du 
of the] dusk [centred star]. If there is a remainder, four-fold it; if it accords 
with the factor once, that is shao ‘Lesser’, if twice, that is ban ‘Half’ , and 
if three times, that is tai ‘Greater’. What is not exhausted, three-fold it; 
if it accords with the factor that is qiang ‘Strengthened’ – let it make up 
qiang [even if] the remainder is [only] over half of the factor. When there 
are 3 qiang that is shao, and when there are four shao that is a du. Two

qiang make shao ruo . [So] you may alternatively make the remainder for 
the sun’s du into shao and qiang, and add them to it respectively.
In this section, we are told what observations and calculations were made in order 
to produce the data in the solar table that follows. The summary explanations 
given here may be supplemented by the details in (Cullen, Christopher 2007a).
The first paragraph refers to the two main sources of actual observational data 
used for the table – an armillary instrument for measuring the sun’s north polar 
distance, and a gnomon for measuring the noon solar shadow. These are to be 
observed on the days corresponding to the 24 qi, the equally spaced divisions 
of the solar cycle from one winter solstice to the next; see Proc. 3.49.
In the second paragraph, reference is made to how the figures for day and night 
lengths at each of the 24 qi are to be calculated. Actual observations are made 
at winter and summer solstice (which are the Nodal Qi referred to here), and it 
is then assumed that the change of each quantity from one qi to the next is in 
proportion to the change in the sun’s north polar distance.
With reference to the third paragraph, as mentioned in section § 6, a star is 
‘centred’ when it crosses the meridian south of the observer. The use of a clepsy-
dra to time the intervals between the ‘centring’ of a sequence of stars was there 
explained. It was customary, as here to pay particular attention to the stars seen 
to be centred at the different seasons of the year – probably because they pro -
vided a means of locating a date in the solar cycle without the need for any 
timing device or measurements of solar shadow. The procedure outlined here 
enables us to find the du between the sun’s position and the position of the 
stars that will cross the meridian at dusk and dawn.
The system of fractions implied in the final paragraph is based on the foundation 
of the three main divisions shao, ban and tai, corresponding to ¼, ½ and ¾. 
These are then modified if necessary by adding 1/12 ( qiang ‘strengthening’) or 
subtracting it ( ruo ‘weakening’). See Table 3.9:

Proc. 3.51 explains how the data in Table 3.11 were produced: actual

were performed, and the other quantities were calculated from them as

中星以日所在為正， 日行四歲乃終， 置所求年二十四氣小餘四之， 如法為少、大，
餘不盡， 三之， 如法為強、弱， 以減節氣昏明中星， 而各定矣． 強， 正；弱， (直)[負]也．
其強弱相減， 同名相去， 異名從之． 從強進少為弱， 從弱退少而強．
Proc. 3.53. [Notation for fractions]:
§255 Centred stars take the location of the Sun as the standard, and [their sequence] 
is accomplished as the sun moves through four years. Set out the Lesser 
Remainders for the 24 qi for the year sought, and four-fold them, and as 
they accord with the factor make shao and tai. As for the remainder that is 
not exhausted, three-fold it, and as it accords with the factor make qiang 
and ruo, with which one subtracts from the dusk and dawn centred stars,

The Han Quarter Remainder system  231
The tabulated centred stars are those that apply if is assumed that the relevant 
qi falls at midnight, so that the midnight position of the sun is as tabulated. In 
fact this is not generally the case. Since qi recur at intervals of 365¼ day, a qi 
that falls at midnight in year 1 will fall a quarter day after midnight in year 2, 
then half a day after midnight in year 3, then three-quarters of a day after 
midnight in year 4, until returning to midnight in year 5. In any given year, the 
Lesser Remainder for that qi is the fraction of a day after midnight when the qi 
falls, at a scale of Medial [ Qi] factor [32]. The procedure given here acts, in 
effect, to produce quarters according to the shao/ban/tai system, followed by 
the conversion of the remainder into ± 12ths according to the qiang/ruo system, 
as outlined in Proc. 3.51. Since the result is the shift in the midnight solar posi -
tion, we may apply the same shift directly to the dusk and dawn centred stars 
positions.
The final sentence is obscure: the rendering here follows Li Rui, who sees it as 
referring to the effect of adding qiang to qiang to make shao ruo, which is clear 
enough, since 
2/12 = 1/4 – 1/12, and of subtracting qiang from shao ruo to make 
qiang, i.e. (1/4 – 1/12) – 1/12 = 1/12.
3.2.10 [The system origin]
從上元太歲在庚辰以來， 盡熹平三年，歲在甲寅， 積九千四百五十五歲也．
§256 From High Origin when the taisui was at gengchen.17, exhausting the 3rd 
year of the Xiping period [174–175 ce] when the year is at jiayin.51, the 
accumulation is 9455 years.
The reference to a date in the late second century makes it plain that the state -
ment just translated cannot date from the time when the Han Quarter Remainder 
was promulgated in 85 ce. The year named is however precisely the year when 
Liu Hong is first said to have been officially consulted on an astronomical topic: 
see Chapter 5, § 73. It therefore seems likely that this text is part of the editorial 
contributions of Cai Yong and Liu Hong.
9455 = 157 × 60 + 35
and 35 + 17 = 52
Thus, as usual, the ‘accumulation’ which ‘exhausts’ a given year includes both 
the initial and final years of the interval specified.
This High Origin fell at the winter solstice at midnight beginning December 15, 
9782 
bce (as usual, in the proleptic Julian calendar), local Luoyang time 
(JD −1 ,668,469.81250). This was also the moment of the (mean) luni-solar con -
junction beginning the first Celestial month. The day then beginning was jiazi.1, 
and the sexagenary name of the year was, as noted here, gengchen.17.

These conditions will repeat at intervals of Origin Factor [4560] years, so that two 
Origins later we find a closer Origin (though not a ‘High Origin’) at the winter 
solstice of late 162 bce. This is the Origin referred to in section § 14. As noted there, 
we need to use the High Origin as our starting point if we wish to calculate lunar 
eclipses and planetary motions, since it is only at the High Origin that we find all 
the luni-solar Origin conditions fulfilled, together with conjunctions of all five 
planets with the sun, and a lunar eclipse at the next full moon. See section § 85 
for a calculation of the interval at which High Origin conditions will repeat.

The material that follows appears to be by the compiler of the monograph now 
included in the Hou Han shu, Sima Biao. He gives a brief outline of the changing 
system origins used in the past, and explains his decision to include the work of 
Cai Yong and Liu Hong in his text.

歷載彌久，暨於黃帝， 班示文章， 重黎記註， 象應著名， 始終相驗， 準度追元，
乃立曆數．

the Two Emblems [Yin  and Yang]. So the distinction between the Two 
Emblems is from long ago. Then there was Sovereign [Fu] Xi; when 
Sovereign Xi held all under Heaven, there was as yet no writing or reck -
oning. As the sequence of years went on and on, it came to Huang Di, 
who first made known written texts. Then Chongli [= Zhuanxu] made 
records and annotations, and set out names in correspondence to the phe -
nomena, so that beginning and end were checked against one another, and 
by measured steps [sc. du] one could go back to the Origin. Thereupon 
he set up the reckonings of the [astronomical] system.

The Han Quarter Remainder system  233
the present, there were changes and innovations in each [period], and they 
did not follow a consistent practice. Thus when the Yellow Emperor made 
his system, the Origin started from xinmao.28, but Zhuanxu used yimao.52, 
Yu [i.e. Emperor Shun 舜] used wuwu.55, Xia used bingchen.53, Yin used 
jiayin.51, Zhou used dingsi.54, and [the state of] Lu used gengzi.37. When 
Han arose it carried on from Qin, and at first used yimao.52. When it came 
to the Yuanfeng period of Wudi, it did not fit together with Heaven, and thus 
gentlemen who were able in reckoning made the Grand Inception system, 
which had its origin at dingchou.14. At the interface with [the reign of] 
Wang Mang, Liu Xin made the Triple Concordance [system], which went 
back 31 Origins before the Taichu, to obtain a year in which the Five Planets 
were in conjunction at gengxu.17, and took that to be the High Origin.
The sexagenary numbers given are those of the years of system origin of the 
systems supposedly used by the ruler or state named. We have no clear reference 
to any one these systems before the later part of the Western Han, and it may 
be that they are simply later reconstructions rather than ancient survivals. Those 
for the Yellow Emperor, Zhuanxu (and hence early Han, as was thought), Yin , 
Zhou and the state of Lu are as found in other sources such as ( Qutan Xida 瞿
曇悉達 c. 725 
ce: chapter 105), but the year more commonly given for Xia is 
yichou.2. I do not know of another early statement of the system origin ascribed 
to Emperor Shun. Whatever these systems may have been, there is general agree-
ment that all of them were of the Quarter Remainder type. Thus their use of  
different origins did not change the intervals between (say) successive winter 
solstices and luni-solar conjunctions, but only (in effect) introduced slight 
displacements in the timing of such events between one such system and 
another.
The Grand Inception system, which was not a Quarter Remainder system, had 
its origin in 104 
bce, which was indeed a dingchou.14 year according to the reck-
oning of years used from the Eastern Han onwards, and the Triple Concordance 
developed from it by Liu Xin had a High Origin in 143,231  bce, a gengxu.17 year 
by the same reckoning.
太初曆到章帝元和， 旋復疏闊， 徵能術者課校諸曆， 定朔稽元， 追漢 
(三)[四]十五年庚辰之歲， 追朔一日， 乃與天合， 以為四分曆元． 加六百五元
一紀， 上得庚申． 有近於緯， 而歲不攝提， 以辨曆者得開其說， 而其元尠與緯
同， 同則或不得於天． 然曆之興廢， 以疏密課， 固不主於元．

[84–86 ce], it in turn had become inaccurate. Those with subtle ability in

to the Yuanfeng period of Wudi, it did not fit together with Heaven, and thus 
gentlemen who were able in reckoning made the Grand Inception system, 
which had its origin at dingchou.14. At the interface with [the reign of] 
Wang Mang, Liu Xin made the Triple Concordance [system], which went 
back 31 Origins before the Taichu, to obtain a year in which the Five Planets 
were in conjunction at gengxu.17, and took that to be the High Origin.
The sexagenary numbers given are those of the years of system origin of the 
systems supposedly used by the ruler or state named. We have no clear reference 
to any one these systems before the later part of the Western Han, and it may 
be that they are simply later reconstructions rather than ancient survivals. Those 
for the Yellow Emperor, Zhuanxu (and hence early Han, as was thought), Yin , 
Zhou and the state of Lu are as found in other sources such as ( Qutan Xida 瞿
曇悉達 c. 725 
ce: chapter 105), but the year more commonly given for Xia is 
yichou.2. I do not know of another early statement of the system origin ascribed 
to Emperor Shun. Whatever these systems may have been, there is general agreement that all of them were of the Quarter Remainder type. Thus their use of 
different origins did not change the intervals between (say) successive winter 
solstices and luni-solar conjunctions, but only (in effect) introduced slight 
displacements in the timing of such events between one such system and 
another.
The Grand Inception system, which was not a Quarter Remainder system, had 
its origin in 104 
bce, which was indeed a dingchou.14 year according to the reckoning of years used from the Eastern Han onwards, and the Triple Concordance 
developed from it by Liu Xin had a High Origin in 143,231 bce, a gengxu.17 year 
by the same reckoning.

reckoning checked and compared all the systems, fixing the conjunctions 
and seeking the Origin, going back to the 45th year of Han, a gengchen.17 
year, where they moved back the conjunction one day, whereupon it fitted 
in with Heaven, and they took that as the Origin for the Quarter Remainder 
system.
[^25] Adding on 605 Origins [4560 years] and 1 Era [1520 years], 
they reached up to gengshen.57 [in 276,0481 bce]. This was near to the 
Wefts,[^26] but the year was not sheti [= one ending in yin 寅]. This gave an 
opening to those who disputed about systems. However, their Origins were 
scarcely in accord with the Wefts, and when they were in accord they did 
not succeed so far as the Heavens [were concerned]. For the success or 
failure of an [astronomical] system depends on a check of its accuracy, 
and is certainly not ruled by the [choice of] Origin.

tion Cai Yong, and the Palace Gentleman Liu Hong added to and continued 
the Monograph on the Pitchpipes and [Astronomical] System [from the Han 
shu]. Yong was able in setting out writings, and in the tuning of bells and 
pitchpipes, while Hong was able in calculations, and in giving an ordered 
account of the Three Luminaries. Now I have examined and evaluated their 
work: its ideas are broad and general, and [the details of] numerical procedures 
are succinct and complete. Therefore I have collected their notes into a first 
and second chapter, and have let them serve as a continuation of the Former 
Treatise, in order to show their point of view.

4.1  INTRODUCTION
4.1.1  Liu Hong and his work
Liu Hong 劉洪 (c. 130–c. 210 ce) was an expert on mathematical astronomy and 
harmonics at the court of the Eastern Han 漢 dynasty (25–220 ce). Writing around 
220–227 ce, the mathematician and astronomer Xu Yue 徐岳 paid him the compli-
ment of saying, ‘Since the time of Liu Xin 劉歆 (c. 50 bce–23 ce) there has been 
no-one equal to Liu Hong’ ( Jin shu 17, 500). Since Liu Xin was amongst other 
things the creator of the Triple Concordance system translated in Chapter 2, this 
was equivalent to rating Liu Hong as one of the foremost astronomical experts of 
about two and a half centuries. The regard in which Liu Hong was held by his con-
temporaries can be seen in the way his opinion was often sought during the debates 
on relevant issues that took place at court during his lifetime (see chapter 5, and 
Cullen (forthcoming) chapter 7).
Liu Hong is the first Chinese astronomer who has left us a complete theory 
of the moon taking into account lunar motion in latitude, as well as the moon’s 
first inequality of motion in longitude. This is set out in his Qian xiang li 乾象曆 
‘Uranic Manifestation [astronomical] system’, which appears to have come down 
to us in its entirety. There is no reason to doubt that this is not only the earliest 
surviving full lunar theory from China, but also the earliest actually created there 
(Cullen, Christopher 2002). The quite detailed discussions of related questions 
in ancient Chinese sources do not refer to any work of this level of detail and 
precision pre-dating Liu Hong, although in the late first century 
ce Jia Kui 賈逵 
did discuss variations in the speed of the moon, and gave a good estimate of the 
monthly displacement of the position of maximum lunar speed (see section 5.3.9).

Liu Hong lived under the Eastern Han dynasty, which had used the Han si fen

236 The Uranic Manifestation system
worked for more than 20 years to develop it (Jin shu 17, 499). His work seems to 
have excited some interest, since we are told that the great scholar Zheng Xuan 鄭
玄 (127–200 ce), his near contemporary, wrote a commentary on it (Hou Han shu 
35, 1212). Once again we see that a reputation for deep learning in the classics did 
not exclude numeracy and an understanding of technical matters at a very high 
level. There was at least one other commentary, by Gan Ze 闞澤 (?–243 
ce), and 
this was still extant when the biographical chapter of the Sui shu was compiled 
around 650 ce (Sui shu 34, 1022). Both commentaries are now completely lost – 
apart, perhaps, from one fragment that appears to have been intruded into the text 
translated here; see Proc. 4.74.
When the Han dynasty fell apart into the so-called Three Kingdoms, the south-
ern state of Wu 吳 (222–280 
ce) adopted the Qian xiang li as its official astronomi-
cal system (San guo zhi 47, 1129). The Qian xiang li continued in use until the end 
of the Three Kingdoms period when Wu was absorbed into a temporarily re-unified 
Chinese state under the Jin 晉.
A unique but apparently fairly complete text of the Qian xiang li is given in 
the monograph on mathematical harmonics and astronomy in the Jin Shu 晉書 
‘History of the Jin dynasty [265–419 
ce]’ completed by Fang Xuanling 房玄齡 
c. 648 ce.
4.1.3  The structur e of the system
Like all early Chinese astronomical systems, the Qian xiang system begins by 
describing conditions at a ‘system origin’ li yuan 曆元 some considerable time 
before the period in which the system was actually in operation, when all con -
ditions are supposed to have been at their initial state. Liu Hong’s term for this 
point is shang yuan 上元 ‘High Origin’. Liu Hong’s High Origin is equivalent to 
midnight, local Luoyang time, beginning January 21, 7172 
bc, JD −898,129.812. 
This instant was chosen to ensure that the system worked well in Liu Hong’s day; 
it was not claimed that ‘origin’ conditions had been fulfilled at that actual moment 
in the remote past, since it was commonly acknowledged that a given astronomical 
system would only work well for a limited range of centuries. The basic structure 
of Liu Hong’s calculations follows the usual pattern of counting off whole cycles 
from the High Origin, and thus finding at what stage in the relevant cycle (solar, 
lunar or planetary) one stands at any given date. The numbers used are slightly dif-
ferent from those used in previous systems; in some cases, particularly in planetary 
motion, they borrow directly from the Han Quarter Remainder, with minor adjust-
ments allowing for the changes in basic luni-solar constants. The major innovation 
in the Uranic Manifestation system lies in its highly complex treatment of lunar 
phenomena, in which Liu Hong appears to be entirely original.
On the basis of the bare text before us it is not impossible to understand just what 
is to be done at each stage of the calculations, but it is not always easy, particularly 
when Liu Hong’s procedures are without precedent in previous systems. The text 
makes no substantive attempt to explain why the given procedures should work, 
or to explain how the data on which they are based were gathered.

The Uranic Manifestation system 237
4.1.4  Organisation of the text
The text begins with a statement of the system origin. It continues with a list of 
basic solar and lunar constants, which leads into instructions for calculating the 
basic data needed for a civil calendar – the beginnings of lunar months, the main 
events in the solar cycle and insertion of intercalary months. Then we are told how 
to calculate the positions of sun and moon in the system of 28 lodges, and when 
lunar eclipses will occur. We then have a note on which hexagrams of the Book of 
Change and which of the Five Phases govern each time of the year.
We then conclude with a method for finding when in a given day any solar or 
lunar event will occur, either with reference to the 12 double-hours or with refer-
ence to the 100 ke into which the running of a clepsydra divided the day. There 
is then a very brief, almost cryptic, reference to how motion with reference to the 
ecliptic may be referred to the equator – clearly based on the method set out by 
Zhang Heng earlier in the second century 
ce.1
Next we move into sections whose content is unprecedented in earlier systems, 
in which we are told how to calculate the true, rather than the mean motion of the 
moon. First there is a table of the cyclical variation in lunar speed, followed by a 
set of further lunar constants, and then a detailed sequence of calculations. These 
enable us to find out where the true moon (rather than the mean moon) is at any 
moment, and when it will be in conjunction with the sun. Next we are told how the 
moon’s distance from the ecliptic may be calculated. As before, we have a table, 
more constants, and methods of calculation set out in sequence. There are strong 
signs that Liu Hong may have succeeded in applying the methods he sets out for 
calculating true lunar positions to the prediction of a solar eclipse that took place 
on November 27, 178 
ce, and of which it was said2:
熹平之際， 時洪為郎， 欲改四分， 先上驗日蝕 . . . 事御之後如洪言， 海內
識真， 莫不聞見， 劉歆以來， 未有洪比.
In the Xiping reign period (172–177 ce), when Hong was a court gentleman, 
he wanted to reform the Quarter Remainder system, so he first checked [his 
methods] into the future by a solar eclipse .  . . . When the reports came in 
they were as Hong had said. Everybody in the empire recognized the truth of 
it, and there was nobody who did not hear or see. Since the time of Liu Xin, 
there has been nobody like Hong.
(Jin shu 17, 1994)
After all this, and a restatement of the date of system origin, we are given a fairly 
conventional set of constants and calculation methods for finding the motions of 
the five planets. In many cases, it becomes clear that the data used for the planets

2 See Cullen (forthcoming) chapter 7.

it today assumes that its reader will use data from the Han Quarter Remainder.
4.1.5   The   question   of   ‘months’  and   the   finding   
of true lunar motion
As already noted, in translating the Triple Concordance and Han Quarter Remain-
der systems, I have only rendered the term yue 月 as ‘month’ (sometimes ‘lunar 
month’) when it refers to the unit of civil time measurement consisting of a whole 
number of days, either 29 or 30, with its first day ideally containing the moment 
of conjunction between sun and moon. When however yue refers to the period 
of time that begins with the instant of one conjunction and ends at the instant of 
the next, I translate it as ‘lunation’, or ‘mean lunation’ (given that a fixed length 
of the lunation is used in these two systems) rather than using the modern terms 
‘synodic month’, or ‘mean synodic month’. A modern value for the mean synodic 
month is 29.53059 days.
In the Uranic Manifestation system, the situation becomes more complicated, 
since this system goes beyond the other two systems, in that it provides means for 
dealing with:
(a) The varying speed of the moon in its apparent orbit. In modern terms, we 
may say that Liu Hong only attempts to deal with the moon’s ‘equation of 
centre’ (or ‘first inequality’ or ‘elliptic inequality’), the variation in its speed 
caused by the fact that the moon’s orbit round the earth is an ellipse. This 
is however by far the largest factor in the moon’s departure from mean 
motion, and leads to its speed varying from about 12° per day to over 14.5° 
over a period of about 27½ days – see below.
4
(b) The moon’s varying latitude, i.e. its changing distance to north and south 
of the ecliptic, caused by the slight (about 5°) inclination of its orbit to the 
plane of the ecliptic.
By considering these factors, Liu Hong is able to calculate the moon’s true ( ding 
定, more literally ‘corrected’) position at any moment, and thus to find the instants 
of true rather than mean conjunction of sun and moon.
5 Moreover, his ability to 
estimate the moon’s distance from the ecliptic at the true conjunction makes it

In modern terms, such discussions require consideration of three other periods 
in addition to the mean synodic month:6
1 The anomalistic month: this is the period between the moon’s returns to 
perigee, the point in its orbit where it is closest to the earth and thus moves 
fastest. It is the length of the cycle of the largest variation in lunar speed, 
the ‘equation of centre’ mentioned above. A modern value for the mean 
length of this period is 27.55455 days, the mean anomalistic month.
2 The nodical (or nodal, or draconitic) month: this is the interval between two 
crossings of the ecliptic in the same direction by the moon as it moves in 
its apparent orbit, inclined about 5° to the ecliptic. It is therefore the period 
with which the moon’s latitude varies. The two crossing points are known 
as ‘nodes’: the node through which the moon moves northwards is called 
the ‘ascending node’ and the other is the ‘descending node’. A modern value 
for the mean length of this period is 27.21222 days, the mean nodical month.
3 The sidereal month: this is the interval at which the moon returns to the 
same position relative to the background of the stars, or more strictly speak -
ing relative to a non-rotating frame of reference – for our purposes this 
distinction can be ignored, since there was no concept of stellar proper 
motion in the period we are discussing, and the stars were taken as fixed 
relative to the heavens. A modern value for the mean length of this period 
is 27.32166 days, the mean sidereal month.
These modern terms do not however correspond precisely to those that Liu Hong 
uses in the relevant parts of his system. The first, the anomalistic month, has a 
fairly close match, but the period in question is not referred to as a month, but as a 
li 曆. We may render li in this case using one of the basic meanings of this word, 
‘sequence’; it refers to a tabulation of the varying speed of the moon over a series 
of days that we are told to ‘enter’ ru 入 at the appropriate point to find the values 
we need. At one point this ‘sequence’ is described as the chi ji li 遲疾曆 ‘Speed 
Sequence’ (literally ‘slowing and speeding up sequence’), a term I have adopted 
in my explanations of the relevant procedures. The sequence consists of 27 whole 
days, and a fractional part of 3303/5969 days, equivalent to a total 27.55336 days, 
which is not far from the modern value for the anomalistic month.

When we look for an equivalent to the nodical month, the situation is at first sight 
quite puzzling. We are given a table for use in finding (in modern terms) lunar 
latitude, with the title yin yang li 陰 陽 曆 ‘yin yang sequence’. Since ‘yin’ in this 
context designates movement in latitude north of the ecliptic and ‘yang’ repre -
sents motion in latitude to the south, I have called this the ‘Latitude Sequence’. 
The length of this sequence is tabulated as 13 whole days, plus a fractional part 
of (5203/7874) days, and it becomes evident that the table represents one half 
of a complete latitude cycle. That implies that the complete cycle would be 27 + 
(2532/7874) days – which will be recognized as the value given above for the 
sidereal month, equivalent to 27.32156 days, rather than the nodical month of 
27.21222 days. At first sight, this seems a grave error on Liu Hong’s part. However, 
as we shall see, the ‘days’ of the latitude sequence are not in fact units of time, but 
rather spatial divisions on the moon’s path from one node to the next, on the basis 
that the complete orbit from a given node and back again is divided into the same 
number of ‘days’ as (in modern terms) the sidereal month. Liu Hong then allows 
separately for the fact that the nodes are not fixed relative to the ecliptic, but shift 
along it in a westerly direction, so that at any given moment the moon will be 
slightly further advanced through the latitude sequence than it would have been 
if the nodes were stationary. As a result of this, the interval between passages of 
the moon through a complete cycle of latitude is slightly decreased, falling from 
27.32156 days to 27.21215 days, a much better approximation to the mean nodical 
month. All this will be explained in detail in the comments on the relevant sections 
of the translation that follows.

4.2.1  [System origin]
上元己丑以來， 至建安十一年丙戍，歲積七千三百七十八年.
Proc. 4.1. [Years elapsed since system origin]:
§1  From the High Origin jichou.26 to the eleventh year of the Jian’an period 
[206–207 ce] bingxu.23, the year accumulation is 7378 years.
What exactly is meant by the ‘year accumulation’ of 7378 years referred to here? 
If this means the number of years elapsed between the winter solstice at system 
origin and the winter solstice preceding the civil year that begins in spring 206 ce, 
then it ought to produce an increase in the sexagenary number of the year by 
57, taking it from 26 to (26 + 57) – 60 = 23.
But in fact, 7378 = 122 × 60 + 58.
Obviously, therefore, for Liu Hong the ‘year accumulation’ in a given year is not 
the number of years that separate the beginning of that year from the beginning 
of the High Origin year, but is one year larger – so that it is the ordinal number of 
the given year, counting the first year of the system as number one. The system 
origin is therefore at the winter solstice 7377 years preceding the year 206 − 7377 − 1 
= 7172 
bce (the extra 1 subtracted allows for the fact that we are using historical 
dating in which there is no year zero, rather than astronomical dating). The 
solstice in question, as reckoned by the Qian xiang system, can be shown to 
correspond in the Julian calendar to local midnight at Luoyang, January 21, 
7172 
bce, JD −898,129.81250, which was also the instant of mean luni-solar 
conjunction at the start of the first Celestial month, and the beginning of a 
jiazi.1 day.

乾法， 千一百七十八．
§2 Uranic Factor 1178.
This is the number of years from High Origin after which winter solstice, midnight, 
mean conjunction of first Celestial month, and day number first repeat their 
initial coincidence.
會通， 七千一百七十一．
§3  Coincidence Compatibility 7171.

This is the number of days in which Extinction Factor [103] ‘extinctions’ of the 
day fraction occur. It is (Circuits of Heaven [215,130]) / 30. Circuits of Heaven is 
defined in section § 5; it is the number of days in Era Factor [589] years. For Era

What is an extinction? To find the number of days in a solar cycle (the interval 
from one winter solstice to the next), we calculate:
(Circuits of Heaven [215,130]) / (Era Factor [589])
= 365 + 145/589
= 6 × 60 + 3090/589
So every year we get a contribution of 3090/589 days to increasing the day 
number. In Era Factor [589] years that amounts to an extra 3090 days, which is 
the Remainder Number (see section § 10). Since 3090 = 60 × 51 + 30, an interval 
of Era Factor [589] years clearly increases winter solstice day number by 30.
We may calculate the increase in day number per day as:
(3090/589) × (589/215,130) = 3090/215,130
Now 3090 = 30 × 103
And 215,130 = 30 × 7171
So 3090/215,130 = 103/7171
Thus in 7171 days, the figure given here as Coincidence Compatibility, we have 
increased day number by precisely 103 – i.e. there have been 103 ‘extinctions’ 
of the fractional part. 103 is the Extinction Factor; see section § 12.

Proc. 4.4. To predict the next month:
§35  Add to the Greater Remainder 29, and to the Lesser Remainder 773. If  
the Lesser Remainder fills the Day Factor [1457], let that go with the 
Greater Remainder. If the Lesser Remainder is upwards of 684, the month 
is long.
As noted above, the number of days in one lunation is:
Compatibility Factor [43,026]/Day factor [1457] = 29 + 773/1457
Thus, suppose we have a month commencing with a conjunction having a given 
Greater Remainder and Lesser Remainder. To find the next conjunction, we add 
29 days to the Greater Remainder to obtain whole days, and 773 parts to the 
Lesser Remainder, to obtain the number of 1/1457 days to be added to the whole 
days. Since 1457 = 773 + 684, a whole extra day will be produced if the Lesser 
Remainder is equal to or greater than 684, and hence to reach the day of the 
next conjunction we must then count 30 days forward rather than 29, and the 
month whose conjunction we have previously calculated will be long.
Example:
Let us start from the month whose first day has just been calculated, which had 
Greater Remainder 36 and Lesser Remainder 294.
So for the next month the Greater Remainder is found from:
36 + 29 = 65
But since the Greater Remainder is a guide to how far we are to move forward 
through the sexagenary cycle, we cast out multiples of 60, to give a Greater 
Remainder of 5, and the Lesser Remainder is 294 + 773 = 1067.
Thus the cyclical day of the start of the next month is
jiazi.1 + 5 = jisi.6

Since the fractional part (‘the Lesser Remainder’) is 1067 > 684, this next month 
is a ‘long’ month, i.e. it will have 30 days rather than 29. The reason for this is 
immediately apparent if we calculate the day when the month after this one 
starts. As before, we add 29 to the Greater Remainder to obtain:
5 + 29 = 34
But this time, when we add 773 to the Lesser Remainder, we obtain:
1067 + 773 = 1840 = 1457 + 383
and 1457 represents one whole day at this scale of calculation.
So we increase the Greater Remainder by a further day to 35, making a 
30-day increase of cyclical days rather than 29 – hence the present month 
is long, since we have to wait 30 days from its first day to the first day of 
the next month, which will fall on jihai.36. This is of course the first day of the 
first month of the civil year of Jian’an 11 according to Liu Hong’s system (Janu -
ary 27, 206 
ce).
This agrees with the prediction of the Han Quarter Remainder system. The true 
conjunction nearest to the start of this month occurred around 01:00 Luoyang 
on January 27 (equivalent to JD 1,796,325.23009).
The remaining Lesser Remainder of 383 calculated here indicates that the con -
junction was expected 383/1457 day after midnight, i.e. at about 06:18. But of 
course what Liu Hong is calculating at this stage is just the mean conjunction. 
His correction to find the true conjunction will come later.

Proc. 4.6. To seek the 24 qi:
§37   Set out the Lesser Remainder of the winter solstice. Add to the Greater 
Remainder 15, to the Lesser Remainder 515, letting what fills 2356 go with 
the Greater Remainder, and count off according to the factor.
Now the number of days from one winter solstice to the next is 365 + 145/589. 
Since there are 24 qi from one winter solstice to the next, the number of days 
between qi is:
(365 + 145/589) / 24 days = 215,130 / (24 × 589)
= 215,130/14,136
= 15 + 3090/14,136
15 + 515/2356
Hence the figures given above.

The day begins at midnight, and is divided into 100 ke. Since a given Lesser 
Remainder represents (Lesser Remainder) / (Day Factor [1457]) of a day, we may 
find the time after midnight at which the calculated phase falls from
(100 ke) × (Lesser Remainder) / (Day Factor [1457]),
as specified here. The unexpired portion of the night clepsydra is the length of 
night remaining after midnight, and by comparing this with the result just cal -
culated we can find whether or not the phase in question falls during the hours 
of darkness, or whether it takes place during daylight. However, since Liu Hong 
does not tell us how to find the night length at the various seasons of the year, 
so unless there was once such a table which has not been preserved, we pre-
sumably have to make use of the table provided by the Han Quarter Remainder; 
see section 3.2.9.
The figure of ‘401 or less’ for the lesser remainder originates as follows. According 
to the Han Quarter Remainder tabulation, at the winter solstice maximum night 
length occurs, and is 55 ke. Half of this, 27½ ke, falls after midnight. In Lesser Remain-
der terms, this amounts to (27.5/100) × 1457 = 401 to the nearest whole number.
If the Lesser Remainder is greater than this, the phase cannot fall during the 
night centering on the given midnight at any time of the year. It seems strange 
that we are not told how to deal with the case of the phase falling late enough 
in the day for it to fall within the darkness commencing that evening.
推沒
置入紀年， 外所求， 以餘數乘之， 滿紀法為積沒， 有餘加盡積為一． 以會通
乘之， 滿沒法為大餘， 不盡為小餘． 大餘命以紀， 算外， 冬至後沒日． 求次沒, 
加大餘六十九， 小餘六十四， 滿其法從大餘， 無分為滅．
Proc. 4.9. To predict extinctions [of day fraction]:
§40   Set out the years into the Era Cycle, with the [year] sought outside. Multiply 
by the Remainder Number [3090]. What fills the Era Factor [589] is accu -
mulated extinctions. If there is a remainder, add to the exhausted accumula-
tions to make one [more]. Multiply by Coincidence Compatibility [7171]. 
What fills the Extinction Divisor 103 makes the Greater Remainder, and 
what is not exhausted makes the Lesser Remainder. Count off the Greater 
Remainder according to the Era Cycle, and what is outside the count is the 
extinction day after the winter solstice. To seek the next extinction, add 69 
to the Greater Remainder, and to the Lesser Remainder 64. What fills its 
factor goes with the Greater Remainder, and when there is no fractional 
part [the fractional remainder] has been wiped out.
The quotient (Remainder Number) / (Era divisor) is 3090/589 = 5 + 145/589, 
which is the excess of year length over 360 days.

Since 360 = 6 × 60, if this quotient is multiplied by the number of years elapsed, 
the integral part of the result is the amount by which the cyclical day number 
of the winter solstice preceding the start of the year has increased compared 
with the day number of the initial winter solstice.
As for the next part of the calculation, its aim is to find how many days elapse 
until the fractional remainder just calculated is ‘extinguished’. The thinking 
works like this: Each year generates a remainder over 360 days of 3090/589 
days. But one year has 215,130/589 days. Therefore the number of days to 
generate one full day of this fractional remainder – an ‘extinction’ – is 
(215,130/589) / (3090/589) days, which on simplification becomes (7171/103) 
days. This is in fact (Coincidence Compatibility [7171]) / (Extinction Factor [103]): 
see section § 3.

Proc. 4.10. To predict the du of the sun:
§41   Multiply accumulated days by the Era Factor [589]. Remove what fills Circuits 
of Heaven [215,130]. From what remains cast out Era Factor [589], and the 
[number of these] obtained is du. Count off the du starting from 5 du before 
Ox, and cast out the successive lodges. What does not fill a lodge is where 
the sun is located at midnight at the Celestial Standard Conjunction.
Accumulated Days is the number of days from High Origin to the midnight com-
mencing the first day of the first month of the Celestial count before the current 
year – which is the 11th Anthropic month of the preceding year.
The sun moves 1 du per day, so the number of du in a complete circuit of the 
heavens is the same as the number of days in the year.
Thus in Era Factor [589] years, the sun moves Circuits of Heaven [215,130] du, 
and the complete circuit made from one winter solstice to the next is 
215,130/589 du.
The procedure above casts this out, and leaves the number of du moved since 
the last winter solstice. We then successively cast out the whole du in each lodge, 
starting from the position of the sun at winter solstice, here taken as 5 du before 
the start of the lodge Ox, and thus arrive at the du of the lodge in which the 
sun is located at midnight preceding the conjunction.

Proc. 4.11. To seek the next day:
§42   Add one du. If this passes through Dipper, take off the parts. If the fractional 
part is too small, then take off one du and make it one Era Factor [589], 
and add it on.
All the lodge widths are whole numbers of du apart from Dipper, which in this 
system will have a fractional part 145/587 du since that is the fractional part of the 
year length and the sun moves 1 du daily. Clearly if the fractional part of solar 
motion is less than 145/589 and the length of Dipper is to be subtracted, one will 
have to ‘borrow’ a whole du and add 589 to the numerator of the fraction before 
the subtraction to find the fractional part of the sun’s position within its lodge.

off as above, then this is the du where the moon is located at midnight at

day, the day fraction scaled up by Era Factor [589] represents the distance in du 
moved by the sun between midnight and conjunction scaled up by 589. So by

moved by the sun between midnight and conjunction scaled up by 589. So by 
adding this to the du of the sun at midnight and scaling appropriately, we have 
the position where sun and moon coincide. As seen above, the fractional part 
of the sun’s midnight du will be scaled by Era Factor [589], so the scales are 
compatible.
求次月
加度二十九， 大分三百一十二， 小分二十(五)[三],9 小分滿會數從大分， 大分
滿紀法後度， 經斗除大分．
Proc. 4.15. To seek the next month:
§46 Add to the du 29, and Greater Parts 312, with Lesser Parts 23. As the Lesser 
Parts fill Coincidence Number 47 let it go with the Greater Parts, and as 
the Greater Parts fill the Era Factor [589] let that go with the du. As you 
pass through Dipper, take off [its] Greater Parts.
The length of a lunation in days is given by
(Compatibility Factor [43,026]) / (Day Factor [1457])
= 29 days 773/1457
= 29 days 773 / (47 × 31)
= 29 days 773 × 19 / (47 × 31 × 19)
= 29 days 14,687 / (47 × 31 × 19)
= 29 days 312 / (31 × 19) + 23 / (47 × 31 × 19)
So the whole days in a complete lunation are 29, the ‘Greater Parts’ are 312, 
and the ‘Lesser Parts’ are 23. Since the sun moves 1 du in a day, this is also the 
distance moved by the sun from one conjunction to the next, and since the sun 
and moon must then coincide, it is also the eastwards displacement of the moon 
from one conjunction to the next.

‘but Li’s original text has 23 for 25’. So it seems that Li Rui may have agreed with my emendation,

260 The Uranic Manifestation system
Take Circuits of Heaven [215,130], which is the number of days in a solar cycle or 
du in a complete revolution at a scale of Era Factor [589] years, and divide by 4:
215,130/4 = 53,782.5
Divide by Era Factor [589], to get:
91 du and 183.5/589,
= 91 du + 183/589 + 23.5 / (47 × 589)
This is the du in one quarter of a revolution – the displacement of the moon 
from new moon to the first crescent on the assumption that the sun does not 
move. However, the pattern of phases of the moon must shift so that for any 
given phase the moon is the required distance from the sun.
So we must add 7 du + 225/589 + 17.5 / (47 × 589), which is the distance moved 
by the sun in a quarter of a lunation, which we have already calculated (see 
Proc. 4.16).
Adding the two, we get:
98 du + 408/589 + 41 / (47 × 589)
Which is the result given in the text, and calculated above.
求日月昏明度
日以紀法， 月以月周， 乘所近節氣夜漏， 二百而一為明分． 日以減紀法， 月以
減月周， 餘為昏分． 各以加夜半， 如法為度．
Proc. 4.18. To obtain the du of the sun and moon for dusk and dawn:
§49   Multiply the night clepsydra-run of the nearest nodal qi by the Era Factor 
[589] in the case of the sun, and the Lunar Circuits [7874] in the case of 
the moon. Take one for 200 to make the dawn parts. In the case of the sun 
subtract from the Era Factor [589], and in the case of the moon subtract 
from the Lunar Circuits [7874], and the excess makes the dusk parts. In 
each case add to the midnight value, and this makes du as it accords with 
the factor [i.e. the Era Factor [589] in both cases].
The ‘night clepsydra-run’ (not actually defined in current text of the Uranic 
Manifestation system, and presumably to be adopted from the Han Quarter 
Remainder System) is the number of ke (1/100 day) from dusk of the previous 
evening until the next dawn. Half therefore falls after midnight, and half before. 
By dividing by 200 we obtain the fraction of the day represented by the period 
midnight to dawn. Assuming the sun and moon move at a steady mean rate, 
their daily motion in du is 589/589 and 7874/589. Hence the result follows from 
the calculation specified here. The ‘dusk parts’ are of course the interval from 
midnight to the dusk of that day.

Proc. 4.19. To predict lunar eclipses:

Cast out Coincidence Years [893]. Multiply the remaining years by 
Coincidence Rate [1882]. Count one Accumulated Eclipse for each accord 
with Coincidence Years [893]. If there is a remainder, add one to the 
accumulation [of eclipses]. Multiply by Coincidence Months [11,045], 
and let the number of accords with Coincidence Rate [1882] be accu -
mulated months. What is not exhausted is the eclipse remainder. Multiply 
the remaining years by Rule Intercalations [7], and what fills Rule Years 
[19] makes accumulated intercalations. Let that be subtracted from accu -
mulated months. For the remainder, cast out Year Medial [ qi] [12] from 
it. For what is not exhausted, count off the number from the Celestial 
first month.
The basis of this section is that in Coincidence Years [893] (the number of solar 
cycles equal to Coincidence Months [11,045] = 893 × 235/19 lunations), the 
number of lunar eclipses is Coincidence Rate [1882]. Thus eclipses will follow 
one another at average intervals of 11,045/1882 = 5 1635⁄
1882 lunations.

node at intervals of 5

the full moon closer to the time when what we may call each ‘eclipse interval’ 
of 5
1635⁄1882 (= 5.8688) lunations expires.

val’ of 5
