pages.raw_text:
262 The Uranic Manifestation system
number of eclipses up to the first one in the year we are considering (since we 
start with the number of years up to the beginning of the present year).
Next, on the basis of this number of eclipses just about to be completed, we work 
out how many months will have expired from the beginning of the current period 
of Coincidence Years [893] until the next ‘eclipse interval’ expires. The ‘eclipse 
remainder’ is the fractional part of the number of months from the start of the 
period until the next ‘eclipse interval’ expires, over a denominator of 1882. If that 
amount is exactly 941, then clearly the eclipse is due halfway through the lunar 
month, just at the instant of full moon, so we may reasonably expect a good eclipse. 
On the traditional view, if the ‘eclipse remainder’ is greater than 941, then there 
will indeed be some sort of lunar eclipse at full moon, but there will also be a solar 
eclipse at the following conjunction; if the ‘eclipse remainder’ is less than 941, then 
there will indeed be some sort of lunar eclipse at full moon, but there will also be 
a solar eclipse at the preceding conjunction; if the ‘eclipse remainder’ is zero, then 
there will be a solar eclipse at the start of the month, and no lunar eclipse.
11
Finally, we work out how many months in all have elapsed since the start of the 
current period of Coincidence Years [893] up to the start of the current year, 
allowing for intercalations. What we are left with is the number of months of 
the current year clear of eclipses. The next month will contain the eclipse.
Example:
Let us try to predict the first lunar eclipse of Jian’an 11, 205–206 
ce.
Accumulated years are 7377.
Cast out Coincidence Years [893] to give ‘remaining years’: 233.
233 × 1882/893 = 491, remainder 43, so we count Accumulated Eclipses as 492.
492 × 11,045/1882 = 2887, remainder 806, so Accumulated Months is 2887, 
and Eclipse remainder is 806.
233 × 7/19 = 85, remainder 16, so accumulated intercalations is 85.
2887 − 85 = 2802
Cast out Year Medial [ qi] [12]: 2802 = 233 × 12 + 6
So the eclipse occurs in (Celestial) month 7, which is month 5 on the usual civil 
(Xia) count. Since the eclipse remainder is close to 940, we should have some 
confidence of a lunar eclipse at full moon of that month, which runs from June 2 4 
to July 22, 206 ce. This was in fact a close miss so far as a lunar eclipse was 
concerned: according to the display by Starry Night, the distance between the 
moon and the edge of the penumbra of the Earth’s shadow cone was about 
1 degree at full moon on July 8, around 03.43 local time at Luoyang.
11 See Nathan Sivin (1969) Cosmos and computation in early Chinese mathematical astronomy . 
Leiden, E. J. Brill, 46.

Proc. 4.20. To find the next eclipse:
§51   Add five months, and a month remainder of 1635. Obtain one month if this 
fills Coincidence Rate [1882]. Take the full moon of the month.
As noted above, lunar eclipses follow on another at the interval 51635⁄

4.2.6  [Pr edicting hexagrams and phases in effect]
推卦用事日
– 509 –
因冬至大餘， 倍其小餘， 坎用事日也． 加小餘千七十五， 滿乾法從大餘， 中孚
用事日也．
Proc. 4.21. To predict which hexagram will be in effect:
§52   Start from the Greater Remainder of winter solstice, and double its Lesser 
Remainder. That is the day when [the hexagram] kan 坎 will be in effect. 
Add to the Lesser Remainder 1075, and let what fills the Uranic Factor 
[1178] go with the Greater Remainder, and that will be the day when [the 
hexagram] zhongfu 中孚 will be in effect.
The length of the solar cycle is 365 + 145/589 days = 365 + 290/1178 days; see 
section § 5).
Li Rui explains the parallels between this and the methods of Jing Fang 京房 
(77–37 bce), which were based on the Quarter Remainder system type (Li Rui 
李銳 (1768–1817) 1993: 779–780). In Jing Fang’s scheme, based on a solar 
cycle 365¼ days long, the four hexagrams Kan, Li, Zhen and Rui were allocated 
to short periods at the solstices and equinoxes and are in effect for 73/80 day 
each. The other 60 were each given equal time allocations of 6 + 7/80 day 
each, except for Yi, Jin, Jing and Da Yu whose time is reduced by 73/80 day 
each to allow space for Kan, Li, Zhen and Rui, and thus get only get 5 + 14/80 
day each.

As Li Rui explains, the solar cycle is divided into five equal periods, one allocated 
to each of the Five Phases. The length of time allocated to each phase is thus:
(days in the solar cycle) / 5
= (Circuits of Heaven 215,130/Era Factor 589) / 5 days
= (860,520/2356) / 5 days
= 73 + 116/2356 days.
The cycle begins at Establishment of Spring, lichun 立春 when Wood comes into 
effect, to be followed by Fire from the Establishment of Summer, lixia 立夏, Metal 
from the Establishment of Autumn, liqiu 立秋, and Water from Establishment of 
Winter, lidong 立冬, after which we are once more at Establishment of Spring, 
returning to the phase Wood. So four of the phases are linked with the four 
seasons. But where is Earth? The time allocated to Earth is in fact divided up into 
four sections, with these quarter-phases being placed at the end of each of the 
four main phases. Thus, after the 73 + 116/2356 days of Wood, there will be a 
period of length
(73 + 116/2356 days) / 4
= 18 + 618/2356 days
devoted to Earth, and similarly at the end of the Fire, Metal and Water phases. 
In other calendrical sources, this period is labelled tu wang yong shi 土王用事 
‘Reign of Earth in Effect’.
12 Later divinatory texts state that the earth should not 
be disturbed by digging during these periods, but I do not know of an early 
imperial source for this. The earliest discussion of the placing of the earth phase 
in all seasons known to me is found in Bai hu tong de lun  白虎通德論 (Compre-
hensive discussions on Virtue in the White Tiger [Hall]), supposedly edited by 
Ban Gu from records of discussions in 79 
ce, although some scholars have sug -
gested a third-century date for the text. 13
The procedure given above starts our count from the start of the Reign of 
Earth after the end of the Water phase preceding the start of Wood at Estab -
lishment of Spring. To find when this is, given that we will have calculated 
when Winter Solstice falls before the start of this year, we make use of the 
fact that the interval of three qi from Winter Solstice to Establishment of 
Spring is:
(15 + 515/2356) × 3 days
= 45 + 1545/2356 days.

推有進退
進加退減所得也． 進退有差， 起二分度後， 率四度轉增少， 少每半者， 三而轉

Proc. 4.26. To predict when there will be advance or retardation:
§57   This is obtained from adding advance and subtracting retardation. There 
are differences in advance and retardation: beginning after the degrees of 
the two equinoxes, the rate is that with every cycle of four du one increases 
it by a quarter, and each time the quarters make up to a half, one takes a 
cycle of three. When the difference mounts up to three du one stops, and 
goes through five du, and then subtracts as before.
This is a very compressed version of a scheme commonly attributed to Zhang 
Heng 張衡 (78–139 ce).14 It is odd that this fragment has no heading, and seems 
out of sequence with the surrounding material. Nor is it used elsewhere in the 
text.
The ‘advances and retardations’ given by Zhang Heng are corrections enabling 
conversion between motion referred to the ecliptic and motion referred to the 
equator, in modern terms ‘the reduction to the equator’. They appear to be 
derived from a graphical method involving a solid sphere marked with graduated 
circles representing equator and ecliptic. Given that, the figures given are useful 
approximations to the true values, with a maximum error of about ¼ du in 
quantities whose magnitude varies from zero to 2¾ du. Each qi begins with two 
four-day periods, during each of which the advance/retardation increases by 
¼ du. After that, the advance/retardation has reached ½ du, and the next ¼ du 
is allocated to only three days. We are not told what happens to complete the qi,

A has been split into columns 1, 2 and 3; B has been split into columns 4, 5 and

Column 1 gives the number of the day of the Speed Sequence, equivalent 
to the day within the anomalistic month; apart from the fractional last day, 
these days are the same length as a solar day, but do not in general begin 
at midnight.
Columns 2 and 3 give the moon’s daily motion in du and (1/19) du, while 9 
gives it in (1/19) du. Column 7 gives the difference between column 9 and the 
mean daily motion of 254/19 du. This column is thus the first difference of 
column 8, which gives the accumulated shift of the true moon from the position 
of the mean moon. Column 4 functions as the first difference of both column 
3 and column 7, with the signs in the first place being given respectively by 
column 5, and column 6 (with the proviso that this gives the sign of change in 
the absolute size of column 7). In column 8 the entry for day 18 has been cor -
rected from 23 in the original for mathematical consistency.
The fractions in the entries for columns 1, 3, 7 and 9 in the final row, repre -
senting the part of a day at the end of the sequence, are supplied following

Circuits [164,466] at a scale of Circuit Divisor [5969], i.e. 29 + 3303/5969 day. 
The length of the Circuit Day is therefore 3303/5969 days.
Now since the accumulated deficit at the end of day 27 is given as 31, and the 
rate of increase is 19 (taking account of the signs of these quantities) the accu -
mulated deficit at the start of the fractional Cycle Day will be 31 − 19 = 12. The 
rate of increase must be such as to reduce this to zero by the end of the day, so 
that we are at the starting conditions for the cycle. So since that rate is in effect 
for only 3303/5969 days, it must be calculated as:
12 / (3303/5969)

The moon’s apparent motion seen by a terrestrial observer is highly complex. As 
mentioned in the introduction to this translation, the main component in the 
variation of its speed from the mean value is due to its elliptical orbit round the 
earth, and has a period of about 27 days. This ‘first inequality’ causes the speed 
to vary between about 12° per day and somewhat over 14½° per day. The ‘second 
inequality’ is smaller but not negligible, and causes a variation of daily speed of 
amplitude about 1.27°, with a period of about 31.8 days. Ptolemy knew of the 
first inequality from his predecessors, but appears to have been the first to describe 
the second inequality, nowadays often known as the ‘evection’. A series of smaller 
inequalities were further discovered by Tycho Brahe, Kepler and Newton.
17
Comparing the Speed Sequence with observation, we may note that the maxi -
mum speed value tabulated is set at 14 10⁄19 du per day, whereas in reality it can 
rise to more than 15 du during some orbital cycles. The minimum value of 125⁄9 du 
per day is more realistic. The smooth curve suggested by the data listed in the 
Speed Sequence, with its simple and clear maxima and minima, will not always 
represent observation very precisely, given the multiple periodic components of 
the observed speed, which will make the actual curve rather irregular and render 
it difficult to decide exactly when maxima and minima occur. See as follows for 
some comparisons of prediction with modern calculations of what was likely to 
have been observed.

amplitude about 1.27°, with a period of about 31.8 days. Ptolemy knew of the 
first inequality from his predecessors, but appears to have been the first to describe 
the second inequality, nowadays often known as the ‘evection’. A series of smaller 
inequalities were further discovered by Tycho Brahe, Kepler and Newton.

mum speed value tabulated is set at 14 10⁄19 du per day, whereas in reality it can 
rise to more than 15 du during some orbital cycles. The minimum value of 125⁄9 du 
per day is more realistic. The smooth curve suggested by the data listed in the 
Speed Sequence, with its simple and clear maxima and minima, will not always 
represent observation very precisely, given the multiple periodic components of 
the observed speed, which will make the actual curve rather irregular and render 
it difficult to decide exactly when maxima and minima occur. See as follows for 
some comparisons of prediction with modern calculations of what was likely to 
have been observed.

§70   Multiply the Greater [11,801] and Lesser [25] Fractional Parts of new moon 
motion by the accumulated months [since] High Origin. Where the Lesser 
Parts fill the Compatibility Number 31 let that go with the Greater Parts. 19 
From the Greater Parts cast out what fills the Sequence Circuits [164,466], 
and for the remainder obtain one day for each time it fills the Circuit [day] 
Divisor [5969]. What is not exhausted is the Day Remainder. Counting off 
the Days, what is outside the count is the entry into the sequence of the 
conjunction which is sought.
We are to calculate (Accumulated Months) × (11,801 + 25/31). We then cast out 
multiples of 164,466 (which evidently represents completed cycles in lunar speed), 
and then divide by 5969 to get days.
This quantity (11,801 + 25/31) represents (in modern terms) the time excess 
of a mean synodic month over an anomalistic month. It is in units such that 
164,466 represents the Speed Sequence, or one anomalistic month. Dividing 
this by 5969 converts to days. Thus it is clear that the implied length of the 
Speed Sequence is:
164,466/5969 = 27.5534 days
which may be compared with the modern value of the mean anomalistic 
month of 27.55455 days. The difference is a deficit of 0.0011 days, which 
mounts up to a deficit of 1 day in something under 1000 lunations, around 
75 years. So if the Uranic Manifestation Speed Sequence is in the correct phase 
relationship to the lunation at a given instant, it will be about a day too early 
75 years later.
Thus maxima of lunar speed will recur at the stated interval, starting at High 
Origin, which is at JD −898,129.81250 (see page 241 above).
The actual displacement of the moon along its apparent path seen by a terrestrial 
observer is complex in detail, but if we make the approximation of calculating 
the moon’s daily displacement in longitude seen from Luoyang using a NASA 
generated online ephemeris for the years 207–209 
ce it may be seen that the 
maxima predicted by the Uranic Manifestation system fall within a few days of 
the maxima of the ephemeris values during this period – bearing in mind that 
as already mentioned the observed values of lunar speed will not always show 
obvious maxima and minima.

without square brackets.

Here for the first time Liu Hong describes how to find a true value from a mean 
value. It will be recalled that the ‘Greater and Lesser Remainders’ for events in 
the lunation are respectively:
Greater Remainder: the number of days to be added onto the epochal cyclical 
day to give the cyclical day of the event;
Lesser Remainder: the fraction of a day after midnight (at a scale of 1457 = 31 × 47) 
when the event occurs.
The object is to use the lunar motion table to correct the values of these quanti -

midnight by simply adding one day: days in the Speed Sequence do not begin 
at midnight, but they have the same length as normal days.
Now if as we step our way through the sequence we find we have reached a 
total of more than 27 days and 3303/5969, we have clearly got into the next 
sequence. Simply deduct that number of days, and start again from the begin -
ning of a fresh sequence. That means we have ‘not set out the Circuit Day’, 
in that we have simply skipped over the final fractional day of the sequence 
which follows the 27th whole day, while making a deduction from the frac -
tional part of the day to allow for its existence. If however our step of one 
day takes us into the fractional ‘Circuit Day’ itself, then if we make another 
one-day step after that, we must increase the Day Remainder by (5969 − 3303) = 
2666, the Circuit Deficit, to allow for the fact that the Circuit Day is not a 
whole day.

Proc. 4.40. To seek the next sequence:
§79   Multiply the Respective Changes by the Circuit Deficit [2666]. Let what 
accords with the Circuit [Days] Divisor [5969] be the ‘Constant Numbers’. 
When the sequence comes to its end, then go on to add [these] to the 
transformation rates [found for the first sequence]. Cast out what fills the 
Respective Changes, and by this process you form the transformation rates 
for the next sequence.
The Transformation Rates found in Proc. 4.39 enabled us to rework the Speed 
Sequence table so that it was tabulated at successive ‘lunation’ midnights, should 
we so wish. Now we deal with the problem of moving past the fractional Circuit 
Day and into the next Speed Sequence. Since the Circuit Day is only 3303/5969 
day, which is 2666/5969 short of a whole day, subsequent midnights will fall 
2666/5969 further into each whole day’s worth of the next sequence. Hence we 
work out here the effect of an extra Day Remainder of 2666 in producing a 
change in the Transformation Rate. The Constant Numbers that result are simply 
an increment to be added to the Transformation Rates already calculated for the 
first sequence, so as to enable them to be used in the second sequence.
But why do we have to cast out from that sum the amount which fills the Respec-
tive Rate? The reason is simple enough. Since both Transformation Rates and 
Constant Numbers are obtained by multiplying the Respective Changes by a 
fraction of the day, then if their sum is greater than the Respective Change, that 
means the sum of the day fractions exceeded unity, and we have moved into the 
next day.

Proc. 4.41. To obtain the true du for midnight of successive days:
§80   Add or subtract the Transformation Rates according as they are additive or 
subtractive to or from the parts for each daily step [i.e. the fractions of du 
given for each day in addition to the whole du]. If the parts are excessive 
or insufficient, let Rule Years [19] leave or enter the du. Let the Compatibility 
Number [31] multiply the parts and the Remainder, and then the daily step 
is added to the midnight du to make the next day. If when you come to the 
end of the sequence you do not set out the Cycle Day, reduce the Remainder 
by 1038, then multiply by the Compatibility Number [31]. If you do set 
out the Cycle Day, then add a Remainder of 837, and 899 Lesser and Greater 
Parts to the Transformation Rates of the next sequence, and seek [results] 
step-wise as before.
In Proc. 4.38 we have already learned how to find the true position of the moon 
in du along the ecliptic at the moment of midnight before conjunction, and this 
midnight is the start of a new civil month. Here we find the distance moved to 
the next midnight position, by simply adding the appropriate tabulated daily 
amount to lunar motion from the speed table, corrected by the Transformation 
Rate for each day to allow for the fact that each midnight falls some time after 
the start of each whole day of the Speed Sequence.
As in the previous calculation of midnight du, we multiply the parts of du by 31 to 
change from a scale factor of 19 as tabulated to the usual factor of 19 × 31 = 589.
The ‘Remainder’ referred to here is the one produced in Proc. 4.38:
‘Multiply the Rate of Lessening or Increase by the [Speed Sequence] Day Remain-
der for entering the sequence at midnight. Obtain one for each time this 
accords with the Circuit [Days] Factor [5969]: what is not exhausted is the 
remainder.’
As explained there, we keep this remainder on one side, and add it to the fen if 
the amount exceeds Circuit [Days] Factor 5969.
As Li Rui explains and justifies in detail, the corrections in the second paragraph 
of the translation are necessary in order for the method sketched out here to 
work consistently if one has to pass from the end of one speed sequence to the 
next. They do not of course arise if one simply starts from scratch within a new 
speed sequence.

We now move on to (in modern terms) the problem of predicting lunar lati -
tude, which varies according to the cycle nowadays known as the nodical or 
draconitic month. As already noted, the title of this section has clearly been 
swapped with that of Proc. 4.27: the ‘Three Roads’ of the moon are to the 
north of the ecliptic, the ecliptic itself, and south of the ecliptic. Clearly there 
are not three separate complete orbits here: the expression is almost certainly 
allusive to older ideas of the moon’s ‘nine roads’ 九道 jiu dao, as discussed in 
Chapter 5.
Using modern concepts, we may say that during the cycle of the nodical month 
the moon spends half its time to the north of the ecliptic, and half to the south, 
following a path inclined at about 5° to the sun’s path, the ecliptic. The points 
of intersection of the two great circles of the solar path and the lunar path are 
the nodes, labelled as ‘ascending’ when the moon is passing from south to 
north and ‘descending’ when the moon passes from north to south. It is clearly 
these nodes that Liu Hong has in mind in the phrase jiao cuo fen tian  交錯分天 
‘Divide the heavens [in half] by its cross-overs’, i.e. the cross-overs of the lunar 
path with the ecliptic. The fact that the nodes shift steadily round the ecliptic 
from east to west is revealed by the fact that the nodical month is just over a 
tenth of a day shorter than the sidereal month. The moon re-encounters a given 
node a little before it has made a complete circuit of the stars since the previous 
encounter.
Whereas the justification of the basic constants for the lunar speed sequence 
was in part cosmological, here and in subsequent sections the argument is based 
firmly on what is known of the eclipse cycle, since eclipses can only occur when 
the latitude of the moon is small near a conjunction (producing a solar eclipse) 
or at opposition (producing a lunar eclipse). The normal modern practice is to 
speak of the sun and moon being close to the same node in the first place, or 
two opposite nodes in the second place. But since the node is not mentioned 
in subsequent discussions in this text, it seems better to avoid language of that 
kind, and speak in terms closer to the thinking that evidently underlies Liu Hong’s 
procedures.

(3)  If therefore we know when the moon leaves one of the nodes, we may 
predict its latitude by simply counting off the days along the graduations 
on the moon’s path, and noting the corresponding latitude.
(4)
  Now we begin to deal with the fact that the lunar path is not a fixed circle, 
but shifts round east to west relative to the ecliptic. For this part of the 
discussion, we treat the lunar path as coincident with the ecliptic, a procedure 
which introduces less than half a percent of error since the inclination is so 
small (cos 5° = 0.9962). We leave in place the graduations into ‘days of the 
sequence’ already made.
(5)
  Suppose then that we want to know the latitude of the moon at some interval 
after it is at a given position on its path. What we do is simply to count off 
the appropriate number of days from west to east along the graduations of 
the ‘days of the sequence’. We then allow for the motion of the nodes to 
the west by imagining the graduated path to be shifted round to the west 
by an amount of space corresponding to the westward motion of the node 
during that period, while the moon stays in place relative to the stars. The 
result will be a slight increase in the reading of ‘days of the sequence’ aligned 
with the moon. We can then read off the corresponding lunar latitude from 
the table. It is clear from this that in general in any given amount of elapsed 
time measured as a number of days, the movement of the moon along the 
graduated ‘days of the sequence’ will be a slightly greater number.

one circuit of the moon relative to the sun. So the following series of events take 
place simultaneously:
The sun makes 893 circuits west to east relative to the stars;
The moon makes 11,045 circuits west to east relative to the sun;
A given node makes 941 circuits east to west relative to the sun.
We may note from this that in 893 years or 11,045 months a node moves from 
east to west by a number of revolutions given by:
941 − 893 = 48.
On this basis it is easy to understand the significance of the quantity derived in 
part (c) of section 43, the New Moon Conjunction Fractional Parts. These relate 
to the movement of the moon relative to the ‘days of the sequence’ graduations 
from one conjunction to another, which may be calculated as follows:
Suppose the moon has just gone through a conjunction with the sun. It has to 
perform one complete circuit back to its starting point relative to the ecliptic – with 
no effect on the ‘days of the sequence’ graduation – and then move the extra distance 
to catch up with movement of the sun since the last conjunction. Since the sun 
performs 893 circuits in 11,045 synodic months, in one month the sun moves through
893/11,045 revolutions, from west to east.
But we also know that since the node moves 48 circuits in 11,045 synodic months, 
that will shift the lunar path through:
48/11,045 revolutions
As a result, from one conjunction to the next, the moon shifts relative to the day 
markings by:
893/11,045 + 48/11,045 = 941/11,045 revolutions.
Now on the lunar orbit the ‘days of the sequence’ marked round the whole 
circumference total:
215,130/7874
So the shift caused by the lunar and nodal motion from one conjunction to the 
next results in a day marking shift:
(941/11,045) × (215,130/7874)
= (215,130 × 941/11,045) / 7874
= 18,328 + 914/220, days of the sequence
Clearly then, the New Moon Conjunction Fractional Part 18,328 is the major 
component of the fractional parts of the ‘days of the sequence’ graduations (at 
a scale of 7874) by which the position of the moon shifts from one conjunction 
to the next. Although it is passed over here, 914 is named in Proc. 4.47 as the 
‘Fine Fractional Parts’ that go with it.

The calculations of Retreat Fractional Parts, Advance Fractional Parts and Differ -
ence Rate that follow in (d), (e) and (f) are similarly easy to follow:
In 893 years the node makes 48 circuits westwards. So (Since 589 = 893 × 31/47) 
in 589 years it makes 48 × 31/47 circuits. Now since one year has 215,130/589 
days, in one day the circuits it makes are:
(48 × 31/47) / (589 × 215,130/589) = (48 × 31/47) / 215,130 circuits.
As before, that can be converted to day-markings as:
(215,130/7874) × (48 × 31/47) / 215,130 days
= (48 × 31/47) / 7874
= (31 + 31/47) / 7874 days of the sequence
So 31 + 31/47 give the ‘Retreat Parts’, that is the number of (1/7874) day we 
have to add on to one day’s eastwards shift to allow for the westward (or retreat-
ing) motion of the node, and make the total shift of the moon relative to the 
‘days of the sequence’ graduations for each day of actual time elapsed. That 
deals with (d).
The addition of Lunar Circuits [7874] in (e) simply results in the addition of the 
whole day to the effect of the nodal ‘retreat’ just calculated. The Daily Advance 
Parts,
7874 + 31 + 31/47 = 7905 + 31/47
thus represents the total daily forward movement of the moon relative to the 
‘days of the sequence’ graduations, in fractional parts at a scale of 7874.
In (f), following Li Rui’s amendment, we multiply this result by 47 and divide by 
31. Thus the ‘Difference Rate’ is equal to:
(7874 + 31 + 31/47) × (47/31) = 11,986
which is equal to the number of circuit of the moon relative to the nodes in 
Coincidence Years [893], 11,045 + 941. This is as specified in the listing of con -
stants, but what purpose does it serve?
The key to this is the prescription in Proc. 4.49:
To determine entry into the sequence at midnight
Multiply the Lesser Remainder for the conjunction by the Difference Rate 
11,986. Obtain one for each accord with Fine Fractional Parts Factor 2209. 
Subtract that from the Day Remainder for entry into the sequence. If that is 
not sufficient, add Lunar Circuits [7874] and then subtract, then go back 
one day. If in going back you get to the fractional day, add that fraction. 
Simplify Fine Fractional Parts by the Coincidence Number 47 to make Lesser 
Parts. This is the entry into the sequence for the midnight on the day of 
conjunction.

In the Speed Sequence Table, the final row had no fractions in the text as it has 
been transmitted to us. Here, however, the lowest entry in column 1 in the 
transmitted text has the figure 5203, which is the length of the fractional day at 
the end of the sequence, in days of the sequence at a scale of Lunar Circuits

25 It is 
necessary in order to ensure that during the fractional day the Rate of Decrease 
and Increase is sufficient to change the Total Number (which represents latitude) 
from 11 to 0, which is the value it must have at the start of the next sequence:
 (5203/7 874) × (16 + 306/473)

that the Speed Sequence Table had its own different Lessening and Increasing

and Increase from 16 + 306/473 to 17 (the value at the start of the sequence)

zero, it is evident that we are just at the point of entry into the yang sequence

whole circuits of the sequence. If we are within the first half of the sequence, 
we are in the Yang sequence (south of the ecliptic), and in the second half we 
are in the  Yin sequence (north of the ecliptic). To convert to actual day gradua -
tions, we have to divide by 7874, as the text tells us.
As for the length of a nodical month, in 11,045 months there are 941 extra circuits 
(since there are 1882 eclipses, and each one represents a shift of one of the nodes 
to another conjunction, i.e. half a circuit), so the length of the nodical month is:
11,045 × (43,026/1457) / (11,045 + 941) = 27.212150735 days
close to the modern value of 27.212220 days.
How well does the timing of passage through the nodes fit in with modern 
calculations?
Calculating as prescribed in Liu Hong’s system, 26 the conjunction of the 12th 
civil month of Jian’an 10 (205–206 ce) falls at JD 1,796,295.92 (mean) and 
1,796,296.323 (true). This conjunction is signalled as ‘within limits’ on the yin-
yang li, and has a ‘total number’ of zero.
The tabulated latitude values from NASA are:
0205-Dec-27 00:30 1 ,796,294.208  −0.58 77836
0205-Dec-28 00:30 1 ,796,295.208   0.58 49442
So it seems that latitude would be zero (and increasing) at about 1,796,294.708: 
This is 1.2 days off the ‘mean’ prediction, and 1.6 days off the ‘true’ value. No 
eclipse occurs.
As Li Rui explains, what Liu Hong is doing is to calculate in effect the angular 
motion of the node from one luni-solar alignment (‘syzygy’) at conjunction or 
opposition to the next. This was based on the notion that a total lunar eclipse 
could be preceded and followed by a ‘just missed’ solar eclipse, and vice versa. 27 
Thus, let us take it that the moon had its syzygy exactly at a node when the 
eclipse occurred. When it gets round to its next syzygy, it misses the opposite 
node by the ‘limit’ amount and just misses the next eclipse.

Calculating as prescribed in Liu Hong’s system, 26 the conjunction of the 12th 
civil month of Jian’an 10 (205–206 ce) falls at JD 1,796,295.92 (mean) and 
1,796,296.323 (true). This conjunction is signalled as ‘within limits’ on the yinyang li, and has a ‘total number’ of zero.
The tabulated latitude values from NASA are:
0205-Dec-27 00:30 1 ,796,294.208 −0.58 77836
0205-Dec-28 00:30 1 ,796,295.208 0.58 49442
So it seems that latitude would be zero (and increasing) at about 1,796,294.708: 
This is 1.2 days off the ‘mean’ prediction, and 1.6 days off the ‘true’ value. No 
eclipse occurs.
As Li Rui explains, what Liu Hong is doing is to calculate in effect the angular 
motion of the node from one luni-solar alignment (‘syzygy’) at conjunction or 
opposition to the next. This was based on the notion that a total lunar eclipse 
could be preceded and followed by a ‘just missed’ solar eclipse, and vice versa. 27 
Thus, let us take it that the moon had its syzygy exactly at a node when the 
eclipse occurred. When it gets round to its next syzygy, it misses the opposite 
node by the ‘limit’ amount and just misses the next eclipse.

as these accord with their factors, and cast out [days that] fill 13, reducing 
the remainder by the fractional day. When the Yin and Yang sequences 
conclude, then enter the start [of the next one]. If one enters the sequence 
within the Earlier Limit Remainder, or after the Later Limit Remainder, 
then this shows the moon is travelling the Middle Road [i.e. it is near the 
ecliptic].
We know that each synodic month we can calculate the extra shift in days of 
the Yinyang sequence by adding:
(18,328 + 914/2209) days, at a scale of Lunar Circuits [7874],
i.e. 2 + (2580 + 914/2209) / 7874 days of the sequence
So here we add 914 to the Fine Factional Parts, and if the total exceeds 2209 we 
add one to the Remainder; to that we add 2580, and if the total exceeds 7874 
we add one to the days.
Suppose the total exceeds the length of the sequence, which is
Sequence Circuits [107,565], at a scale of Lunar Circuits [7874], i.e.
107,565/7874 days = 13 days 5203/7874.
Then we have to take 13 from the shift in ‘days of the sequence’, and 5203 
from the remainder to find entry into the next yinyang sequence. As in the case 
of the speed table, the last entry of the sequence is (in modern terms) the 
fourteenth day, but it is not so numbered. Instead, since it is incomplete, it is 
labelled fen ri 分日 ‘fractional day’, just as the last entry of the speed table was 
labelled zhou ri 周日 ‘circuit day’.

limits, calculated on the traditional basis that if sun or moon are eclipsed exactly 
on a node, then a possible eclipse (of moon or sun respectively) half a month 
away will just be missed.

graduations that will represent an eclipse just missed, we start with the 
moon in conjunction with the sun precisely at a node i.e. exactly at the start

opposition to the sun, but while it will still be close to a node it will (accord -
ing to the traditional view) just miss a lunar eclipse. The position of the 
moon relative to the ‘days of the sequence’ graduations will have increased 
from zero to:
½ × (18,328 + 914/2209) / 7874 days of the sequence
= 1 + (1290 + 457/2209) / 7874

This is 1 day with a remainder 1290/7874, and Fine Fractional Parts of 457.

Working the other way round, if we want to find the conditions for the moon 
just to miss an eclipse half a synodic month before an eclipse occurs with the 
moon precisely at a node, then given that the total length of a sequence is 13 
days 5203/7874, if we subtract 1 du and 1290/7874, with a ‘Fine Parts’ remainder 
of 457, we find as the result:
12 + (3912 + 1752/2209) / 7874
So we have a remainder of 3912 + Fine Parts 1752 into the 13th day, under which 
the ‘later limit’ is shown, as is appropriate.
If we want to convert the Earlier and Later Limit Remainders to modern angular 
terms, we can do so by recalling that the entire sequence occupies 360°, and 
that it contains 215,130/7874 days.
(360° / (21,510/7874) × (1 + (1290 + 457/2209) / 7874)
= (360°/215,130) × (7874 + (1290 + 457/2209))
= 15.3°
On that basis the two limits are placed 15.3° on either side of a node. We may 
compare this value with modern figures as follows:

node) from a node at the instant of opposition if a lunar eclipse is to be 
possible.
Solar eclipse limit – superior 18.4°: an eclipse is impossible if the sun and moon 
are further from the node than this at conjunction; inferior 15.4°: an eclipse must 
take place if the sun and moon are closer to the node than this at conjunction.
Liu Hong’s eclipse limit is close to the inferior solar eclipse limit, and is therefore 
a useful predictor for solar eclipses.

Proc. 4.48. To find the true numbers for conjunction and full moon:
§97   In each case set out the greater and lesser parts of the Excess or Deficit 
from the Speed Sequence. Multiply the lesser part by the Coincidence 
Number [47] to make Fine Parts, 29 and taking the Day Remainder in the 
Yinyang [sequence] subtract from it for Excess or add to it for Deficit. If 
the Day Remainder is in excess or deficient, settle it by advancing or retreat-
ing a day. By the true Day Remainder multiply the Rate of Decrease or 
Increase, counting one as it accords with Lunar Circuits [7874], and by that 
subtract from or add to the Total Numbers, to make the true numbers for 
the time of occurrence.
We now proceed to correct the moon’s position in the yinyang (latitude) 
sequence, using our previous result for how far the moon is in advance of or 
behind its mean position. In Proc. 4.34, we were told how to find the Excess 
or Deficit (the departure of the moon from the position given on the basis of 
mean motion), and we saw that this will involve ‘greater and lesser parts’. We 
then use this Excess or Deficit to correct the position in the latitude sequence 
previously calculated on the basis of mean motion and thus find the corrected 
value, which will appear as a corrected Total Number, i.e. lunar latitude in  du 
at a scale of 12.
推夜半入曆
以差率乘朔小餘， 如微分法得一， 以減入曆日餘， 不足， 加月周而減之， 
却一日.却得分日加其分， 以會數約微分為小分， 即朔日夜半入曆．
Proc. 4.49. T o determine entry into the sequence at midnight:
§98   Multiply the Lesser Remainder for the conjunction by the Difference Rate 
[11,986]. Obtain one for each accord with Fine Parts Factor [2209]. Subtract 
that from the Day Remainder for entry into the sequence. If [the Day 
Remainder] is not sufficient, add Lunar Circuits [7874] and then subtract, 
then go back one day. If in going back you get to the fractional day, add 
that fraction. Simplify Fine Parts by the Coincidence Number [47] to make 
Lesser Parts. This is the entry into the sequence for the midnight on the 
day of conjunction.
The Lesser Remainder for a conjunction is the fraction of a day that the conjunc -
tion falls after the midnight beginning that day, at a scale of Day Factor [1457]. 
29 See the explanation at the end of the commentary on Proc. 4.44.

The Uranic Manifestation system 313
§105   In each case, the Cycle Rate and Solar Rate are made by simplifying 
together Termination Days and Degrees of Heaven.
There now follows a series of notes on how to calculate the quantities that 
will later be listed for each planet. The names for those quantities are given 
in slightly different form from that used in the subsequent lists; I have 
shown missing text as insertions in square brackets for the sake of 
clarity.
Termination Days is the duration of planet’s cycle in days (i.e. its synodic period). 
It is stated as a number of days and parts of days at a scale of the planet’s Day 
and Du Factor.
Degrees of Heaven evidently means the number of  du in one circuit, which is 
the same as the number of days in a solar cycle. Cycle Rate is the number of 
synodic cycles that take place in Solar Rate years.
Thus for Jupiter, we have:
Termination [Days] =
= 398 days 3,484,646 parts
= 398 × Jupiter Day and  Du Factor [3,959,358] + 3,484,646 parts
= 1,579,309,130 parts, at a scale of 3,959,358
While degrees of heaven is Circuits of Heaven [215,130] at a scale of Era Factor 
[589]
So Termination Days/Degrees of Heaven
= (1,579,309,130 × 589) / (215,130 × 3,959,358)
= 930,213,077,570/851,776,686,540
= 1.092085627922756
This should be close to Solar Rate/Cycle Rate for Jupiter
= 7341/6722
= 1.0920856887831, which is identical to 7 significant figures.
Or alternatively we may make the comparison by noting that if we multiply 
numerator and denominator of 7341/6722 by 126,714,766, we obtain
930,213,097,206/851,776,657,052, which we may compare with:
930,213,077,570/851,776,686,540, Termination Days/Degrees of Heaven as set 
out above.
The numerators and denominators match to seven significant figures, well within 
the four figure precision of Solar Rate and Cycle Rate in the form in which the 
text states them.

Proc. 4.58. [Derivation of Conjunction Lunation Factor]:
§106   If Rule Years [19] multiply Cycle [Rate], it makes the [Conjunction] Luna-
tion Factor.
Cycle Rate × Rule Years = number of solar cycles in Cycle Rate Rule Cycles
This is the quantity later referred to as the he yue fa 合月法 Conjunction Lunation 
Factor for a given planet.
章月乘日， 為月分.分如法， 為[合]月數.
Proc. 4.59. [Derivation of Conjunction Lunation Number]:
§107   If Rule Months [235] multiply Solar [Rate], it makes Lunation Parts. As 
Parts accord with the [Conjunction Lunation] Factor, that makes [Conjunc-
tion] Lunation Number.
Solar Rate × Rule Months = number of lunations in Solar Rate Rule Cycles. Simi -
larly to the previous quantity, the listing of constants for each planet prefaces 
the name of this quantity with the word he 合 ‘conjunction’.
Taking the two preceding sections together, we are to calculate:
(Solar Rate × Rule Months) / (Cycle Rate × Rule Years)
= (Solar Rate/Cycle Rate) × (Rule Months/Rule Years)
This will yield the number of lunations in one synodic cycle. In the listing 
for each planet, it is labeled as he yue shu 合月數 Conjunction Lunation 
Number. Also listed for each planet following this quantity is the remainder 
from that calculation, labeled as [ he] yue yu [ 合]月餘 [Conjunction] Luna-
tion Remainder, which is the remainder produced in the calculation of 
Conjunction Lunation Number above, at a scale of Conjunction Lunation 
Factor.
通數乘月法， 日度法也.
Proc. 4.60. [Derivation of Day and Du Factor]:
§108   The Compatibility Number [31] multiplies the [Conjunction] Lunation 
Factor, and that is the Day and Du Factor.

patibility Number [31].

Proc. 4.61. [Derivation of [Planet] Dipper Parts]:
§109   Dipper Parts [145] multiply Cycle Rate, to make [Planet] Dipper Parts. 
The Day and Du Factor uses Era Factor [589] to multiply Cycle Rate, so 
this is similar [in] multiplying it by parts.
Dipper Parts [145] are a general solar constant, whose derivation is explained in 
section § 121. It is the fractional part of a day in one solar cycle, at a scale of 
Era Factor [589]. By multiplying by Cycle Rate, we change the scale to Day and  
Du Factor for the planet in question, which is Era Factor [589] × Cycle Rate for 
the planet. Each planet thus has its own value for [Planet] Dipper Parts.
五星朔大餘、小餘.
以通法各乘月數， 日法各除之， 為大餘， 不盡為小餘.以六十去大餘.
Proc. 4.62. [Derivation of] the [Planet] Lunar Conjunction Greater Remain-
der, and [Planet Lunar Conjunction] Lesser Remainder for the Five 
Planets:
§110   In each case multiply the [Planet] Lunation Number by Compatibility 
Factor [43,026], and in each case cast out the Day Factor [1457]. That 
makes the Greater Remainder. What is not exhausted makes the Lesser 
Remainder. Cast out 60 from the Greater Remainder.
Here I use ‘Lunar Conjunction’ to render shuo 朔 (conjunction of the moon with 
the sun), so as to distinguish it from he 合, the term referring to conjunction of 
the planet with the sun.
Compatibility Factor [43,026] is the number of days in Day Factor [1457] lunations. 
Multiplying by Compatibility Factor/Day Factor converts [Planet] Lunation Number 
into the number of days. Casting out 60 leaves us with the number to add to the 
epochal day number jiazi.1 to find the day number for the Conjunction.

各以通法乘月餘， 以合月法乘朔小餘， 并之， 會數約之， 所得各以日度法除
之， 則皆是.

Planets:

Factor [43,026], and in each case cast out the Day Factor [1457]. That

Proc. 4.63. [Derivation of] the Days and Day Remainder of Entry into the 
Lunation for the Five Planets:
§111   In each case multiply the [Conjunction] Lunation Remainder by the Com -
patibility Factor [43,026], and multiply the Lunar Conjunction Lesser 
Remainder by the Conjunction Lunation Factor. Combine them, and sim -
plify them by Coincidence Number [47]. Cast out Day and Du Factor from 
what you obtain, and it is this in every case.
[Conjunction] Lunation Remainder represents the fraction of a lunation left after 
the whole months in a synodic period of the planet, at a scale of Conjunction 
Lunation Factor.
If we multiply this by Compatibility Factor [43,026], we change the scale of the 
fraction to Conjunction Lunation Factor × Compatibility Factor [43,026].
We then in effect divide by Coincidence Number [47], and then finally by Day 
and Du Factor, which is Compatibility Number [31] × [Conjunction] Lunation 
Factor.
That changes to scale of the lunation fraction to
Compatibility Factor [43,026] / (1457). But this is the number of days in a luna -
tion, and so the result is in days.
Lunar Conjunction Lesser Remainder is the fraction of a day by which the last 
lunar conjunction of the synodic period falls after midnight, at a scale of Com -
patibility Factor [43,026].
If we multiply this by Conjunction Lunation Factor (Rule Years [19] × Cycle Rate), 
we obtain days at a scale of Compatibility Factor [43,026] × Rule Years [19] × 
Cycle Rate.
We then divide as before, by Coincidence Number [47], and then finally by Day 
and Du Factor, which is Compatibility Number [31] × [Conjunction] Lunation 
Factor. The scale of the fraction then becomes: Compatibility Factor [43,026] × 
Rule Years [19] × Cycle Rate / (47 × 31 × Rule Years × Cycle Rate.
= Compatibility Factor [43,026]/1457, which again produces a result in days.
The total is thus the days that the conjunction falls into the final lunation of the 
synodic period, with parts of a day at a scale of Day and  Du Factor.

318 The Uranic Manifestation system
Proc. 4.64. [Derivation of] the [Planet] Du Number and Du Remainder for the 
Five Planets:
§112   Subtract [the lesser] from the greater to make Du Remainder Parts, and 
multiply by Circuits of Heaven [215,130]. Simplify by Day and Du Factor, 
and what you obtain makes du, while what is not exhausted makes [Planet] 
Du Remainder. If it goes past Circuits of Heaven, cast it out, with Dipper 
Parts.
Li Rui points out that ‘the greater’ is either Cycle Rate or Solar Rate, depending 
which is greater.
Suppose that Solar Rate is the greater, then we are calculating:
(Solar Rate – Cycle Rate), which is the number of times of solar circuits of the 
heavens while Cycle Rate conjunctions take place, minus the number of 
conjunctions, i.e. the number of complete cycles of motion of the planet 
relative to the sun. This is therefore the number of circuits of the heavens 
made by the planet in Cycle Rate conjunctions. If we multiply by Circuits 
of Heaven [215,130], we get the number of du moved by the planet in Cycle 
Rate conjunctions, at a scale of Era Factor [589].
Day and Du Factor = Cycle Rate × Era Factor [589], so dividing by this gives us 
the number of du moved by the planet in one conjunction, with parts at a scale 
of Day and  Du Factor.

tions relating to the planets. All of them but one (Dipper Parts) have already 
been stated in the listing near the beginning of the text. This restatement may 
perhaps be placed here for reasons of convenience. Alternatively, it may (like the 
repetition of the data for High Origin, see Proc. 4.54) suggest that the material 
on the planets in the Uranic Manifestation system may once have existed as an 
independent document.

The Uranic Manifestation system 329
置上元盡所求年， 以周率乘之， 滿日率得一， 名積合， 不盡為合餘.
§192   Set out the [years from] High Origin so as to exhaust the current year . 
Multiply by Cycle Rate, and obtain 1 for each filling of Solar Rate. This 
is called Accumulated Conjunctions. What is not exhausted is Conjunction 
Remainder.
The instruction to ‘Multiply by Cycle Rate, and obtain 1 for each filling of Solar 
Rate’ effectively divides by the number of solar cycles elapsed by synodic period, 
which is (Solar Rate/Cycle rate). Accumulated Conjunctions is the number of com-
plete conjunction cycles that have occurred up to the winter solstice at the end of 
the present solar cycle. Conjunction Remainder is the fraction of a conjunction (at 
a scale of Solar Rate) that remains uncompleted at the time of the solstice.
以周率除之， 得一， 星合往年.二， 合前往年.無所得， 合其年.
§193   Cast out Cycle Rate from this. If you get 1, the conjunction was in the 
preceding year. If 2, the conjunction was in the year before the preceding 
year. If one gets nothing, the conjunction is in the year in question.
Since a conjunction takes (Solar Rate/Cycle Rate) years, we can find how many 
solar cycles Conjunction Remainder amounts to by calculating:
(Conjunction Remainder/Solar Rate) × (Solar Rate/Cycle Rate)
= (Conjunction Remainder/Cycle Rate): this is a fraction of a solar cycle.
If it is more than one, the conjunction must have started before the last solstice. 
If more than two, then it is before the preceding solstice. If this is less than one, 
the incomplete conjunction started since the last solstice.
合餘減周率為度分.
§194  Conjunction Remainder is subtracted from Cycle Rate to make Du Parts.
Conjunction Remainder = Cycle Rate × fraction of solar cycle since last 
conjunction
So Du Parts = Cycle Rate × (1 − fraction of solar cycle since last conjunction)
This is Cycle Rate × fraction of solar cycle completed since preceding solstice at 
last conjunction.
Now this goes with the denominator Day and Du Factor. According to Li Rui, 
Day and Du Factor is the product of Cycle Rate and Era Factor [589].

§195   For Metal [V enus] and Water [Mercury], if Accumulated Conjunctions is 
odd, it is the dawn, and if it is even it is the evening.
Since dawn and evening appearances alternate.
推星合月
以月數、 月餘各乘積合， 滿合月法從月， 不盡為月餘.以紀月去積月， 餘為入
紀月.副以章閏乘之， 滿章月得一閏， 以減入紀月， 餘以歲中去之， 命以天正
算外， 合月也.其在閏交際， 以朔御之.
Proc. 4.67. To predict the month of planetary conjunction:
§196   By the month number and the Lunation Remainder multiply in each case 
Accumulated Conjunctions. Let what fills Planet Conjunction Lunation 
Factor go with months, and what does not fill is the Lunation Remainder. 
Cast out Era Months [7285] from Accumulated Months, and the Remainder 
is months entered into Era. Separately multiply it by Rule Intercalations 
[7], and obtain one intercalation for each time this fills Rule Months [235], 
then by that subtract from Era Months. From the remainder cast out Year 
Medials [12], and count it off from the Celestial First Month. Outside the 
count, it is the month of planet conjunction. If it is on the edge of an 
intercalation, manage it according to the conjunction.
This is a restatement in slightly different words of the procedures given in the 
Han Quarter Remainder system, beginning at Proc. 4.38. We find out how many 
whole lunations and parts of lunations correspond to the accumulated conjunc -
tions of the planet so far, and then cast out multiples of completed cycles of 
months, before casting out any completed years, together with the intercalary 
months they contain. This enables us to find in which month of the current year 
the latest planetary conjunction will fall.

以通法乘月餘， 合月法乘朔小餘， 并以會數約之， 所得滿日度法得一， 則星合
入月日也.不滿為日餘， 命以朔算外.

Proc. 4.68. To predict the Day of Entry into Lunation:
§197   Multiply Lunation Remainder by Compatibility Factor [43,026]. Planet 
Conjunction Lunation Factor multiplies Conjunction Lesser Remainder. 
Combine them, and simplify by Coincidence Number [47]. From what 
you get, obtain 1 for each filling of Day Du Factor. Then that is the days 
of entry into the lunation of the planet’s conjunction. What does not fill 
is the day remainder, count it off outside the count for the [luni-solar] 
conjunction.
Again, this is close to the Han Quarter Remainder procedure. We find how many 
days correspond to the fraction of the lunation remaining, and then find the sexa-
genary day of the planet’s conjunction by counting off from the day of the 
luni-solar conjunction preceding it.
推星合度
– 526 –
以周天乘度分， 滿日度法得一度， 不盡為餘， 命度以牛前五起.右求星合.
Proc. 4.69. To predict the du of planet conjunction:
§198   Multiply Du Parts by Circuits of Heaven [215,130], and obtain 1 du for 
each time this fills the Day and Du Factor. What does not fill makes the 
remainder. Designate the du by starting from 5 du before Ox. What is 
above seeks for planet conjunction.
The wording here is very close to that in the Han Quarter Remainder. As we saw 
in Proc. 4.60, Du Parts = (fraction of solar cycle completed since preceding solstice 
at last conjunction) / (Era Factor [589]).
Since Day and  Du Factor = Cycle Rate × Era Factor [589], (Circuits of Heaven) 
× Du Parts / (Day and  Du Factor) gives the distance moved by the sun from 
winter solstice to conjunction with the planet, as specified here. The starting 
point ‘5 du before Ox’ is the location of the winter solstice, from which we 
may count off the  du, while (although this is not stated explicitly) casting 
out the total du of each lodge through which we pass during this process 
so as to end up with the  du in the lodge in which the conjunction takes 
place.

The point of the final note is that we shall next look for the conjunction of the 
moon (rather than the planet) with the sun. The text actually says ‘to the right’, 
referring to writing in columns from right to left.
求後合月
以月數加月數， 以月餘加月餘， 滿合月法得一月， 不滿歲中， 即合其年 ；滿去
之， 有閏計焉， 餘為後年 ；再滿， 在後二年.金、水加晨得夕， 加夕得晨.
Proc. 4.70. To find the month of the next conjunction:
§199   Add Lunation Number to the number of the month, 33 and Lunation 
Remainder to the month remainder, obtaining one month when [the 
remainder] fills Conjunction Lunation Factor. If [the resulting months] 
do not fill Year Medials [12], then there is a conjunction in the [pres -
ent] year. If it does fill, cast it out, reckoning in [any] intercalation, 
and the remainder is in the next year. If it fills twice, it is in the second 
year after. For Venus and Mercury, if one adds to a dawn conjunction 
one gets a dusk [conjunction], and if one adds to a dusk [conjunction], one 
gets dawn.
Here we simply add on the extra lunations and parts to get to the next conjunc -
tion, allowing for the possibility that it may fall in the current year, the next year, 
or the year after.
求後合朔日
以朔大小餘，加合月大小餘，上成月者，
又加大餘二十九， 小餘七百七十三， 小餘滿日法從大餘， 命如前.
Proc. 4.71. To find the day of lunar conjunction for the next planetary 
conjunction:
§200  Add to the greater and lesser remainders for the month of planetary con -
junction the greater and lesser lunar conjunction remainders, and let what 
makes a lunation go up [to add to the lunations].
33 Yue shu 月數 has two different meanings. Translated as ‘Lunation Number’, it is the quantity 
given for the number of lunations between any two given conjunctions. Translated as ‘the num -
ber of the month’, it is the number of the month in the year in which the conjunction previously 
found takes place. Similarly, yue yu 月餘 refers to both the Lunation Remainder in one planetary 
conjunction, and to the remainder that tells us the position in the month of the conjunction previ -
ously found.

moved by the planet between conjunction and the moment of dawn appearance,

accord with half the factor or greater, then accordingly obtain one.

du counts as 1  du, and 1.7  du counts as 2  du.

5.1  INTRODUCTION
In this chapter I present translations of two sources from the Eastern Han period, 
both of which narrate and document discussions and decision-making in relation 
to li. The first translation is by way of prelude to the second, which is considerably 
more substantial.
The first source translated here is found at the end of the first part of the writ-
ings by Ban Gu 班固 on harmonics and astronomical systems in the Han shu 漢
書. It was probably completed some time before his death in 92 
ce, although we 
cannot exclude some modification by those who later worked to complete the Han 
shu, including his sister Ban Zhao 班昭. In this text he speaks as editor, and from 
its concluding sentences, he evidently intended this material to lead into the next 
chapter, in which Liu Xin’s Triple Concordance system is presented.
Ban Gu’s writing begins with a summary of the development of astronomical 
systems from the time of the grandson of the mythical Yellow Emperor down to 
the beginning of the Han dynasty. The main value of this material in the context 
of this book however lies in its detailed account of the Grand Inception reform of 
104 
bce, and of the dispute about the validity of the new system that began in 78 
bce and continued until 75 bce. Finally we are told of Liu Xin’s creation of the 
Triple Concordance system early in the first century ce.
It is clear that the earlier parts of this text are adapted from the account given 
by Sima Qian 司馬遷 in Shi ji 26, 1255–1260. Sima Qian served as Grand Clerk 
Tai shi 太史, with overall responsibility for astro-calendrical affairs, and might 
therefore have been expected to play a central role in the making of the new 
system. His account of the Grand Inception reform is however much briefer 
than that given by Ban Gu, possibly because (according to the Han shu account) 
he appears to have been displaced from the decision-making process by other 
experts, some of them from outside official structures. Further, since Sima Qian 
died somewhere around 86 
bce, there is no mention in his writing of any later 
developments. I have therefore not thought it worthwhile to give a separate 
translation of Sima Qian’s text.
In the second part of this chapter I translate a source of unparalleled value for 
the historian of astronomy, both in early imperial China and the ancient world as a  
Han discussions of astronomical 
systems and their development

104

tells us:
光和元年中， 議郎蔡邕、 郎中劉洪補續律曆志， [. . . ] 今考論其業, 義指博
通， 術數略舉， 是以集錄為上下篇， 放續前志， 以備一家．
In the first year of the Guanghe period [178 ce], the Gentleman for Con -
sultation Cai Yong, and the Palace Gentleman Liu Hong added to and 
continued the Monograph on the Pitchpipes and [Astronomical] System 
[from the Han shu ]. Now I have examined and evaluated their work: its 
ideas are broad and general, and [the details of] numerical procedures are 
succinct and complete. Therefore I have collected their notes into a first 
and second chapter, and have let them serve as a continuation of the For -
mer Monograph, in order to show their point of view.
The ‘Former Monograph’ refers to the sections of the Han shu from which comes 
the material by Ban Gu discussed above. The ‘first and second chapter’ nowadays 
appear as the second and third parts of the Lü li zhi 律曆志 ‘Monograph on mathe-
matical harmonics and astronomical systems’, which appear as zhi (monographs) 2 
and 3 in the current Hou Han shu. Zhi 2, translated here, contains a series of official 
documents – memorials, edicts and so on, linked by detailed narrative sections that 
are also clearly based on official sources. Zhi 3 is a description of the Han Quarter 
Remainder astronomical system, prefaced by an essay on the observational basis 
of such systems: see the translation in chapter 3.
While engaged in their work of compilation, Cai and Liu were allowed to 
consult the archives of the Dong Guan 東觀 ‘Eastern Pavilion’, in which con -
fidential state papers were kept.
2 The result is a rich repertoire of documents 
that gives us a much deeper insight into the events of the Eastern Han that 
concern us than we could ever hope to have for the Western Han. A glance at 
the translated material below will make the nature and variety of this material 
clear. For the convenience of the reader, we may note the following broad topic 
divisions of the text.
1 On the general issue of the monographs, see Mansvelt Beck (1990).
2 Hou Han shu, zhi 3, 3083, commentary, zhi 3, 3083, commentary, quoting a memorial of Cai Yong.

office of Grand Clerk and was a major literary figure as well as a constructor of instruments and 
expert on celestial calculation. He was never allowed the access he sought: Hou Han shu 59, 1,940.

Sections 5.3.1 to 5.3.6: The adoption of a new system
This series of documents relates to discussions of the need for a change in the 
official li not long after the beginning of the Eastern Han dynasty, and continues up 
to the decision to adopt the new Han Quarter Remainder system in 85 ce. The first 
memorial on the subject was submitted in 32 ce; it pointed out that the Triple Con-
cordance system was making incorrect predictions of the times of conjunctions of 
sun and moon. Though this was certainly the case, the emperor shelved the matter on 
the grounds that there were more urgent matters to attend to. It is worth noting that 
neither of the two persons submitting the memorial had any direct responsibility for 
li – but as later documents will show, it was not seen as unlikely or inappropriate that 
those who were not technical specialists might have sufficient knowledge of such 
matters to express an opinion, and that their opinion might deserve serious attention.
Sections 5.3.2 to 5.3.4 deal with the revival of interest in this question 30 years 
later, and take us up to the eve of its final settlement 20 years after that. Two 
notable points emerge. First, those who were the first to become involved did not 
hold regular official posts, but were in the ‘Expectant Official’ dai zhao category – 
talented younger recruits to the administration who did not yet hold a designated 
post. Second, we see the first instance of one frequent mode of official response 
to the raising of a question relating to li, which was to commission a prolonged 
programme of meticulous observation and recording. This involved not simply 
checking on what day conjunction of sun and moon appeared to fall – an event 
that could only be observed directly on the rare occasions when a solar eclipse 
occurred – but also when lunar eclipses occurred, a much more readily observed 
datum which indicated the moment of opposition of sun and moon. By 69 
ce no 
final resolution had been reached, but it was agreed that crescents and full moons 
were to be predicted by methods based on the constants used in quarter-remainder 
type systems. However for the conjunctions – which were the foundation on which 
the civil calendar was based – the Triple Concordance remained in use.
But by 85 
ce, we are told, it had become clear that the discrepancies between the 
Triple Concordance and observation were too large to be tolerated. All observers (hou 
zhe 候者) recognised that conjunctions were being predicted three-quarters of a day 
too early, and that the sun’s position was 5 du behind prediction – so that rather than 
being at the start of the lodge Ox at winter solstice, it was at 21 du of the preceding 
lodge, Dipper. But the officials of the Grand Clerk, tai shi 太史, who would normally 
have handled questions relating to li, could not resolve the situation. The emperor 
therefore turned for advice to two persons who were evidently not connected with that 
group, but who were never the less able to zhi li 治曆 ‘handle li’, Bian Xin and Li Fan.
We are not told much about the arguments put forward by Bian and Li, or on 
what evidence they were based, but they were evidently effective, for the next 
document cited is a long edict issued in March of 85 
ce, in which the emperor pro-
claimed his determination to enact a reform in the official li, so that from then on 
a quarter-remainder type system would be used for all purposes. This new system 
was the one referred to in this book as the ‘Han Quarter Remainder system’. The 
document has a number of features worthy of remark.

Han discussions of astronomical systems 359
It stresses the duty of the ruler to maintain a li that is in accord with the heavens, 
and points out that if he fails to do so, the resultant cosmic disorder may show 
itself through natural disasters. One instance of this is mentioned particularly: if 
the customary spring amnesty is granted a day too early because of a faulty li, seri-
ous problems will arise because an ordinance appropriate to spring (when mercy 
to criminals is in order) has been observed while it is still winter (when harsh 
punishments are appropriate).
It is claimed that any li will need reform after a few centuries, since initially 
small discrepancies are bound to build up over time. (As we have seen, however, 
the initial solar and lunar positions of the Grand Inception system which formed 
the basis of the Triple Concordance were in fact wrong from the outset.)
The edict cites a number of texts of a kind we have not before encountered in 
relation to li: these are the so-called chen wei 讖緯 ‘prognostications and weft’ 
books, sometimes called ‘apocrypha’ by westerners, which first appear around the 
beginning of the Common Era, but which were often thought to contain secret 
teachings handed down orally by disciples of Confucius.
3 Much of the content of 
these texts relates to supposed cosmic influences and omens on one side or another 
of current political conflicts, but some appear to have contained astronomical and 
calendrical references which favoured the li adopted in 85 
ce – which certainly 
suggests they had been written not long before.4
After the edict, a short paragraph brings a certain Jia Kui onto the scene, who 
held a role that gave him responsibility for all Expectant Officials. He pointed out 
one fault in the proposals for the new system – the proposal that it should with 
a long 30-day month after system origin – which could only have the effect of 
including two conjunctions in that month, and depriving the next month of its con-
junction. This was corrected. But this was not the last of what Jia Kui had to say.
Sections 5.3.7 and 5.3.8: Jia Kui on astronomical  
systems, and the ecliptic
The editors tell us that Jia Kui, already a widely respected scholar learned in 
the classics (and an advocate of the ‘apocryphal’ books) wrote a comprehensive 
resumé of what had been learned when, from around 89 to 104 
ce, the officials 
in charge of li were tasked to accumulate regular observations of lunar phases in 
3 Wei 緯 means the cross-wise ‘weft’ threads in a piece of weaving, as opposed to the main ‘warp’ 
threads, called jing 經, which was also the word used to refer to the recognized classical texts to 
which the ‘wefts’ were thought by some to be an essential supplement.
4 On  these texts in general, see for instance Twitchett, Loewe and Fairbank (1986), 179, and Jack 
L. Dull (1966). “A historical introduction to the apocryphal, ch’an-wei, texts of the Han Dynasty.” 
University of Washington, PhD. Both these sources use a slightly different modern reading of the 
first character in the name rendered here as chen-wei. In later centuries the Han apocrypha fell into 
disfavour and were deliberately destroyed, so that today we only know them through quotations. 
The importance of the apocrypha in the present context was noted by Yabuuti Kiyosi (1974) “The 
calendar reforms in the Han dynasties and ideas in their backgrounds.” Archives Internationales 
d’histoire des Sciences 24: 51–65.

relation to the so-called Nine Ways procedure. In the lengthy extracts that follow, 
Jia Kui covers a number of topics in depth.
First, he notes that the new system’s position of the sun at winter solstice, at 
21¼ du of the lodge Dipper, rather than at the beginning of the lodge Ox as had 
been posited by the Triple Concordance, fits in with what a considerable number 
of respected texts, including apocrypha, state is the case. He then turns to a matter 
referred to in the emperor’s edict – the need for periodic revision in the official 
li to deal with secular change. Like the emperor (or rather those who drafted the 
edict issued in his name), he quotes an apocryphal text that says that any li will 
need revision after three centuries, and he backs this up with further material from 
the Book of Change – but unlike the emperor he also provides solid observational 
data to support his claim. These come from a total of 70 dated records of solar 
eclipses since the start of the Western Han – and because a solar eclipse is an infal-
lible sign of a conjunction of sun and moon, he can easily check the accuracy of 
any given system by seeing whether it would have put the eclipse on the first day 
of the corresponding lunar month. From 206 
bce to 104 bce, the Grand Inception 
(which provided the calendrical core of the Triple Concordance), is the clear win-
ner – showing, he says, that its adoption in 104 
bce was a century overdue. But the 
closer he moves to his own day, the more the position changes, until from 26 ce to 
89 ce the Han Quarter Remainder is obviously superior, and the time for reform 
had arrived – three centuries after the time when the Grand Inception should have 
been adopted. It is, he points out, inevitable that all systems will fail in the end, 
since even if they match the phenomena of their own day precisely, they use con-
stant finite numbers to define their basic constants, and thus there must always be 
a slow accumulation of difference between prediction and reality.
5
He then moves on to make a claim with little precedent in writings before his 
time – that the true reference for the motions of sun and moon is not the equator, 
but the ecliptic. He points out that the Grand Clerk’s officials’ practice of using the 
equator as reference often led to the conclusion that the sun and moon were moving 
irregularly, when in fact they were not, and cites observations made in the Western 
Han as well as a systematic investigation made from 85 
ce to 89 ce in support.
Jia Kui himself died in 101 ce, but his statement is followed by an editorial note 
that in 103 ce an edict was issued ordering that a new armillary instrument with an 
ecliptic ring should be constructed, and we are given the spacings of the lodges as 
marked on this ring. We are however told that the Grand Clerk’s officials resisted 
using it, as they claimed that it ‘made observation difficult’.
5 Nathan Sivin (1995). “On the limits of empirical knowledge in Chinese and Western science,” in 
Medicine, philosophy and religion in ancient China: researches and reflections . Aldershot, Vari-
orum, 165–190, 170 interprets this statement as supporting his wider case that it was common in 
pre-modern China to view astronomical knowledge as subject to ‘indeterminacy’. Without entering 
into Sivin’s general claim, I do believe that a proper technical understanding of the terms used by 
Jia Kui in the instance cited makes it clear that he is making a relatively straightforward arithmetical 
point whose implications are intended to be purely practical – see the translation that follows for 
further details.

Han discussions of astronomical systems 361
Sections 5.3.9 and 5.3.10: Jia Kui on variation  
of lunar speed
We now return to material by Jia Kui. Having eliminated effects due to a wrong 
frame of reference, he now discusses a real variation in lunar speed. His investiga-
tion had begun by showing the unreliability of an attempt to predict this variation 
by using numerology based on the Book of Change, and went on to suggest on the 
basis of observational records that in reality the position of maximum speed in the 
moon’s apparent orbit shifted by 3 du for each lunar circuit of the heavens, so that in 
nine years it moves through a complete cycle. This is in fact in quite close accordance 
with modern values for this shift, based on the difference between the anomalistic 
month (the period of return to lunar perigee, hence maximum speed) and the sidereal 
month.
6 What is more, Jia Kui does not merely note that the moon’s speed varies, but 
points out that knowledge of this variation can lead to more accurate predictions of 
conjunctions of sun and moon – a suggestion has says he has tested on 38 records of 
lunar eclipses from 25 
ce onwards. With this, the material by Jia Kui ends.
The editorial note that follows indicates that attempts to develop this method 
further were made over the century that followed Jia Kui, but that no marked suc-
cess followed. As we shall see, it was Liu Hong himself who proposed a complete 
theory of lunar motion, late in the second century.
Section 5.3.11: Jia Kui on variation of lunar speed
The editors now turn to another matter. In 102 
ce an Expectant Official under the 
Grand Clerk7 pointed out that the seasonally changing lengths of day and night 
marked on official clepsydras were adjusted by a fixed amount up or down every 
nine days. In modern terms, seasonal day-length variation was being modelled by 
a step function. This, it was noted, was often far from reality. The Clerk’s officials 
conceded this point – though only after pointing out that they had been acting in 
strict accordance with the regulations then in force. It was suggested that matters 
would be improved it the calibration was instead based on the sun’s north-south 
motion. An edict ordered that this idea should be adopted. The editors state that all 
the data related to this decision are to be found tabulated in the following chapter 
on the Han Quarter Remainder system – as indeed they are.
8
Section 5.3.12: Discussions of system origins
The material in this section deals with three major disputes about the question of 
system origin in the second century ce. As the editors’ short introduction explains, 
6 Modern values are 27.3216 days (mean sidereal month) and 27.55455 days (mean anomalistic month). 
The difference between these, 0.233 days, is the amount by which each passage of perigee will fall earlier 
in successive sidereal months. Since, in quarter remainder terms, the moon moves 365¼ du in a whole 
sidereal month, then in this time it moves (0.233/27.3216) × 365¼ du = 3 du, to the nearest whole du.
7 He was one of 37 such officials attached to the Grand Clerk: see Hou Han shu , zhi 25, 3572 
(commentary).

Sections 5.3.9 and 5.3.10: Jia Kui on variation 
of lunar speed
We now return to material by Jia Kui. Having eliminated effects due to a wrong 
frame of reference, he now discusses a real variation in lunar speed. His investigation had begun by showing the unreliability of an attempt to predict this variation 
by using numerology based on the Book of Change, and went on to suggest on the 
basis of observational records that in reality the position of maximum speed in the 
moon’s apparent orbit shifted by 3 du for each lunar circuit of the heavens, so that in 
nine years it moves through a complete cycle. This is in fact in quite close accordance 
with modern values for this shift, based on the difference between the anomalistic 
month (the period of return to lunar perigee, hence maximum speed) and the sidereal 
month.
6 What is more, Jia Kui does not merely note that the moon’s speed varies, but 
points out that knowledge of this variation can lead to more accurate predictions of 
conjunctions of sun and moon – a suggestion has says he has tested on 38 records of 
lunar eclipses from 25 
ce onwards. With this, the material by Jia Kui ends.
The editorial note that follows indicates that attempts to develop this method 
further were made over the century that followed Jia Kui, but that no marked success followed. As we shall see, it was Liu Hong himself who proposed a complete 
theory of lunar motion, late in the second century.
Section 5.3.11: Jia Kui on variation of lunar speed
The editors now turn to another matter. In 102 
ce an Expectant Official under the 
Grand Clerk7 pointed out that the seasonally changing lengths of day and night 
marked on official clepsydras were adjusted by a fixed amount up or down every 
nine days. In modern terms, seasonal day-length variation was being modelled by 
a step function. This, it was noted, was often far from reality. The Clerk’s officials 
conceded this point – though only after pointing out that they had been acting in 
strict accordance with the regulations then in force. It was suggested that matters 
would be improved it the calibration was instead based on the sun’s north-south 
motion. An edict ordered that this idea should be adopted. The editors state that all 
the data related to this decision are to be found tabulated in the following chapter 
on the Han Quarter Remainder system – as indeed they are.
8
Section 5.3.12: Discussions of system origins
The material in this section deals with three major disputes about the question of 
system origin in the second century ce. As the editors’ short introduction explains,

The difference between these, 0.233 days, is the amount by which each passage of perigee will fall earlier 
in successive sidereal months. Since, in quarter remainder terms, the moon moves 365¼ du in a whole 
sidereal month, then in this time it moves (0.233/27.3216) × 365¼ du = 3 du, to the nearest whole du.

the point of departure in each case was in some way related to the apocryphal 
books cited in the 85 ce edict that promulgated the Han Quarter Remainder system. 
In addition to his careful citations of observational evidence Jia Kui treats these 
books as a respected source of support for the case he makes. In each of the three 
disputes recorded here, the claim was made that instead of the gengshen.17 year 
in which the system origin of the new official system fell, it would be more fitting 
to change to a jiayin.51 year, as set out in several of the apocrypha. In addition, 
there were those who argued that it had been a mistake to abandon the Grand 
Inception system of 104 
bce, effectively embodied in the Triple Concordance sys-
tem replaced by the Han Quarter Remainder. In each case, however, a determined 
opposition was mounted, and the new official system was successfully defended. 
In the last of the three instances, Cai Yong himself was the major advocate for the 
defence, so the evidence provided is of particular interest.
One feature of all these discussions is striking, and that is the question of 
who takes part in them. In the first place, it is clear that although officials 
from the Grand Clerk’s office do play a role, many others whose job titles 
have nothing to do with observation of the heavens, or with calendrical mat -
ters, also make significant contributions. What is more, these are not small-
scale debates. In the first of the three, we hear of groups of 40 and over 80 
officials collectively indicating support for different points of view. In the 
third instance, the matter was settled in what appears to have been a plenary 
meeting of the officers of the central administration based at the capital. And 
at some stages the discussion involved the Three Excellencies san gong 三公, 
who were the highest officers of state. We have no record of anything similar 
from any other ancient culture.
The accounts given by Cai and Yong are detailed records of what appears to 
have been vigorous hand-to-hand intellectual combat, and are not easily sum -
marised. The following notes can only give the reader a general indication of what 
to expect in each section.
1 122 ce A return to the Triple Concordance?
Two persons made separate claims – one that a change in system origin to a 
jiayin.51 year was needed in order to accord with both the heavens and the apoc-
rypha, and one that a return to the Triple Concordance was advisable. These claims 
attracted heavyweight support, including the Grand Defender, Tai wei, one of the 
Three Excellencies. The counterattack was made by the Director of the Impe -
rial Secretariat, a bureau which included those responsible for drafting imperial 
documents. He pointed out that periodical revision of the official li was not only 
normal, but also essential, and attacked some of the bases on which Liu Xin had 
constructed the Triple Concordance. He mentions the wrong position of the winter 
solstice sun, and calls on the observations and practice of the Grand Clerk’s offi-
cers as evidence that the new system was correct. His submission was accepted 
by the emperor.
