2 143 ce A fractional correction to the Triple Concordance?
A more subtle attack was mounted on this occasion. After recounting the author-
ity given to the Grand Inception in 104 bce, and the careful check of its validity 
made two decades later, a member of the Imperial Secretariat made the claim that 
after the Grand Inception had been in use for 171 years (which is nine Rules of 19 
years each), i.e. in 68 
ce, the calendrical officials ought to have realised that it was 
appropriate to remove 63/81 day from the time of prediction of conjunctions of sun 
and moon – which would of course have dealt with the problem of late predictions. 
This claim was based in part on the apocrypha, and in part on an interpretation of 
Liu Xin’s ‘station-skipping’ rule for finding the position of Jupiter.
9 The matter was 
referred to the Three Excellencies for consideration, and they invited comments. 
This time the response was led by the Grand Clerk himself. He pointed out that 
the essential basis of a li was twofold: the establishment of a system origin, and 
the choice of constants defining the motions of the celestial bodies. There was no 
way that a li could be run on the basis that from time to time one trimmed off an 
inconvenient fraction, since such quantities represented actual motion of celestial 
bodies, which could not perform the ‘jumps’ forwards or backwards that this would 
imply. Again, the defence was successful.
3 175 ce Cai Yong defends the Han system against the final attack
Cai Yong’s personal involvement in this incident is no doubt reflected in the 
detailed narration given, and in the long citations from his own submissions. One 
again, the claim was made that the jiayin.51 origin should be adopted, on the 
basis of support from the apocrypha, and also, it was argued, because the use of 
an incorrect origin was leading to social and natural disorder. Further, those who 
supported the current system should be punished for their role in bringing about 
such disasters.
This attack on the Han Quarter Remainder system was the most serious to date, 
and it was made the subject of a formal confrontation of the two sides in a plenary 
assembly of officials, one of the great deliberative meetings known as yi 議 which 
were held during this period.
10 Cai Yong’s counterattack, launched in that meet -
ing, appears to have been comprehensive, covering all the usual points made on 
previous occasions, but introducing several new ones, including a challenge to his 
opponents to produce new astronomical instruments whose observational results 
might support their claims. Finally, however, since this is ultimately a political 
 9  The basis of this is set out in the Triple Concordance system, in the division entitled ‘Year Workings’ 
sui shu 歲術. It is there stated that in 144 years Jupiter will move through 145 ‘Jupiter stations’, the 
12 equal divisions of the heavens that define its path. Jupiter will normally move through one station 
each year, but by the end of the 144-year period will be found to have ‘skipped’ an extra station.
10 For discussion of these debates and their place in Han political life, see Christopher Cullen (2007b) 
“Actors, networks and ‘disturbing spectacles’ in institutional science: 2nd century Chinese debates 
on astronomy.” Antiquorum Philosophia 1: 237–268.

given authority to the current system. His arguments were evidently persuasive. 
The assembly decided in his favour, and the presiding Three Excellencies rec -
ommended that the objectors should be subject to criminal sanctions of the kind 
they had demanded for their opponents. Interestingly, the emperor was unwilling 
to proceed – a reluctance that one commentator, while praising Cai Yong for his 
principled stand, attributes to a wish to preserve a principle of free expression said 
to have been enunciated by Confucius.
Section 5.3.13: Liu Hong and lunar eclipses
In the last section, the third set of documents selected by Cai Yong and Liu Hong 
was of particular relevance to the former. The final section of their monograph 
reflects the interests of Liu Hong, and relate to lunar phenomena.
This section begins by reviewing the method for predicting lunar eclipses in 
use immediately after the 85 
ce adoption of the Han Quarter Remainder system. 
It was, it appears, an adaptation of the Triple Concordance method, but with 
an ad hoc shift of system origin. However, after 89 
ce it was decided to adopt 
the proposals of a certain Zong Gan, who did not at the time hold any official 
post, but was recruited to the Grand Clerk’s office in recognition of his exper -
tise. These proposals are presumably those embodied in the account of the Han 
Quarter Remainder system given in the next part of Cai and Liu’s document 
collection, Hou Han shu, zhi 3. Zong Gan’s procedures were in use for the next 
50 years, but by 146–147 
ce problems began to be evident. However it was not 
until 174–175 ce that proposals for revision of the system were made, initially 
by Liu Hong, followed by others. The situation was complicated when Zong 
Gan’s grandson appeared at court, claiming to have a revised version of the 
methods proposed by his grandfather. The Grand Clerk’s office also put forward 
its own proposals. When the time came to compare the predictions of the various 
proposals available, cloudy weather made it impossible to check who was right. 
A report was commissioned from the Grand Clerk’s immediate superior, the 
Chamberlain of Ceremonials Tai chang 太常, in the hope that the matter could 
be settled, and Liu Hong was recruited to the drafting committee. The commit -
tee did not succeed in ending what was by now a fierce quarrel, and in the end 
the parties involved were subjected to administrative sanctions to restrain them 
from further open conflict.
The next contender to present himself, Wang Han, was, like Zong Gan, a pro-
vincial worthy from outside the government bureaucracy. He presented records of 
93 lunar eclipses, some dating back nearly a century, which had apparently been 
gathered by earlier generations of his family. Liu Hong was asked to report on 
these, and on Wang’s use of a jisi.6 epoch for eclipse prediction. Liu’s criticisms 
fall into two parts. First, he points out that jisi.6 is simply another obsolete datum, 
like those used in the apocrypha; more particularly, it is the epochal year of the 
Zhuan Xu system thought in Eastern Han times to have been used under the Qin, 
and in the early Western Han. Second, the figures he uses in his calculations are

faulty in detail. We are told that Wang Han could make no reply to these attacks, 
apart from saying that he was simply citing what was in his ancestors’ books, and 
that as a result he was sent home to his village – luckily for him without any other 
sanctions being imposed.
Here the narrative and documentary part of the collection of Cai and Liu ends; 
the next part, zhi 3, consists of a description of the Han Quarter Remainder sys -
tem, translated as Chapter 3 in this book. Ten years after the events involving 
Liu Hong just recounted, the warlord Dong Zhuo burned Luoyang, and forced 
the emperor to relocate to the old capital at Chang’an. Vast losses of documents 
took place during the chaotic circumstances of the time, and it is unlikely that 
further large-scale discussions of li took place during the years that remained of 
nominal Han rule.

天也.創業變改， 制不相復， 推傳序文， 則今夏時也.臣等聞學褊陋， 不能明.陛
下躬聖發憤， 昭配天地， 臣愚以為三統之制， 後聖復前聖者， 二代在前也.今
二代之統絕而不序矣， 唯陛下發聖德， 宣考天地四時之極， 則順陰陽以定大

§5  At that time, the Imperial Counsellor Ni Kuan excelled in the exposition 
of the classics, so the emperor addressed him by edict as follows ‘You 
shall deliberate together with the Academicians, on the question of what 
the Standard Conjunction ought now to be, and what colour should be 
given precedence in ritual.’ Ni Kuan deliberated with the Academician 
Ci and others, and they all said ‘Emperors and Kings always reform the 
Standard Conjunction, and change the colour of ritual garments, as a 
means of showing that they have received the mandate to rule from 
Heaven. They innovate and reform, and their ordinances do not simply 
add to those of their predecessors. If we extrapolate from the traditions 
and writings, now is [like] the time of the Xia dynasty. Your ministers’ 
learning is shallow, and we cannot comprehend [this matter]. Your maj -
esty’s imperial person has roused up Your ardour, and equals heaven and 
earth in brilliance; Your ministers foolishly conceive that in the institu -
tions of the Three Concordances, the later sages imitate the former sages, 
and there are two dynasties before our time. The continuity with the 
Concordances of those two dynasties has been broken; only if Your High -
ness manifests his sagely virtue, and proclaims an examination of the 
limits of the Four Seasons, then the Yin and Yang will be rendered har -
monious so as to correct the ordinances of the great brilliance, and serve 
as a model for a myriad generations.’
於是乃詔御史曰 ： 「乃者有司言曆未定， 廣延宣問， 以考星度， 未能讎也.蓋
聞古者黃帝合而不死， 名察發斂， 定清濁， 起五部， 建氣物分數. 然則上矣.書
缺樂弛， 朕甚難之.依違以惟， 未能修明.其以七年為元年.」
§6  Thereupon an edict [from Wudi] was issued to the Imperial Clerks, saying 
‘Now, the officials have said that the degrees of the stars have not yet been 
determined. A broad enquiry for advice has been widely promulgated, so 
as to set the degrees of the stars in order, but they have not yet been able 
to reach a conclusion. Now We have heard that formerly the Yellow Emperor 
accorded [with the cosmos] and did not die. He named and examined the 
advance and retreat of the seasons, he corrected the pitch [of musical notes], 
he drafted the order of the Five Phases, he established the numerical basis 
of [seasonal] qi phenomena. So [such matters] evidently go back to the 
remote past. But to Our great sorrow, the writings are lost and the musical 
tradition is debased. We are undecided, and have not been able to follow 
[the Yellow Emperor’s] brilliance. Let this seventh year become the first 
year [of a new period].’

§9  Their method derived the astronomical system from the regulating [pitch-
pipes]. They said: ‘The [Yellow Bell] regulating pitchpipe has a capacity of 
1 yue, which is a volume of 81 cun. So that is the divisor for one day. It is 
commensurable with the length. The regulator is 9 cun long, and a 171-fold 
division takes us back to the conclusion. After three repeats, one [again] 
obtains jiazi.1 [as the day number].
23 The regulators are yin and yang, [cor -
responding to] nine and six, from which the lines of the hexagrams of the 
Book of Change are generated.
24 Thus the Yellow Bell is called a ‘regulator’ 
since it gives the guiding thread for the original qi. ‘Regulator’ means ‘pat -
tern/divisor’, and there is nothing that does not take its pattern from it.’ This 
agreed with what Deng Ping had determined. Thereupon they observed new 
du for the stars, and the motions of sun and moon, and recalculated in accor -
dance with the pattern of [Luoxia] Hong and [Deng] Ping. The pattern was 
that the days of one lunation were 29 and 43/81 days.
25
23 An Origin Factor, 9 × 171 × 3 = 4617, giving the number of years after system origin when winter 
solstice and the conjunction of the first Celestial month once more coincide at midnight beginning

乃詔遷用鄧平所造八十一分律曆， 罷廢尤疏遠者十七家， 復使校曆律昏明.宦者淳
于陵渠復覆太初曆晦朔弦望， 皆最密， 日月如合璧， 五星如連珠.陵渠奏狀， 遂用
鄧平曆， 以平為太史丞.
§10  Then [Sima] Qian was ordered to use the system that Deng Ping had devised 
based on the regulators, with a factor of 81, and to discard 17 methods that 
were less accurate, so as to use dawn and dusk timings that were in accord 
with the astronomical system and the regulators. The Palace Eunuch Shunyu 
Lingqu reworked the last days of lunations, conjunctions, crescents and 
oppositions for the Grand Inception system, and they were all extremely 
accurate, with ‘the sun and moon like joined jade disks, and the five planets 
like a string of pearls’. [Shunyu] Lingqu memorialized accordingly, where-
upon Deng Ping’s system was put into use, and [Deng] Ping was made 
Deputy Grand Clerk.
5.2.3  [Zhang Shouwang]
– 978 –
後二十七年， 元鳳三年， 太史令張壽王上書言 ： 「曆者天地之大紀， 上帝所為.傳
黃帝調律曆， 漢元年以來用之.今陰陽不調， 宜更曆之過也.」 詔下主曆使者鮮
于妄人詰問， 壽王不服.
§11  [T wenty-seven] years later, in the 3rd year of the Yuanfeng period26 [78 
bce], the Grand Clerk Zhang Shouwang sent up a memorial, saying: ‘The 
astronomical system is the great thread guiding heaven and earth, made by 
the Supernal Lord. From the beginning of the Han [up to the Grand Incep-
tion reform], the dynasty made use of the Yellow Emperor’s Tiao lü [‘har-
monising the standard pitchpipes’] system. Now [under the new system] 
the yin and yang are no longer in harmony, and it is time to put right the 
faults in the astronomical system.’ An edict was issued to the Master of li 
officers Xianyu Wangren to conduct an investigation, but [Zhang] Shouwang 
would not co-operate.
妄人請與治曆大司農中丞麻光等二十餘人雜候日月晦朔弦望、 八節二十四
氣， 鈞校諸曆用狀.奏可.詔與丞相、 御史、 大將 軍、 右將軍史各一人雜候上林
清臺， 課諸曆疏密， 凡十一家.以元鳳三年十一月朔旦冬至， 盡五年十二月， 各
有第.壽王課疏遠.
26 This is not the same as the Yuanfeng ‘Epochal Enfeoffment’ period referred to earlier; the charac-
ter with the modern pronunciation feng is different in this case, so that the name means ‘Epochal 
Phoenix’.

§12  [Xianyu] Wangren requested that he should be allowed to work with the 
expert in li Ma Guang, [holder of the office of] Palace Assistant to the Grand 
Supervisor of Agriculture, and other persons [amounting to] more than twenty 
in all, to make varied solar and lunar observations, including last and first 
days of lunations, crescents and oppositions, the eight main divisions of the 
solar cycle and the 24 qi, and to make comparisons of the merits in use of 
various li. His request was approved. An edict ordered that one person from 
each of the staffs of the Chancellor, the Secretary to the Imperial Counsellor, 
the General in Chief, and the General of the Right should make various 
observations on the Pure Terrace in the Shanglin [Park],
27 and to evaluate the 
accuracy of various li, of which there were eleven in all. From the third year 
of Yuanfeng, the eleventh month, conjunction and winter solstice, up to the 
twelfth month of the fifth year, they ranked them all. And Zhang Shouwang’s 
[system] was [found to be] very far out.
案漢元年不用黃帝調曆， 壽王非漢 曆， 逆天道， 非所宜言， 大不敬.有詔勿
劾.復候， 盡六年.太初曆第一， 卽墨徐萬且、 長安徐禹治太初曆亦第一.壽
王及待詔李信治黃帝調曆， 課皆疏闊， 又言黃帝至元鳳三年六千餘歲.丞相 
屬寶、 長安單安國、 安陵桮育治終始， 言黃帝以來三千六百二十九歲， 不與壽
王合.壽王又移帝王錄， 舜、 禹年歲不合人年.壽王言化益為天子代禹， 驪山
女亦為天子， 在殷周間， 皆不合經術.
§13  W e may observe that at the beginning of Han the Yellow Emperor’s Tiao 
lü system was not in fact used. Shouwang denied the Han system, and 
went contrary to the way of Heaven, using inappropriate words, which 
amounted to lèse majestè. But an edict ordered that he should not be 
prosecuted. [The persons above] observed once more, up to the end of the 
sixth year, and the Grand Inception came out in top place; when Moxu 
Wanqie and Xu Yu from Chang’an handled the Grand Inception system it 
was also in top place. Shouwang and the Expectant Official Li Xin handled 
the Yellow Emperor’s Tiao lü system, but all its results were inaccurate. 
They also said that from the time of the Yellow Emperor down to the 3rd 
year of the Yuanfeng period was more than 6000 years. The Chancellor’s 
staff member Bao, and Dan Anguo from Chang’an, and Bei Yu from Anling 
worked from the ends and beginnings [of reigns], and stated that it was 
3629 years since the Yellow Emperor, which was not consistent with 
Shouwang’s [statement]. Shouwang also shifted the order of emperors and 
kings, so that the regnal years and ages of Shun and Yu were inconsistent 
with [normal] human age. Shouwang also said that [a certain] Hua Yi took 
over from Yu as Emperor, and that the Lady of Li Mountain also reigned 
27 The ‘Pure Terrace’, of which this is the only mention in such a context, appears to have played the 
role of astronomical observatory. From the first century ce onwards the term ling tai 靈臺 ‘numi-
nous terrace’ replaces it.

壽王曆乃太史官殷曆也.壽王猥曰安得五家曆， 又妄言太初曆虧四分日之

28誦不詳之辭， 作祅言欲亂制度， 不道.奏可.
§14  The li used by Shouwang was in fact the  Yin system used by the Clerk’s 
officials. But Shouwang wildly claimed that he had gained possession of 
the li of the five schools. He further said that the Grand Inception cut off 
¾ day, and had removed 705 parts from the Lesser Remainder,
29 so that the 
Yin and Yang were out of tune, which he said was causing worldwide 
disorder. The judicial officers [proposed to] punish Shouwang with a fine 
of 800 piculs of grain, since he given utterance to inauspicious expressions, 
and made up baleful words in order to cause disorder, which was not in 
accordance with the Way. Their memorial was approved.
壽王候課， 比三年下， 終不服.再劾死， 更赦勿劾，  遂不更言， 誹謗益甚， 竟
以下吏.故曆本之驗在於天， 自漢曆初起， 盡元鳳六年， 三十六歲， 而是非
堅定.
§15  Shouwang was sent for trial after three years of observational testing, but 
to the end he remained obdurate, so he was once more condemned to death, 
but then was pardoned in an amnesty. Thereafter he did not change the way 
he talked, and uttered even worse slanders, so that in the end he was sent 
for trial. Thus it is clear that the basis of the li is to be checked against the 
heavens. From the first use of the [Grand Inception] Han system, up to the 
6th year of the Yuanfeng [period], it had been 36 years, and the rights and 
wrongs were definitively settled.
– 979 –

§16  When it came to the time of Xiao[di] [r. 31–7 bce] and Cheng[di] [r. 7–1 
bce], Liu Xiang gave a comprehensive treatment of the Six Systems, setting 
out what was right and wrong, and wrote his Wu ji lun 五紀論 ‘Discussion 
of the Five Eras’. [Liu] Xiang’s son [Liu] Xin investigated every subtle 
detail, and wrote the Triple Concordance system and a listing to explain 
the Spring and Autumn annals.
30 His methods of prediction are precise and 
important, so I have set them out here.

5.3.2  [Failur e of the Grand Inception system in early 
Eastern Han; proposals for revision deferred]
自太初元年始用三統曆， 施行百有餘年， 曆稍後天， 朔先於曆， 朔或在晦， 月
或朔見． 考其行， 日有退無進， 月有進無退．
§1  The Triple Concordance system began to be used from the first year of the 
Grand Inception period [104 bce]. It had been in use for more than a century, 
and the system lagged slightly behind Heaven, [so that] the conjunction fell 
in advance of the [predictions of] the system, [with the] conjunction some -
times falling on the [predicted day of] the end of the lunation, and the moon 
sometimes being visible on the [predicted day of] conjunction. Examining 
its movements, the sun was retarded [from its predicted position] and never 
advanced [beyond it], while the moon was advanced [from its predicted 
position] and was never retarded.
建武八年中， 太僕朱浮、 太中大夫許淑等數上書， 言曆朔不正， 宜當改更． 時分
度覺差尚微， 上以天下初定， 未遑考正．
§2  In the eighth year of the Jianwu period [32 ce] the Chamberlain for the Impe-
rial Stud Zhu Fu, and the Superior Grand Master of the Palace Xu Shu, with 
others, memorialised that the conjunctions [given by] the system were incorrect, 
and that it would be appropriate to revise it. [But] at that time the observable 
discrepancies of the fractions and the degrees were still quite subtle; since the 
empire had only just been settled, the emperor felt he did not yet have the 
leisure to examine and correctly determine [such matters].
5.3.3  [Observed err ors in lunar eclipse predictions in  
62–69 ce lead to experiments in partial use of  
Quarter Remainder methods]
至永平五年， 官曆署七月十六日月食． 待詔楊岑見時月食多先曆， 即縮用筭
上為日， 因上言「月當十五日食， 官曆不中」 ． 詔書令岑普候， 與官曆課． 起七
月， 盡十一月， 弦望凡五， 官曆皆失， 岑皆中． 庚寅， 詔書令岑署弦望月食官， 復
令待詔張盛、 景防、 鮑鄴等以四分法與岑課．
§3  When it came to the fifth year of the Yongping period [62 ce], the official system 
set out that the moon would be eclipsed on the sixteenth day of the seventh 
month [September 8, 62 
ce].32 [But] the Expectant Official Yang Chen saw that 
at that time lunar eclipses where generally in advance of the [predictions 
of] the system, so he [simply] counted one back to find the day, and hence sent 
32 The Triple Concordance predicts a lunar eclipse at the full moon of this month, which is day ding-
wei.44 while the month begins on day renchen.29, so that the prediction is indeed for the 16th day, 
which commences at Luoyang at JD 1743953.18778, September 8. However according to the Starry 
Night Pro planetarium software, the eclipse actually began with penumbral contact at about 18:00

§5  Before this, in the ninth year [66 ce] the Expectant Official attached to the

the matter was referred to the Three Excellencies. Those of the office of the

35 who understood li made divergent formal 
submissions, but up to the fourth month of the tenth year, there were none 
who were able to distinguish what was reliable.
至元和二年， 太初失天益遠， 日、 月宿度相覺浸多， 而候者皆知冬至之日日
在斗二十一度， 未至牽牛五度， 而以為牽牛中星， 後天四分日之三， 晦朔弦望
差天一日， 宿差五度． 章帝知其謬錯， 以問史官， 雖知不合， 而不能易， 故召治
曆編訢、 李梵等綜校其狀．
§6  When it came to the second year of the Yuanhe period [85 ce], the 
Grand Inception was missing the Heavens by an increasing distance, 
and the lodge degrees of the sun and moon were perceived as increas -
ingly excessive, while the observers all realised that on the day of the 
winter solstice the sun was at 21 du of [the lodge] Dipper, and was 5 
du short of [the start of the lodge] Ox, which they took [as marked by] 
the middle star of the Ox [asterism]. [The system] lagged ¾ day behind 
heaven. So the [predicted] last days, conjunctions, crescents and full 
moons were a day different from heaven, and the lodges were five du 
different. Zhangdi became aware of these errors, and enquired of the 
Clerk’s officials concerning them, but even though they knew things 
did not fit, they could not change anything. So he ordered Bian Xin 
and Li Fan, who could handle li, to make a comprehensive comparison 
of all the circumstances.

need for revision, and commands use of the Quarter

Heavenly Seasons. The He tu36 says “The Red meets together in harmony; 
there is Brilliance in the tenth generation; and Resurrection in the eleventh 
generation”. It further says “In the age of the Nine Names, the Lord will 
practice virtue, and restrain oppressive government”. We, in Our lack of 
virtue, do take up and uphold the great task; morning and evening We are 
in reverent awe, and do not dare to be dissolute and idle. We the insignificant 
child put Our trust in the accomplishment of the [cosmic] reckonings. How 
should We not rise up in continuation, honouring and glorifying Our progeni-
tors and ancestors, supporting and relieving for epoch after epoch? The Shang 
shu xuan ji qian
37 says “Give an account of the age of Yao, and pass on the 
civilisation of Tang”. The Di ming yan says “Follow the reverend virtue of 
Yao, and initiate the period by setting up the counterpart”  ’.
且三、 五步驟， 優劣殊軌． 況乎頑陋， 無以克堪， 雖欲從之， 末由也已． 每見
圖書， 中心恧焉． 閒者以來， 政治不得， 陰陽不和， 災異不息， 癘疫之氣， 流傷
於牛， 農本不播． 夫庶徵休咎， 五事之應， 咸在朕躬， 信有闕矣， 將何以補之？

§9  ‘The Chun qiu bao qian tu says ‘In three hundred years the Dipper system 
changes its order’. If in the Grand Inception system of Deng Ping used by the 
Clerk’s officials there was to be a single fraction left over, then in the space of 
three hundred years the degrees of motion would move into error, and [the whole 
system] would be imbued with falsity, so that the ji and heng would be out of 
order, and there would be no insight into the patterned counterparts. Now on the 
day of the winter solstice, the sun is at 21 du of Dipper, but according to the 
[Grand Inception] system it is [at] the middle star of Ox. One day before the 
[official] day of Establishment of Spring, then it is the day of Establishment of 
Spring according to the Quarter-Remainder reckoning. If on that basis one was 
to open prisons and end great punishments, one would at once be violating the 
qi; to look for peace and tranquillity following the principle of the seasons would 
be a distant prospect. Now We shall change to following the Quarter Remainder, 
in order to follow in the footsteps of Yao,
39 and in order to accord with the saintly 
Confucius upholding the patterning of Heaven, trusting that all gentlemen will 
go ahead of the people, and with concordant hearts respectfully deliver [the 
seasons], so that there will be great good order, such that Our Ancestors great 
achievements may be made illustrious.’

this context they probably refer to the Pole Star and the Northern Dipper, though later they were

39 Y ao was a legendary sage emperor in High Antiquity.

於是四分施行． 而訢、梵猶以為元首十一月當先大， 欲以合耦弦望， 命有常
日， 而十九歲不得七閏， 晦朔失實． 行之未期， 章帝復發聖思， 考之經讖， 使
左中郎將賈逵問治曆者衞承、 李崇、 太尉屬梁鮪、 司徒掾嚴勗、 太子舍人徐

§10  At this, the Quarter Remainder [system] was promulgated for use. How -
ever Xin and Fan took it that the eleventh month at the head of the first 
Origin ought first to be long, with the intention that this would best fit 
in with the crescents and full moons, and the counting-off would have 
a fixed day [to start from]. But [this way] there would not be seven 
intercalations in a nineteen-year period, and last days and conjunctions 
would miss their real [dates]. It had not been in practice for long, when 
Zhangdi once more turned his sagely consideration to the matter, and 
examined it in accordance with the classics and the prognostications. 
He instructed the Left Commander of Palace Gentlemen, Jia Kui, to 
enquire of those who could handle li, Wei Cheng, Li Chong, Liang Wei 
the associate of the Commandant, Yan Xu of the office of the Excellency 
over the Masses, Xu Zhen the Houseman of the Heir Apparent, Su Tong 
the Eighth Order Grandee
40 from Ju Lu, [Bian] Xin and [Li] Fan, and 
others, ten in all.
以為月當先小， 據春秋經書朔不書晦者， 朔必有明晦， 不朔必在其月也． 即
先大， 則一月再朔， 後月無朔， 是明不可必． 梵等以為當先大， 無文正驗， 取欲
諧耦十六日望， 月朓昬， 晦當滅而已． 又晦與合同時， 不得異日． 又上知訢、 梵
穴見， 敕毋拘曆已班， 天元始起之月當小． 定， 後年曆數遂正．

on the fact that when the Spring and Autumn Annals 41 recorded conjunc-
tions it did not record last days. If there was a conjunction [recorded], 
then there was a clear last day, but if there was no conjunction [recorded] 
then [one could only say that the day in question] was in [the given] 
month. If one had a long [month] first, then the first month would have

impossible. Fan et al. had no textual basis on which to verify that the 
first month should be long; they just got it from their wish to fit in with

of the year after next were correct.

asterism] Ox. At the ancient winter solstice of the Yellow Emperor, 
Xia, Yin , Zhou and Lu systems, 42 the sun is at the Establishment Star, 
and the Establishment Star is our modern Dipper Star. On the Grand 
Inception system, Dipper has 26 du and 385 fen, and Ox has 8 du.
43 
Referring to the notes of the Clerks in charge of these affairs, at the 
winter and summer solstices the sun regularly fell short of the [position 
predicted by] the Grand Inception system by 5 du, so that at the winter 
solstice the sun was at 21¼ du of Dipper. The Star Canon of Master 
Shi
44 says “The Yellow Road circles through the beginning of Ox and 
is level at 20 du of Dipper, when it is 25 du further from the pole than 
the Red Road.” This is 21 du of Dipper on the equator. Quarter-
Remainder methods agree with the degrees of heaven in the observa -
tional notes of the responsible officials. [According to the] Shang shu 
kao ling yao “Dipper: 22 du, with no remaining fraction, and the winter 
solstice is at the place where Ox starts from.” Further, the present 
position of the sun relied on by Bian Xin and others is five du short 
of the middle star of Ox, which is 21¼ du of Dipper, close to the [value 
in the] Kao ling yao , which makes matters clear. In the eighth month 
of the second year of the Yuanhe period [85 
ce] an edict declared “One 
may not depart from Shi.”’
令兩候， 上得筭多者． 太史令玄等候元和二年至永元元年， 五歲中課日行及
冬至斗二十一度四分一， 合古曆建星考靈曜日所起， 其星閒距度皆如石氏故
事． 他術以為冬至日在牽牛初者， 自此遂黜也．  」
§14  It was ordered that observations should be doubled up, and that those that 
agreed with calculation to the greatest extent should be submitted to the 
throne. The Grand Clerk Xuan and others carried out observations from the 
second year of the Yuanhe period [85 
ce] to the first year of the Yongyuan 
period [89 ce], and in those five years checked that the sun reached the 
winter solstice at 21¼ du of Dipper, which fitted in with the Establishment 
Star of the ancient systems, and the sun’s starting point in the Kao ling yao. 
42 T hese are five of the ‘six ancient systems’ that by the end of Western Han were thought to have 
been in use in pre-imperial times, together with the Zhuan Xu system. The latter was named after 
supposed ancestor of the Qin royal house, who was the grandson of the mythical Yellow Emperor. 
However it is unlikely that these systems date back to pre-imperial times, rather than being more 
recent creations. See Cullen (forthcoming), chapter 3.
43
 The number of du in a complete revolution is Circuits of Heaven [562,120]/Concordance Factor 
[1539], which is equal to 365 + 385/1539. The fraction is all allocated to Dipper. Dipper is stated in 
the Han shu account of the Triple Concordance to be 26 du, and Ox is 8 du. See T
able 2.6. page 119.
44 ‘Master Shi’, otherwise known as Shi Shen 石申, was said to have been an expert in sky-lore of the 
pre-imperial period. The book referred to is now only known through quotations in later sources 
such as this one.

逵論曰 ： 「以太初曆考漢元盡太初元年日(朔)[食]二十三事，其十七得朔，四
得晦，二得二日；新曆七得朔，十四得晦，二得(三)[二]日.
§15  Jia Kui said: ‘Looking into 23 instances of solar eclipses from the Han 
epoch [206 bce] to the first year of the Grand Inception period [104 bce] 
using the Grand Inception system, 17 come out as at the conjunction, four 
come out as on the last day, and 2 come out as on the second day. With 
the new system, 7 come out as at the conjunction, 14 come out as on the 
last day, and 2 come out as on the second day.’
以太初曆考太初元年盡更始二年二十四事， 十得晦；以新曆十六得朔， 七得
二日， 一得晦．
§16  ‘Looking into 24 instances from the first year of the Grand Inception period 
[104 bce] to the second year of the Gengshi period [24 ce] using the Grand 
Inception system, ten come out as on the last day. 45 With the new system 
16 come out as on the conjunction, 7 come out as on the second day, and

384 Han discussions of astr onomical systems
[The incommensurability of cosmic constants; consequential  
necessity of inexactitude of all systems and their cumulation  
of errors; hence no system can be exact outside its limited  
period of validity, and revisions are inevitable]
天道參差不齊， 必有餘， 餘又有長短， 不可以等齊． 治曆者方以七十六歲斷
之， 則餘分消長， 稍得一日．
§19  ‘The alignments and discrepancies of the way of heaven are not commen -
surable. There must be remainders, and those remainders [themselves] will 
themselves differ in ways that cannot be made commensurable through 
equalising.
46 Those who manage astronomical systems [arbitrarily] chop off 
a period of 76 years [for commensurability of day, lunation and solar cycle, 
the Obscuration period of the Quarter Remainder], so the fractional remain-
ders gradually increase until they build up to a day.’
故易金火相革之卦象曰 ： 『君子以治曆明時． 』又曰 ： 『湯、 武革命， 順乎天
應乎人． 』言聖人必曆象日月星辰， 明數不可貫數千萬歲， 其閒必改更， 先
距求度數， 取合日月星辰所在而已． 故求度數， 取合日月星辰， 有異世之術．
§20  ‘So in the Book of Change, the image for the hexagram of metal and fire 
controlling each other says ‘The Gentleman clarifies the seasons by regulat-
ing the system.’ It also says ‘When Tang [founder of the Shang dynasty] 
and Wu [founder of the Zhou dynasty] changed the mandate, they accorded 
with heaven and responded to Man.’ That means the Sage must systematise 
and image the sun, moon and stellar markers, but in clarifying the reckon -
ings he cannot run the same reckonings through thousands of myriads of 
years, but there must be revisions during that interval. At the first setting 
of a standard, when one seeks for the reckoning of the degrees, one just 
gets them by fitting in with the locations of the sun, moon and stellar mark 
46 The references to qi 齊 here are I suggest more technical than might seem, as is the mention 
of qi deng 齊等. I believe that what is referred to here is the aim of the Chinese astronomical 
system-builder to represent the behaviour of the heavens by a series of (possibly large) whole 
numbers. Success in doing this requires that all the celestial cycles should be commensurable, 
i.e. that they can all be expressed as multiples of some one quantity, which may be set as equal 
to unity to simplify matters. The term qi is used in a similar way by Liu Hui 劉徽 around 
ad 
263 in describing what is done to fractions with different denominators which are to be added: 
母互乘子知以齊其子也 ‘the reciprocal multiplication by denominators is what renders the 
numerators commensurable’ Guo Shuchun 郭書 (1990) Jiu zhang suan shu 九章算術 ([Critical 
edition of the text] Mathematical Procedures in Nine Sections) . Shenyang, Liaoning Educa -
tion Press, 184–185. The reference to deng ‘equalised may refer’ to the process of finding the 
common factors of numbers by alternate subtraction until equal differences are found. At any 
rate, it does not seem likely that Jia Kui is just talking in a general way about the difficulty of 
representing particular cosmic constants exactly, nor is he making any claim that such constants 
change over time. The real difficulty as he sees it is apparently that of building a system using 
finite whole numbers.

太初曆不能下通於今， 新曆不能上得漢元． 一家曆法必在三百年之閒． 故讖
文曰『三百年斗曆改憲』． 漢興， 當用太初而不改， 下至太初元年百二歲乃

明效也． 」
§21  ‘The Grand Inception system cannot be extended down to today, and the 
new system cannot reach back up to the first year of Han. The rules of the 
system of a given school are [rightly] located within a particular three 
hundred year period. So the text of the Apocrypha says “In three hundred 
years the Dipper system must change its basic rule.” At the rise of Han, it 
would have been right to use the Grand Inception system but they made 
no change. The change was only made 102 years later when it came to the 
first year of the Grand Inception period. So at the start there were conjunc -
tions one day before the last day of the month, and when it came down to 
the time of Chengdi and Aidi, the second day [of the lunation] was taken 
as the conjunction. So this is a clear explanation of the frequent occurrence 
of the conjunction on the last day of the month.’
[The necessity of measuring solar and lunar motion with  
reference to the ecliptic and not the equator; work of Fu An,  
ignored by today’s officials; a check of records requested and  
carried out; conclusions of Fu An supported by this; support  
also given from observations by Geng Shouchang; necessity  
for officials to use ecliptic]
逵論曰： 「臣前上傅安等用黃道度日月弦望多近． 史官一以赤道度之， 不與日
月同， 於
– 3029 –
今曆弦望至差一日以上， 輒奏以為變， 至以為日却縮退行． 於黃道， 自得行
度， 不為變． 願請太史官日月宿簿及星度課， 與待詔星象考校． 奏可．
§22  ‘Y our servant has previously submitted a memorial pointing out that when 
Fu An and his colleagues 47 used the Yellow Road to measure the [posi -
tions of] sun and moon at half and full moons, they were mostly correct. 
47 W e do not know who Fu An was, or when he and his colleagues worked. But it sounds as though 
this took place in Jia Kui’s time, since he tells us that his intiative followed on from what Fu An 
had done.

386 Han discussions of astr onomical systems
But the astronomical officials, who only used the Red Road, were not in 
agreement with the sun and moon. They were often more than a day 
wrong in comparison with the present system, so they went ahead and 
memorialised this as being a portent, even to the extent of making out 
that the sun had suffered a setback and moved retrograde! On the Yellow 
Road the degrees of motion turn out naturally, and no such “portents” 
occur. I requested that the Grand Clerk’s records of the lodges of the sun 
and moon, together with the stellar data should be checked, and compared 
with the stellar phenomena [observed] by the Expectant Officials. My 
memorial was approved.’
臣謹案： 前對言冬至日去極一百一十五度， 夏至日去極六十七度， 春秋分日
去極九十一度． 洪範『日月之行， 則有冬夏』． 五紀論『日月循黃道， 南至牽
牛， 北至東井， 率日日行一度， 月行十三度十九分度七』也．
§23  Y our servant respectfully notes: I have previously answered that at the 
winter solstice the sun is 115 du from the pole, that at the summer solstice 
it is 67 du from the pole, and that at the spring and autumn equinoxes it 
is 91 du from the pole. 48 According to the Great Plan [chapter of the Book 
of Documents] ‘From the movements of the sun and moon, there result 
winter and summer’. The Wu ji lun
49 says ‘The sun and moon follow the 
Yellow Road, going south as far as Ox, and north as far as Well. The 
rates are that the sun moves one du in a day, and the moon moves 13
7⁄19  
du in a day.’
今史官一以赤道為度， 不與日月行同， 其斗、 牽牛、 東井、 輿鬼， 赤道得十
五， 而黃道得十三度半；行東壁、 奎、 婁、 軫、 角、 亢， 赤道七度， 黃道八度 ；
§24  Now the Clerks all use the Red Road as a scale for measuring the degrees, 
which is not in accord with the motions of the sun and moon. In Dipper 
and Ox [near the winter solstice] and Well and Ghost [near the summer 
solstice] one gets 15 du on the Red Road while getting 13½ du on the 
Yellow Road. When moving through Wall, Straddler and Harvester [near 
the spring equinox] and through Axletree, Horn and Gullet [near the 
autumn equinox] it is seven du on the Red Road for eight du on the 
Yellow Road.
48 These figures given in the solar table of the Han Quarter Remainder system (see Chapter 3, Proc. 
3.52) were 115 du for winter solstice and 67 1/12 du for summer solstice.The mean of these two 
values would be 911/24 du. A quarter of a complete circuit of 365¼ du would be 915/16 du. Jia Kui’s 
figures are clearly given to the nearest du. They imply that a value for the obliquity of the ecliptic 
(the angle by which the its plane is inclined to that of the equator) of 24 du. This is the value given 
by Zhang Heng, Hou Han shu, zhi 3, 3076, quoted in commentary).
49 This (now lost) book ‘Discussion of the Five Eras’ was written by Liu Xin’s father, Liu Xiang 劉
向, as mentioned at the end of the Han shu material translated above.

或月行多而日月相去反少， 謂之日却． 案黃道值牽牛， 出赤道南二十五度， 其直東
井、 輿鬼， 出赤道北二十五度． 赤道者為中天， 去極俱九十度， 非日月道， 而以
遙準度日月， 失其實行故也．
§25  Or the moon’s motion may be [supposedly] in excess, while the distance 
between the sun and moon on the contrary decreases, which they call ‘solar 
setback’. I would note that when the Yellow Road runs level through Ox, 
it goes 25 du to the south of the Red Road, and when it runs level through 
Well and Ghost, it goes 25 du to the north of the Red Road. The Red Road 
is the middle of Heaven, and is all of it 90 du from the pole.
50 It is not the 
path of the sun and moon, and [the effect alleged above] is because one 
has used such an incorrect standard to measure the sun and moon, and 
missed the real motions.
以今太史官候注考元和二年九月已來月行牽牛、東井四十九事， 無行十一度
者；行婁、角三十七事， 無行十五六度者， 如安言．
§26  If one uses the observational records of the present Grand Clerk from 
the ninth month of the second year of the Yuanhe period [85 ce Oct 7 
to Nov 5] onwards to examine 49 instances in which the moon has moved 
through Ox and Well,
51 there is none in which [the actually observed 
motion along the path of the moon from day to day] has been 11 du [as 
one would have expected if it had moved 13 du on the Red Road]. And 
for 37 instances in which it has moved through Harvester and Horn, there 
is none in which [the actually observed motion across the heavens from 
day to day] has been 15 or 16 du [as one would have expected if it had 
moved 13 du on the Red Road].
52 This is just as [Fu] An said.
問典星待詔姚崇、 井畢等十二人， 皆曰『星圖有規法， 日月實從黃道， 官無其
器， 不知施行』 ．
§27  I asked the Expectant Star-Clerks Yao Chong, Jing Bi and others, twenty 
persons in all, and they all stated that [the present] star maps have the 
compass pattern,
53 [whereas] the sun and moon really follow the Yellow 
50 These figures are slightly different from those given two paragraphs earlier. The implied winter 
solstice polar distance of the sun is (90 + 25) du = 115 du as already stated, but the summer solstice 
value would be (90 − 25) du = 65 du rather than 67 du. The stated value of the obliquity is also 
different from the 24 du implied above. I can think of no obvious reason for this discrepancy.
51 Forty-nine complete lunations would take us to the end of the intercalary 7th month of yongyuan.1, 
August 25–September 22, 89 ce.
52 He is about right: the actual daily motion of the moon across the celestial sphere does not fall below 
11° or rise much above 15.5°. See Cullen (forthcoming) chapter 6.
53 Possibly meaning that they were planispheres with all circles centered on the celestial pole?

疾意． 永平中， 詔書令故太史待詔張隆以四分法署弦、 望、 月食加時． 隆言能
用易九、 六、 七、 八爻知月行多少． 今案隆所署多失． 臣使隆逆推前手所署， 不
應， 或異日， 不中天乃益遠， 至十餘度． 梵、 統以史官候注考校，
§33  Jia Kui said: ‘Further, when the Clerks today predict the times of occurrence 
of conjunctions, crescents, full moon and lunar eclipses, their figures mostly 
miss the mark. This is because they do not understand the concept of the 
moon’s slowing and acceleration. In the Yongping reign period [58–75 
ce] 
an edict ordered the former Expectant Official attached to the Grand Clerk 
Zhang Long to use Quarter-Remainder methods to set out the times of 
occurrence of crescents, full moons and lunar eclipses. Long said he was 
able to use the numbers 9, 6, 7 and 8 of the hexagram lines of the Book of 
Change in order to understand the amount of the lunar motion. But I now 
report that [the results] that Long set out were mostly wrong. I, your vassal, 
caused Long to reproduce what his own hand had previously set out, but 
it did not answer, sometimes being on the wrong day and the amount by 
which it missed [corresponding with] the heavens was even greater [than 
before], up to as much as over ten du. Fan and Tong examined and compared 
these results with the observation notes of the Clerks.
月行當有遟疾， 不必在牽牛、 東井、 婁、 角之閒， 又非所謂朓、側匿， 乃由月
所行道有遠近出入所生,率一月移故所疾處三度， 九歲九道一復， 凡九章， 百七 
十一歲， 復十一月合朔旦冬至， 合春秋、 三統九道終數， 可以知合朔、 弦、 望、 月食
加時． 據官注天度為分率， 以其術法上考建武以來月食凡三十八事， 差密近， 有
益， 宜課試上． 」

not consistently [linked to position] between Ox, Well, Harvester and Horn 
[the lodges corresponding to the solstices and equinoxes], nor is it what is 
called tiao or ce ni,

the moon varies in distance and goes to south and north of [the Yellow 
Road]. The rule is that one month shifts the old position of [maximum]

文選 (Selected literature), 58, 1249.

reconstruct a ‘Nine Roads’ procedure for the moon]
案史官舊有九道術， 廢而不修． 熹平中， 故治曆郎梁國宗整上九道術， 詔書下
太史， 以參舊術， 相應． 部太子舍人馮恂課校， 恂亦復作九道術， 增損其分， 與
整術並校， 差為近． 太史令颺上以恂術參弦、 望． 然而加時猶復先後天， 遠則

§35  Note that previously the Clerks had the Nine Roads method, but it was 
abandoned before it had been perfected. In the Xiping  period [175–176 ce], 
the former Gentleman in charge of the calendar of the kingdom of Liang, 
Zong Zheng submitted [his own] Nine Roads method, and an edict was 
issued to refer the matter to the Grand Clerk. When it was compared with 
the old method, they answered to one another. Feng Xun, Houseman of the 
Heir Apparent checked and compared; Xun accordingly made a further Nine 
Roads method, adding to and subtracting from the fractional parts. When it 
was compared together with Zheng’s method, the differences were close. 
The Grand Clerk Yang submitted that he had checked Xun’s method against 
crescent and full moons, but the times when they fell were still further before 
and after Heaven, in the extreme case more than 10 du.

rate for the ke [graduations on] official clepsydra graduations is that they are 
increased or decreased by one ke [each] nine days.60 This is not answerable 
to the heavens: sometimes the difference in timing is as much as 2½ ke. This 
is not as accurate as the Xia system.’
詔書下太常， 令史官與融以儀校天， 課度遠近． 太史令舒、 承、 梵等對 ： 「案
官所施漏法令甲第六常符漏品， 孝宣皇帝三年十二月乙酉下， 建武十年二月
壬午詔書施行． 漏刻以日長短為數， 率日南北二度四分而增減一刻． 一氣俱十
五日， 日去極各有多少． 今官漏率九日移一刻， 不隨日進退． 夏曆漏刻隨日南
北為長短， 密近於官漏， 分明
– 3033 –
可施行． 」
§37  An edict was sent down to the Chamberlain for Ceremonials, ordering that 
the Clerks should, together with Rong, compare their instruments with the 
heavens, and check whether the measurements were far out or nearly cor -
rect. The Grand Clerk Shu, with Cheng, Fan and others replied: ‘We note 
that method for using clepsydras practised by the officials is modelled on 
Order A, [section] number 6, category ‘Perpetually correct clepsydras’, of 
the third year of the Filial [late] Xuandi [69 
bce], the twelfth month, day 
yiyou.22, which was ordered to be followed by an edict of the tenth year 
of the Jianwu period [34 ce], second month, day renwu.19. Clepsydra gradu-
ations take their numbers from the varying length of the day, the rate being 
that for every 2¼ du southwards or northwards they are increased or 
decreased by 1 graduation. One qi is 15 days, and [for each qi] the sun’s 
polar distance varies. Now the rate for official clepsydras is to shift by one 
graduation for each nine days. This does not follow the advancing or retreat-
ing of the sun. In the Xia system the clepsydra graduations do follow the 
southwards and northwards [movement] of the sun in their lengthening and 
shortening, and this is more accurate than the official clepsydra. Clearly 
this may be put into practice.’

§38  That same year, in the eleventh month, day jiayin.51 [December 14, 102 
ce], an edict stated: ‘Let it be announced to the Minister of Education, 
and to the Minister of Works: the clepsydra serves to regulate the divi -
sions of time, to fix darkness and daylight. The varying lengths of dark -
ness and daylight arise from the variations of the sun’s polar distance. 
The way of the sun follows round in a circle, and cannot be divided up 
according to calculated rates: one has to rely on instrumental measure -
ments, and align it with the sundial shadow. Now the official clepsydra 
divides up darkness and daylight by calculated rates, and adds or subtracts 
one graduation each nine days, which is contrary to reality, and at the 
extreme may lead to an inaccurate number derived from an arbitrary 
method. The Expectant Grand Clerk Huo Rong has sent up a memorial 
saying “This is not answerable with the heavens”. The Clerks of the 
Chamberlain for Ceremonials have operated their instruments and let 
water flow down, [and found that] the officials’ clepsydra misses the 
heavens by as much as three graduations. Using the sundial shadow to 
make the graduations diminishes the error, and its accuracy can be veri -
fied. Now we decree 48 indicator-rods [lit. “arrows”] for the clepsydra 
graduations [from the] sundial shadow, [garbled phrase omitted] for use 
in official establishments; when the reckoning clerks come on duty, let 
them take charge of [appropriately] issuing the 48 indicator-rods.’
文多， 故魁取二十四氣日所在， 并黃道去極、 晷景、 漏刻、 昬明中星刻于下.

clepsydra, and the graduations of darkness and daylight and the centred stars.

had been made clear. When we come to the Quarter Remainder, that was 
[begun] in the Jianwu period [25–54 ce], promulgated in the Yuanhe period 
[84–86 ce] and settled in the Yongyuan period [89–104 ce] – 70 years, and 
only after that were all the patterns and forms completely established, so 
that those in charge of observations had a standard [to rely on]. Celestial 
matters are obscure and subtle, and that is how difficult they are.
中興以來， 圖讖漏泄， 而考靈曜、命曆序皆有甲寅元． 其所起在四分庚申元
後百一十四歲， 朔差卻却二日． 學士修之於草澤， 信向以為得正． 及太初曆以
後天為疾， 而修之者云「百四十四歲而太歲超一辰， 百七十一歲當棄朔餘六
十三， 中餘千一百九十七， 乃可常行」 ． 自太初元年至永平十一年， 百七十一， 當
去分而不去， 故令益有疏闊．
§41  After the renaissance of our dynasty, the tu and the chen [apocrypha] were 
all-pervasive, and the Kao ling yao and Ming li xu both used the jiayin.51 
epoch. The starting point for this was 114 years after the gengshen.57 origin 
of the Quarter Remainder.63 The difference in new moons amounted to two 
days. Scholars worked on this in the backwoods, and their trust in it all 
made them sure they were right. When it came to the fact that the Grand 
Inception system had the fault of lagging behind Heaven, then those who 
worked on it said ‘The Tai sui skips one year-name every 144 years;
64 in 
171 years one must take out a conjunction remainder of 63, and a Medial 
[qi] remainder of 1197, then the system can be run as usual. From the first 
year of the Grand Inception period [105 
bce] to the eleventh year of Yong-
ping [68 ce] is 171 [years]. The fractions should have been removed but 
was not. So that made things more and more inaccurate.’ 65
此二家常挾其術， 庶幾施行， 每有訟者， 百寮會議， 群儒騁思， 論之有方， 益於
多聞識之， 故詳錄焉．
§42  Now these two schools each clung to their doctrines, and when [either] was 
put into practice, there were advocates on each side. The assembly of 
63 T he system origin of the Han Quarter Remainder system used for calendrical purposes was 161 
bce, which was a gengchen.17 year. However, if we go back one Era [1520 years], we reach 1681 
bce, which is a gengshen.57 year. After another 114 years, we reach 1567 bce, which is indeed 
a jiayin.51 year. This is the system origin of the  Yin system, one of the Six Ancient li referred to 
above.
64 See note 72.
65 I end the quotation here, which makes better sense, despite the editors of the Beijing edition, who 
punctuate otherwise. If one looks at the predictions of the Triple Concordance for 68 bce, we find 
that the conjunction beginning the first Celestial month preceding the relevant civil year was pre-
dicted to fall on December 25, 69 bce, a xinyou.48 day, at 63/81 of a day after midnight, while the 
winter solstice (the first medial qi) fell on the same day (as expected, given that this was a Rule 
Head), but at 1197/1539 of a day after midnight. The suggestion made was thus that both these 
fractions should be reduced to zero, thus resetting the system to Concordance Head conditions.

§43  In the second year of the Yanguang period of Andi [122 ce], the Palace 
Receptionist Dan Song stated that it would be right to use a jiayin.51 
origin. Liang Feng from Henan said it would be right to return to using 
the Grand Inception. The Secretarial Court Gentlemen Zhang Heng and 
Zhou Xing both had abilities in calendrical reckoning.
66 They raised 
objections to Song and Feng, to some of which they did not reply, and 
to some of which they stated that they were in error and mistaken. Heng 
and Xing checked and reported on the records [from] instruments, 
examined the past and compared it with the present, and took the view 
that the Nine Roads method was the most accurate. An edict ordered 
that the matter should be referred to the ducal ministers for detailed 
submissions.
太尉愷等上侍中施延等議 ： 「太初過天， 日一度， 弦望失正， 月以晦見西方， 食不

應， 合圖讖， 可施行． 」 博士黃廣、大行令任僉議， 如九道．

dant Shi Yan and others, saying ‘The Grand Inception goes past the heavens, 
the sun [doing so] by one du, and the crescents and full moons miss the 
correct time. The moon is seen in the west on the last day of the month, 
and the eclipses do not correspond to heaven. In the Yuanhe period [84–86 
ce] a reform led to the use of the Quarter Remainder, but even though it is 
more accurate than the Grand Inception, it is still not correct, and neither 
is fit for use. The jiayin.51 origin corresponds to the heavens, and fits with

§45  Y in Zhi of Henan, and the Houseman to the Heir Apparent Li Hong and 
others, forty in all, submitted: ‘If the jiayin.51 [origin] is used, then 114 
years would have to be removed from the interval between the beginning 
of things and the capture of the Lin as mentioned in the Yuan ming bao,
68 
and in predicting intercalations one would not set out the months, while 
there would be more than one instance when the last days, crescents full 
moons and the lodge degrees for the 24 qi would not match up. In using 
the Nine Roads for the conjunctions, the months would have three long 
ones for two short ones. All of this is far out. The Yuanhe reign period 
system reform [in 85 
ce] was in correspondence with the saying in the text 
of the Yuan ming bao “Every three centuries the Dipper system changes its 
rule”. The Quarter Remainder system originally came from the Charts and 
Apocrypha, and gets closest to accuracy. It would not be right to change 
it.’ Kai and others, 84 persons in all made a formal submission, [saying] 
that it would be proper to follow the Grand Inception.

of the various persons who follow the Grand Inception have any other 
comparison or verification than this – they seize on the excuse that Shizong

that it would be proper to follow the Grand Inception.

prodigies suddenly went to the extreme, and there was no favourable response 
[from the cosmos]. Your vassal hereby submits that when sage kings arise,

he did not examine preceding ages, and offended against the canon of the 
emperors. When Taizong [Wendi] made his reforms, the Three Grades were 
at peace, yellow dragons appeared, the guilty were punished and all five 
things were complete. But in the time of Aidi and Pingdi, while they both 
maintained the Grand Inception, evil prodigies came in droves, and there 
were not a few disasters. Those who make submissions [advocating the 
Grand Inception] have not done so by aligning completed reckonings, and 
examining the real to seek the substantial, but wildly select some crazy 
doctrine, attributing all blessings to the Grand Inception, and putting all 
blame on the Quarter Remainder.’
太初曆眾賢所立， 是非已定， 永平不審， 復革其弦望． 四分有謬， 不可施行． 元
和鳳鳥不當應曆而翔集． 遠嘉前造， 則表其休；近譏後改， 則隱其福． 漏見曲
論， 未可為是．
§47  ‘The Grand Inception system was established by many worthy men, and 
the rights and wrongs of it have been settled. In the Yongping period [59–75 
ce] it did not pass muster, so they made further revisions to the crescents 
and full moons, but the Quarter Remainder [still] had errors, and could not 
be promulgated for use. In the Yuanhe period [84–86 
ce] it would not have 
been fitting for phoenix birds to have gathered together in droves in response 
to the [new] calendar. When distant blessings are created earlier, then their 
advantages are shown forth: when recent faults are later reformed, then the 
[resultant] goodness is concealed. [Such] deficient views and biased reason-
ing can never be right.’

were the most accurate when compared to contemporary methods, but it 
still could not be extended back to antiquity. Turning to the aim of [Liu] 
Xiang’s son [Liu] Xin to fit in with the [data] of the Spring and Autumn 
Annals, he arbitrarily cut across the reckoning of the years, diminishing 
the Xia [dynasty] and adding to the Zhou [dynasty]. Looking into this 
through tables and annals, the errors are several hundred. Checking the 
two systems against one another, in 6156 years the Grand Inception is 
one day in excess.
69 It says that the winter solstice sun is in Ox, although 
it [goes] level through Dipper. It is too inaccurate for further use. That 
things obviously are this way is common knowledge amongst the Clerks 
– not just to Heng and Xing. Previously it was held that the Nine Roads 
[method] was accurate; now those who make submissions [in favour of 
the Grand Inception system] say it is faulty. When we come to [the 
proposal for changing to] a jiayin.51 origin, again it has many contradic -
tions and mistakes. None of this can be taken as correct. In the past, 
Confucius corrected the expression “[Duke Ding of Lu] borrowed a 
horse”, in order to pay respect to the meaning of being a prince;
70 how 
much more is [such attention to correct expression] needed in the case 
of the reckonings of the celestial system. One cannot trust in the dubious 
and follow the empty, making wrong into right!’ The emperor accepted 
what he said, and so put an end to the business of revising the astronomi -
cal system.

a dubious practice has become established. Few of them have been able 
to “hook out what is profound and attain to what is distant”: in order to 
become aware of this one only has to take note of the [incorrect predic -
tions] of the crescents and full moons].’
詔書下三公、百官雜議． 太史令虞恭、治曆宗訢等議： 「建曆之本， 必先立

§51  An edict referred the matter to the Three Excellencies, and all the officials 
made diverse submissions. The Grand Clerk Yu Gong, and the calendrical 
expert Zong Xin, with others, submitted: ‘The basis of establishing a system 
inevitably lies in first establishing an origin. When the origin is correct, 
only then may one fix the Day Divisor, and only when the Day Divisor is 
fixed can one measure out the circumference of heaven and fix the equinoxes 
and solstices. When these three follow in sequence, then the system may 
be completed. The “middle Era” origin [period] of the Quarter Remainder
74 
began in the third year of the Houyuan reign period of Wendi [161 bce],

Han discussions of astronomical systems 401
§52  Each year is supported by its predecessor, from below to above, and their 
upholding of one another is without error. This is how a clear scriptural 
warrant for the system origin of the Quarter Remainder is set out in the 
Charts and Apocrypha. In the first year of the Grand Inception reign-period, 
the year was at dingchou.14. Going right up all the way to its [High] origin, 
that should have been gengxu.47, but it was said to be bingzi.13.
75 They 
said that every 144 years the year skips a station, and that in all there had 
been 993 skippings, so that the year had 82 and a fraction “void circuits”,
76 
and thus reached bingzi.13. 77 Note that as for the year having a “skip”, at 
the celestial origin, in the eleventh month, on day jiazi.1 the instants of 
midnight, conjunction and winter solstice coincided, and the sun and moon 
set off together. The sun moves one du [each day] and when it had accu -
mulated 365¼ du it had made one circuit of the heavens, what we call a 
year [sui, i.e. a solar cycle]. Each year [the sexagesimal count] advances 
by one station. If the sun is unable to make a “void circuit” of the heavens, 
then the year has no means of skipping a station.’
案百七十一歲二蔀一章， 小餘六十三， 自然之數也． 夫數出於杪曶， 以成毫
氂， 亮氂積累， 以成分寸． 兩儀既定， 日月始離． 初行生分， 積分成度． 日行一
度 ，一歲而周， 故為術者， 各生度法， 或以九百四十， 或以八十一． 法有細觕， 以
生兩科， 其歸一也．
§53  ‘Note that 171 years is two Obscurations [76 years] and one Rule [19 years], 
[leading to] a lesser remainder of 63: these are the natural quantities. Numbers 
come from minute amounts, which form tiny quantities, and as these tiny 
quantities accumulate, they make [such small but measurable quantities as] 
fractions and whole inches. When the Two Principles [of yin and yang] have 
been fixed, then the sun and moon first separate; in their inception of motion 
they give rise to fractions, and these accumulate to form du. The sun moves 
one du [per day] and makes a circuit in one sui. So those who lay down 
algorithms each produce a “degree divisor”, some using 940 and some 81. 
These divisors have small differences, and so the two categories [of system] 
are produced, but they are basically the same.’
日法者， 日之所行分也． 日垂令明， 行有常節， 日法所該， 通遠無已， 損益
毫氂， 差以千里． 自此言之， 數無緣得有虧棄之意也． 今欲飾平之失， 斷法垂
75 Dingchou.14 was the year-name of 104 bce according to the reckoning used in the Eastern Han, and 
continued thereafter. The High Origin of the Triple Concordance system was at the winter solstice 
preceding the civil year 143,231 bce, which was gengxu.47 on the same reckoning. That year was 
however specified as being bingzi.13 by Liu Xin in the Triple Concordance. Applying his ‘station-
skipping’ rule, 104 bce thus also became bingzi.13. See Proc. 2.26.
76 One circuit of the heavens contains 12 Jupiter stations, so 993 skipped stations is equivalent to 
993/12 = 82¾ circuits.
77 The 993 ‘skippings’  introduce a shift in cyclical year of 993 mod 60 = 33.

分， 恐傷大道． 以步日月行度， 終數不同， 四章更不得朔餘一． 雖言九道去課
進退， 恐不足以補其闕． 且課曆之法， 晦朔變弦， 以月食天驗， 昭著莫大焉．
§54  ‘The day fraction is [what gives] the fractional part of the sun’s [annual] 
motion. The sun clearly sends down its ordinance, and its motion has its 
constant rules. What the day fraction defines is valid indefinitely without 
any end. If one decreases it or adds to it by a mere trifle, [eventually] the 
result will be thousands of li out.
78 Speaking of it this way, there is no basis 
for getting the notion of trimming off and discarding [small amounts] from 
the numbers. Now it is desired to excuse [Deng] Ping’s errors by chopping 
off the divisor and dropping a fraction. I fear that this will do injury to the 
great Way. In pacing out the degrees of motion of the sun and moon, the 
ultimate numbers will not be the same, nor in four Rules will one obtain a 
conjunction remainder of 1. Even though it [might be] said that the Nine 
Roads depart from the calculated [mean motions] through their advances 
and retardation, I fear that [this] is not enough to repair the deficiencies. 
Moreover, the rule for checking the system, as last and first days change to 
crescents, is by means of the celestial verification [given by] lunar eclipses 
– nothing could be more clear and obvious than this.’
今以去六十三分之法為曆，驗章和元年以來日變二
– 3037 –
十事， [一]月食二十八事， 與四分曆更失， 定課相除， 四分尚得多， 而又便
近.孝章皇帝曆度審正， 圖儀晷漏， 與天相應， 不可復尚． 文曜鉤曰： 『高辛受
命， 重黎說文． 唐堯即位, 羲和 立(禪)[渾]. 夏后制德， 昆吾列神． 成周改號，
萇弘分官． 』運斗樞曰： 『常占有經， 世史所明． 』洪範五紀論曰： 『民閒亦有
黃帝諸曆， 不如史官記之明也． 』

the dates of 20 solar events and 28 lunar eclipses from the first year of the 
Zhanghe reign period [87 
ce] onwards,79 then its accuracy falls further short 
of the Quarter Remainder, and if we look at the differences in predictions 
and observed events, then the Quarter Remainder not only succeeds in more

they could not be improved. The Wen yao gou says “When Gao Xin [great

80 The Yun dou shu says “There are the handbooks of

自古及今， 聖帝明王， 莫不取言於羲和、常占之官， 定精微於晷儀， 正眾疑,
祕藏中書， 改行四分之原． 及光武皇帝數下詔書， 草創其端， 孝明皇帝課校其

§56  ‘So from antiquity down to the present, there has been no sage emperor 
or perceptive king who has not taken advice from officials such as Xi, 
He and Chang Zhan, determining the essential subtleties of the gnomon 
shadow, settling dubious points, and recording them confidentially in 
the palace archives, so as to reform and put into practice the origin of 
the Quarter Remainder. When we come to Guangwudi, several edicts 
were issued that created the starting point. Mingdi observed and verified 
the reality of it, and Zhangdi proclaimed that its methods should be put 
into practice. Three sage princes have succeeded in turn, and several 
decades have passed, making it reliable and proved, well-known and 
accepted in practice. Its [system] origin goes back to the beginning of 
the cosmos, and its numbers restore the ancient Quarter Remainder. It 
would be right to accord with the precedent laid down in the edict [issued 
on] the jiayin.51 [day].’
82 This submission was accepted [by the Emperor].
[175 ce proposal for use of jiayin origin; successful opposition  
by Cai Yong in a great assembly of officials]

所用代周之元． 太史[治曆郎](治治曆)
83中郭香、劉固意造妄說， 乞本庚申元

§57  In the fourth year of the Xiping reign period of Lingdi [175–176 ce] the 
Gentleman of the Interior for Miscellaneous Uses Feng Guang 84 and the 
Accounting Clerk to the Chancellor of Pei, Chen Huang stated: ‘The 
system origin is incorrect, so that evil folk are rebelling and thieving in 
Yizhou, and robbers and bandits make endless trouble. Although the 
system should use a jiayin.51 origin, it uses a gengshen.57 origin. Among 
the Charts and Wefts, there is none that uses a gengshen.57 origin. It is 
near to the origin that Qin used in supplanting Zhou. The Palace Gentle -
man for Regulating the Calendar Guo Xiang and Liu Gu thought up wild

議郎蔡邕議， 以為：
– 3038 –
曆數精微， 去聖久遠， 得失更迭， 術無常是． 漢興承秦， 曆用顓頊， 元用乙卯. 
百有二歲， 孝武皇帝始改正朔， 曆用太初， 元用丁丑， 行之百八十九歲．孝 章
皇帝改從四分， 元用庚申．
§59  ‘The Court Gentleman for Consultation Cai Yong gave his views as follows: 
“The reckonings of an astronomical system are refined and subtle. As we 
move further away from the sages, successes and failures alternate, and 
there is no method that is always correct. When the Han rose in succession 
to Qin, for an astronomical system they used the Zhuan Xu [system], and 
for origin they used yimao.52.
87 [After] 102 years, Wudi took the initiative 
to change the Standard Conjunction; for an astronomical system he used 
the Grand Inception, and for an origin he used dingchou.14. They followed 
this for 189 years. Then Zhangdi changed to follow the Quarter Remainder, 
and for an origin he used gengshen.57”.’
88
今光、晃各以庚申為非， 甲寅為是． 案曆法， 黃帝、顓頊、 夏、 殷、 周、 魯,  
凡六家， 各自有元． 光、晃所據， 則殷曆元也． 他元雖不明於圖讖， 各自一家之
術， 皆當有效於當時． 武帝始用太初丁丑之元， 六家紛錯， 爭訟是非． 太史令張
壽王挾甲寅元以非漢曆， 雜候清臺， 課在下第， 卒以疏闊， 連見劾奏， 太初效
驗， 無所漏失． 是則雖非圖讖之元， 而有效於前者也． 及用四分以來， 考之行
度， 密於太初， 是又新元有效於今者也．
§60  ‘Now Guang and Huang both say that gengshen.57 is wrong, and that 
jiayin.51 is correct. I would note that each of the astronomical systems of 
the Yellow Emperor, Zhuan Xu, Xia, Yin, Zhou and Lu, six schools in all, 
had its own origin. The one relied on by Guang and Huang is the origin of 
the Yin system. Even though the other origins are not made clear in the 
Charts and Apocrypha, each one stands in its own right as the method of 
one school, and all must have had validity at the corresponding time. When 
Wudi took the initiative to use the dingchou.14 origin of the Grand Incep-
tion, the six schools were thrown into confusion, and wrangled over the 
rights and wrongs. [In 78 
bce] the Grand Clerk Zhang Shouwang clung to 
the jiayin.51 origin in order to reject the Han system. After various 
87 Cullen (1996), 28 notes that Chen Jiujin and others make the Zhuan Xu epoch jiayin.51. Chen 
ascribes this to the fact that the sexagenary system used by Liu Xin in the Triple Concordance was 
not continuous with the system of early Han, so that the station-skipping meant that there was dif-
ference of one in the count.
88
 As already noted. the epochal year of 161 bce is actually gengchen.17. This gengshen.57 epoch is 
one Era period of 1520 years further back, in 1681 bce. 161 bce is the Celestial Era Head, and 1681 
bce is the Anthropic Era Head.

observations on the Pure Terrace, it was checked and put down as a failure,

deficiencies or errors. This is a case where a system origin was shown to 
be valid in the past, even though it did not appear in the texts of the Charts 
and Apocrypha. When we come to the time from when the Quarter Remain-
der was used, if one checks the degrees of motion, it is more accurate than 
the Grand Inception. This additionally is a case of a new system origin 
being valid today.’
延光元年， 中謁者亶誦亦非四分庚申， 上言當用命曆序甲寅元． 公卿百寮參
議正處， 竟不施行． 且三光之行， 遲速進退， 不必若一． 術家以筭追而求之， 取合
於當時而已． 故有古今之術． 今術之不能上通於古， 亦猶古術之不能下通於
今也．
§61  ‘In the first year of the Yanguang period, [122 ce] the Palace Receptionist 
Dan Song himself attacked the gengshen.57 epoch of the Quarter Remainder, 
and memorialised that one should use the jiayin.51 origin of the Ming li 
xu. The ducal ministers and the various office-holders compared reports and 
correctly settled the matter, and in the end the proposal was not adopted. 
Moreover, the motions of the Three Luminaries, in their slowings and 
accelerations and their advances and retardations are not invariably the 
same. When experts try to chase after them through calculation, all they 
can do is to seek a fit at the corresponding time. So there are ancient meth -
ods, and also modern ones. The inability of modern methods to be extended 
back to antiquity is the same as the inability of ancient methods to be 
extended forward to modern times.’
元命苞、乾鑿度皆以為開闢至獲麟二百七十六萬 歲；及命曆序積獲麟至
漢， 起庚午蔀之二十三歲， 竟己酉、戊子及丁卯蔀六十九歲， 合為二百七十
五歲． 漢元年歲在乙未， 上至獲麟則歲在庚申． 推此以上， 上極開闢， 則元在
庚申． 讖雖無文， 其數見存． 而光、晃以為開闢至獲麟二百七十五萬九千八
百八十六歲， 獲麟至漢百六十一歲， 轉差少一百一十四歲． 云當滿足， 則上違
乾鑿度、元命苞， 中使
– 3039 –
獲麟不得在哀公十四年， 下不及命曆序獲麟至漢相去四蔀年數， 與奏記譜注
不相應.

beginning of the cosmos to the capture of the Lin. When we come to the

sui of the gengwu.7 Obscuration, and extends through the jiyou.46, wuzi.25 
Obscuration and the 69th sui of the dingmao.4 Obscuration, making 275 sui 
in all. In the epochal year of Han the sui was at yiwei.32; if one goes back

to the capture of the Lin, then the sui was at gengshen. 57. Extending on 
backwards from this until one comes to the start of the cosmos, then the 
origin is at gengshen.57. Even though the Apocrypha have no [relevant] text, 
the reckonings are there before us. But Guang and Huang take it that from 
the start of the cosmos to the capture of the Lin is 2,759,886 sui
89 and that 
it is [only] 161 years from the capture of the Lin to the Han. They have 
made a difference of 114 years less. If one says that this is to be made up, 
then far back it will contradict the Qian zao du and Yuan ming bao, in the 
intervening period it will mean that the capture of the Lin did not fall in the 
14th year of Duke Ai [of Lu, i.e. in 481 
bce] and finally it will not reach 
the number of years [specified in] the Ming li xu  for the four Obscurations 
[of 76 years each] from the capture of the Lin to the Han, so that this will 
not be answerable to the data noted in the memorial.’
蔡邕月令論曰： 「顓頊曆術曰： 『天元正月己巳朔旦立春， 俱以日月起於天廟
營室五度． 』今月令孟春之月， 日在營室． 」　 　
§63  [NOTE FROM COMMENTARY]: Cai Yong’s Comments on the ‘Monthly 
Ordinances’ states ‘According to the Methods of the Zhuan Xu system “In 
the first month, day jisi.6 conjunction occurs at midnight, which is also the 
inception of ‘Establishment of Spring’. At that time the sun and moon start 
off together from the 5th du of [the lodge] House in the Celestial Shrine.”
90 
Now in the ‘Monthly Ordinances’, the sun is said to be in House in the 
month of Early Spring.’ 91

at the central star of Ox. The Establishment of Spring of the Quarter

§67  ‘Formerly Yao ordered Xi and He to systematise and make counterparts 
for the sun, moon and celestial markpoints, and Shun rectified the seasons 
and months to correct the days; Tang and Wu changed the Mandate, settled 
the system and clarified the seasons – we can call this “correcting”. But 
[all these sages] still met with floods and encountered drought, and they 
received warnings such as “the Man and Yi [tribes] are treacherous to the 
Chinese, bandits, thieves and evil villains”. But Guang and Huang say that 
all the derangement of yin and yang, all evil ministers, robbers and thieves, 
are the fault of the [system] origin. This is really not the pattern [things 
follow].’

§69  The Commandant Chen, the Minister of Education Gui, and the Minister 
of Works Xun indited Guang and Huan for lèse majesté on account of 
Yong’s report, and sentenced them to penal banishment. But an edict ordered 
that their offence should not be proceeded against.
臣昭曰： 不有君子， 其能國乎？觀蔡邕之議， 可以言天機矣． 賢明在朝， 弘益遠
哉！公卿結正， 足懲淺妄之徒， 詔書勿治， 亦深「盍各」之致．
§70  [NOTE FROM COMMENTARY]: The vassal [Liu] Zhao says: Without 
gentlemen, how could one have a state at all? Looking at Cai Yong’s 
report, one can say it gets to the basic workings of Heaven. If the worthy 
and perspicuous are at court, then their vast benefits reach afar. If the 
ducal ministers bind themselves to rectitude, than is enough to settle 
mean and irresponsible people. The edict ordering that the prosecutions 
[of Guang and Huang] should not proceed is surely a full expression of 
[the spirit of] ‘Why not all [speak your mind]’ [as in the Analects of 
Confucius].

the fourth month [May 24–June 22, 179 ce]; Xun’s method had it in the 
3rd month, and the official system had it in the 5th month. 101 The Grand 
Clerk submitted that they should be checked, and when the time came the 
one that hit the mark should be followed. On day dingchou.14, an edict 
replied that this was approved.
其四年， 紺孫誠上書言： 「受紺法術， 當復改， 今年十二月當食， 而官曆以後年
正月． 」到

§75  In the 4th year [of the Xiping period, i.e. 175–176 ce] [Zong] Gan’s grandson 
[Zong] Cheng submitted a memorial saying ‘I have received the model 
methods of Gan. They require to be revised. In the present year there will 
be an actual eclipse in the twelfth month [December 31, 175–January 28, 
176], while the official system has it in the first month of the next year.’
102 
100 What these were is unclear. I suggest that the reference may be to the ‘six ancient systems’, the 
Triple Concordance and the Han Quarter Remainder, which would give us eight different system 
origins.
101 This sentence appears to be (in modern terms) an editorial footnote. It breaks the sequence of the 
narrative by jumping ahead several years to comment on a failure to predict an eclipse by both 
Xun and the official system. Starry Night Pro shows a very slight penumbral eclipse on June 7, 
09:58 local Luoyang time, JD 1,786,594.6027, but at that time the moon was invisible, 60° below 
the western horizon, so the eclipse could not have been observed. The Han Quarter Remainder 
does indeed predict an eclipse for the full moon of the 5th civil month, which would have been 
July 7, when no eclipse took place. The use of the word ‘ought’ suggests that Liu Hong (who is 
presumably the editorial voice here) had made his own prediction – and in fact if we make use 
of his Uranic Manifestation system, it does indeed predict a lunar eclipse for the full moon of the 
4th month, on June 7.

lunar eclipse was in fact visible on that day, reaching its maximum with slight immersion into 
the umbra at 06:20 local Luoyang time, JD 1,785,354.451, when the moon was still 9° above the 
western horizon. It had begun 2 hours earlier, when the moon’s altitude was 32°. The Han Quarter

When the time came, it was as he had said. Cheng was given the post of 
Houseman. On day bingshen.33 [March 2], an edict ordered that Cheng’s 
method should be attended to and put into practice.
到光和二年歲在己未， 三月、 五月皆陰， 太史令修、 部舍人張恂等推計行度,
以為三月近， 四月遠． 誠以四月． 奏廢誠術， 施用恂術． 其三年， 誠兄整前後上
書言： 「去年三月不食， 當以四月． 史官廢誠正術， 用恂不正術． 」整所上正屬
太史， 太史主者終不自言三月近， 四月遠． 食當以見為正， 無遠近．
§76  W hen it came to the second year of the Guanghe period [179–180 ce], when 
the year was at jiwei.56, the third and the fifth months were both cloudy. 
The Grand Clerk Xiu, and the Houseman of his office Feng Xun [reading 
Feng 馮 for Zhang 張 as in the collation note, in view of the appearance 
of Feng Xun elsewhere] and others used calculations to predict the degrees 
of the motions, and held that the third month had been close [to an eclipse] 
but the fourth month was far out. Cheng made it the fourth month.
103 It was 
proposed to reject Cheng’s method, and to promulgate Xun’s method for 
use. In the third year [180–181 
ce] Cheng’s elder brother Zheng sent memo-
rials one after another to the effect that ‘Last year there was no eclipse in 
the third month, but it actually happened in the fourth month. The Clerks 
have rejected Cheng’s correct method, and used Xun’s incorrect method.’ What 
Zheng submitted was properly the concern of the Grand Clerk. Those in charge 
of the Grand Clerk’s [office] never [actually] stated themselves that the third 
month was near and the fourth month was far out. In eclipses, it should be 
visibility that decides what is correct – there should be no ‘near’ or ‘far’.
詔書下太常： 「其詳案注記， 平議術之要， 效驗虛實． 」 太常就耽上選侍中韓
說、 博士蔡較、 穀城門候劉洪、 右郎中陳調於太常府， 覆校注記， 平議難問. 
恂、 誠各對．
Remainder does indeed predict an eclipse for the full moon of the first month, on February 13, 
176 ce, when no eclipse took place – although the moon had just missed the earth’s penumbra by 
about half a degree around 21:00 on the preceding evening.
103 The Han Quarter Remainder system predicted an eclipse on July 7, the full moon of the 5th 
month; no eclipse took place on that day. There was a very slight penumbral eclipse around 
10:00 local Luoyang time on June 7, the day after the predicted full moon of the 4th month, 
but the moon was then 62° below the horizon and nothing would have been seen. Since we are 
not told that full moon day of the 4th month was cloudy, the absence of a visible eclipse was 
presumably noted, hence the rejection of Cheng’s method. There was however a good pen -
umbral eclipse with the moon 38° above the horizon in the preceding month, with maximum 
around 00:20 local Luoyang time on May 9, which was the predicted full moon day of the 3rd 
month. We may note that Liu Hong’s Uranic Manifestation system predicted an eclipse in the 
4th month – could this have anything to do with the favour shown to Cheng’s predictions in the 
conclusions below?

§77  An edict sent the matter down to the Chamberlain for Ceremonials: ‘You 
shall make a detailed examination of the records of observation notes, and 
make a fair report on the essentials of the methods [proposed], checking 
and verifying the baseless and the solid’. The Chamberlain for Ceremonials 
Jiu Chen submitted that he had gathered the Palace Attendant Han Shuo, 
the Erudit Cai Jiao, the Watch Officer at the Gucheng Gate Liu Hong, the 
Palace Gentleman of the Right Chen Diao in the Chamberlain for Ceremo-
nials’ office, to comprehensively compare the records of observation notes, 
and to report equitably and debate matters. Xun and Cheng each made 
responses.

§78  [The report stated:] ‘Xun’s method took as its pattern that there were 961 
eclipses in 5640 months. He multiplied and divided to make complete months.105 
Making predictions from the Jianwu period [began 56–57 ce] onwards, in all 
he obtained 327 eclipses, of which 15 eclipses were wrong. Note that when 
the officials searched their observation notes, 98 eclipses seen in the heavens 
corresponded with both methods, and 2100
106 were false.’

踰． 各引書緯自證， 文無義要， 取追天而已．
§79  Cheng’ s method took as its pattern that there were 135 eclipses in 23 months. 
He multiplied and divided to make complete months, and from the Jiankang 
period [144–145 ce] backwards deducted 41, while from the Jiankang period 
onwards he deducted 35 on the grounds that none of these was an eclipse. 
Xun’s method revised the old pattern, while Cheng’s method additionally 
subtracted and diminished midway along. If we analyse their good and bad 
points, neither goes beyond the other. Each one cited the Wefts [apocrypha] of 
the Book of Documents to justify itself, and their writing had nothing that got 
to the essential meaning; they were just trying to chase after the Heavens.

§80  In the methods for the sun and moon, the sun follows the Yellow Road, 
and the moon follows the Nine Roads. According to the equatorial instru-
ment, the distance of the sun at the winter solstice from the pole is 115 du. 
As for its entry into the lodges, on the Red Road it is at 21 [du] in Dipper, 
while on the Yellow Road it is at 19 [du] of Dipper. Comparing the two 
instruments [ecliptic and equatorial] with one another, then in the motion 
of sun and moon, there are differences from the curvature and straightening 
of their paths, through which advances and retardations are produced. Thus 
when the moon goes through Well and Ox, [it moves] more than 14 du [in 
a day]. When it is in Horn and Harvester, [it moves] more than 12 du [a 
day].
107 Throughout if one does not keep answerable to the rate [of motion] 
it will not work.
以是言之， 則術不差不改， 不驗不用． 天道精微， 度數難定， 術法多端， 曆紀
非一， 未驗無以知其是， 未差無以知其失． 失然後改之， 是然後用之， 此謂允
執其中．
§81  Speaking of it this way, then if a method has no errors it is not changed; 
if it does not check out it is not used. The way of heaven is refined and 
subtle, the reckoning of the degrees is hard to fix. The patterns of the 
methods have many aspects, and the succession of astronomical systems is 
not uniform. If there has not yet been a verification, there is no way to 
know something is right. If there has not yet been an error, there is no way 
to know something is at fault. Changing something only when it is wrong, 
using something only when it is right – this is called sincerely holding to 
the mean.
今誠術未
– 3042 –
有差錯之謬， 恂術未有獨中之異， 以無驗改未失， 是以檢將來為是者也．
§82  Now Cheng’s method has not yet acquired the blame of being in error, nor 
has Xun’s method yet acquired the distinction of being the only one to hit 
the mark. To change something that has not yet failed using something as 
yet unverified, this would be treating something only to be checked in the 
future as if it was correct.
107 Note the contradiction of Jia Kui’ s earlier assertion that this does not happen.
